By Mike Dunn 

SEATTLE—Pay ’n Save wiill 
launch early in 1984 the first of a 
chain of huge cash-and-carry 
wholesale warehouses catering 
to small businesses and select 
groups. 

The 100,000-sq.-ft. deep-dis- 
count operation, called Price 
Savers Wholesale Club, will 
open in Salt Lake City. Sites 
are also being considered in 
Seattle and Tacoma, Wash. 
and in Honolulu and Anchor- 
age. 

Although the new high-vol- 
ume venture will be located in 
Skaggs’ heartland, competition 
will not be head to head. The 
Price Savers Wholesale Club 
will not contain a pharmacy or 
sell OTC products. However, a 
small selection of vitamins and 
health and beauty aids will be 
carried. 

The new unit will concentrate 
on major appliances, house- 
wares, hardware, tools, sport- 
ing goods, seasonal merchan- 
dise, tobacco products, baby 


Pay’ n Save to open no-frills ‘warehouse’ 


needs, plants, stationery and 
office supplies, books and food 
products. Most products will be 
bought direct from manufactur- 
ers. 

Calvin Hendricks, vice chair- 
man of the Pay ’n Save board of 
directors, said the Price Savers 
Wholesale Club will not be com- 
peting against Skaggs because 
of the different product mix and 
because the buying club will be 
selling to a dissimilar type of 
consumer. 

“Many of our customers will 
be other businesses. We will act 
like a wholesaler,” he said. 

But the store also is expected 
to draw the ordinary consumer 
who belongs to a group. “We 
believe the warehouse concept 
of merchandising offers a for- 
mula that will be readily accept- 
ed and appreciated by the cost- 
conscious consumer,” said M. 
Lamont Bean, Pay ’n Save 
chairman.

concepts at the new division

NWDA sets management seminars 


MAUI, Hawaii—The National Wholesale Druggists Asso- 
ciation (NWDA) will present a series of management seminars 
on Monday, Oct. 24. 

The seminars, which are a part of the NWDA’s annual 
meeting in Maui, Hawaii, will include an evaluation of third- 
party programs, a report on innovations in home health care, 
an update on the status of corporate physical fitness programs 
and a session on attracting and retaining key management 
personnel. In addition, there will be a one-time seminar on 
communications. 

The seminars will begin at 8:15 and will be repeated once at 
10:15 a.m. They will conclude at noon. 

Representatives from more than 50 of the nation’s leadin 


drug wholesalers are expected to attend the meeting whic 
begins Oct. 22. 


Drug store sales rise 10.5% 


WASHINGTON—Drug and proprietary store sales in- 
creased a healthy 10.5% to $3.55 billion in September, up from 
$3.213 billion in August, according to advance unadjusted 
figures from the U.S. Commerce Department. 

The advance September 1983 sales figure was 24.2% better 
than the $2.86 billion reported for September 1982. 

Drug and proprietary sales in September 1983 outper- 
formed the entire retail industry, according to the Commerce 
Department figures. 


Best Buy plans more combos 


_WEST PALM BEACH, Fla.—Best Buy Drugs Inc. is plan- 
ning to raise $1 million in a public stock offering to fund its 
continuing conversion of drug stores into mini food and drug 
combination stores. Money raised from the offering, which is 
being underwritten by Helfer Broughton Inc., also will be 
used for expansion. 

Best Buy operates nine units in the 7,500- to 8,000-sq.-ft. 
range. Two more stores are scheduled to open by February 
1984. Eight of the nine existing units have pharmacies. 


Deep-discount Super D to open 


MEMPHIS—tThe Super D division of Malone & Hyde will 
open its first deep-discount drug store next year in Memphis, 
where Revco has already opened a deep-discount unit. Don 
Lasseter, president of Super D, said Tom Hanemann, sr. vp 
and general manager of the drug division, will oversee the new 
venture. Bob Billings, who had been vp of marketing, will 
become director of operations for Super D. 


Malone & Hyde acquires 13 Auto Shacks 


MEMPHIS—Malone & Hyde Inc., which operates and 
franchises Super D and other drug stores, has signed an 
agreement to acquire Auto Shack Inc., a company that has 13 
retail auto parts stores in the Phoenix area. The transaction 
involves a tax-free exchange of Auto Shack shares for an 
undisclosed number of Malone & Hyde shares. Malone & Hyde 
also operates 121 Auto Shack stores in seven mid-South states 
that have been developed internally and is opening new auto 
parts stores at the rate of one a week. 


Group acquires Nature’s Organics 


PARAMUS, N.J.—The financially ailing Nature’s Organics 
Plus was recently purchased by a private group of investors 
headed by William Weiss and Harvey Polly, two of the princi- 
pals of Helena Rubinstein. 

Under the terms of the agreement (for an undisclosed sum) 
Polly becomes president of Nature’s Organics. The offices will 
remain here and all marketing and sales will be handled by 
DeKama Associates, a newly formed company directed by Joe 
DeKama, former president of Nature’s Organics. 


3 join Medicare-Glaser board 


ST. LOUIS—Harlan Steinbaum, president of Medicare- 
Glaser Corp., has announced that the following individuals 
have been elected to the company’s board of directors: Landon 
Y. Jones, Stanley M. Rosenblum and Stuart L. Bascomb.

Court rules consumers not misled 
by ‘gray market’ shipping methods 


WASHINGTON—Imports 
of so-called “gray market” mer- 
chandise are not likely to create 
confusion among consumers, a 
Federal appeals court in New 
York ruled earlier this month. 

The decision, a key defeat for 
multinational manufacturers 
pressing for new restrictions on 
foreign supply sources of Unit- 
ed States drug chains, figures 
to complicate Treasury Depart- 
ment plans to issue controver- 
sial regulations = “oray 
market” shipments. Eckerd 
and Revco are among the giant 
retailers that are rigorously re- 
sisting such a ban. 

The New York ruling paral- 
lels a Florida Federal court de- 
cision earlier this year permit- 
ting a group of Miami fragrance 


distributors to continue pur- 
chasing perfumes overseas for 
sale in this country despite ob- 
jections raised by the foreign 
manufacturer’s United States 
subsidiary. 

In that case the Miami Feder- 
al judge rejected the manufac- 
turer’s request for an injunction 
against such transshipments, 
ruling that there is no evidence 
that the “‘public is being 
harmed” by gray market trans- 
actions. 

In the more recent New York 
case, the trial court initially 
ruled in favor of a major Ja- 
panese camera supplier, con- 
cluding that snl im- 
ports of Mamiya photographic 
equipment by a Brooklyn cam- 
era wholesaler violated the 


Federal trademark law. 

According to the initial dis- 
trict court ruling, the whole- 
saler’s unauthorized imports of 
legitimate, Mamiya cameras 
could lead to “a substantial like- 
lihood of confusion” among con- 
sumers. 

The appeals court, however, 
lifted the district court’s gray 
market injunction against fur- 
ther imports by the wholesaler, 
ruling that the manufacturer 
“has not shown that the sale of 
the subject camera equipment 
by another distributor is likely 
to cause any consumer to be 
misled about the product he or 
she purchases.” 

Although both the Florida 
and New York court actions

Arbor store becomes set for TV ads 


TROY, Mich.—Arbor Drug 
has hit the highly competitive 
Detroit-area market with a se- 
ries of five TV commercials fea- 
turing actor William Schallert 
as chain spokesman. 

Schallert, who is best known 
for his role as the father on the 
Patty Duke Show, filmed the se- 
ries of commercials for the 34- 
store chain on the topics of ge- 
neric drugs, Arbortech (Ar- 
bor’s pharmacy computer sys- 
tem), the 2-for-1 photo offer and 
Christmas. oe 

The 30-second spots, airing 
during all hours of the day, are 
reaching shoppers in all six of 


the major Detroit area counties 
consisting of about 9.7 million 
consumers. 

According to Lavid Mazur, 
account executive for Kolon, 
Bittker & Desmond Inc., the 
advertising agency that de- 
vised the ads, Arbor wanted a 
spokesman who “was recogniz- 
able by any age group, but not 
such a big star that he could, in 
a sense, overshadow the store. 
Schallert is perfect because 
most people know that they rec- 
ognize his face ... but they 
don’t know from where.” 

Arbor first started TV adver- 
tising last fall with a “Welcome 


to Arbor” awareness campaign. 
According to Mazur, with Ar- 
bor’s increasing store count, 
the cost per thousand is “well 
worth” putting the message on 


In the Michigan area, Per- 

—the No. 1 chain by market 
share—is the heaviest TV ad- 
vertiser. Other contenders on 
TV include Revco and Meijers 
Thrifty Acres. Although Mazur 
would not release Arbor’s ad 
budget, he did note that it is a 
“large sum” that will probably 
make Arbor the second-largest 
chain drug television advertiser 
in the market.

Study sees whopping 4-year sales gain 


NEW YORK—Drug and 
proprietary stores are expected 
to generate $55.2 billion per 
year in annual sales by 1986, 
according to retailing study by 
Dun & Bradstreet Credit Ser- 
vices. 

The U.S. Commerce Depart- 
ment reported sales in the cate- 
gory last year were $35.85 bil- 

on. 


For the four-year period from 
1983 to 1986, the stud — 
sales will total $172.3 bi lion. 

Overall retail sales are ex- 

cted to increase to $1.2 tril- 
ion this year, up 9% from 1982, 
according to the study. 

Annual gains of 10%, 10% 
and 11% are expected to bring 
total retail sales to $1.6 trillion 
in 1986. 


The study divides retailing 
into 13 areas ranging from drug 
and proprietary stores to con- 
sumer electronics, hobbies, 
building materials and auto 
parts stores. Entitled “Retail- 
ing for 1980’s—A Strategic and 
Financial Analysis,” the study 
is designed to enable executives 
to measure their company’s 
performance. 


“Significantly,” Fantle told a 
meeting of security analysts 
here, “comparable store sales 
rose 12%.” 

Fantle said the performance 
reflected “our strong pharmacy 
operations, which now account 
for 25% of total sales and the 
growth in our seasonal and pro- 
motional merchandise.” 

Another important factor, 
according to the chief execu- 
tive, was the consolidation pro- 
ea in Indiana under which all 

aag stores were brought un- 
der the Peoples logo and mer- 
chandising format.

key mission of the wholesale drug industry. However, as this illustration 

depicts, new equipment, new customers and new products are rapidly changing 
the way wholesalers go about their business.

Compuiers, hospitals spur growth in ’83 : 


By Allen Mundth 


roduct, performance and produc- 
tivity—the three P’s—are the 


focus of the nation’s drug whole- 
saling industry this year as members 
strive to top near record results report- 
ed in 1982. 

Indeed, as the National Wholesale 
Druggist Association’s 1982 operating 
survey indicates, America’s drug whole- 
salers “have come a long way during the 
past five years.” It was just six years 
ago that the association’s chairman 
warned members that “adequate prof- 
itability continues to elude the drug 
wholesale industry.” 

Like many of its key financial indica- 
tors, the levels of optimism, enthusiasm 
and pride in the drug wholesaling com- 
munity have reached all time highs. 
Why? The numbers speak for them- 
selves: 

@ Estimated sales of all United States 
drug wholesalers grew an estimated 
18.6% to $10.2 billion in 1982; NWDA 
members accounted for all but $1.2 bil- 
lion of the total. 

@ Operating expenses as a per cent of 
gross profit dropped to 74.39%, while 


overall expenses dropped to 7.79%. 
e Average return on investment topped 
an industry goal of 15% for the first time 
ever. 
@ An unprecedented 14.2% return on 
net worth put drug wholesalers even 
closer to the average returns achieved 
by most of their suppliers, and 
@ Net profit, which had sunk to below 
1% in the mid-1970’s, continued its 
gradual ascent, settling at 1.41% in 
1982. 

Subtle changes 

While the blend of customers ser- 
viced by America’s drug wholesalers 
remained stable last year, certain dis- 
tinctions reflect subtle changes in the 
overall delivery of health care products 
and services to United States consum- 
ers. 

While retail drug stores, primarily in- 
dependents and small chains, still ac- 
count for the bulk (56.1%) of all whole- 
saler revenues, the long term decline of 
this market segment continued in 1982. 
In 1981, 57% of all sales were to retail 
customers. Sales to retail drug stores 
increased 17% last year, compared to 
the 18.6% sales increase overall. Sales 
by wholesalers to chain drug ware- 


houses and mass merchandisers also 
dipped last year, with chain drug stores 
accounting for 3.4% of all revenues. 

The most significant change in the 
wholesalers’ customer mix involves hos- 
pital and institutional customers, which 
accounted for 15.6% of all sales in 1982, 
compared to 14.1% in 1981. Rapid 
growth of this segment, which offers 
wholesalers comparativelv lower gross 
margins, was cited for a slight drop, 
from 2.74% in 1981 to 2.68%, in operat- 
ing profit margins. 

Pharmaceutical, toiletry and sundry 
products continued to pace the overall 


product mix offered by both general line 
and specialized wholesalers. However, 
sales of proprietary goods sunk to 15.5% 
of total sales, believed to be a 10-year 
low. 
Gradual recovery 
Revitalization of the wholesale drug 
industry has been gradual, triggered by 
the realization more than a half decade 
ago that significant changes, in sys- 
tems, services and product selection, 
were needed to ensure long term 
viability.

WATER iLS 


Frequent deliveries, fair pricing and credit allowances, plus strong deals and 
discounts are among the most important things that independent retail pharma- 
cists look for from their wholesalers. 

And, according to a recent National Association of Retail Druggists member- 
ship survey, the wholesalers are getting good grades on all these counts from 
independent pharmacists. 

Overall, 71% of the NARD members polled said that they preferred using 
wholesalers instead of buying direct from manufacturers. 

Kighty-five per cent of the independents surveyed said they were satisfied 
with prices and credit policies offered by their wholesalers, although 47% felt 
that they could get better pricing by forming co-ops. 

More than 80% approved of the discounts and deals wholesalers provide. By 
the same wide majority, 87% of the respondents said they were getting deliver- 
ies on a frequent enough basis. 

While most NARD members said they were satisfied with the relationship 
with their wholesalers, 50% disapproved of the return-goods procedures. In 
addition, 50% of the respondents said they were not being supplied with enough 
front-end merchandise. Among the items they said they want to carry more of 
are cosmetics, home health care products and school supplies. 

The broader problem of shortages and out-of-stock products, and specifically 
the difficulty in obtaining generic drugs, were among the other areas of concern 
frequently voiced by the independents. 

Generally, NARD members said they were pleased with the level of service 
from their wholesalers. However, a number of independents said they wanted to 
receive additional merchandising assistance, marketing and advertising pro- 
grams, as well as more internal management reports, inventory controls and 
expanded computer capabilities. 

| 3 On the question of whether an independent should work with one wholesaler, 
The impact of the computer, both in the internal operations of wholesalers and slightly more than half of the NARD members leaned toward using more than 
in providing retail services, has been a major factor in bringing about changes one wholesaler. 
in the drug wholesaling industry.

Fred Meyer 
goes public 
—again 


By Mike Dunn 

PORTLAND, Ore.— Fred 
Meyer Inc., is going public 
again, but it will not be the 
same company that was taken 
private on Dec. 11, 1981. 

It will continue to be a multi- 
department retailer that oper- 
ates 62 pharmacies in 69 stores 
averaging 104,000 sq. ft. And it 
will continue to be a major com- 

etitor of Pay ’n Save and Pay 
Can Northwest. 

But the new company re- 
ports sharply lower earnings 
than the old one, and a major 
reason is that Fred Meyer no 
longer owns its real estate. 

A second reason is that the 
company must repay high-in- 
terest loans secured two years 
ago. Those loans were either at 
the prime rate or at 17%. 

Although Jerry Sadis, Fred 
Meyer’s executive vp of finance, 
concedes the new ag ed has 
a different financial base, he 
also said it has the same ability 
to increase its earnings.

NACDS to offer booths at ’85 
pharmacy affairs conference 


ALEXANDRIA, Va.—The National Asso- 


meetings—-Cosmetics/Fragrances and Mer- 


ciation of Chain Drug Stores will hold its first 
“booth show” at the 1985 Pharmaceutical Af- 
fairs Conference, according to Robert J. 
Bolger, president of the association. 

Bolger said pharmaceutical manufacturers 
will be invited to set up booths at the show, 
which is tentatively set for Chicago. The con- 
ference had been scheduled for the third week 
in July, Bolger added, “but we are trying for 
mid-September.” 

The addition of revenue-producing booths to 
the Pharmaceutical meeting is the latest in a 
series of changes that NACDS has made or is 
considering making in an effort to respond to 
the needs of chain and associate members. 

Although the NACDS Board has discussed 
including booths at other product-oriented 


chandising—no decision has been made. 

In 1984, the association will take the first 
step in its revised approach to meetings with 
its “SuperSCOPE” conference. 

SuperSCOPE is a combination of four pre- 
viously separate meetings—SCOPE (pri- 
marily financial management); MIS (data 
processing and management of computer- 
generated information); Loss Prevention, 
and human resources. 

The clustering of these four nonproduct-ori- 
ented meetings is being done because the sub- 
ject matter of the four often overlaps and be- 
cause it will reduce the financial burden of the 
chains. The meeting will be held Oct. 14-17 at 
the Crown Center Hotel in Kansas City.

RPM legislation clears Senate 


WASHINGTON—Legislation cutting off all Federal fund- 
ing for the Justice Department’s campaign for softer resale 
hes maintenance restrictions cleared the Senate and was 

eaded for a final Capitol Hill showdown. 

The measure, introduced by Sen. Warren Rudman (R- 
N.H.) and a bi-partisan group of Senate leaders, was approved 
by voice vote as an neuen to the department’s new 
gag i fs bill. 

udman’s bill, which attracted support from the National 
Association of Chain Drug Stores and other key retail industry 
organizations, prohibits Justice antitrusters from using Gov- 
ernment funds “for any activities the purpose of which is to 
overturn or alter the per se prohibition on resale price mainte- 
nance in effect under the Federal antitrust laws:”

growth in three regions 


WOONSOCKET, R.I.—An- 
ticipating the opening of at least 
50 new stores each year, Con- 
sumer Value Stores (CVS) has 
announced tentative plans for 
the construction or lease of a 
150,000-sq.-ft. bulk storage 
and promotional goods ware- 
house here. 

The facility would replace 
much of the storage space cur- 
rently leased by CVS in two 
Woonsocket-area buildings, 
one of which houses most of the 

romotional merchandise sold 
in the chain’s 500 health and 
beauty aid stores. Many of 
these stores contain pharmacy 
departments. 
he announcement follows 
the recent construction of a 35,- 
000-sq.-ft. addition to the 
chain’s central distribution cen- 
ter here. With 24 loading docks, 
the newly expanded center re- 
flects the chain’s efforts to 
streamline merchandise ship- 
ments to its 483 stores in 
Maine, New Hampshire, New 
York, Massachuseits, Connect- 
icut, Rhode Island and New 
Jersey, as well as 15 health and 
beauty aid stores and two drug 
stores in southern California. 

The chain is also reviewing 
various options for the con- 
struction, acquisition or lease of 


a new distribution center in 
southern California, as well as 
the addition of a “full-size dis- 
tribution center” in southern 
New Jersey, northeast Penn- 
sylvania or northern Maryland. 
Approximately 35% of the 50 
new CVS stores expected to 
open in calendar year 1983 are 
located in that tristate area. 

Except for a second new drug 
store in southern California, 
the balance of the new store 
openings this year are concen- 
trated in CVS’ conventional 
markets, including New En- 
gland, New York, Pennsylvania 
and northern New Jersey. 

Tentative plans for de- 
centralizing its distribution 
system reflect the company’s 
long-range growth plans. 

“Distribution center growth 
will continue to run parallel 
with CVS store growth,” Dave 
Jonson, senior vp for adminis- 
tration and control, said in a re- 
cent message to company em- 
‘sacghaae “Expansion activity 

as been planned for almost 
every year.” 

Although the chain has fallen 
short of its original goal for an 
accelerated store opening pro- 
gram on the West Coast, CVS is 
still intent on carving out a 
strenger market share in Cali- 


fornia, and possibly several 
other Western states. The 
chain’s inability to locate and 
secure satisfactory store sites 
has been a major impediment to 
its West Coast expansion. 

CVS president Stanley Gold- 
stein emphasized, however, 
that the zhain’s first pharmacy 
in California, which opened last, 
March in Los Angeles, is “doing 
well.” He said CVS is looking 
forward to several more phar- 
macy openings in California 
during fiscal year 1984. Its sec- 
ond California pharmacy store 
opened earlier this month in the 

orth Ridge section of Los An- 
geles. 

According to Goldstein, CVS 
expects to compound its prv- 
jected base of 56 new store 
openings per year by an addi- 
tional five per year. 

Much of this expansion will 
occur in freestanding, nonmall 
locations. However, sites in lo- 
cal and regional malls still ac- 
count for a substantial share of 
new CVS stores, especially in 
malls where the chain’s parent 
company, the Melville Corp., 
operates other retail outlets, 
such as Thom McAn shoes, Fox- 
moor, Chess King, Marshall’s, 
Linen’s ’N Things, Wilson’s 
Leather and Kay-Bee Toys.

Talking scanner: the end 
of the silent screen? 


PLYMOUTH TOWNSHIP, Mich.—Family Discount Drug, 
a 22,100-sq.-ft. drug store operated by Allied Supermarkets, 
has installed talking cash registers. 

The supermarket chain believes this is the first talking cash 
register to be used by a United States chain drug store. 
According to Joseph Moenik, vp and general manager of Al- 
lied’s Great Scott Supermarkets and Family Discount Drug 
division, a cashier S a product over the scanner and a 
female voice calls out the price of each item. The identity and 
price are printed on a display panel as well as on the itemized 


receipt. : 
_ Mocnik said the talking scanners will be installed in addi- 
tiona] Family Discount Drug Stores. Currently, Allied oper- 
ates three other drug units in the Metro Detroit Area. Indus- 
try sources expect Allied to convert several existin 
supermarkets into drug outlets and become another competi- 


tor in the Michigan drug store arena.

at Bindley Western for the

Chain Rx dept. performance hits jackpot 


By Joe Caputo, R.Ph. 

NEW YORK—Chain drug phar- 
macy departments are enjoying a 
banner year, with continued growth 
in script count, increased dollar vol- 
ume, higher gross margins and 
greater pharmacist productivity, ac- 
cording to Drug Store News’ latest 
national pharmacy survey. 

The survey, completed last month, 
drew responses from drug chains 
operating 2,246 pharmacy depart- 
ments. 

The results clearly indicate the 
pharmacy’s key role in overall sales 
performance. In virtually every 
area measured, prescription depart- 
ments emerged as winners. For ex- 
ample: 
®@ Scripts dispensed per hour of op- 
eration increased to 9.8 from 9.4 in 
1982, and scripts filled weekly per 
pharmacist rose to 360 from 348. 


@ Dollar volume per hour of opera- 
tion reached a total of $104 from $92 
in 1982, and dollar sales per pharma- 
cist increased to $3,823 per week 
from $3,408. 
@ Sales per square foot rose to 
$1,093 from $982 last year. 
Increases were also chalked up in 


the average cost of prescription de- 
partment inventory (up $2,450); 
turnover hit a new high of 7.4 times a 
year, and the size of the average de- 
partment increased to 382 sq. ft. 
The survey also found a substan- 
tial increase in the percentage of 
pharmaceuticals shipped directly to

In addition, the salary of the aver-

remained unchanged, however. The 
average pharmacy department now

NUTS—EVERYTHING THEY’RE 


Health conscious 
consumers 

view nutsas , 

a fun and tasty 
way to meet their 
nutritional needs. 


ue to reduced export 
opportunities, United 
States growers of tree 
nuts placed extra emphasis 
on domestic promotions of 
several major varieties last 
year. 

The results seemed to 
pay off, as per capita con- 
sumption of tree-grown nuts 
topped the 2-lb. mark for 
the first time ever. Con- 


sumption increases were 
greatest last year for al- 
monds, filberts and mac- 
adamias. 

Whether in their pure 
form or blended into a vari- 
ety of snacks, tree grown 
nuts are being included in 
the diets of more American 
consumers than ever before. 

Almonds and walnuts are 
among the primary ingre- 
dients used in a large as- 
sortment of prepackaged 
trail mixes and other snacks 
sold in the natural depart- 
ments of many chain drug 
stores. Because they are 
wholesome, nutritious, easy 
to consume and crunchy, 
they are being commonly 
substituted for more con- 
ventional snacks, such 
as candy bars and

NATURAL CENTERS SPUR VITAMIN 


SALES GROWTH 


Recognizing their 
success in drug 
stores, 
supermarkets 
and mass 
merchandisers 


are expanding 
vitamin 


departments to 
attract increased 
sales. 


M ost major drug store 
merchandise depart- 
ments have at least one 
product category that 
serves as an anchor. 

In natural departments, 
that category is without 
doubt, vitamins. 

With annual retail sales 
of nutritional supplements 
(primarily vitamins) esti- 
mated at $2.6 billion last 
year, this category has long 
been a traditional drug 
store commodity. But it’s 
only in recent years that 
mass market retailers, such 
as K mart, Sears and even 
7-Eleven have moved de- 
cisively to create, and then 
capture, a larger segment of 
this growing business. 

The $2.6 billion figure 
represents a 6% increase 
over vitamin sales through 
all retail outlets in 1981 
according to the Council for 
Responsible Nutrition, a 
trade association represent- 
ing manufacturers of vi- 
tamins, minerals and other 
food supplements. Vitamin 
sales in 1981 were 17% 
ahead of the prior year. 

Whether the decline in 


the growth rate indicates a 
maturing industry is uncer- 
tain. As one health foods 
distributor commented, 
“only 50% of the population 
today is taking vitamins. 
Therefore, every 1 per cent 
increase represents a sub- 
stantial amount of business 
for retailers.” 

Based upon research 
from various sources, the 
CRN estimates that vi- 


tamins account for the lion’s 
share of the nutritional sup- 
plement market with $2.23 
billion in sales last year. 
Minerals accounted for $250 
million in retail sales; pro- 
tein supplements (powders 
.and tablets) $105 million, 
and other categories $10 
million. 

In the vitamin segment of 
the business, multiples ac- 
counted for an estimated 


39% of all sales, followed by 
vitamin C with 22%; vi- 
tamin E with 16%; B-com- 
plex vitamins with 18%, and 
all others, 5%. 

While chain drug and 
other mass merchandise 
outlets account for the bulk 
(31%) of all nutritional sup- 
plement sales, their share 
slipped by one percentage 
point last year, while that of 
supermarkets grew by two 
points to 16%. The share of 
supplement sales through 
health food stores increased 
last year by 1% to 28% of 
the market. 

Natural product depart- 
ments in supermarkets, 
drug store and other mass 
merchandise stores ac- 
counted for a significant 
portion of the growth last 
year in vitamin, mineral and 
other supplement sales. 

Supplement sales in su- 
permarket natural product 
departments grew to $136 
million in 1981, and then 
jumped another 40% last

BOOKS, MAGAZINES KEEP 


CUSTOMERS INFORMED 


With most mass 
market natural 
departments 
operated ona 
selfservice basis, 
books and 
magazines can 
be effective 
tools in helping to 
educate 
consumers. 


A Ithough their locations 
are often not as conve- 
nient as those of chain drug 
stores, health food stores do 
hold a definite edge in their 
ability to educate consum- 
ers about the products on 
their shelves. 

In fact, this prompt, per- 
sonalized service is perhaps 
the key factor separating 
the pure health food store 


from the mass market seller 
of natural products. In 
keeping with their self-ser- 
vice formats, most drug re- 
tailers have kept specia! 
staffing of their natural 
products departments to a 
minimum. Often, these sav- 
ings are passed along to 
consumers in lower prices. 

Many chains use spe- 
cialized books, magazines 
and in-store informational 
aids as a low cost way to 
educate consumers about 
natural products. 

SupeRx, which has at- 
tributed its initial problems 
with natural foods to an 
uneducated consumer, has 
included 4-8 ft. book and 
magazine sections in dozens 
of its larger nutrition cen- 
ters. 

Consumer magazines, of 
course, not only help edu- 
cate customers about health 


related issues and products. 
They also promote, often 
with cents-off coupons, 
many of the products fea- 
tured in natural product de- 
partments. In drug stores, 
pharmacists will often refer 
a customer with specific 
questions to a book or mag- 
azine. 

Prevention, the leading 
consumer publication in the 


health products industry, is 
currently expanding its 
newsstand program to at- 
tract a larger number of 
nonsubscription readers. 
Radio spots are being used 
in key metropolitan areas 
such as Los Angeles, to 
inform customers that Pre- 
vention is now available at 
their neighborhood food or 
drug store.

DRUG STORE NEWS, November 14, 1983 


® Special report: 
Rx operations survey 


Rx productivity, 
script price gains 
boost sales 12% 


NEW YORK—Pharmacy 
sales increased 12% in the aver- 
age chain pharmacy this year, 
reflecting productivity gains as 
well as increases in the price of 
an average script, according to 
Drug Store News’ annual phar- 
macy survey. 

The survey shows that the 
san chain pharmacy is ring- 

up $104 in average hourly 
ales, $11.53 higher than in 
1982. 

Most of the gain stems from 
script price increases, as newer, 
more expensive drugs find their 
way into the department’s 
product mix. Script prices 
climbed 9% to an estimated 
$10.63 from $9.79 last year. 

The 9% advance in script re- 
tail price combined with a 3% 
gain in number of scripts re- 


sulted in the 12% gain reported 
by the average chain pharmacy 
department. 

Overall, the survey shows 
that the typical chain pharmacy 
is generating $417,461 on an an- 
nual basis, a year-to-year gain 
of $45, 344. Sales per pharma- 
cist are also up 12%, to $3,823. 

Sales per square foot jumped 
sharply in the average phar- 
macy department this year, ac- 
cording to the survey. Despite a 
small increase in average 
square footage, the typical 
pharmacy is generating $1,093 

er square foot, an increase of 
$111 since last year. 

Average gross margin re- 
mains relatively constant this 
year at 35.5%, compared to 
35.4% in 1982. After retailers 
pay for the cost of merchandise 
sold, funds available for ex- 
penses and operating profits are 
estimated at $148,200, signifi- 
cantly greater than the $131,- 
730 available in 1982. 

It is predicted by some indus- 
try sources that 1983 will prove 
to be another banner year for 
ponigceny. but only if chains can 

eep the growth of expenses at 
a level equaling inflation or be- 
low it. In addition, they say, 
new products must continue to 
be launched regularly. 

Dampening their enthusi- 


~asm, however, is the lid on reim- 


bursement for third-party 
scripts. They point out that 
costly new drugs are increasing 
inventory values, but fixed fees 
are cutting margins for third- 
party scripts. 

If third-party business con- 
tinues to grow —— any in- 
crease in dispensing fees, they 
say, it will mean a Sevens ero- 
sion of return on investment in 
the prescription department.

the average chain drug pharma- 
cist has increased a hefty 16% 
this year, rising to $31, 337 from 
$27,120 in 1982. 

This is one of the main find- 
ings of Drug Store News latest 
national survey of chain drug 
pharmacy operations. 

Other findings include the 
following: 

@ The typical chain pharmacy 
employs 2.1 pharmacists and 
1.5 technicians, substantially 
unchanged from 1982. 

e The department remains 
open 77.2 hours per week, down 
from 77.4 in 1982. 

@ Each pharmacist generates 
sales of g1 198,791 per year. 

e The average pharmacy’s 
sales yield $70,791 in gross mar- 
gin dollars per pharmacist. 

Although the average phar- 
macist’s salary nationwide is 
$31,337 a year, the survey 
shows wide regional variations 
in pay. For example, pharma-

WASHINGTON—Drug store sales rose in October, but not 
as fast as the rest of the retail industry. | : 
Preliminary unadjusted figures from the U.S. Commerce 
Department indicate drug store sales for October were $3.178 
billion, up 1.2% from $3.14 billion in September. 
The October figure was 7.6% better than the $2.953 billion 


For all retailers, sales for October 1983 were $100.006 bil- 
lion, up 2.1% from $97.873 billion in September. October 1983 
sales for all retailers ran 9.6% ahead of October 1982, when 
sales of $91.416 billion were reported.

SCOPE focuses on educating 
workers to lower benefit costs 


PHILADELPHIA—In- 
creasing the amount employees 
must pay for health insurance 
and reducing insurance cover- 
age are two approaches drug 
chains are taking to reduce spi- 
raling costs. 

But senior chain executives 
at the NACDS SCOPE meet- 
ing here agreed that employees 
must be educated that higher 
health care expenses paid by 
the chains leaves less money for 
salaries. 

“Employees consider bene- 
fits their rights,” said Robert 
Primm, director of personnel 
for SupeRx. Primm said em- 
ploy zes resist giving up those 
“rights.” 

rimm was part of a benefits 
panel that included Walter Felt- 
man, executive and opera- 
tions director at K&B; William 
G. Combs, vp of administration 
and treasurer of Longs, and 
James A. Norton, a principal 
with William M. Mercer Inc., 
an employee benefits consulting 
firm. The moderator was Bruce 
Berg, vp of store operations at 
Fay’s Drug. 

Combs put the problem of 
health benefits into perspective 
by stating the cost of benefits in 
the retail industry is expected 
to rise from 10% of salaries in 
1982 to 17% in 1986 and 30% by 
1990. 

Until the 1970’s, chains saw 
benefits as a way to lure em- 
ployees. Those benefits were 
not then considered a substan- 
tial cost. Now, with benefits ris- 
ing faster than wages and sales, 
chains have to rethink their 
strategy. 

Last year, Longs began edu- 
cating its employees to prepare 
for changes in their medical in- 
surance. “We notified our em- 
ployees that increases in medi- 
cal expenses were exceeded 
only by increases in energy ex- 
penses. We faced a 31% in- 
crease in medical expenses in 
1981 and another 24% increase 
in 1982,” Combs said. 

- To combat this trend, Longs 


offered its employees the option 
of less coverage or the same cov- 
erage with a contribution b 

employees, coming as a payroll 
deduction. With this c ae 
Longs managed to reduce what 
had een projected as a “sub- 
stantial increase” in its benefits 
costs by $400,000 to $500,000. 

At K&B, the ratio of health 
insurance to sales has increased 
to 0.5% of sales, according to 
Feltman. Although K&B pays 
the cost for its employees, it 
raised the deductibles for de- 
pendents from $100 to $200. 

K&B also requires its hourly 
employees to be employed for 
one year before they qualify for 
medicakh coverage. At most 
chains, the period is three 
months for hourly employees 
and one month for salaried em- 
ployees. 

At SupeRx, Primm said, 
health benefits costs have m- 
creased 50% in the past three 
years. The chain pays 100% of 
the premiums for its employees 
and their families. 


Cohen joins staff of DrSN 


NEW YORK—Harold 
Cohen, a registered pharmacist 
for 15 years, has joined the staff 
of Drug Store News as assistant 
pharmaceutical editor. 

Cohen is a 1969 graduate of 
Rutgers University, College of 
Pharmacy. Soon after graduat- 
ing from school and obtaining a 
license as a registered pharma- 
cist, he went to work at a Sho 
Rite pharmacy owned by Food- 
arama, Freehold, N.J. ie rose 
to the position of manager at 
Shop Rite and later ieft to open 
ge pharmacy in Jackson, 

Cohen comes to Drug Store 
News with an in-depth knowl- 
edge of retail pharmacy and 
store operations. 

He resides in Ocean Town- 
ship, N.J., with his wife Roz and 
their two children, Jodi and 
Rachel. 


But Primm added, “Being 
the leader in the industry is ex- 
pensive.” 

Norton, the benefits consul- 
tant, said the expensive part of 
health care is the treatment of 
employees at hospitals. He rec- 
ommends that chains require 
their employees to get a second 
opinion before surgeries that 
are often not required, such as 
hysterectomies. _ 

At Longs, if the physicians’ 
opinions differ, the chain will al- 
low a third opinion and pay 
100% of the cost. Longs also 
pays more of the costs of em- 
ployees who seek a second opin- 
ion. 

In addition to reducing un- 
necessary surgery, Longs also 
attempts to have its employees 
treated as outpatients instead 
of in the hospital whenever pos- 
sible. 

Chains also are finding they 
can reduce medical expenses by 
encouraging their employees to 
eat better, exercise and, above 
all, not to smoke.

quiver with anxiety: fixed fee reim-

also breeding opportunity.

Washington Perspective 


Importers oppose ‘anticounterfeiting’ bill 


By Ken Rankin 

The chain 
drug store in- 
dustry is not 
alone in its con- 
cern that pend- 
ing Federal 
“‘anticounter- 
feiting” legisla- 
tion could be 
used to frus- 
trate consumer 
acceptance of 
iower-cost generic drugs. 

The American Free Trade Associa- 
tion—a group of H&BA importers and 
distributors opposed to the controver- 
sial bill—echoed fears raised earlier by 
the National Association of Chain Drug 
Stores that the unprecedented “search 
and seizure” powers granted to brand- 
name manufacturers by this legislation 
could be used to discourage pharmacies 
from even stocking generics. 

The stated goal of this legislation is 
not to hamper price competition at the 
retail level, but rather to halt the dis- 
tribution of goods bearing counterfeit 


trademarks. It would accomplish this 
through stiff new criminal penalties for 
“traffickers” (up to five years in prison, 
plus $1 million fines), and by enabling 
brand-name manufacturers to orches- 
trate “ex parte” (no warning) search and 
seizure raids against retailers sus- 
pected of dealing in pirated goods. 

Understandably, that “ex parte”’ 
search and seizure provisions has come 
under sharp attack by a variety of retail 
industry groups in and out of the drug 
store field. 

Earlier this month, in fact, the broad- 
ly based American Retail Federation 
adopted an NACDS-supported policy 
statement charging that the so-called 
anticounterfeiting measure is “inequita- 
ble, overboard and has the real potential 
for injuring our industry.” 

Significantly, ARF joined with 
NACDS in expressing concern that the 
bill’s vague definition of a “counterfeit” 
product as one bearing a “spurious” 
trademark could lead to serious prob- 
lems for the nation’s drug stores. 

“The bi!!’s scope is not restricted to 
intentional out-and-out piracy of brand- 


name products” and “its drasti¢ penal- 
ties and procedures could be invoked 
even in ‘garden variety’ trademark in- 
fringement disputes between compet- 
ing” manufacturers, the Federation 
charged. 

“As a result, private label products, 
generic drugs and other beneficial trade 
practices may be sii nae ” ARF 
concluded. 

In an even more detailed expression 
of concern, the American Free Trade 
Association warned Congress that the 
bill’s vague definition of counterfeit 
merchandise “could easily be applied to 
properly labeled goods in packaging 
similar in size, color and shape to that of 
trademarked goods.” 

Specifically, AFTA warned that de- 
spite the Supreme Court’s landmark /n- 
wood v. Ives ruling last year clearly le- 
galizing so-called generic “look-alike” 
drugs, the pending anticounterfeiting 
legislation could be used to halt the dis- 
tribution of “properly labeled goods in 
packaging of substantially similar color, 
size and shape” as brand-name prod- 
ucts. 


Drug store H&BA market share down 2% 


NEW YORK—Drug store market 
share of 25 leading health and beauty 
aids categories fell by two percentage 
points in July-August vs. the same peri- 
od last year, according to the latest data 
available from A. C. Nielsen. 

In comparing retail drug sales with 
those of food stores and mass merchan- 
disers, Nielsen found that the drug 
store share decreased to 32.2% from 
34.2% a year ago. 

The decline came despite an overall 
increase. in drug store sales of the 25 
leading product categories to $743 mil- 
lion from $726 million last year. 

Most of the drug store loss was picked 
up by food stores, continuing the long- 
term shift of H&BA volume to higher 
traffic supermarkets as they aggres- 
sively pursue nonfood sales. 

Food stores gained 1.3 share points tc 
52.7% as their sales rose to $1.2 billion 
from $1.1 billion in the same period a 
year ago. The remaining 0.7 of a per- 
centage point was gained by mass mer- 
chandisers, whose dollar volume grew 
to $349 million from $306 million. 

In a comparison of July-August fig- 
ures with those of May-June 1983, the 
survey found that the drug store share 
of dollar sales for the 25 leading prod- 
ucts decreased to 32.2% from 32.9%, 
while mass merchandisers increased to 


15.1% from 14.4%. 
Drug store share of unit volume also 


declined on a year-to-year basis, to 
28.6% from 30.6%. Food store share of 
unit volume increased to 54.2% from 
53.4%. 

In a year-to-year comparison of per- 
formance in the four major H&BA cate- 
gories—men’s products, remedies, oral 
hygiene and women’s products— drug 
stores did not fare well. 


While dollar sales were up in all four 
categories, unit movement declined in 
the two biggest volume producers— 
remedies and women’s products. 

For remedies, unit volume declined to 
68.2 miliion

porarily abandon his foxhole to jump for 
joy. 

Clearly the retail pharmacists sur- 
veyed by Drug Store News weren’t just 
sitting around on their hands waiting for 
times to get better. They were reassess- 
ing their businesses and their dilemmas 
and coming up with programs that gave 
them the momentum to carry on. 

Many were reaping the rewards of 
having installed pharmacy computers, 
while others were revamping their dis- 
tribution systems. 

Clearly the growth wasn’t coming 
through higher prices. Average mar- 
gins in 1983 were just 0.1% higher than 
in 1982. But inventory turnover was 
better—7.4 times in 1983 as opposed to 
7 in 1982. And merchandising and ad- 
vertising were obviously better. 

This doesn’t mean, of course, that the 
industry should give up the fight against 
unnecessary evils such as MAC and 
fixed-fee reimbursement programs. 

But it does mean that good business 
planners can not only survive but actu- 
ally prosper if they work hard and 
they’re clever. 

So, for pharmacists who have gotten 
their share of bad news in 1983, the 
Drug Store News survey hopefully 
proves there’s something to cheer about 
too. Now the challenge is to keep on 
struggling to acquire those skills and 
those programs that will make 1984’s 
survey results even stronger.

Malone&Hyde income up Begley Drug profits drop 


MEMPHIS—Malone & 
Hyde reported 2: net income 
gain of 28.3% and an 11.4% 
sales increase for the quarter 
ended Sept. 17. 

Net income for the first quar- 
ter was $6.8 million, up from 
$5.3 million for the first quarter 
last year. Sales for the quarter 
were $611.6 million, up from 
$549 million. 

Earnings per share for the 


first quarter were 42¢, up 
27.3% from 33¢ in the compara- 
ble quarter last year. 

J. R. Hyde III, chairman and 
president, said he foresees con- 
tinued strong earnings for the 
remainder of the year, but add- 
ed that “the rate of increase 
should slow as we compare re- 
sults against prior year periods 
in which sales and profits have 
already been enhanced.” 


Kroger income plummets 


CINCINNATI—The Kroger

By Jim Ricchiuti 


fter nearly two years of relatively 
flat sales, drug retailers are 
poised for a strong showing fron 

the sunglasses category next year. 
This year, sales of sunglasses showed

unit growth was down by as much as 
10%, according to some industry sourc-

“We are anticipating a 15% increase in 
dollar sales in 1984,” says Dick Fore- 
back, sunglasses buyer at the Atlanta, 
Ga.-based Reed Drugs, a division of 
Peoples Drug Stores. “We feel that this 
is not unreasonable. The increases could 
even be better if the economy continues 
to be strong.” 


Buyers expect sunglass recovery in ‘84 


Not only will a strong economy have a 
stimulative effect on sales, many chain 
drug buyers say the consumer’s sense of 
fashion—the desire to have sunglasses 
that match his or her lifestyle and dress- 
ing habits—now plays an even greater 
role in the multiple sales of sunglasses. 

A number of buyers agree with 
Reed’s Foreback, who says that “a large 
part of the business is fashion.” 

“As people have more money to 
spend, I think they will buy more sun-

selling sunglasses is to keep current 
with fashionable styles. “You really 
have to be on top of what style and what 
shape is selling,” Schultz says. 

In regions of the country that experi- 
ence a much shorter selling season, 
buyers are cautious about making any 
sales predictions for next year. In these 
areas the selling season for sunglasses 
may only be three months and weather 
more often than not means the dif- 
ference between a good year and a bad

According to Jim Whitticom,

Whitticom like many other

cial to get the right product 
from suppliers and offer it at

Buyers for chains located in 
rural areas say consumers are 
generally reluctant to spend 
over $15 for a pair of sun- 
glasses. These same buyers 
note that the bulk of sunglass 
sales in drug stores are in the 
$10 to $11 range.

most to drug retailers.

to $790 million, according to

pected to reach 75 million. In

Outsize plush toys pose two problems for retailers: Where to find 
the space to display the super-bulky items and how to keep little 
hands away from them. A Pay Less store in Oakland found the 
answer by suspending them on overhead wires. This way they get 
high visibility without using floor space and they do not become 
the darlings of the “play set.”

Longs income jumps 21% 
WALNUT CREEK, Calif.—Net income at Longs for the 
third quarter increased 21% to $7.7 million from $6.3 million 


for the comparable quarter last year. 
Sales for the quarter ended Oct. 27 were $290.6 million, up 


Earnings per share for the quarter were 72¢, up from 60¢. 

For the three quarters ended Oct. 27, net income was $25 
million, or $2.36 per share, up 18% from $21.1 million, or $2 
per share, for the similar period last year.

ers are expecting to ring in the

markets.

that much ahead of last year a 
along, and we expect it to con-

chandise out during the first 
week in November, which was 
earlier than in the past. 

“The discounters and depart- 
ment stores hac their merchan- 
dise or wn so we e to com- 
pete,” Sprabary said. 

Page is hacking the trend at 


most chains by stocking holiday 
inventory at a level that is 15% 
higher than last year’s. Few 
chains are going with inventory 
levels more than 9% higher than 
in the Christmas 1982 selling 
season. 

So far, Page already has 
made some right decisions. The 
chain was able to latch on to 
some Cabbage Patch dolls, 
which appear to be the hottest 
item this year. Most chains 
were unable to get them.

Page include imported plush,

and can openers that fit under

After a year, Thrifty still testing 
recipe for convenience food dept. 


LOS ANGELES—After 
testing a convenience food de- 
partment at its headquarters 
store for almost a year, Thrifty 
Drug has expanded the section 
and continues to test at this 
store without any further com- 


mitment. 


The original sectinn—consis- 
ting of two 30-ft., 4-shelf facing 
gondola sides—remains. The 
addition is an 18-ft., 4-shelf sec- 
tion on the reverse side of one 
gondola. Thrifty has also added 


a 3-ft. bread rack. No dairy, 
deli, or frozens are carried. 
In addition to adding space, 


Thrifty has redefined its mer- 


chandising approach on food. 


Now all the items on the two 30- 
ft. facing gondolas (canned 


juices, canned vegetables, 
coffee, tea, bread, crackers, ce- 
real, shortening, jams-jellies, 
canned fish and meats, sauces 
and dressings, raisins, pasta, 
soup, gelatine, packaged din- 
ners) are basic staples. Mer- 
chandise on the 18-ft. section 
consists of special buys and ad 
carryovers. 

The 18-ft. section is across 
the aisle from chips, snacks and 
nuts, ard adjoins liquor-bev- 
erage, thus ensuring strong im- 
pulse pick-up of related items. 

Ad items are positioned on 
bay ends throughout the store, 
as well as on four of the 15 4-ft.- 
by-4-ft. midaisle tables. Three 
of these tables, stocked with 
food, abut the food gondolas. 


Reactions of execs differ 


SELLERSVILLE, Pa.— 
Lemmon Company’s decision to 
halt the production of 
Quaalude, its brand name for 
methaqualone, was greeted by 
mixed reactions from chain 
drug executives. 

While some execs praised the 
decision because of the abuse 
problem associated with the 
drug, others maintained that 
controlled distribution should 
continue as long as there re- 
mains a legitimate medical need 


for the drug. 

Michael Zagorac, spokesman 
for the Jack Eckerd orp., was 
one exec who reacted favorably 
to Lemmon’s action. “We dis- 
continued the sale of metha- 
— almost two years ago,” 

agorac said, “to bring higher 
public visibility to the abuse 
problem associated with it.” 

Zagorac pointed out that the 
banning of methaqualone sales 
had helped reduce Eckerd’s 
pharmacy-related crime by 


Safeway broadens tests 
of Rx computer systems 


OAKLAND, Calif.—After 
testing the IBM Series 1 stan- 
dalone pharmacy terminal for 
five months in two San Fran- 
cisco superstores, Safeway will 
expand the IBM test early in 
1984. 

In addition, Safeway will test 
National Semiconductor phar- 
~— terminals next year. 

IBM Series 1 is being in- 
stalled in superstores with IBM 
scanning systems and National 
Semiconductor terminals are 
being installed in stores with 
National Semiconductor scan- 
ners. Safeway’s rationale: It’s 
easier and more convenient for 
one vendor to service both 
pharmacy terminals and scan- 
ners in the same store. : 

National Semiconductor 
Data Checker/DTS will not re- 
veal produc® information on its 
new pharmacy terminal at this 
time. Hewever, Safeway will be 
the company’s first test in- 
stallation. 

Based in California’s famed 
Silicon Valley, National Semi- 
conductor is a prime supplier of 
scanners for the nation’s super- 
markets. Established in 1972, 
National Semiconductor has 
924 scanner installations (or 


39% of the market) among the 
nation’s top 10 supermarket 
chains. 

Safeway has been testing 
pharmacy terminals since 1980, 
when two stores in the Wash- 
ington, D.C. division installed 
the Healthroom on-line system. 
In 1981, Safeway installed the 
OSI standalone (hardware b 
IBM, software by G & H Ltd. 
Galena, Kan.). At the same 
time, Safeway tested the Phar- 
matrex on-line pharmacy ter- 
minal (hardware by Nixdorf of 
Germany, software by Blodgett 
of Salt Lake City). 

After testing, Safeway elect- 
ed not to go further with any of 
these systems, but “to go back 
and look at the pharmacy com- 
puter concept,’ according to 
one Safeway exec. 

Safeway did make one deci- 
sion: to go with standalone. Al- 
though the chain will not com- 
ment on its reasoning, a 
pharmacy terminal expert says 
that “standalone works best for 
Safeway because their phar- 
macies are in clustered areas. 
The system has the ability to 

oll data at night at a central 
ocation. This saves many after-

Pay ’n Save boosts | 


net income by 104% 


SEATTLE—Net income at 
Pay ’n Save for the quarter end- 
ed Oct. 31 increased 104% to 
$6.8 million from $3.3 million 
for the comparable quarter last 
year. 

Sales for the quarter were 
$284 million, up 11% from $255 
million for the same year-ear- 
lier period. 

Earnings per share for the 
quarter were 54¢, up from 30¢. 

For the first three quarters of 
the fiscal year, net income in- 
creased 102% to $16.7 million 
from $8.3 million from the cor- 
responding period last year. 
Sales for the first three quar- 
ters rose 10.5% to $813.4 mil- 
lion, from $736.2 million. Earn- 
ings per share for the period 
were $1.40, up from 75¢. 

Same store sales for the 


quarter increased 10%. Inter- 
est expenses declined nearly 
$1.5 million because of reduced 
borrowing levels, and the com- 
pany benefited from effective 
expense controls and strength- 
ening gross margins. 

“We achieved solid earnings 
“ae in each of our three major 

usiness lines: drug, home cen- 
ter and apparel,” said Cal 
Hendricks, vice chairman of the 
board. “Earnings increases 
were particularly outstanding 
in our Pay ’n Save drug division 
and our Lamonts apparel divi- 
sion.” 

Three of six new stores 
planned for the year opened in 
the third quarter: a Pay ’n Save 
and an Ernst Home Center in 
Missoula, Mont., and a Pay ’n 
Save in Hawaii. 


Eckerd pushes net income 


CLEARWATER, Fla.—The 
Jack Eckerd Corp. has turned 
the corner with a 20.9% gain in 
net income for the first quarter, 
reversing the disappointing 
1.5% profits increase posted for 
fiscal 1983. en 

Net income for the quarter 
ended Oct. 29 was $11.1 million, 
up from $9.2 million for the 


comparable quarter last year. 
Sales increased 15% to $542 
million from $472.1 million. 
Earnings per share for the 
quarter were 30¢, up from 25¢. 
The earnings improvement 
reflects a LIFO charge of 3¢ for 
the quarter instead of 4¢ for the 
first quarter last year. 
Stewart Turley, chairman

MELVILLE, N.Y.—Net in- 
come at Genovese for the quar- 
ter ended Nov. 4 increased 
46.8% on an 18.8% sales gain. 

Net income for the chain’s 
third quarter was $737,000, up 
from $502,000 for the compara- 
ble quarter last year. Sales 
were $42.7 million, up from $36 


million. 

For the first three quarters, 
net income increased 47.7% to 
$2.1 million from $1.5 million. 
Sales increased 21.2% to $139.1 
million from $114.8 million. 

Earnings per share for the 
first three quarters were 53¢, 
up from 37¢.

MAC creates ‘2nd-class citizens,’ chains say 


WASHINGTON—Federal 
Maximum Allowable Cost Rx 
regulations place the Medicaid 
recipient “into the position of a 
second-class citizen, forced to 
accept the lowest-priced drug,” 
chain drug store industry leac- 
ers told the Department of 
Health and Human Services. 

Ina fi of comments sub- 
mitted to H.H.S. after a two- 
day hearing on Medicaid drug 
reimbursement regulations 
earlier this year, a number of 
key drug store chains charged 
that pharmacies “can no longer 
survive” under the present sys- 
tem. 

Among other things, the 
chain leaders blasted a provi- 
sion of the Medicaid reimburse- 
ment rules that requires drug 
stores to provide services to 
Medicaid recipients who can 
not afford to share the cost of a 
prescription, forcing phar- 
macies to absorb the loss. 

“While this may appear to be 


compassionate public policy, 
the result is to deny providers 
the recovery of a significant por- 
tion of the cost incurred in fill- 
ing the prescription,” Hook 
Drug’s Government affairs di- 
rector Raymond Rizzo told 
Federal Medicaid regulators. 
In separate comments, Medi 
Mart Drug Stores voiced simi- 
lar concerns and urged H.H.S. 
to change the copayment rules. 
Specifically, the chain recom- 
mended that Rx drugs be ex- 
empted from the copayment 
uirements or that the regu- 
lations be revised so that the 
“state Medicaid agency and the 
Federal Government are the 
payor of the last resort on all 
uncollected copayments.” 
According to chain drug 
store industry leaders, Medi- 
eaid recipients and the general 
public are also adversely af- 
fected by the MAC program.

tions r.quire pharmacists to

Giant opens with updated computer 


By Harold Cohen, R.Ph. 

ROCKVILLE, Md.—Giant 
Food has introduced a modified 
version of its IBM pharmacy 
computer system with the 
opening of its new 60,000-sq.- 
ft. prototype combo store here 
last month. 

As a result of the modifica- 
tions, patients will be notified 
by the pharmacist when a dru 
they are currently takin will 
interact with a new drug being 
filled at that time. 

The computer is alse capable 


of offering patients a consulta- 
tion sheet with additional infor- 
mation about their medications. 
This may include special stor- 
age directions or other specific 
information concerning when 
and how to take the medication. 
Sheldon Pelovitz, R.Ph., di- 
rector of Pharmacy Computer 
Services, said that a serious 
drug interaction will occur in 1 
out of 3 prescriptions filled. 
The computer is also capable 
of giving information concern- 
ing generic substitution. This is 


Revco and Rite Aid curing the 
public hearing on Medicaid re- 
imbursement in September. 
At that meeting chain 
spokesmen denounced the co- 
payment rules and criticized as 
unfair the “lower of” MAC 
provisions requiring pharma- 
cists to accept reimbursement 
for Medicaid prescriptions at 
the lowest of the MAC cost of 
the drug plus a disvensing fee 
or the pharmacist’s “usual and 
customary” charge,

especially important because 
Giant operates pharmacies in 
several states. The computer is 
preprogrammed with substitu- 
tion information from each of 
these states, which will avoid 
filling a prescription with a ge- 
neric permitted in one state 
that may not be allowed in an- 
other. The computer will also 
suggest the least expensive 
substitute from a supplier rec- 
ognized by the state in which 
the pharmacy is located.

An initial lesson in deciphering Government regulations| 


PRAC, MAC, EAC, MiniMAC and PRBs read like 
some sort of new alphabet soup to most people, but to 


Areas identified as major trouble spots are: 
@ Inadequate dispensing fees. 


practicing pharmacists these acronyms have come to 
— just about everything that is wrong with 
the profession of pharmacy. 

In reality the letters signify various aspects of regu- 
lations that were established over the years to set 
reimbursement limits on prescription drugs provided 
under Medicaid. 

Another major problem which has more significant 
ramifications centers on the dictatorial methods em- 
ployed by some public and private third-party pre- 
scription plan intermediaries. For example, many of 
these “intermediaries” routinely make unilateral 
changes in provisions which then directly affect the 
providers of pharmaceutical services. 

But that’s another story. 

The issues swirling around the Maximum Allowable 
Cost program trace directly to some overzealous ad- 
ministrators at the Health Care Financing Adminis- 
tration (part of Health and Human Services) who 
seem intent on wringing extra savings for public pro- 
grams when in fact none may exist. This in turn means 
that pharmacists sometimes have to subsidize scripts 
for MAC products out of their own pockets. This 
situation occurs when HCFA establishes a MAC price 


Joseph Caputo, RPh 
Pharmaceutical Editor 


for a drug, but the drug isn’t available to most phar- 
macies at the price stipulated. It means the pharma- 
cist must refuse to fill a Medicaid patient’s script, or 
fill it with a higher cost drug (more than allowed under 
MAC limits) and suffer a loss. 

In fact the situation deteriorated to such an extent 
that a two-day public hearing was recently held in 
Washington and the hearing was chaired by a repre- 
sentative from HHS. 

Testimony was submitted by virtually every faction 
of pharmacy and comments about the program were 
=! quite negative—pretty much as everyone 
expected. 


Inadequate product availability at MAC price lev- 
els. 

e “Lower of” regulations with, at times, product 
losses. 

e@ Unfair proposed copayment provisions. 

@ Required maintenance of dual inventories. 
@ Slow sn dageoien for services rendered. 

_ But these problems represent just the tip of the 
iceberg. Many private third-party programs follow on 
the heels of any government program restriction 
which seems to produce savings. 

The question most pharmacists are now asking 
themselves is “Will all the testimony submitted in 
Washington produce any tangible benefits for practi- 
tioners?” 

Being optimists, some pharmacists noted an indi- 
rect benefit the profession may receive in the process: 
Pharmacy’s often bickering factions have actually 
a age on an issue that has significant economic im- 
pact. 

Who knows, in the future the profession may once 
again wrench control of its own destiny from the tight 

asp of third-party insurance programs... but 

on’t bet on it.

Rx computer 
newsletter 
is launched 


TWINSBURG, Ohio—A 
Revco subsidiary has developed 
a computer newsletter for phar- 
macists and a schedule of meet- 
ings to discuss pharmacy com- 
puters. 

The Revco subsidiary, Gener- 
al Computer Corp., is a major 
developer of retail pharmacy 
systems. 

Richard Pilarezyk, General 
Computer’s president, said fu- 
ture meetings will provide an 
opportunity for participants to 
i information about their 
computer experiences, hear 
news of software enhancements 
and take part in roundtable dis- 
cussions on future develop- 
ments. 

Named “SIG,” the newslet- 
ter is designed to provide a new 
two-way information channel 
between users and the comput- 
er professionals, noted Pil- 
arczyk. 

Information about the users’ 
group and the newsletter are 
available for General Computer 
Corp., 2045 Midway Drive, 
Twinsburg, Ohio 44087.

year.

differently this year, the results showed 
that impulse buying was on the rise.

ing was higher among frequent shop- 
pers (five or more trips a month) and 
among high-income shoppers ($25,- 
000+ a year). 

What stimuli do shoppers respond to 
when it comes to impulse buying? L-F 
researchers read three statements to 
the interviewees and asked them to ex- 
press various levels of agreement or dis- 
agreement. 

On the first statement, designed to 
find out if shoppers look for in-store 
signs and special promotions to guide 
them to “good buys,” 3 out of 4 re- 
sponded affirmatively. 

More than half also said they often 
will pick up items such as razor blades, 
lighters or batteries that they had not 
anticipated buying but realized as a 
need when they saw the items displayed 
at the checkout counter. 

The cluttered look that an abundance 
of signs and special displays often cre- 
ates did not seem to disturb most shop- 
pers. Only 37% said signs and special 
displays clutter a store and make shop- 
ping confusing.

f the study reveals anything about 

consumer attitudes, it is that the typ- 

ical drug store shopper is satisfied 
with her regular store. In fact, more 
than half of the respondents who shop at 
one store regularly (58%) could find 
nothing wrong with it. The level of satis- 
faction was particularly strong among 
older consumers, 72% of whom had 
nothing negative to say. 

There were some gripes, however. 
And in at least two areas there were 
more complaints from shoppers who 
regularly shop a chain store than from 
their independent store counterparts. 

Twenty-four per cent of the shoppers

who regularly shop a chain drug store 
said they did not appreciate the slow 
checkout service they sometimes expe-

with inexperienced store clerks and

had this complaint. 

But the leading irritation was that

other headache mentioned by 12% of the 
consumers.

Pharmacists are 
drug stores’ edge 


n the competitive struggle among 

drug stores, supermarkets and dis- 

count stores, drug stores have at 
least one potent weapon—the pharma- 
cist. 

Primary shoppers of drug stores, su- 


permarkets and discount stores were 
asked to rate those types of retail out- 
lets on 10 selected characteristics. On 
“trustworthy pharmacist,” three quar- 
ters of the primary shoppers rated drug 
stores excellent or very good. In con- 
trast, discount stores and supermarkets 
received high marks from only 30% of 
the consumers. 

On most of the other characteristics 
on the list, drug stores scored well, and 
so did supermarkets. For example, on 
“in store environment and general 
cleanliness,” drug stores received an ex- 
cellent/very good rating from 69% of the 
primary shoppers, and supermarkets 
from 66% of the supermarket primary 
shoppers. Discount stores, on the other 
hand, got high marks from 46% of the 
sample who were primary discount 
shoppers. 

In addition, both drug stores (64%) 
and supermarkets (59%) scored better 
than discount stores (40%) on “quality of 
merchandise carried.” 

On five other characteristics, drug 
stores were rated excellent/very good 
from at least 1 out of every 2 consumers: 
“accessibility to home/work” (62%), 
“fast and efficient checkout” (57%), “va- 
riety of brands” (55%), “sales as- 
sistance” (54%) and “sale merchandise 
always in stock” (49%). 

On those same characteristics, super- 
markets also got generally good marks: 
“accessibility to home/work” (61%), 
“fast and efficient checkout” (49%), “va- 
riety of brands” (58%), “‘sales as- 
sistance” (46%) and “sale merchandise 
always in stock” (50%). 

The consumer report card for dis- 
count stores, in contrast, was generally 
less favorable: “quality of merchandise 
carried” (40%), “accessibility to home/ 
work” (39%), “fast and efficient check- 
out” (32%), “variety of brands” (43%), 
“sales assistance” (27%) and “sale mer- 
chandise always in stock” (37%). 

Only on “sale prices” did supermar- 
kets and discount stores outshine drug 
stores. The tally: supermarkets (48%), 
discount stores (47%) and drug stores 
(39%). 

On everyday prices, none of the three 
types of retail outlets fared particularly 
well: supermarkets (44%); discount 
stores (42%), and drug stores, in their 
lowest rating, (37%).

Drug stores still dominate in home remedies 


s the price of physician office vis- 

its skyrockets and more products 

are shifted from prescription to 
OTC status, self-medication is becom- 
ing a more viable alternative for con- 
sumers. 

Drug stores, with their recognized 
supremacy in the distribution of OTC 
products, are in the prime position to 
capitalize on this long-term trend. 

Of the primary drug store shoppers 
surveyed by Drug Store News, 98% said 


they use OTC medications. And among 
these users, the drug store ranks as No. 
1 supplier. Approximately 80% of all in- 
terviewees said they last purchased an 
OTC medication at a drug outlet. Super- 
markets, with a 10% share and discount 
stores with 6% rank a distant second 
and third. 

But a big percentage of the primary 
drug store shoppers surveyed are also 
the primary supermarket and discount 
store shoppers in the households. As a 


result, these outlets could be primed for 
a significant entry into a market tradi- 
tionally dominated by drug stores. Ac- 
cording to the survey, chains outper- 
formed independents in attracting 
users of OTC medications. Among those 
consumers who said they last purchased 
an OTC medication in a drug store, 53% 
bought the product in a chain outlet and 
47% in an independent store.

Vitamin buyers prefer drug stores hands down 


ing medications, free-wheeling 

lifestyles (heavy smoking and 
drinking), and skipped meals can all con- 
tribute to vitamin deficiences. 

Consumers are beginning to recog- 
nize these facts and have taken steps 
necessary to correct their nutritional 
shortfalis. Of al! primary drug store 
shoppers surveyed by Drug Store News, 
92% said they have at some time taken 
supplemental vitamins. 

Drug stores rated very high as an 
outlet where consumers purchase these 
nutritional products. In fact they were 
the No. 1 outlet where most shoppers 
said they last purchased their vitamins. 
Virtually 71% of all vitamin users inter- 
viewed said they made their most recent 
vitamin purchase at a drug outlet. And 
82% claimed this outlet as the only place 
where they ever purchased vitamins— 
indicating a high consumer loyalty to 
drug outlets. 

Statistically, chains ranked higher 
than independents in terms of the pro- 
portion of shoppers that stated where 
they shopped for -heir latest vitamin 
purchase. Fifty-five per cent of the sam- 
ple said they last bought vitamins in a 
chain drug store, while 45% mentioned 
independents 


S pecial reducing diets, nutrient kill- 


Discount stores and supermarkets 
placed a distant second and third as 
noted by their 11% and 9% market 
shares among vitamin users. Health 
food stores captured 4% and depart- 
ment stores netted only 2% 

Drug stores’ strength as the primary 
distribution point for vitamin products 
is further illustrated in that most drug 
store shoppers also characterized them- 
selves as primary shoppers of super- 
markets, convenience stores and dis- 
count centers. 

In absolute numbers, females repre- 
sent the largest single group of shop- 
pers that purchase vitamins in drug out- 
lets. This group registered a proportion 
of 5 to 1 compared to their male counter- 
parts. The proportion, however, reflects 
the sample’s composition. When per- 
centages of vitamin shoppers are used 
as a yardstick of measure, males are just 
as likely to purchase vitamins as 
females in drug stores. 

All age groups analyzed—under 35, 
35-49, and 50 and over—purchased vi- 
tamins in drug stores about equally. Ap- 
proximately *% of all respondents said 
drug stores represent the outlet where 
vitamins were last purchased. In abso- 
lute terms, however, the largest single 
age group of vitamin shoppers are those 


under age 35. 

In terms of marital status, singles 
represent a disproportionately large 
percentage of vitamin shoppers, but 
their numbers are small relative to 
other groups. Indeed, 3 of every 4 (72%) 
singles who are vitamin users last pur- 
chased vitamins in a drug store. 

Interestingly, those spending the 
most on their last shopping trip ($21 or 
more), purchased vitamins in propor- 
tionally higher percentages than those 
spending $10 less on their last trip to the 
drug store. 

The survey revealed few differences 
in terms of regions of the country and 
household location. For example, drug 
stores captured approximately 2 out of 3 
of all rural, urban, or suburban based 
shoppers. And drug outlets are the pri- 
mary source of vitamins across all re- 
gions of the country—especially the 
South atlantic region. 

On the other hand, supermarkets 
chalked up above average shares in New 
England (19%) and in the Western re- 
gion (16%). 

Approximately half of all vitamin 
users that last purchased vitamins in 
drug stores typically shopped two or 
less times per month, a reflection of the 
sample.

Sports medicine remains a sure winner 


elastic bandages, analgesic rubs 

and heating pads, are without 
question a key drug store commodity, 
according to results of Drug Store News’ 
third annual consumer survey. 

Two of every three primary drug 
store shoppers surveyed (71%) said they 
had made their last purchase of a sports 
medicine product in a drug store. Other 
outlets where survey respondents said 
they made their last purchase of a 
sports medicine product included super- 
markets (11%) and discount stores 
(11%). Only 6% of the 750 primary drug

never bought or used a sports medicine 

Nearly three-fourths (73%) of the pri- 
mary drug store shoppers who said they 
had made their last purchase of a sports 
medicine product in a drug store were 
under 35 or over 50 years of age. 

Persons living in households with 
total annual incomes exceeding $25,000 
accounted for the bulk of all survey re- 
spondents, and likewise, for the bulk 
(40%) of the most recent sports medi-

cine purchase in a drug store. By a 
slight margin (54% vs. 44%), survey re- 
spondents indicated they typically pur- 
chased sports medicine products in a 
chain drug store rather than in an inde- 
pendent drug store. 

Though typically labeled and mer- 
chandised sports medicine products, 
elastic bandages, analgesics rubs, heat- 
ing pads and related items are often 
used by persons who have sustained 
strains, sprains or other injuries not re- 
lated to athletic activities. On-the-job 
injuries, and even home and garden 
chores, often result in many of the same 
aches and pains that afflict part-time 
athletes. 

Unless these injuries appear severe, 
resulting in sharp, enduring pain, per- 
sons typically consult their neighbor- 
hood pharmacist for advice on what 
product or products to use for treat- 
ment. Rest, ice, compression and eleva-

The drug stores’ stake in the rapidly 
expanding home health/self care market 
cannot be underestimated. 

According to the Bennett Group, a 
Washington-based consulting and plan- 
ning organization specializing in the 
home health care field, the product seg- 
ment of the home/self care market 
topped $1.8 billion in sales in 1981. By 
1985, the product segment of the mar- 
ket (excluding professional services) is 
expected to exceed $3.3 billion in annual 
sales. Products and services combined 
are expected to generate sales of $9.1 
billion annually by 1985. 

While incontinence and urological 
products are expected to continue to 
dominate the home/self care market in 
the next decade, other categories are 
expected to pick up a greater share. 

By 1985, major growth categories and 
their annual projected sales will include 
high technology items ($665 million), 
respiratory equipment ($516 million), 
durable medical equipment ($319 mil- 
lion), rehabilitation equipment ($510 
million) and pressure sore/skin care 
products ($357 million).

the convenience offered by the drug

latest consumer survey revealed that 
46% of those questioned last purchased

That should come as welcome news to 
drug store operators, who have been 
upgrading the mix and decor of their 
departments in hopes of improving their 
share of the $10.3 billion cosmetics mar- 
ket. Their efforts have apparently paid 
off in the race for market supremacy 
with department stores, supermarkets 
and discount stores. 

Based on the survey, only 12% que-

partment store. Supermarkets were 
mentioned by 8% of those surveyed, a 
surprisingly high response rate consid-

selection. Discounters, such as K mart, 
Target and Wal-Mart, were popular 
among the sample, with 13% reporting 
that their last purchase was at a dis- 
count outlet. 

Another competitive challenge is 
coming from the door-to-door mar- 
keters including Mary Kay and Avon. 
Almost 7% of the sample last used this 
source to buy cosmetics. 

It is the drug store, however, that 
tends to entice the younger, more afflu- 
ent shopper who is prepared to pick up 
an item on impulse. To this end, drug 
chains are improving their merchandise 
presentations and bettering customer 
service. This has been apparent in the 


T he average consumer today prefers 


major chains. Sixty per cent of the drug 
store shoppers noted that they shopped 
a chain rather than an independent.

Halston and Ricci are proper for the 
more affluent shopper frequenting the 
drug store. About 40% of those last pur- 
chasing cosmetics in a drug store have 
household incomes exceeding $25,000. 

Many drug chains are now going one 
step farther by adding prestige cosmet- 
ics lines to the mix. These brands, often 
secured via diverters, help set drug 
stores apart from food stores. 

In the drug cosmetics mix, fra- 
grances produce the bulk of sales, fol- 
lowed closely by pegged cosmetics. The 
fastest growing segment is the facial 
treatment area, whose expansion is 
being fueled by the aging of the popula- 
tion. 

Total cosmetics growth has flattened 
over the years, making it more crucial 
than ever for drug chains to entice for- 
mer department store shoppers. Over- 
all, cosmetics sales last year increased 
only 1% to 2%, while drug chains man- 
aged to squeeze out an 8.9% sales 
growth. 

While almost 50% of those surveyed 
last purchased cosmetics at a drug 
store, an even greater percentage, 76%, 
reported that they have at sometime 
purchased cosmetics at a drug store. 

Based on the total number of shop- 
pers who last purchased in a drug store, 
it is apparent that cosmetics is a high- 
impulse category.
