Drug store lead in toiletry 
sales boosted by image 


rug stores are the outlet that 

the majority of people surveyed 

in Drug Store News’ Consumer 
Study last purchased a toiletry item. 

In fact, 40% of those questioned had 
selected a drug store, compared with 
33% who last shopped in a supermarket. 
Over the past few years, these two out- 
lets have engaged in a fierce battle to 
command the toiletry market. Al- 
though drug stores fared better overall, 
supermarkets outperformed drug out- 
lets in the New England and South Cen- 
tral States. Those who did ot last pur- 
chase in a drug outlet often made less 
than two trips to the store and had a 
household income under $10,000. 

The image of the drug store—the 
health atmosphere provided by the 
pharmacy—helps keep drug stores 
ahead of food units when it comes to 
toiletry goods. Additionally, drug stores 
are willing to devote greater space to 
these heavily sku’d areas. 

The loyalty to the drug store is even 
more dramatically demonstrated by ex- 
amining the answers of customers when 
asked if they ever shop a drug store for 
toiletries. Almost 90% said yes, making 
toiletries one of the categories custom- 
ers associate with drug stores. 

This toiletry shopper is likely to be a 
frequent visitor to her favorite drug 
stores. For example, only 14.5% of the 
total survey said they shop at a drug 
store as many as five times per month. 
Of those shopping a drug store for toi- 
letries, however, almost 18% said they 
visit the store five or more times. 

And she’s prone to impulse pur- 
chases—perhaps the new shampoo fea- 
tured in a floor display or the sun care 
item on the endcap. Twenty per cent 
said they'll always buy on impulse while 
47% said they’ll sometimes make an im- 
pulse purchase. 

Drug stores also tend to attract the 
single shopper more often than other 
outlets. Only 10% of those shopping for 
toiletries in a supermarket were single, 
while 16% of those last purchasing toi- 
letries in a drug store were. 


This single shopper is upwardly 
mobile with a decent discretionary in- 
come that she is prepared to spend on 
toiletry items. This has enabled drug 
stores to realize an 8% sales gain in toi- 
letry sales last year for a total of $3.3 
billion. This category, which accounts 
for 12% of total chain sales, is one of the 
areas drug chains now stress as they 
take a back-to-basics approach to mer- 
chandising their stores. 

One of the fastest growing segments 
of toiletries is skin care accounting for 
almost 12% of toiletry sales. Deodor- 
ants command about the same share fol- 
lowed by men’s toiletries and shampoos. 

Conditioners are also gaining in popu- 
larity as are new hair care goods, includ- 
ing free-styling mousse items. 

Another area with potential in toilet- 
ries is ethnic hair care, now an $800 
million market. Drug chains currently 
offer as much as 40-ft. of ethnic hair 
goods. 

Although drug units must continue to 
fight the battle against supermarkets, a 
new foe appears to be the discount 
store, mentioned as the site of the last 
toiletry purchase by 19% of those sur- 
veyed.

in a supermarket or liquor 
store. They also usually buy 
their snacks, foods and soft 
drinks in a supermarket. 

Still, drug stores ranked 
third as the location where out- 
lets for liquor, wine, and beer 
and groceries were last pur- 
chased, second as the place 
where soda and snacks were 
last purchased. 

Only 6% of all beer pur- 
chasers in the third annual 
Drug Store News consumer 
study said they made their last 
beer purchase in a drug store. 
That was less than the 49% who 
bought the product in a super- 
market and the 31% who 
bought it in a liquor store. How- 
ever, the number of beer con- 
sumers who last bought beer in 
a drug store was triple the n:m- 
ber who bought it in depart- 
ment and discount stores and 
nearly double the number who 
bought it in convenience stores. 

For wine and liquor sales, 
drug stores remained in third 
place. Eight per cent of the 
users said they made their /ast 
purchase in a drug store. That 
was less than the 51% who 
made their last purchase in a 
liquor store and the 33% who 
made their last purchase in a 
supermarket. 

Once again, drug stores were 
more than twice as popular an 
outlet for such purchases than 
discount stores (3%), conve- 
nience stores (1.7%) and de- 
partment stores (0.5%). 

Although the percentages of 
men and women who made 
their last beer, wine and liquor 
purchases in a drug store were 
approximately equal, men were 
more likely to ever have bought 
the products at some time in 
their lives in drug stores. 

Twenty-six per cent of the 
men surveyed said they bought 
beer at some time in a drug 
store, or twice the number 
(13%) of women. 

In the wine and liquor cate- 
gory, 21% of the men s::rveyed 
said they once bought such 
products in a drug store. 

Only 16% of the women sur- 
veyed bought in a drug store. 

Alcohol consumption at all 
outlets decreased as consumers 
aged, but older people gave up 
beer faster than they gave up 
wine and liquor. 

In the under 35 age group, 
85.2% of those surveyed said 
they drank beer and 84.6% said 
they drank wine and liquor. In 
the 35 to. 49 age group, 69.7% 
said they drank beer and 74% 
said they drank wine and liquor. 

In the 50 and over category, 
only 53.6% said they drank beer 
and 64.6% said they drank wine 
and liquor. 

Single people were more like- 
ly to drink, with only 18.7% re- 


porting they do not drink beer, 
compared to 28.7% of the total 
population. 

With wine and liquor, only 
13.2% of single people reported 
they do not drink compared to 
25.1% of the total population. 

When it comes to snack 
foods, 5.3% of those surveyed 
said they made their last pur- 
chase at a drug store. That was 
behind the 86.4% who said they 
made the last purchase at a su- 
permarket, but nearly double 
the 2.7% who said they made 
the last purchase at a discount 
store. 


A GROWING FAMILY 


Buying habits were similar 
for soda. Eighty-three per cent 
of those surveyed said they 
made their last soft drink pur- 
chase at a supermarket and 
5.1% said they made the last 
purchase in a drug store. 

Drug stores were twice as 
popular among soft drink buy- 
ers as discount stores, where 
2.1% said they bought their last 
soda, and convenience stores, 
where 2.3% said they bought 
their last soda. 

With groceries, 94.8% of 
those surveyed said they bought 
the products in a supermarket.

NEW YORK—Revco, Supe- 
Rx, Medi Mart and Drug Fair of 
New Jersey have joined the 
growing list of both large and 
small chains planning to launch 
limited in-store tests of check- 
out scanning systems early this 
year. 

Along with Florida-based 
Eckerd Drug, which also plans 
a limited test of scanning equip- 
ment early this year, these 
chains will venture into a seg- 
ment of retail technology that is 
fast becoming commonplace in 
the grocery store industry. 

Under the auspices of a Chi- 
cago marketing consultant, 
several drug chains ‘have al- 
ready installed laser scanners 
in stores located in Marion, 
Ind., Midland, Tex., Pittsfield, 
Mass., and Eau Claire, Wis. In 
addition, Revco has installed 11 
scanners in its first low margin 
H&BA store in Memphis. 

Both Giant Foods and the 
Jewel Companies, through its 
Osco and Sav-On drug store di- 
visions, are also testing scan- 
ning equipment in freestanding 
drug or food/drug combination 
stores. 

However, the tests to begin 
this year by Eckerd, Revco, 
SupeRx, Medi Mart and Drug 
Fair N.J. represent the initial 
foray into scanning by drug 
store chains themselves. 

Although a rapid conversion 
to checkout scanning in drug 
stores is unlikely, top manage- 


ment at several chains has rec- 
ognized that, in the words of 
Eckerd Drug chairman and 
president Stewart Turley, “it’s 
getting close to the point where 
scanning will be more feasible” 
in drug stores. 

Industry sources now esti- 
mate that at least 60% of all 
merchandise carried in the typ- 
ical chain drug store is UPC 
coded and that 80% of all check- 
out transactions are comprised 
of products carrying the UPC 
code. With the number of UPC- 
coded items going up, and the 
price of buying, installing and 
maintaining scanning equip- 
ment coming down, the move- 
ment toward checkout scanning 
in drug stores is gradually pick- 
ing up steam.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 9, 1984 


Special report: 
Diabetics 


PHARMACY 


Diabetics need full line of monitoring devices 


NEW YORK—Many of the 
nation’s leading diabetologists 
now believe that the best hope 
for diabetics lies in close control 
of blood glucose levels. 

Maintaining levels as near to 
normal as possible appears vital 
in managing diabetes. Control 
is defined operationally as the 
achievement of “normal” blood 
g'ucose values before, and 
three to four hours after, any 
given meal and through the 
nighttime hours. 

Control is achieved by physi- 
clan care, proper diet, exercise 
and medicine when needed. But 
the success of this program 
hinges on diabetics knowing 
their own blood sugar levels at 
all times. 

Depending on the condition 
and needs of individual diabet- 


ics, there is a “hierarchy” of 
testing, which means that a 
complete range of products 
must be available to consumers. 
These items include both urine 
and blood testing devices, and 
reagent strips. 

Untilas recently as 1980 urine 
testing was the only monitoring 
method available to diabetics for 
use at home. However, for many 
diabetics—notably type I—ur- 
ine tests for sugar are insuffi- 
cient for close control. 

The amount of glucose in the 
urine does not always accu- 
rately reflect the “immediate” 
glucose level in the blood. Spe- 
cifically, urine tests don’t al- 
ways indicate when blood glu- 
cose is dangerously low; urine 
tests do not become positive un- 
til glucose levels in the blood

have been high for several 
hours, and urine glucose levels 
may falsely appear negative if 
the patient has recently had a 
large amount of liquid to drink. 

Type I diabetics also have the 
option of using blood tests to 
monitor their diabetes manage- 
ment. 

Frequency of monitoring var- 
ies with the Severity of diabetic 
symptoms. Most insulin-de- 
pendent diabetics monitor 
blood glucose levels four to five 
times a day for optimum con- 
trol. And during periods of ill- 
ness or stress, monitoring is 
more frequent to avoid abrupt 
changes in blood glucose levels. 

Pregnant diabetics are often 
advised to monitor seven to 
eight times a day. In a study 
conducted at New York Hospi- 


tal-Cornell Medical Center, dia- 
betic women on regular blood 
glucose self-monitoring were 
able to achieve near normal 
blood sugar levels. These same 
women delivered healthy 
babies with no diabetes-related 
hospitalizations during preg- 
nancy. 

Monitoring also minimizes 
the unexpected highs and lows 
which can occur when a diabetic 
misses a meal, is ill or under 
stress. And monitoring also 
provides diabetics with a means 
of associating daily activities 
with the effects of blood sugar 
levels. 

To foster more patient self 
care, some physicians have 
formed Diabetes Self-Care Pro- 
grams so that patients can learn 
how to monitor their conditions

Diabetes 
incidence 
growing 


NEW YORK-—Approxi- 
mately 5% of the United States 
population has some form of di- 
abetes. And while the incidence 
of the disease grows, research- 
ers remain stumped about the 
cause of the increase. 

In 1980, it was estimated that 
eight million to 8.5 million 
Americans suffered from type I 
(insulin-dependent) or type II 
(not-insulin-dependent) di- 
abetes. 

By 1983, this estimate grew 
to 10 million to 11 million peo- 
ple. And of this total, half, or 
about five million people, don’t 
even realize they have the dis- 
ease. 

Failure to recognize diabetes’ 
early warning signs, including 
blurred vision, obesity and slow 
healing of cuts, helps explain 
why the disease is the nation’s 
third largest killer. Other warn- 
ing signs are excessive thirst, 
constant hunger, frequent uri- 
nation, fatigue, rapid weight 
loss and acetone breath. But 
these clu:s are not observed 
among a!’ patients. 

So blood glucose and urine 
tests are used to confirm and 
monitor the disease. 

Aside from its rapid growth, 
diabetes is an often-misun- 
derstood disease, and making 
people aware of symptoms 
serves a critical community 
need. By improving awareness, 
many of the disease’s life- 
threatening complications— 
blindness, kidney failure, heart 
disease, leg/foot amputations— 
can be avoided. 

If diabetes is left uncon- 
trolled during pregnancy, it can 
lead to spontaneous abortion or 
retarded and physically de- 
formed or impaired children. 

When unchecked, diabetes 
can result in blindness. A re- 
ported 5,000 cases occur each 
year. Diabetics are also 17 times 
more likely to have kidney dis- 
ease, five times more likely to 
develop gangrene and lose a 
limb, am twice as susceptible 
to heart attack.

Like other chains that have

health care market, Walgreens 
views home health care as a nat- 
ural extension of its main busi- 
djrug stores.

Pay ’n Save chooses Wash. 


sites for 2 Price Savers 


ryvryy 


Price Savers Wholesale Club 
set to open next month in Salt 
Lake City, Pay ’n Save has 
picked sites closer to home for 
its next two ventures into the 
hot new buying club trend that 
is Sweeping the nation. 

Pay 'n Save’s newest 100,000- 
sq.-ft. stores, which operate on 
margins averaging 104%, will 
be located in Seattle and Fife, 
Wash. In Seattle, the chain will 
be going up against Costco, a 
relatively new entry into high- 
volume discounting. 

But Pay ‘n Save and Costco 
will meet head-on before the 
Price Savers Wholesale Club in 


Seattle is completed. 

Costco and Pay ‘n Save are 
racing to be the first to com- 
plete a warehouse-style retail 
outlet in Salt Lake City. 

Two units in a medium-size 
city probably saturate a mar- 
ket, so it is imperative that pro- 
spective operators of the stores 
stake out their territory quick- 
ly. 

When Pay 'n Save announced 
it was opening its first unit in 
Salt Lake City, the retailer also 
announced it planned to open 
units in Seattle, Tacoma, An- 
chorage and Honolulu. 

That kind of announcement 
was meant to forestall competi- 


tors who were looking for new 
sites. The originator of the con- 
cept, Price Club of California, 
has been expanding and similar 
operations also are growing. 

When Pay ’n Save announced 
its units in Fife and Seattle, di- 
versified retailer also indicated 
it still plans to open in Honolulu 
and Anchorage. 

But claiming an area may not 
be enough. Operators of this 
type of store know that they will 
open units only in some of the 
sites they announce. Announc- 
ing expansion plans in several 
cities is meant to kept the op- 
position guessing.

Execs to speak at conference 

DALLAS—Three top chain drug executives will discuss 
merchandising strategies for the home fieaith care market as 
part of the NACDS Small Chain Conference here Jan. 22-25. 
The execs are J. Douglas Reeves, chairman and president of 
Hook Drug, Robert J. Begley, chairman and president of 
Begley Drug and James I. Harrison Jr., president of Harco 
Drug. Other conference highlights include a study of the 
Dallas retail drug market presented by Howard L. Green, 
president of a consulting company that bears his name and a 
presentation on controlling vendor theft by Jack Henry of 
Security Training Programs. 


Rite Aid promotes Martin Grass 

NEW YORK—Martin Grass, vp real estate of Rite Aid, has 
been promoted to senior vp. Alex Grass, Martin’s father, 
announced the appointment before the New York Retail Ana- 
lysts society. At the same meeting, Grass also announced that 
the chain’s board of directors has also agreed to a dividend 
increase and a stock split. 

The split is Rite Aid’s third in three years and the fifth since 
the company first went public in 1968. An original share pur- 
chased in 1968 would be equal to 24 shares today. The dividend 
increased 28% to 20.5¢ per quarter. 


APhA names interim president 


WASHINGTON—The American Pharmaceutical Associa- 
tion Board of Trustees has elected Maurice Q. Bectel as inter- 
im president, succeeding Dr. William S. Apple, who died last 
month at the age of 65. Bectel, a practicing pharmacist in 
Muskegon, Mich., has resigned his position as chairman of the 
APhA Board of Trustees to which he was recently re-elected. 
Bectel said he would be serving “temporarily” as interim 
a and would “definitely not be a candidate for presi- 

ent.” 


Malone & Hyde tests Ike’s 


MEMPHIS—Malone & Hyde has firmed up plans for the 
first of its deep-discount variety stores, “Ike’s,”. which will 
open Feb. 1 ina former supermarket in the Eastgate Shopping 
Center. 

Although there will be no pharmacy, the 33,000-sq.-ft. unit 
will be operated along the lines of deep-discount drug stores. 
Sixty per cent of Ike’s product mix will be H&BA and general 
merchandise such as ight bulbs, toys, pet foods, plastics and 
greeting cards. Snack foods, soft drinks and household prod- 
ucts will occupy the rest of the store. 

Tom Hanneman, senior vp and former head of the Super D 
drug chain, said Ike’s pricing is designed to be 20% to 50% 
lower than conventional pricing. 

“We will stock only highly consumable name brand products 
with fast turnover. Our massive, high-volume buying of only 
manufacturers’ deals will enable us to maintain the lowest 
possible expenses and pass the resulting savings to the con- 
sumers,” he said. 

This store will be the testing ground for Malone & Hyde's 
concept, which Hanneman dubbed the “store of the future.”

and other drug store formats as 


well.”

was “particularly interested” in 
looking at the deep-discount

defensively.”

fascinating format that may 
turn out to be for drug stores 
what the super centers were to 
the traditional supermarket en- 
try,” Leiberman said. 

While not revealing the loca- 
tions of the new freestanding 
drug stores, Lieberman said 
that they would probably be 
opened “within Pathmark’s ad- 
vertising umbrella.”

Pathmark’s H&BA and pre- 
scription pricing strategies.

Walgreens debuts Perfection line cosmetics 


DEERFIELD, Il.—Backed 
by the success of its imported 
Perfection personal care appli- 
ance line, Walgreens is dipping 
into other areas, including cos- 
metics accessories. 

This past Christmas, the 
chain turned to the Orient to 
produce a quality line of cos- 
metics kits that could be pro- 
moted as a Christmas gift idea. 
The result was a series of four 
items attractively packaged in 
navy enamel with Oriental 
flowers. Price points ranged up 
to $7. Sell-through was report- 
edly brisk and stores were left 
with only a few pieces after the 
holiday rush. 

Since 1982, Walgreens has 
carried its Perfection brand, 
which now consists of nine hair 


care appliances plus cosmetics 
brush applicators. The most re- 
cent test of makeup cases, 
packed under a Pretty Face 
logo with a Perfection tag line, 
hints that the chain may move 
further into private label cos- 
metics. 

The Perfection hair care line, 
produced in Hong Kong, has 
been steadily improving thanks 
to Walgreens emphasis on qual- 
ity control. In the chain’s re- 
cently released annual report, 
vp marketing Vern Brunner re- 
ported that sales “are particu 
larly strong for the Perfection 
personal care appliances.” 

Overall, Walgreens store 
brands are enjoying healthy 
sales increases. In fact, during 
1983, house brand volume rose 


19%, according to the annual 
report. 

Walgreens and Eckerd have 
been the two chains most ag- 
gressive-in extending private 
label into appliances and ac- 
cessories. However, other 
chains including Peoples have 
expressed interest in providing 
an alternatively priced brand 
that would net the chain a hefty 
gross margin at the same time. 
Personal care, because the 
business is now mostly in re- 
placement items, was a natural 
start. 

Sources at other drug chains 
add that cosmetics accessories 
and novelties were a natural 
move. “These items fly out of 
the stores at Christmas,” one 
buyer says.

Rite Aid splits stock 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa.— 
Rite Aid has announced a 2- 
for-1 stock split payable Jan. 30 
to stockholders of record at the 
end of Jan. 16. 

The dividend was increased 
on the old share basis from 16¢ 
to 20'4¢. 


quarter were 49¢, up from 41¢. 

For the two quarters ended 
Nov. 12, net income was $31.4 
million, up 27.4% from $24.6 
million for the comparable peri- 
od last year. Sales for the first 
two quarters were $889 million, 
up 15.4% from $771 million. 

Earnings per share for the 
first half of the fiscal year were 
97¢, ri from 80¢. 

In the second quarter, stores 
which have been open at least 
one year produced sales that 
were 12.1% better than they 
did in the second quarter last 
year. 

In the first quarter of fiscal 
1984, same store sales were up 
11.6%. For fiscal 1983 same 
store sales were 12.3% better 
than in fiscal 1982. 

During the seven quarters 
that Revco produced double 
digit same store sales increas- 
es, earnings increases exceeded 


sales gains. 

Sidney Dworkin, chairman, 
attributed the trends to the re- 
cession resistant nature of 
Revco’s drug store business, 
effective expense controls and 
steady improvement in the re- 
sults of the former Skillern 
drug stores and Revco’s man- 
ufacturing subsidiaries. 

“Sales of these [former Skill- 
ern| stores exceeded the chain- 
wide like-store average during 
the second quarter, and we are 
progressing toward a level of 
profitability comparable to the 
Revco chain as a whole,”’ 
Dworkin said. 

During the first two quar- 
ters, Reveo added 63 stores 
chainwide, up from 26 for the 
comparable period last year. 
Between 110 and 120 stores are 
expected to be opened during 
fiscal 1984. 

At the end of the second 


quarter, there were 1,720 
stores in 28 states. 

In the second quarter, Revco 
opened its first deep discount 
store, the “Get It For Less” 
unit in Memphis. Dworkin said 
one or two more may be opened

operate drug stores. The test 
will determine if this type of re- 
tailing ‘‘represents a viable 
form of diversification for 
Revco,” Dworkin said.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 23, 1984 


® Special report: 
Eye care products 


HARMACY 


Ads, counseling boost sales 


of extended wear lens aids 


New York—Despite longer 
wearing times, extended wear 


lenses still require periodic im- 
mersion in lens care solutions. 
Retailers say they merchan- 
dise extended wear lens solu- 
tions by using point-of-sale ads 
and patient counseling to re- 
mind lens users that they need 
to treat their lenses just as 
carefully as if they were prod- 
ucts they washed each day. 
Although extended wear 
lenses remain on the eyes for as 
long as 30 days and nights, they 
still require cleaning and disin- 
fecting with the same systems 
that are designed for daily con- 
tact lenses—either with heat or 


chemical solutions. 

Many retailers prompt sales 
by reminding their customers 
that the buildup of surface de- 
posits on extended wear lenses 
can be prevented by using a 
sterile saline solution mornings 
and evenings as an eyewash. 

They also point out to shop- 
pers that protein and other de- 
posits from eye fluids build up 
on these lenses just as they do 
on contact lenses worn daily. 

To prevent these deposits 
from accumulating and perhaps 
irritating the eye, retailers sug- 
gest that shoppers remove their 
lens periodically and wipe them 
with a surface cleaner or that

Eye care merchandising 


@ Promote eye care products regularly, at least three times 
each month. Most chains feature two or more lens care sys- 
tems in weekly newspaper and circular ads. 

e Group products together by system—Bausch-Lomb, AI- 
lergan, Alcon/op, Barnes Hind, Cooper Vision. Blairex, ete. 
This allows consumers to recognize the system initially recom- 
mended by their optometrist. Group other eye care products 
such as decongestants, washes, artificial tears and ointments 
by class. 

@ Don’t stint on stock; eye care is among the highest contribu- 
tors to sales per square foot. Contact lens solutions average 
$600 per square foot when merchandise in an &-ft. section. 

@ Stock 85-90 sku’s in a 6-ft. or an 8-ft. section. Large drug 
stores feature eye care in sections up to 40 linear feet. Bantam 
stores utilize’sections of 20 to 24 linear feet. 

@ Price competitively. Although discounting exists it hasn’t 
destroyed margins.

screen. 

At present, consumers can 
choose from some 125 items, 
but this number will increase to 
300 starting February 1984. 
McKesson currently warehous- 
es 35 of the items, but this in- 
ventory will also increase. 

Nine of the 11 stores ship di- 
rect to the consumer’s home; 
two (Shaw’s and Bon Appetit) 
are shipped from McKesson’s 
warehouse to the consumer. 
Eventually, more items will be 
shipped from McKesson’s ware- 
house. 

Retailers and other locations 
receive $100 per month or 5% of 
the gross sales—whichever is 
most—during the one-year iri- 
al period. 

How does the terminal work? 

When a customer approaches 
within 3 ft., a sonar detector 
triggers a 30-second “welcome” 
audiovisual message, explain- 
ing the video shopper. 

The screen then asks, “Are 
you interested in hearing 
more?” If so, the customer en- 
ters a credit card (Master 
Charge, Visa or American Ex- 
press) in a slot and touches a 
visual block 1'2-in. square. 

Inserting the credit card 
does not obligate the customer 
in any way. Its aim is to sepa- 
rate adults desiring information 
from children playing with the 
terminal. 


Read classified ads 


The second. audiovisual se- 
quence provides such informa- 
tion as customer service, guar- 
antees, delivery, names of 
vendors. 

The system is interactive: 
Customers can get computer- 
generated answers to their 
questions. A computerized 
order-processing system, de- 
veloped and operated by Com- 
puFill, keeps track of all trans- 
actions, validates credit-card 
purchases and transmits orders 
to participating merchants. 

Jim Belka, secretary-trea- 
surer at Martinez, Calif.-based 
Valeo Drug, said it was “a little 
premature” to evaluate the new 
shopping device. “The public is 
not totally ready to accept the 
concept,” he said. “It would 
work better in an airline termi- 
nal or shopping mall, where 
people have more time to 
browse.” 

Although Valco is testing one 
terminal at present, Belka says 
there will be three or four addi- 
tional installations in 1984. 

Belka also notes that “people 
are hesitant about putting a 
credit card into a slot just to 
look at products. A typical re- 
sponse is, ‘Oh, oh, I’ve signed 
up for something.’ ” 

Chuck Mortensen, partner in 
Encina Drug in Walnut Creek 
said, after one week: “The con- 
cept is good. It should provide 
added sales. All items are guar- 
anteed and customers are given 
full credit on returns.” 

But “returns” is one of the 
risks retailers will have to take, 
Mortensen believes. “As a con-

Highlights 

Currently Ruble estimates 
that approximately &5% of all 
the products ina Rite Aid store 
are UPC coded. That includes 
private label items, which are 
coded at the warehouse. By the

chainwide, he thinks the per- 
centages will be in the low to 
mid-90’s. Already most high- 
velocity items are coded, he 
says. For the remaining items 
that are not coded, iy ch 
plans to ring them up in-the 
usual way. 

In addition to pricing sav- 
ings, scanners also help super- 
markets realize a significant

creases in front end productiv- 
ity, or through-put. However, 
because the average drug store 
transaction is so much smaller 
than a supermarket, Rite Aid 
doesn’t feel as if it will enjoy the 
same advantages. 

“In fact,” says Ruble, “we 
worry about whether our 
through-put mightn’t slow 
down a little.”

office and perhaps one more 
micro at some strategic point in 
the store.

yields margins of 35% and up 
and is less inventory-intensive. 

Besides its Home Medical 
Centers, Walgreens offers a se- 
lection of home health care in 
most drug stores. In addition, 
customers in every Walgreens 
market will soon be able to 
order products through a Home 
Medical Center catalog.

sidering more centers. How- 
ever, industry sources report

‘an offer convenience service

Walgreens sales rise 16.4% 


DEERFIELD, Ill.—Led by 
strong gains in its drug store 
division, Walgreens’ sales for 
the first quarter ended Nov. 30 
increased 16.4% to $613 million. 

Fred F. Canning, president, 
attributed the advances in drug 
store sales to “solid marketing 
strategies and excellent phar- 
macy performance.” 

For the quarter, net earnings 
reached $12.5 million, or 41¢ a 
share, from $9.6 million, or 31¢ 
a Share, for the same year-ear- 
lier period. 

Chairman Charles R. Wal- 
green III said that net earnings 
from United States operations, 
up 49.8% for the quarter, “indi- 
cated the company’s ability to 
generate strong sales from an 
expanding store base, while 
maintaining iirm control on ex- 


The LIFO charge for the first 
quarter this year was 7¢ per 
share, vs. 10¢ last year. 

December sales for the 
chains were up $13.6% to $338.5 
million. That increase came de- 
spite inclement weather in most 
of the company’s markets, Wal- 
greens reported. 

Walgreen added, “A favor- 
able sell-through of seasonal 
merchandise will aid profit- 
ability. We anticipate an excel- 
lent business climate in 1984, 
and a very successful year for 
Walgreens. ’ 

The drug store division is 
scheduled to open 80 new drug 
stores and remodel 70 in fiscal 
1984. “Company expansion is 
on target,” Walgreen said. “We 
will reach a company milestone 
this year when we open the 


two more of its Home Medical 
Centers bringing the company 
total to three. According to 
Walgreen, the chain is evaluat- 
ing the potential for expansion 
in this field. 

Growth plans for the compa- 
ny’s food services include the 
addition of Wag’s stores in F lor- 
ida and Chicago. Walgreens 
concluded the year with a total 
of 1,043 units compared with 
979 last year.

By Jim Ricchiut! 


he sunecare industry will attempt 
to top 19&3’s sizzling selling sea- 


new facial and specialty suntan prod- 
ucts and by continuing to place a heavy 
emphasis on products with a high sun 
protection factor. 

In recent vears, many of the new 
products launched by the industry 
have had a decidedly cosmetic appeal, 
which is not surprising considering 
that the suncare market is made up 
almost entirely of women consumers. 

Retailers have picked up on the in- 
dustry’s strategy and in addition to 
merchandising these products in the 
traditional endecaps and seasona! sec- 
tions, some chains are now moving 
high ticket suncare products into avail- 
able cosmetics department space. 

At Kerr Drugs, based in Raleigh, 
N.C., buyer Johnny Kerr said the 
chain is strategically placing its high- 
end lotions in glass gondolas and on 
promotional shelving in the cosmetics 
department. 

“We mass them around the cosmet- 
ics department and try to tie in just 
about everything you can think of with 
them,” Kerr said. 

Among the notable products being 
introduced for the 84 season are a fa- 
cial gel and a tanning spray oil from 
Charles of the Ritz, an Aloe Vera SPF 
6 lotion and a waterproof SPF 15 block 
out lotion from Carter- Wallace, a new 
Tropical Blend product with a tequila 
fragrance and a reformulated lip pro- 


son by introducing a variety of 


New suncare items 
to stress cosmetics 


tection product with an SPF of 15 from 
Plough and a water-resistant sun- 
screen lotion and a sunburn relief 
product with Aloe Vera from Tanning 
Research Laboratories. 

Buyers surveyed by Drug Stor 
News said that as with many of the 
new H&BA introductions, they will be 
cautious in their approach to the new 
suncare products. However, many 
drug retailers also pointed out that be- 
cause the advertising dollars allocated 
to support these products are so heav- 
ily concentrated during the relatively 
short selling season, new products can 
often secure a high degree of brand 
awareness among consumers in a 
short time. 

“Most of the lines are on a guaran- 
teed sales basis, so there’s not much 
risk,” Kevin MeGivne, buyer at Gen- 
ovese Drugs, based in Melville, N.Y., 
also noted. 

One product that created a great 
deal of interest last vear in the South 
will be brought into more chains this 
vear. Panama Jack, as the product is 
known, was one of the hottest items in 
the category last year, according to 
buyer Johnny Kerr. In much the same 
manner that Hawaiian Tropics was 
launched, Panama Jack was sold on the 
beaches of south Florida, the proving 
ground for many suntan products. A 
small sales force has been selling the 
product store to store along with Pan- 
ama Jack T-shirts, and, according to a 
number of buyers, it has really taken 
off.

Retailers are increasingly integrating high-end suncare products into their cosmet- 


ics departments. 


- Sunglass market demands heavy promos 


ineteen eighty-four is shaping up 
to be a crucial year for the sun- 
glasses category in chain drug 
stores, a year in which drug chains are 
going to have to promote more heavily if 
they are to combat the market share 
inroads by discount stores and super- 
markets. 

For the past few years sunglass sales 
have not been overly strong in drug 
stores. Many retailers have linked the 
poor showing to consumer buying resis- 
tance created by the recession. 

However, with the economy running 
with considerable more steam, it would 
seem logical that drug retailers would 
enjoy a strong season. But statistics ob- 
tained from the A. C. Nielsen Company 
suggest the problems affecting the sun- 
glass category in drug stores may be 
more complex than just a poor economy. 

Figures compiled by Nielsen indicate 
that the two main retail outlets that are 
in direct competition for the low-end 
sunglasses market, which drug stores 
traditionally have been strongest in, 
showed substantial sales increases over 
1982. 

For the first 10 months of 1983, dis- 
count store sales of sunglasses were up 
an extraordinary 29% over the same pe- 
riod in 1982, according to Nielsen. And 
while the Chicago-based research com- 
pany said that the increase may have 
been inflated somewhat by the addition

Nielsen figures, chain and independent 
drug stores measured collectively 
showed no net sales gain at all from 
January to October last year over the 
same period in 1982. And chain drug 
stores fared only slightly better than 
independents. Chains recorded a 1% in- 
crease in sales. 

While drug stores are in no immedi- 


ate danger of losing their dominance 
over supermarkets and discount stores, 
the increased competition is becoming a 
growing problem. In 1982, Nielsen re-’ 
ported that food stores and discount 
stores generated increases in market 
share. These increases have come at the 
expense of drug stores. 

Drug stores in 1982 controlled ap- 
proximately 60% of the low-end sun- 
glasses market. Supermarkets generat- 
ed an estimated 23% of the volume and 
mass merchandisers accounted for 18% 
of the market. However, these figures 
are certain to change after the inroads 
made by discount stores are considered 
this year. 

What are discount stores doing that 
drug stores aren’t? One industry source 
points out that they have been much 
more aggressive promotionally. But he 
sees drug chains changing their strat- 
egies this year. “Chains are going to 
promote earlier and more often this 
year to get a jump on the market.” 

Most drug retailers would agree that 
they could do a better job with the sun- 
glasses category. In some cases, chains 
have been spoiled by their past suc- 
cesses in the category. However, like a 
number of other “core” drug store cate- 
gories, retailers are realizing that they 
will have to either become more com- 
petitive .

Initially some buyers feared 
the vast number of line exten- 
sions in recent years would re- 
sult in lines cannabalizing one 
another. However, few buyers 
believe this will happen now. 
The general consensus among 
buyers is that the suncare con- 
sumer is becoming increasingly 
sophisticated about the prod- 
ucts on the market and is will- 
ing to purchase more than one. 

Many chains now kick off the 
season by heavily promoting 
products that have a lower sun 
protection factor (SPF). As the 
season progresses, buyers said, 
they push the sun blocks more 
heavily. As one buyer at a major 


chain based in the South noted, 
“Anybody who has «tan by July 
isn’t going to buy more suntan 
lotions, unless it’s a sun block.” 

The rapid growth of the sun 
block category is still coming as 
a surprise to some chains. Sev- 
eral buyers reported that the 
unseasonably hot summer last 
year caused them to sell out 
products with higher SPF’s 
much faster than they antici- 
pated. 

“Last year the sunscreen cat- 
egory really took off,’ said 
Nathan Roach, buyer at Medi- 
care Glaser, based in St. Louis, 
Mo. “Sales increased dramat- 
ically over the year before. This 
year we're going to double the

noted, “Sun blocks are the real 
hot category right now. 

“We're probably advertising 
the sun blocks more than we 
were four to five years ago,” 
Sullivan continued. “We realize 
that it is a big part of the busi- 
ness today.” 

As successful as the suncare 
category was last year for many 
drug chains, several buyers re- 
ported that they are going to 
step up promotions and employ 
some different merchandising 
techniques this year. 

“IT think that there were a lot 
of things that we didn’t do last 
year that we could have done to 
generate more interest,” said 
Medicare Glaser’s Koach. This 
year he said the chain will 
planogram its sunecare endcap

last year was that every item 
could not be seen by the cus- 
tomer,’’ Roacn said. “By 
planogramming our endcaps

likely to compete more ag: 
gressively this vear using 
strategies that include in- 
creased advertising and heavy 
discounting. 

“Consumers are ready for 
price point sunglasses,” 
Bill Baxley, vp, marketing at

N.C. “For the average consum 
not the name on the 
it's the look and the

price. 

Baxley became convinced 
last year when the chain tested 
a limited assortment of no 
name sunglasses at price points

The low-end glasses showed the 
biggest sales increases in the 
category. 

In addition to price, most 
drug retailers consider service 
to be one of the most Important 
elements in a sunglass pro- 


gram. 

“You are just as strong as the 
people vou have calling on you, ” 
notes a buyer for the Deerfield, 
[ll.-based Walgreens. 

“The biggest fear among 


many retailers is that the ven- 
dor is just going to load them up 
with product that isn’t going to 
sell,” said a buyer for a large 
southern-based drug chain. 
Some chains such as Perry 
Drug Stores, based in Pontiac, 
Mich., have tried to solve ser- 
vice problems by going the di- 
rect import route. According to 
Dave Peterson, Perry’s as- 
sistant vp of merchandising, 
the chain opted for a direct im- 
port program because it want- 
ed to take advantage of the 
higher margins and to obtain 
tighter control over the sun- 
glasses department, but pri 
marily because the chain was 


unhappy with the service end of | 


the supplier business. 

But there are risks inherent 
in a direct import program and 
retailers are well aware of 
them. Sunglasses have long 
been considered a fashion item, 
and consumers are fickle when 
it comes to fashion. What’s in 
one year can just as easily be 
out the next.

A direct import program can 
also present maintenance prob- 
lems at the store level. Tradi- 
tionally, the sunglasses catego- 
rv has been one department in 
which store personnel have 
generally had little involve- 
ment. Before a direct import 
program can be successful a 
chain must get its store person- 
nel to actively service the de- 
partment, many retailers point 
out. 

For the most part retailers 
say they are satisfied with the 
attempts made by many sup- 
pliers to improve their overall 
programs. 

“They [the suppliers] are 
spending more time and effort 
servicing the stores,’ 
Tom Rosenthal, vp and mer- 
chandise manager at Standard 


notes 


oo 


Drug in Richmond, Va. Rosen 
thal said that Standard went 
back to a service program after 
warehousing sunglasses be- 
cause of problems in getting 
emplovees to learn the busi- 
ness. 

The improved service pro- 
grams may also be the reason 
that fewer chains are changing 
suppliers. While there is still a 
tendency to go with different 
manufacturers to clean out old 
stock, a number of buyers said 
that they are staying with their 
current suppliers longer than 
they were a few vears ago. In 
addition to improvements In 
service programs, buyers say 
they are more confident dealing 
with a company that they have 
been working with for a few 
vears.

Christy to replace Eads as prez 


By Lou Karney 

SEATTLE—Pay ’n Save, the 
industry’s 13th largest drug 
chain, has just acquired North- 
western Drug, the largest drug 
wholesaler in the state of Wash- 
ington. 

Industry sources say that it 
is the first time that a major 
drug wholesaler has been pur- 
chased by a chain drug retailer. 
Pay ’n Save, which will operate 
Northwestern as a wholly 
owned subsidiary, paid be- 
tween $3 million and $4 million 
to acquire the company. Last 
year Northwestern’s sales to- 
taled $130 million, up 30% from 
1982. 

Joe Christy, Pay ’n Save’s vp 
administration, will replace 


Ken Eads as president of 


Northwestern. Eads. who also 


owned Northwestern, will 
lease to Pay ’n Save a 258,000- 
sq.-ft. distribution center 
which he still owns. The lease is 
effective for the next 25 years. 


— 


Sefore the acquisition, 
Northwestern had supplied 22 
Pay ’n Save drug stores plus five 
Bi-Mart’s, Pay ’n Save’s dis- 
count drug stores. Now that the 
acquisition is completed, 
Northwestern will begin ser- 
vicing a total of 64 Pay ’n Save 
stores located in Washington 
and Idaho, plus all 32 Bi-Marts 
in Washington and Oregon. 

Other Pay ’n Save operations 
based in California, Alaska and 
Hawali will continue to be 
served by their local whole- 
salers because they are outside 
Northwestern’s current dis- 
tribution range. 

Cal Hendricks, vice chair- 
man of Pay ‘n Save, said that the 
acquisition will give the Pay ‘n 
Save store “more depth in lines 
and better in-stock conditions.” 

Eventually, said Hendricks, 
management will begin buying 
and distributing general hard- 
ware lines through Northwest-

Pneumo ’83 net gains 51% 


BOSTON—Helped by a 
strong performance from its 
food drug group, which in- 
cludes Carls Drug, Pneumo 
Corp. posted a 51% increase in 
net earnings for the vear ended 
Nov. 30, 1983. 

Net profits for the company 
rose to $35.7 million, or $2.53 a 
share, from $23.6 million, or 
$1.69 a share, the previous 
vear. Pneumo reported that the 
increase “resulted from higher 
sales, improved operating effi- 
clences and increased interest 
income.” Earnings per share 
were restated to reflect a 2- 
for-1 stock split in May 1983. 

Sales for the vear climbed 6% 
to $1.2 billion from $1.1 billion 
In fiscal 1982. 

According to Gerard A. 
Fulham, chairman and ceo, the 
food drug group, which also in- 
cludes P&C Food Markets, Svyr- 
acuse, N.Y., realized an 18% in- 
crease in operating profit and a 


7% advance in sales. 


While Pneumo’s Aerospace 
Industrial Group accounted for 
only 27% of corporate sales, it 
contributed 74% 
profits. 

“We are very pleased with 
Pneumo’s pe rformance in 1985, 
4 period of many economic un- 
certainties,” Fulham said. “Fis- 
cal 1983 was the most produc- 
tive vear in the history of the 
company and a period in which 
the soundness of our business 
strategy was again confirmed.” 

According to Pneumo, return 
on average stockholders’ equity 
increased to 25% from 22% in 


1982, and stockholders’ equity 


rose by 65% to a record level of 


$178.5 million. 

In the fourth quarter, earn- 
ings rose 538% to $10.8 million 
from $7.1 million in the compa- 
rable 1982 period. Earnings per 
share were 74¢ compared to 
92¢. Sales for the period in- 
creased to $322.8 million from 

$294.8 million.

Playing cards are an important item 
for drug chains because of a fairly high 
turnover rate of 4.5 to 5 times and a 
return-on-investment in the 60 and up 
range. 

Recause of this, many chains have de- 
veloped techniques to boost sales ‘to

Since many games including bridge 
and gin rummy require multiple decks, 
retailers are selling decks on 2-for-1 or 
3-for-1 deals. Walgreens, for instance, 
recently advertised three packs of Stud 
playing ecards for $2.29. 

Begley Drug in Richmond, Ky., also 
capitalized on the impulse nature of the 
category by placing two combined decks 
on endeaps. “If we sell them regularly 
one pack for $1.39, we'll sell two decks 
for $1.99," said Orlando Segneri, sr. vp 
for Begley. 

At Ribordy, executive vp Ausen- 
baugh has found that multiple decks sell 


“real well” when promoted via direct- 
mail coupon books. The chain normally 
sells a pack of cards at price points rang- 
ing from 98e to $1.39. 

Still others have dipped into private 
label cards that can be packaged for 2- 
for-1 promotions. Eckerd, for instance, 
introduced private-label cards about a 
vear ago. Rite Aid has private label 
cards produced in the United States and 
Kerr Drug in Raleigh, N.C., has an im- 
ported brand carrying the chain's logo. 

“We buy them direct from the Orient, 
put them in our own package and sell 
them three for $1,” explained Kerr's Bill 
Baxley. 

Location of playing cards varies from 
chain to chain. Some prefer to snare 
impulse sales at checkouts—others pre- 
fer more in-line locations.

STIMULATES SALES 


Line extensions have enabled retailers 
to target school supplies by age group 
and satisfy the growing needs of 


t used to be that school supplies 

were regarded as seasonal 

items In some drug and general 

merchandise outlets. But in ad- 
dition to their obvious appeal dur- 
ing the August and September 
back to school period, school sup- 
plies are now steady sellers 
throughout the vear. 

Indeed, only 2% of the drug, dis- 
count and general merchandise 
buyers responding to the Lebhar- 
Friedman Research survey said 
they carry school items on a sea- 
sonal basis. 

School supplies actually are the 
leading stationery sellers in most 
mass merchandise outlets. When 
measured collectively school sup- 
plies generate 37% of the station- 
ery department sales in discount 
stores and 41% in drug stores. 
Moreover, 78% of the buvers said 
that they expect school supply 
sales to Increase in the coming 
vear. 

The projected increased de- 
mand for school supplies, a result 
of growing enrollments in day and 
night schools, has prompted many 
chains to increase their space al- 
lotments especially for ring bind- 
ers, spiral notebooks, filler paper, 
pads and folders. In fact, accord- 
ing to the L-F survey, 42% of the 


buyers expect to provide more 


shelf space for school supplies dur- . 


ing 194. 

While overall year-round sales 
of school supplies are up, the lucra- 
tive back to school period con- 
tinues to be the driving force in 
the category. A new survey con- 
ducted jointly by Chain Store Age 
General Merchandise Edition and 
Better Homes & Gardens maga- 
zine revealed that the average con- 
sumer who purchased merchan- 
dise during the BTS period

their total expenditures for sta- 
tionery and school supplies. The 
only other categories where con- 


sumers spent more were apparel, 
shoes and text books.

porting that they are extending 
some of their school supply lines.

are interested in better quality 
merchandise.

ers are upgrading are portfolios, 
report covers and higher grades of 
writing tablets. The trend among 
students is toward more util-

Thrifty’s quest: a profitable Rx dept. 


LOS ANGELES—Thrifty 
Corp., which realized a profit 
growth of better than 25% in 


fiscal 1983 and the first quarter 


of 84, is making a concerted 
drive to bring its unprofitable 
pharmacy department into the 
black. 

A big part of the effort will 
focus on increasing pharma- 
cists’ productivity through a 
phased rollout of pharmacy 


computer terminals. 

The attempt to restore prof- 
itability is a key element in the 
strategic plans of the chain, 
which operates almost 540 
Thrifty Drug and Discount 
Stores in nine Western states, 
because prescriptions account 
for 10% of volume. 

Four years ago, Leonard 
Straus, Thrifty chairman, said 
that in fiscal 1979 the compa- 


ny’s prescription department 
“made money for the first time 
in its history.” 

But Thrifty failed to sustain 
the pace and dropped back into 
the red. “We are now getting 
close to breaking even because 
of improvements during the 
past three years,” Richard Eils, 
president, told Drug Store 
News.

New drug approvals dropped 50% last year 


ROCKVILLE, Md. —The 
number of “totally new” drugs 
approved by the Food and Drug 
Administration dropped by 50% 
last year despite pledges by the 
Reagan Administration to 
“streamline” Government re- 
views of important new phar- 
maceuticals. 

During calendar year 1983 
F.D.A. granted marketing ap- 
proval for only 14 “new molecu- 
lar entities’—down from 28 
NME’s approved by the agency 
in 1982, and 27 such approvals 
in 1981. 

Moreover, of the 14 totally 
new drug products cleared by 


the agency last year, nine are 
categorized as providing little 
or no therapeutic advantage 
over other pharmaceuticals al- 
ready on the market, F.D.A. of- 
ficials confirmed. 

The abrupt decline in NME’s 
approved by F.D.A. during 
1983 reverses a distinct upward 
trend in new drug approvals 
over the past two years and 
casts doubt on claims by Rea- 
gan Administration health offi- 
cials that their efforts to “re- 
form” Government drug review 
practices are beginning to pay 
off. 

Two years ago then-Health 


and Human Services Secretary 
Richard Schweiker credited the 
sudden (1981) upsurge in NME 
approvals to a series of “signifi- 
cant steps” taken by the Ad- 
ministration to enable “benefi- 
cial new drugs to reach those 
who need them faster.” 

As a result of the “leader- 
ship” of Reagan Administration 
F.D.A. appointees, he said, 
Government approval of NMC’s 
during 1981 reached its highest 
level since passage of the 1962 
Federal drug law amendments, 
and more than doubled the out- 
put (12 NMF’s) of the last year 
of the Carter Administration 


(1980). 

“We promised the American 
people we would reform the 
drug approval process, and last 
vear marked a long step toward 
that goal,” Schweiker said in 
1981. “Speeding the review of 
lifesaving new drugs will allow 
the public to benefit from medi- 
cal advances without needless 
delay.” 

Among the specific steps cit- 
ed by Schweiker to accelerate 
the drug approval process: a 
series of “new management ini- 
tiatives” to “enhance account- 
ability for moving [NDA] ap-

Marketplace pricing: one solution to dwindling margins 


The facts are in, and 1983 goes into the record books 
as another banner year for nation’s pharmacy depart- 
ments. Total scripts dispensed rose 2% while script 
prices surged 14 points over January 1983 levels. 

Expensive new drugs, price increases by manufac- 
turers and greater quantities of dosage units per 
script account for a large percentage of the price 
gains. 

Price advances combined with the growth in total 
scripts yielded a bountiful harvest of sales dollars for 
retail pharmacy departments. 

But despite this promising performance, storm 
clouds may be gathering on the prints Pharmacists 
from both chain and independent community drug 
store settings say margins In their pharmacy depart- 
ments are s rinking. 

So in spite of impressive sales growth, margin dol- 
lars (the money used to pay expenses) are on a down- 
ward trend. And lowered margins cut into retailers’ 
return on investment in inventory. 

The culprit creating all the problems are fixed dis- 
pensing fees and the “lower of” provision written into 
many third-party prescription contracts. 

This canbe sa really becomes acute when expensive 


BENCHMARKS 


By Joseph Caputo, R.Ph. 
Pharmaceutical Editor 


medications are dispensed, and it’s important to re- 
member that an increasing mix of drugs on pharma- 
cists’ shelves are categorized as expensive. 

Third-party administrators typically lock pharma- 
cists to low fees that are not regularly updated. So as 
expenses climb pharmacists have no way to recoup 
their inventory investment except one: They can 
charge their private pay patients more for the same 
drugs which are dispensed at lower prices to patients 
enrolled in third-party rograms. 

If this price shifting doesn’t work another dilemma 
is created: Pharmacists can either walk away from 


participating in third-party programs (and face a loss 
of store traffic which accompanies these plans), or 
accept low returns from what was and should be the 
premier department in the store. 

A number of solutions could get pharmacists out of 
the corner they are painted into. One answer may be a 
return to marketplace pricing. Another solution cen- 
ters on separating the distributive function from 
other services that pharmacy is capable of providing, 
and setting separate remuneration rates for the dif- 
ferent functions. A third-solution focuses on elimina- 
tion of the “lower of” provision 

In an economy that hinges on return on investment, 
the degree to which market place pricing is accepted 
may determine the number of pharmacy departments 
and scope of pharmacy practice in the future. 

Unfortunately it appears neither pharmacists nor 
consumers will have a say in the matter. The parties 
welding the greatest clout presently are state govern- 
ment officials, insurance company administrators and 
personnel officers in large corporations. 

These are the power blocks which may set the scope 
of pharmacy practice in the future—and have been 
setting it for the past several years.

larger doses later in the cycle. 
This mimics more closely the 
normal hormone pattern @uring 
a woman’s foliicular (phese 1) 
and luteal (phase 2) patterns.

SEATTLE—The Pay ‘n Save 
Corp. reported a 54° increase 
in earnings for the year ended 
Jan. 28. Sales for the year rose 
IZ. 

According to M. Lamont 
Bean, chairman, net profits for 
the diversified retailing compa- 
ny increased to $30.1 million on 
sales of $1.22 billion, compared 
to earnings of 319.6 million on 
sales of $1.09 billion in the pre- 
vious fiscal vear. 

Farnings per share were 
$2.02, up from $1.41 a vear ear- 
lier. 

Sales and earnings figures 
for the two vears were restated 
to reflect the combined results 
of Pay ‘n Save and Schuck’s 
Auto Supply, which Pay ‘n Save 
acquired in a “pooling of inter- 
ests” transaction on Jan. 27 of 
this vear. Earnings per share 
were also restated to reflect a 2- 


for-1 stoek split in May 1983. 

Bean said the improved earn- 
ings were the result of “solid 
sales increases combined with 
good control over growth in op- 
erating and administrative ex- 
penses.” He added that gross 
margins improved “modestly,” 
while interest expense declined 
to $17.9 million from $22.6 mil- 
lion a vear earlier.

ings Increased 17% to $10.8 mil- 
lion, or 70e@ a share, from 39.5 
million, or 66e a share, in the 
vear-earlier period. Sales rose 
14% to $362.4 million from 
$318.8 million. 

At the close of the vear, Pay 
‘n Save Was operating a total of 
315 stores, including 111 Pay ‘n 
Save drug stores, ¢9 Ernst 
Home Centers, 58 Schuck’s 
Auto Supply stores, 32 Bi-Mart 
discount stores, 24 Lamonts ap-

parel stores, 15 Sportswest 
sporting goods stores, three 
Yard Birds general merchan- 
dise stores and three Von To- 
bel’s home liaprovement cen- 
ters. 

In a letter to shareholders, 
Bean mentioned other accom- 
plishments for the vear, includ- 
Ing: 

@ Raising $30 million in equity 
capital through the sale of com- 
mon stock. 

@ Completion of a long-term 
plan for upgrading its manage- 
ment information systems.

hen it comes to beverage 
sales—soft drinks and in 
states where the law permits 
their sale, beer, wine and liquor—drug 
retailers tend to pay more attention to 
turns than they do to profit margins. 

The reason, of course, 1s competl- 

lon. Drug stores are one of many out- 
le ‘ts for alcoholic and nonalcoholic bev- 
erages, and not always the first choice 
among consumers. Consequently, 
chains that do the biggest business are 
usually those with the sharpest pen- 
cils. 

Drug chains use soft drinks in much 
the same way they merchandise other 
food items—primarily as a traffic 
draw. But a growing number of drug 
stores now feature planogramed de- 
partments, both on shelves and 1 
coolers. 

By selling soda on an everyday 
basis, a chain can make up some of the 
margin it loses when promoting items 


ine and liquor showing as big 


Most chains recognize that with items 
such as beer, turns are frequently more 
important than profit margins. 


such as two-litre bottles. “Ivy you're 
going to stick to promotional sections, 
vou won't make any money,” says Fred 
Van Laare, executive vp of Shoppers 
Drug Mart’s Florida division. 

Van Laare said that the chain began 
testing permanent soda sections 1n Its 
Florida stores during the past vear. 
The 16-ft to 20-ft. section includes an 
assortment of 1l-litre bottles and 6 
pack cans, which Van Laare said con- 
sumers are more inclined to purchase 
at regular prices. 

Chains that have broadened their 
soft drink departments to include per- 
manent sections can realize profit mar- 
gins in the 20% range. While not spec- 
tacular compared to other drug store 
departments, the margins coupled 
with turns of 20 to 30 make the ecatego- 
rv “extremely viable,” as one buyer for 
a western-based chain noted.

section MtIS mpit te ,/ iif 


ecause the over-the-counter prod- 

uct category is one of the key de- 

partments in today’s retail phar- 
macy, accounting for about 15% of chain 
drug sales, Drug Store News, in this 
issue, launches its first OTC movement 
study. 

The rankings are based on warehouse 
withdrawal data from a variety of major 
retail drug chains operating more than 
2,000 stores in every region of the coun- 
try. 

To filter cut skewed results based on 
seasonal variations, such as the winter 
jump in cough/cold sales, the study in 
cludes data from a full year of product 
movement. 

The heart of our study is the unit 
movement chari, which ranks products 
according to how quickly they sell 
through retail drug stores. Also in- 
cluded are charts that rank the same 
products within their own individual 
subcategomes, such as analgesics and 
cough/cold. 

Chap Stick, for instance, is the leader

in overall movement, and, of course, Is 
also the undisputed Tyrannosaurus rex 
within its own subcategory of topical 
Creams. 

The second most popular topical 
cream, Vicks Vaporub 1.5 0z., is a good 


33 points behind Chap Stick, while the

Chap Stick, however, does not make it 
into our Top 10 or even Top 20 in dollar 
sales ranking, and that is primarily be 
cause it carries such a low ticket, a sug 
gested retail of 95¢. Chap Stick is also 
low in doller volume because it is a hotly 
promoted item particularly during the 
cold weather months. 

In tracking drug store ads through 


the month of January, Assistant Phar- 
macy Editor Harold Cohen, R.Ph., 
found that Chap Stick was frequently 
advertised and often at incredibly hot 
prices, as much as 49% below its 61¢ 
average Wholesale price (AWP). 

For that reason, Drug Store News ed 
itors based their analysis of the survey 
data more on unit movement than on 
dollar movement. Because unit sales 
show the actual velocity of a product 
through the drug retail universe, we felt 
it was a better variable for making mer 
chandising decisions. 

Chain merchandisers and buyers 
know the importance of the top 100 OTC 
drug/proprietary items, products are 
routinely discounted because they rep 
resent added value to consumers who 
regularly purchase them. 

The importance of the OTC health 
aids department Is also reflected by the 
fact that it contributes about 15% of a 
chain drug store’s overall sales volume, 
second to the prescription department. 

Drug Store News compiled these 
product rankings by unit and dollar vol 
ume because drug store patrons are ex 
tremely sensitive to prices of frequently 
purchased products. And added mer 
chandising opportunities are created 
when this merchandise is competitively 
priced,

In organizing our over-the-counter 


health product survey, we deliberately 
restricted the study to only those prod 
ucts having a remedial application: anal 


gesies Which relieve pain or fever, for 


example, or vitamins to relieve stress, 
We excluded such borderline prod 


ucts as razor blades, skin creams or 
shampoos that we decided were better 


classified as health and beauty aid prod 


icts. 


After we had computerized our sam 
ple and ranked each product in descend 
ing order of volume, we found that 24 
of all the unit sales volume was generat 
ed by cough/cold products and an equal 
percentage by analgesics. Another [9% 
went to antacids, while 10% went to 
topical creams and eye lens care prod- 
ucts. Laxatives captured 5 of the total 
top 100 unit volume while appetite sup 


pressants, vitamins and antihemor

Focus on cough/cold 

Cough cold products grabbed three 
spots among the top 10-in. unit sales:

The breakdown of sales in the cough 
cold category seems to suggest that 
manufacturers, in their marketing cam- 
paigns, have succeeded in convincing 
customers to buy several 
what is essentially the same product. 

Shoppers seem to be buying a night- 
relief cough product like Nyquil to com- 
bat symptoms while they sleep, then 
turning right around and buying a regu- 
lar cough product 
Vicks to fight those same symptoms in 
the davlight

McNeil earns top spot 
among manufacturers 


An outstanding marketing effort has 
earned McNeil Consumer Products Co., 
manufacturer of Tylenol, the top posi- 
tion among the 37 companies repre- 
sented in Drug Store News’ survey of 
the 100 fastest-moving OTC products. 

Tylenol, in its various sizes and dos- 
age forms, claimed 10 places on the top 
100 list, followed by Vicks and Bur- 
roughs Wellcome Co., each with seven 
positions. 

While it is evident that Tylenol is well 
represented in the consumer's medicine 
cabinet, no particular Tylenol item ap- 
pears among the top 10 fast movers. 
However, five items do make their ap- 
pearance in the top 20. Tylenol also ae- 
counts for 10 of the 24 analgesic prod- 
ucts that placed among the Top 100, tar 
above any other manufacturer.

Key legislator reverses stand on Rx crime bill 


WASHINGTON—In a move 
that significantly improves 
prospects for tough new phar- 
macy crime legislation this 
year, House Crime Subcommit- 
tee Chairman William Hughes 
(D-N.J.) reversed course 
abruptly and introduced his 
own measure to treat the theft 
of controlled substances as a 
Federal offense. 

Hughes, considered by drug 
store industry lobbyists to be 
the chief Congressional road- 
block to enactment of such leg- 
islation, had been expected to 
join with House Judiciary Com- 
mittee Chairman Peter Rodino 


(D-N.J.) in attempting to side- 
line this year’s pharmacy crime 
measure. 

His sudden conversion repre- 
sents a major legislative victory 
for chain, and wholesale drug 
lobby groups which have been 
pressing hard for Congression- 
al action on such a bill. 

The primary remaining 
obstacle to passage of the phar- 
macy crime legislation this 
year: Lingering concerns 
among independent druggists 
who raised objections to several! 
provisions in the Hughes mea- 
sure hours before the bill was 
scheduled for final subcommit-

Giant cancels sex education tapes 
WASHINGTON—Giant Pharmacy officials abruptly dis- 
continued offering taped sexual advice over the chain’s new 
health information telephone “hotline” following protests from 
Washington, D.C.-area religious and antiabortion groups. 


Although the chain will continue to offer phone-in prere- 


corded advice on some 200 other health topics, tapes dealing 
with such issues as abortion, masturbation, homosexuality 
and birth control have been discontinued, Giant officials said. 

The eight controversial “sexology” tapes had been approved 
by the Maryland State Medical Society as well as a separate 
“sereening” committee. But Catholic Church leaders as well 
as “pro-life” antiabortion activists termed the recorded sex 
education messages “extreme.” 


Carter named Eckerd vp 


CLEARWATER, Fla.—Eckerd Drug Co. named James 
Michael Carter, manager of the Georgia-Alabama division, as 
a company vp. Carter will continue to supervise the division's 
207 stores. Carter, who joined the chain in 1966 as a pharma- 
cist, came to the Georgia-Alabama division from Florida, 
where he served as district manager in Orlando and Clearwa- 
ter. 


McKesson plans AMBI buy 

SAN FRANCISCO—McKesson Corp. has signed a letter of 
intent to purchase AMBI Medical Management Systems in a 
stock buyout valued at over $3 million. AMBI, which processes 
claims and provides billing, computer services, marketing 
consultation and training for durable medical equipment re- 
tailers, will become part of SunMark Home Health Care, a 
separate McKesson subsidiary that specializes in DME equip- 
ment for home convalescents. 


Waigreens Feb. sales rise 19% 


DEERFIELD, Il].—Walgreen Co. announced February 
sales of $213.5 million, an increase of 18.9% from $179.5 million 
for the same month in 1983. Charles R. Walgreen said the 
healthy increases came from strong prescription sales, the 
excellent performance of its restaurants and continuing drug 
store expansion.

Perry cuts prices in Mich. mkt. war 


PONTIAC, Mich.—Perry 
Drug’s discount program, en- 
acted to combat the tough com- 
petition in its primary market 
of Michigan, has bolstered sales 
without negatively impacting 
margins. 

“We knew we had to do some- 
thing,” explained Perry's vp 
merchandising Dave Peterson. 
Peterson was referring to the 
hotbed of competitive activity 
that includes not only deep dis- 
counters such as F&M and 
Warehouse Way but also sharp 
drug store operators like Ar- 
bor. 

Perry’s answer, according to 
Peterson, was to cut prices on 
several key categories whose 
suggested retails allow room for 
discounting. 

Huge signs touting discounts 
of up to 40%, as well as a print, 
TV and radio campaign telling 
shoppers they'll “never have to 
pay a full price again,” ham- 
mered home the discount image 
to Perry customers. 

The result? “We've been able 
to hype sales without a negative 
impact on gross margins,” Pe- 
terson said. “Initially, we had 
some cherrypicking, but now 
we have increases throughout 
the entire mix. We've been able 
to expose more shoppers to our 
broad mix and to high gross 
profit departments.” 

Categories discounted in 
Perry include: Timex 30% off; 


franchised cosmetics, about 
20% off; Goody hair care, Whit- 
man and Sanders Candy and 
Westinghouse light bulbs, 40%. 

According to Peterson, Per- 
ry began testing the concept 
last August in its Kalamazoo 
and Battle Creek outlets. “We 
first wanted to see what would 
happen to our margins,” he 


Exec tells NWDA 


noted. Although he wouldn't re- 
veal how much sales have risen, 
the program has been so suc- 
cessful that all drug chains now 
have the discount policy in 
place. 

Although the signs mimic the 
stvle of a deep-discount unit, 
Perry has not realigned its buy- 
ing strategies.

commonplace and hospitals be- 
gin to discharge patients ear- 
lier, many of these patients will 
end up in soa homes. 

“The growth of the long-term 
care industry is very dramatic,” 


explained Webster. “We went 
from 200,000 beds in 1960 to 1.5 
million in 1980. With earlier dis- 
charges from hospitals, this 
number will most definitely 
gTOW. ” 

Because most of these nurs- 
ing homes do not have the pro- 
fessionals or facilities to offer 
pharmacy and other health care 
supplies on their own, they will 
be looking to retail companies 
to supply these needs. Webster 
pointed out that the average 
nursing home patient has 6.1 
medication orders, which 
translates into five scripts per 
patient per month.

sional at a nursing home is at 
the LPN level or less,” said 
Webster. “That leaves a real

different ages, income levels, 
sexes and race used OTC’s. The 
only major difference was that 
the elderly, those with lower in- 
comes and less education used 
professional help more often 
than other Americans, and 
pregnant women used self med- 
ication the least: Only 18% used 
OTC’s compared to 33@ in the 
population at large. 

The more serious the prob- 
lem, the more likely Americans 
are to seek medical help. Infec- 
tions, ulcers and asthma had 
high levels of professional in- 
volvement, while problems like 
age or liver spots, baldness, 
over- or underweight and bruis- 
es were generally ignored. 

Over-the-counter products 
were used most commonly to 
treat such problems as head- 
aches, lip problems, athlete’s 
foot, chronic dandruff and the 
common cold. 

The study also showed that 
the majority of Americans are 
cautious about the way they in- 
gest self medication. Only those 
Americans with relatively se- 
rious discomfort chose to use an 
OTC product on the first day of 
their problem: 81% of those 
who had over-indulged in alco- 
hol, for instanee, did use an 
OTC on the first day. 

In contrast, just 16% of those 
with bunions cr calluses used 
OTC treatments the first day as 
did 19% of those with acne 
problems and 24% of those with 
athlete's foot. 

The overall satisfaction level 
with OTC products was high: 
92% of all those who used OTC 
products said they were satis- 
fied. But certain remedies elic- 
ited even higher levels of satis- 
faction. For instance, 98% of 
those respondents who used 
OTC to treat back problems, 
97% who used OTC's to treat 
minor cuts, scratches and pre- 
menstrual problems and 96% 
who used OTC’s for upset stom- 
achs, indigestion and insect 
bites reported they were satis- 
ited,

Careful consumers detail 
self-medication practices 


According to the findings of 
the Proprietary Association's 
recent study of medication 
treatment patterns, the average 
American has a highly responsi- 
ble attitude toward self-treating 
their medical symptoms. 

Ninety-five per cent of the re- 
spondents in the survey agreed 
that a consumer should be 

“careful” when using OTC’ 
and 96% agreed that a consum- 
er should read the instructions 
before taking an OC for the 
first time and that they should 
only take medication when it 
was “absolutely necessary.” 

Ninety-five per cent of the re- 
spondents said they felt it was 
not safe to take as many OTC’s 
as they might wish. 

Only 10% of the respondents 
believed prescription products 
were more effective than 
OTC’s, and over 70% believed 
that OTC products are just as

because parents are more cau-

Most adults either tend to ig-

treat them with home reme-

those ailments that could be- 
come serious over a long period 
of time.

Association survey, 37% of a 
total of 9,148 reported ailments 
were ignored and another 14% 
were treated with home reme- 
dies. Together these choices 
make up 51% of the possible ac-

taken about an ailment. This 


compares to the 35% of prob-

counter drugs.
