MERCHANDISER 


Mini-electronics make small-sized batteries big 


ith many consumer electronics 
products shrinking in size, 
sales growth in the small-size 
battery category is expected to outstrip 
gains made in the larger-sized batteries 
in the next few years. 

The new miniature cassette player re- 
eorders, radios and calculators that 
have swept the country in recent years 
have led to an upsurge in demand for 
double A, triple A and button cell bat- 
teries. 

The shift in the battery market has 
provided a degree of uncertainty to a 
normally stabie category. Retailers 
have reacted by stocking additional 
sku’s of small batteries. In addition, 
some chains, which in the past have 
merchandised “button cell” batteries in 
jewelry, photo and consumer electronics 
departments, are now placing blister- 
packed “button cells” with their conven- 
tional batteries. 

The battery category is generally re- 
garded by many drug retailers as a good 
profit center that can also be used to 
bring people into the stores. Margins 
can frequently range from 30% to 40%, 
depending on deals from manufactur- 
ers. Turns usually average five to eight 
times a year. 

Chains allocate approximately 4 ft. to 
6 ft. for batteries in most stores. The 
displays are usually placed in the front 
end of the store to stimulate impulse 
sales or in the photo and electronics de- 
partments where they provide a natural 
complement to that merchandise. 

Unlike many other price-sensitive 
drug store categories, consumers are 
less likely to shop around for the best 
prices on batteries. Consequently, drug 
retailers say that batteries can generate 
a healthy return on investment. 

The growth of the smaller-sized bat- 
teries also comes at a time when more 
consumers are switching to alkaline bat- 


Food 
stores 
44.7% 


teries. According to one industry 
source, the alkalines controlled approx- 
imately 65% of the market in 1982. That 
compared with 18% for heavy-duty bat- 
teries and 16% for general-purpose bat- 
teries. 

Industry projections are that the al- 
kaline category will continue to grow at 
a rate of about 12% a year. By 1987, 
alkalines may account for as much as 
71% of the total sales. Heavy-duty bat- 
teries may represent 20% of the market, 
while the general-purpose batteries are 
expected to dwindle to about 9%. 

Overall, chain drug battery sales in- 
creased by 10% last year, according to 
figures from A. C. Nielsen. The drug 
segment, including both chains and in- 
dependents, controlled approximately 
33% of the market in 1983, down from 
34.5% in 1982. However, chains man- 
aged to actually increase their share of 


‘Drug 

stores 

33.0% 

Food 
stores 
44.0% 


the retail drug market, going from 7&% 
in 1982 to 79% in 1983. 

Mass merchandisers made the big- 
gest gains in the battery category last 
year. The discounters were able to in- 
crease their share of the market from 
20.8% in 1982 to 23% in 1988. The food 
segment dropped slightly from 44.7% to 
44%, 

While retailers expect strong gains in 
the small battery category, particularly 
the double A segment, sales of D size 
alkalines have also increased. Buyers at- 
tribute much of the increase to the 
growing popularity of large box radios. 

In the alkaline category, which ac- 
counts for approximately 55% of all 
chain drug battery sales, D size bat- 
teries represent about 18% of sales. 
Double A batteries are the biggest sell- 
er with approximately 45% of the cate- 
gory sales. C batteries and 9-volts ac- 


count for 16% and 9%, respectively. 
Lantern batteries, triple A and button 
cells make up the remaining 12%. How- 
ever, industry sources say that the re- 
cent growth of the button cells and tri- 
ple A batteries has probably been 
understated. 

Retailers say that the 9-volt battery 
segment is declining in importance, 
mainly because manufacturers of toys 
and electronics have been switching to 
double A and in some instances to triple 
A batteries as the power source. 

One chain in the Midwest reported 
sales of 9-volt batteries were down 20% 
to 30% last year, but that sales of double 
A batteries rose more than 30%. 

Another major development in the 
battery category last year was the in- 
creasing number of chains which have 
begun selling rechargeable batteries. 
With nearly all of the major battery 
manufacturers currently marketing re- 
chargeables, the category is expected to 
be a factor over the next few years. 

But while chains such as Skaggs, Wal- 
greens and Eckerd and smaller retailers 
like Lewis Self Service Drugs in Sioux 
Falls, S.D., are carrying a limited selec- 
tion of rechargeables, many chain 
buyers say it is still too early to predict 
their success. 

One of the big problems with the re- 
chargeable category, buyers say, is edu- 
cating consumers about the long-term 
benefits. The prices of rechargeables 
are often two to three times higher than 
disposable batteries. And if a consumer 
also has to spend between $9 and $15 for 
a charging unit, the initial purchase can 
cost more than $25 in some cases for two 
batteries and a charger. 

However, manufacturers of nickel 
cadmium rechargeable batteries say 
that they could account for as much as 
5% of all retail battery sales within the 
next three years. 


he Guild store in Newport Beach, 
Calif., a high-income city, which 
borders even higher-income Corona 
Del Mar, does more volume in picture 
frames than any of the other 10 stores in 
the chain. 

Certainly it helps to have affluent 
shoppers who take a lot of pictures—but 
competition is more intense here, too. 

So it boils down to merchandising 
skills—and that’s where store manager 


“Use the gondola end for an uptraded line 


of frames,” is one of Guild store manager 
i ’s 10 commandments. 
Jim Hoover 


Jim Hoover excels. Hoover is the dean of 
Guild managers, having been with the 
chain for 18 years, 17 as a manager. 
“Picture frames are often viewed as 
“just another department,” he says. 
“But not in my book. Any category that 
yields 40% to 50% gross margins, with 
unit prices up to $20 and six turns a 
year—with an inventory investment of 
$800 at retail—is worth working at.” 
Here are Jim Hoover’s Ten Com- 
mandments on selling picture frames: 

1. Locate the department away 
from photo to funnel traffic into other 
areas of the store—but still put it in a 
highly visible place near the front. 
“Frames are part of a purposeful shop- 
ping trip,” says Hoover, “not impulse. 
People pick up their processing, go 
home and decide on the enlargements— 
and then return to the store for the 
frames.” 

2. Use the gondola end for an up- 
traded line of frames. Guild pulled low- 
profit paper from the picture frame end 
and replaced it with a wood-stained fix- 
ture (furnished by the supplier) for 
$7.80 to $20 frames. In a companion 
move, accessories (7 lineal feet) were 
moved from hardware to adjoin the 
frames (20 lineai feet). 

3. Split off the top ticket line of bev- 
eled frames (up to $34) to glass shelves 
in the gift section because they are pri- 
marily purchased for gifts. 

4. Carpet the shelves of the picture 
frame gondola to upgrade the depart- 
ment and prevent frames from slipping 


Merchandising skill moves frames at Guild unit 


off the shelf. 


5. Select a knowledgeable supplier 


and keep abreast of the best sellers. 


6. Code-date incoming merchandise 
at the same time it is priced, and keep 
the department looking good by assign- 
ing one clerk to spend a few minutes 
daily straightening the stock. 

7. Rotate the frames, with new 
stock in back of the old. “If you don’t,” 
says Jim Hoover, “old styles can stay 
hidden for months.” 

8. Mark down items 50% aftei six 
months. If carryover stock still re- 
mains, work out a credit arrangement 
with the supplier. 

9. Use framed pictures for promo- 
tions only. “We’ve had success only with 
advertised items [16 in. x 20 in. and 20 
in. x 24in.],” says Hoover, “but not with 


staples. Certain styles appeal to people 
in certain areas. Items often become 
fads and you end up selling 2 out of a 
selection of 20.” 

10. Be flexible in your shelf layout. 
Most stores graduate the sizes—from 
the smallest on top to the largest on the 
bottom. “We flip-flopped 5x7 with 8x10 
sizes which account for 80% of the busi- 
ness, putting the 8x10’s on top. We 
found out from the photo department 
that 8x10 is the most popular enlarge- 
ment in this store. Also, instead of hav- 
ing small frames (2'2 x 3%, 3% x 5, 4x5, 
etc.) in a horizontal position on the top 
shelf, we broke them into a two-shelf 
vertical display. This gives them higher 
visibility while maintaining an un- 
broken line of 8x10’s and 5x7’s on the 
two top shelves,” Hoover concluded.

DRUG STORE NEWS 


1984 REFERENCE FOR 
PHARMACY PRACTICE 


This year Drug Store News has updated last year's issue of the Reference For Pharmacy Practice. It has been 
determined through interviews with numerous pharmacists that a need exists for business-oriented information 
and more generic product information. 


The BUSINESS SECTION is a commercial section that contains a myriad of business data useful to practicing 
pharmacists. Included in the section are the top 200 drugs, both by business terms and by manufacturer, profiles 
of leading drugs, a bulk buying guide, manufacturers’ trade terms to retailers and wholesalers and many more 
features. Numerous sources have been used to compile this section. 


The GENERIC SECTION presents information helpful to all pharmacists specifying the top generic products to 
stock, the brand of products pharmacists usually select in an open call situation, and generic to brand name 
reference guides. This newest section is in response to the added demands placed on the pharmacist by drug 
products selection laws. 


The CLINICAL SECTION contains background material on some OTC products, drug/drug interactions, low 
sodium products and sugar free products. Also in this section is information on contact lens care and a guide to 
leading drugs. 


The CONTINUING EDUCATION SECTION contains a 100 question quiz based on the material presented in the 
Clinical section of the book. Following successful completion of the test, pharmacists will be better prepared to 
instruct their patients and advise physicians on such matters as unwanted side effects of leading prescription 
drugs.

Second Ike’s store is planned 


MEMPHIS—Following the success of its first “Ike’s” deep- 
discount drug store here, Malone & Hyde said it will open a 
second unit in the fall that “will mirror” the original 33,000- 
sq.-ft. store. Malone & Hyde said the new Ike’s will also use a 
circus decor theme, with Ike the elephant as its mascot. 

Operating on margins averaging 14%-18%, the stere banks 
on high volume to generate profit dollars. Customer savings 
are in the 20%-50% range. Sixty per cent of the product mix is 
H&BA and general merchandise, and the rest is convenience 
merchandise, such as snack foods, soft drinks and household 


Most of the merchandise consists of deals and closeouts 
direct-shipped to the store. Malone & Hyde is considering 
other Memphis locations for future Ike’s units. 


Snyder’s announces appointments 


MINNETONKA, Minn.—Mike Pann has been promoted to 
vp of retail operations for Snyder’s drug stores, Don Beeler, 
president of the chain, announced. Pann, who joined Snyder’s 
in 1969 as a manager trainee, has held various positions, the 
most recent of which was assistant vp of retail operations. 

Beeler also announced the appointment of Rich Oorlog to vp 
of human resources. Oorlog transferred from Gambles, an- 
other division of Wickes Company, where he was vp-human 
resources. Snyder's operates 55 corporate stores and 148 inde- 
pendent retail outlets in Minnesota, Wisconsin, South Dakota,

make the robbery of controlled 
substances from a pharmacy a 
Federal offense, it appeared 
likely at presstime that some 
type of pharmacy crime legisla- 
tion would finally be enacted 
into law this year.

1983, the other three will open

CVS profits up 16% 


WOONSOCKET, R.I.— 
Melville Corp. reported that 
CVS, Melville’s drug and 
health and beauty aids store 
chain, posted operating profits 
of $61.2 million for the year end- 
ed Dec. 31, 1983, 16% higher 
than the $52.7 million in profits 
for the previous year. 

Sales for CVS increased 
19.2% to $734.1 million from 
$615.8 million in 1982. 

The profit increase for 1983 


was the second strong perfor- 
mance in a row. In 1982, CVS 
operating profits rose 31%. 

For the Melville Corp. as a 
whole, net earnings increased 
to $176.3 million from $142.1 
million, a 24% advance. Sales 
rose 20.3% to $3.9 billion from 
$3.3 billion in 1982. 

At the end of the year, CVS 
was operating 513 drug and 
health and beauty aids stores, a 
net increase of 47 stores. 


Pay Less NW dividends rise 


WILSONVILLE, Ore.— 
The directors of Pay Less NW 
voted to raise the quarterly div- 
idend on the company’s com- 
mon stock to 8'42¢ from 6%4¢, a 
26% increase. 

The dividend will be paid 
July 16 to shareholders of rec- 
ord on June 22. The increase 


raises the indicated annual rate 
to 54¢ a share, two times the 
rate in effect three years ago. 

Commenting on the board’s 
action, Pay Less president Ed 
Hart said, “We are raising the 
dividend again in view of our 
continued earnings growth and 
our outlook for fiscal 1985. 


Malone & Hyde earnings 
Jump 14% in third quarter 


MEMPHIS—Malone & 
Hyde Inc., the food and drug 
Wholesaler and retailer which 
operates Super D drug stores, 
said that fiscal 1984 third quar- 
ter earnings rose 14% to $9.4 
million from $8.2 million during 
the prior year’s quarter. 

Earnings per share for the 
third quarter, ended March 3, 
increased 16% to 58¢ from 50¢ 
last year. 

Third quarter sales were up 
3.6% to $627 million from $695 
million during the same period 
last year. However, exciuding 
the sales of operations discon- 
tinued during the previous 
year, sales rose 7.2%. 

Sales for the 36-week period 
were $1.9 billion, a 5.7% in- 


crease from the $1.8 billion gen- 
erated during the first three 
quarters of fiscal 1983. Exclud- 
ing sales of discontinued opera- 
tions in 1983, sales rose 11%. 

Net income for the first three 
quarters of fiscal 1984 was up 
21% to $25.6 million from $21.2 
million for the previous year. 

J. R. Hyde III, chairman and 
president of Malone & Hyde, 
commenting on the results said: 
“We were pleased with our 
overall operating results for the 
quarter. Importantly, we con- 
tinued to make progress in fur- 
thering our strategic objec- 
tives. 

“We are well-positioned to 
confidently predict profitable 
growth and record results for 


the fiscal year,” Hyde added. 

Malone & Hyde’s net-to-sale 
ratio for the first three quarters 
of 1984 was 4%. During the first 
three quarters of fiscal year 
1983, the Memphis based re- 
tailer had a net-to-sales ratio of 
3.9%. 

Hyde also credited the suc- 
cessful launch of the company’s 
new deep-discount drug opera- 
tions for the strong showing. 

“Initial customer response 
has been exceptionally strong 
for our newest retail venture, 
ike’s, a deep-discount variety 
store which opened Feb. 25,” 
Hyde said. “We plan to open the 
second Ike’s this summer, and 
look toward opening a third by 
the end of the calendar year.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 16, 1984 


Eckerd tests ‘department store’ prototypes 


Continued trom page J 

downtown Clearwater mer- 
chants to draw shoppers back 
to the downtown area. The two 
other main stores in the Cleve- 
land Plaza, F. W. Woolworth 
and Publix Super Markets, 
have also been remodeled. One 


source said that management of 


those two stores reported sales 
had picked up by about 40% 
since the remodeling, and that 
the stores were attracting a 
higher class of clientele. 

The Eckerd store also ap- 
pears to be quite upscale. The 
traditional Eckerd “supermar- 
ket’’ aisle design has been 
tossed out in favor of a depart- 
ment store race track format, 
and the severe white and blue 
decor has been softened to 
shades of beige and taupe. 

Unyielding long aisles have 
been replaced by boutiques and 
islands, which are linked by a 
two-tone floor that funnels the 
customer through each section 
of the store.

In Cleveland Plaza, the drug 
store is in the back, with its 
core—the pharmacy—nestled 
into the rear left wall. 

Cosmetics, photo and elec- 
tronics departments have been 
moved to the center of the 
store, where individual atten- 
tion can be given by service 
clerks. There is one center 
land that displays franchise cos- 
metics facing the front of the 
store and in the Back, watches 
and radios. To the left of the 


lS- 


island, as you w alk to the rear of 


the store, is the television and 
sterev alcove. 

The “opening wall” doesn't 
begin until the customer gets 
halfway into the store. Midway 
along the track the customer 
discovers a broad expanse of 
H&BA, OTC, feminine and 
baby products that flow di- 
rectly into the pharmacy area. 

Pulls right 

When shoppers enter the 
store, they can choose between 
aright and left'track. However, 
the pull is to the right toward 
the expanded greeting card 
section and past the power sea- 
sonal] aisle. If customers decide 
to go left, they will find the to- 
bacco, wine, liquor and conve- 
nience food departments. 

Because each department 


has been carved into a cove or 


harbor, each section is dis- 
tinctly apart from the others. 
Therefore, customers who are 
in the greeting card area are 
segregated from those in cos- 
metics or electronics. 

“Some are looking to buy a 
stereo,” says the manager, “and 
they don’t necessarily want to 
be bothered by someone brows 
ing for a toothpaste or greeting 
card. Here they can go into the 
section, talk about the products 


we have on display and make a 
decision quiet tly. If they need 
help they can call across to the 
girl on the island checkout 
stand.” 

There are five registers In 
the store, two at the front en- 
trance for convenience pur- 
chases, one in the pharmacy de- 
partment and two in the gift 
aisle. Shelves are high, about 50 
or 60 in., allowing the addition 
of about 20% more items with- 


out having to expand the size of 


the department. 

Besides the regular stacking 
of products, Eckerd has also be- 
gun to slant merchandise so the 
shopper can get a full view of 
packaging. 

Customer reaction to the new 
look is promising. Two weeks 
after the new planograms were 
in place at the Cleveland Plaza 
store, customers were telling 
clerks what a great pleasure it 
was to shop in the new environ- 
ment.

Only 48% of the 27,282 pur- 
chases cataloged in the survey 
were “planned,” a full 39% were 
completely unplanned or spon. 
taneous, another 4.6% were 
substitute sales, while 13.4% 
were general sales (i.e., the 
customers meant to buy tooth- 
paste, but didn't specifically 
know what brand. The decision 
to select one brand over all the 
others was made at the store 
level). 

In-store decision-making, 
the POPAT findings suggest, 
affect almost 50% of all drug 


store purchases actually made. 


Prescriptions, of course, gen- 
erate the lowest levei of impulse 
purchase activity: 
all prescriptions sete ps are 
unplanned. However, 32 of the 
remaining 39 key categories 


venerated more than half their 


sales through impulse buying. 
Fight out of every 10 pur- 


chases in jewelry/leather 


goods, cards and seasonal prod- 
ucts were impulse sales. More 
than 7 out of every 10 candy 
gum sales, stationery and home 
office supplies, were un- 
planned, while 6 out of every 10 
sales for toys/sporting goods, 
garden supplies, cosmetics,

housewares, pet 
supplies, food, first-aid, hard- 
ware and paint, vitamins, 
household cleaning aids and pa- 
per goods were impulse-gener- 
ated. 

The findings show why the 
retail drug outlet has more con- 
trol over individual purchasing 
behavior than the typical manu- 
facturer seems to realize. 

While a company like Gillette 
may be spending $27 million in 
total ad revenues for a brand 
like Right Guard, more than 
half the sales in the deodorant 
category are actually generated 
at store level. 

The findings imply that the 
retailer is in a strong position to 
affect purchase rates through 
in-store merchandising. 

In addition to its analysis of 
what prompts sales in a specific 
category, the POPAI study also 
looks at the impact of different 
demographics on consumer 
spending. 

It also tabulates the most 
common cross purchases be- 
tween categories. For instance, 
the study can determine if a 
male who buys contraceptives 
is also likely to buy cologne. 

The study also charts how 
deeply drug stores have gone 
into such product lines as beer 
wine, home health care, sports 
medicine, food, photo process- 
ing, ete. 

In our April 30 sequel, Drug 
Store News will chart some of 
the initial findings more deeply.

directions. We have always

new superstores will have phar-

ture superstores will be 44,000 
sq. ft., and combos, 60,000 sq.

Ten-unit Best Buy 


WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. 

—Best Buy Drugs, a 10-unit 
chain of health and convenience 
stores, is preparing to go pub- 
lic. 

The 20-year-old company, 
which currently has about 120 
private owners, hopes to raise 
between $1.25 and $1.75 million 
from the stock sale, which could 
be consummated this week. 

If the sale goes through, Best 
Buy plans to use the proceeds 
to launch an ambitious expan- 
sion drive in its home market. 
President Robert Pickett, who 
is also one of the company’s 11 
founders, says he hopes to open 
a total of 40 stores over the next 
five vears. 

Ground has already been 
broken on two stores that will 
open this calendar year, and the 
company is about to sign a new 
lease for a third store. 

“We're going to definitely 


open two stores in 1984, and we 
may have a total of five opened 
by the time our fiscal vear ends 
inJuly 1985,” says Pickett. Part 
of the money would also be 
spent to at least double the 
chain’s current 6,000-sq.-ft. 
warehouse as well as to bring in 
new computers and software 
programs. 

sest Buy earned $150,182 on 
sales of $9.4 million in fiscal 
1983 ended July 31. Sales for 
the period were up 12% over the 
prior year, while the earnings 
put Best Buy back into the 
black after the chain, in 1982, 
lost money for the first time in 
its 20-year history. 

The $143,919 loss, said Pick- 
ett, was aggravated by a num- 
ber of factors including the 
adoption of the LIFO account- 
ing system, the expense of re- 
modeling some existing stores 
to the company’s new growth

Medicare-Glaser names Barney 
chief of deep-discount di vision 


ST. LOUIS ney, 
former president of the Jax, 
deep-discount stores in Cleve- 
land has been named to head 
Medicare-Glaser’s newly 
formed specialty retailing divi- 
sion. He'll oversee the chain’s 
entrance into the deep-dis- 
counting business. 

Barney will be joined by Jer- 
ry Gaddis, who leaves his job as 
vp of purchasing at Fisher's Jax 
division to serve as vp for Medi- 
care-Glaser’s specialty retailing 
division. 

Cash rich from its recent 
public offering, 
Glaser will unwrap its first 
deep-discount store this sum- 
mer in its home market of St. 
Louis. No name has been given 
the unit, which according to 
Barney, will resemble Jax. 

“You don't tamper with suc- 
cess,” Barney said. 

That means the store will 
have full-line department in- 


prototype, and the fact that the 
chain was highly leveraged at 
what Pickett feels “was the bot- 
tom of the recession.” 

In fiscal 1984, the underwrit- 
ers are also anticipating a 
“small loss” for the company 
but they attributed it to am- 
bitious investment spending. 
“They’re in the process of con- 
verting all their stores to their 
new protctype,” says Steve 
Hirsh, a broker for Helfer- 
Broughton, one of the two un- 
derwriters. “‘They’ve just 
opened three new stores and 
they've remodeled one. They’re 
remodeling several more and 
two more are about to open, but 
we think these new stores will 
wind up at break-even or better 
their first year because they’re 
in excellent locations.” 

Pickett, who is trying to lo- 
cate most of his new stores in 
shopping centers, says he won’t 
even consider a site if it hasn’t 
the potential to crack $1 mil- 
lion. 

One of the two new stores un- 
der construction is projected to 
open at $2 million, while the 
average new prototype store 
does between $1.4 million and 
$1.5 million. Break even for a 
new store is between $1.1 mil- 
lion and $1.2 million.

or the chain drug industry, the 

past year has been one in which 

many of the promises of 1982 
were fulfilled. 

The previous year, chains had 
been tested by the faltering econo- 
my, but they had emerged in good 
shape, leaner and tougher. And the 
lessons learned in a tight economy 
carried over. 

As the economy mended and infla 
tion remained quiescent, consumer 
confidence rebounded, and drug 
chains were among the benefici- 
aries, with sales rising 11% to $22.

billion and profit growth running 
even higher. 
The record profits earned by chain 


after chain were partly the result of 


lowered inflation, which cut LIFO 
charges, partly of lower interest 
rates and partly of the leaner oper- 
ating styles adopted in 1982. 

Apart from the record operating 
results, the past year was marked 
by a number of trends and high- 
lights. Among them: 

—The reawakening of aggressive 
growth strategies that charac 
terized earlier years. Chains that 


had pulled back on the reins, began 
to loosen them once again as increas- 
es in interest rates and building 
costs slackened and shopping center 
developers began to return to ac- 
tion. Revco, for example, appears 
likely to meet its current-yeur goal 
of 110 to 120 new stores after a year 
in which the worid’s largest drug 


chain was able to achieve only half of 


its objective of 10% growth in retail 
footage. 

—~With more cash to invest, 
chains branched out aggressively 
into other businesses—both retail 


and nonretail. Drug chains had long 
hedged their retail drug bets with 
side wagers on other types of ven- 
tures. But there was a flurry of di- 
versification activity this past year 
that made other years seem tame by 
comparison. 

—QOn the acquisition front, chains 
remained subdued for much of the 
year, preferring instead to concen 
trate on strengthening their share of 
existing markets with small buys 
and new store openings.

buster: Imasco Ltd., parent compa- 
ny of Shoppers Drug Mart, Can- 
ada’s largest drug chain, made a 
$320 million offer to purchase Peo- 
ples Drug Stores, the 11th largest 
American drug chain. It was the 
largest acquisition ever in the chain 
drug industry, and Peoples became 
the first major American chain to be 
purchased by a foreign company. 

The deal was a good one for both 
companies. Imasco got a well-man- 
aged and expansion- -minded drug 
chain, and Peoples would get access 
to additional resources for its 
growth objectives. 

—Technology assumed an even 
greater part in chain operations. 
The pharmacy computer, with its 
power to improve productivity and 
enhance the pharmacist’s role as a 
health care specialist, made its way 
into more and more prescription de- 
partments . Virtually every major 
uncommitted chain finally made the 
decision to go chainwide, following 
several years of careful testing. 

Many chains also began tests of 
checkout scanning as the cost of the 
equipment came down and the per- 
centage of UPC-coded items in- 
creased. For the drug chains, higher 
throughput at the checkout counter 
was far less important than the 
chance to improve accuracy and 
swiftness of price updates, get a bet- 
ter handle on item movement and 
strengthen inventory control. In 
this, the role of the MIS executive 
became even more crucial. 

—The year brought other high- 
lights, which are detailed: in the 
pages that follow. They included: 
Eckerd’s return to strong profit 
growth after two years of flat earn- 
ings; Walgreens’ decision to renew 
its attack on the New York City mar- 
ket and Pay ’n Save’s acquisition of a 
wholesale company—Northwestern 
Drug—and the controversy that en- 
sued.

goes into high gear 

A::viie: chain drug company 
was announcing its plunge into 


a new type of business.

ADAP, Carport: These were just a 
few of the unfamiliar names that 
flowed through the news pages dur- 
ing the year. 

Behind the headlines was a famil- 
lar story: Drug chains were sailing 
into uncharted waters as a way to 
direct substantial cash flow into

The heaviest play was in areas 
akin to their main line of business, 
like deep-discount drug and health 
and beauty aids stores or home 
health care centers. 

But there were other areas poles 
apart from the drug store industry 
that chains entered aggressively. 
Auto parts retailing was a prime ex- 
ample.

as Perry, Dart, Thrifty and Malone

Continuéd from page 48 

Aid and Pay ’n Save acquired auto- 
motive chains and made ready to ex- 
pand them with their substantial re- 
sources. 

The reason was simple: Auto 
parts retailing offers net profits in 
the 4% to 6% range, higher than 
what the average drug chain gener- 
ates. Also, the boom in do-it-your- 
self auto repairs has steadily risen 
with the price of new cars. More- 
over, it’s a hard parts business that 
requires few markdowns. 

While deep discounting, home 
health and auto parts were the main 
events, there was other action tak- 
ing place in smaller arenas. 

Rite Aid, which the year before 
had moved into the retail toy busi- 
ness with the purchase of the 12%- 
store Circus World chain, acquired 
the rights to another retailing con- 
cept called Heaven. Started in Cali- 
fornia, it featured a mix consisting of 
designer sweat shirts and T-shirts, 
sophisticated greeting cards and 
other paper products and nostalgia 
records. 

Rite Aid quickly launched several 
3,000-sq.-ft. Heaven stores in the 
East, and made plans to open more. 
By early 1984, there were seven 
Heaven outlets, and Rite Aid was 
planning 10 to 15 more this year and 


three more areas to the list: whole- 
saling, auto parts retailing and a 
warehouse-style, membership only 
outlet called Price Savers Wholesale 
Club. 

Price Savers was announced first. 
Pay 'n Save targeted Salt Lake City 
for its first venture into the growing 
price club phenomenon. These are 
huge (100,000-sq.-ft.) no-frills, 
cash-and-carry outlets catering to 
small businesses and members of or- 
ganizations, who can realize sub- 
stantial savings on a wide variety of 
merchandise by joining the club. 

The outlets operate on margins of 
10% to 11% and generate high turn- 
over and tremendous volume. The 
breakeven point is said to be $25 mil- 
lion a year, and projections are that 
the outlet will eventually do $50 mil- 
lion. 

Two more Price Savers have been 
slated, one in Fife, Wash., and the 
other in Seattle. Next year, units 
will be launched in Honolulu and An- 
chorage, Alaska. 

Then, early this year, Pay 'n Save 
purchased Schuck’s, a 58-store auto 
parts chain. Pay ’n Save paid $70 
million to acquire the stores and an 
85,000-sq.-ft. warehouse. 

But neither Price Savers nor 
Schuck’s stirred as much interest as 
Pay ‘n Save’s third! diversification

In 1983 the headlines began to tell 
the story: 
@ Giant installed scanners in its 
first freestanding drug store in 
Bethesda, Md. 
@ Reveo introduced scanners in its 
first deep-discount store, Get It For 
Less, in Memphis. 
@ Eckerd, which already had a pro- 
grammable nonscanning POS sys- 
tem in place in 100 stores, was now 
preparing to test the addition of 
scanning. 
@ Rite Aid joined the trend with 
three test stores in the East. The 
Shiremanstown, Pa.-based chain 
planned to follow the lead of super- 
markets and gradually eliminate 
item price-marking. 
@ Pay ‘n Save tested a system for 
three months and was ready to roll it 
out. 
@® SupeRx, Medi Mart and Drug 
Fair of New Jersey were also poised 
to launch limited scanning tests. 

An industry first 

The first company to introduce 
scanning into a freestanding drug 
store was not a drug chain at all. 
Giant Food Inc., the Landover, Md.- 
based food drug combo operator, 
opened the country’s first free- 
standing drug store equipped with 
state-of-the-art laser scanners in 
Bethesda. 

Giant’s plunge began a trend that 
would continue throughout the vear: 
Many of the chains that announced 
scanning plans were associated with 
parent companies that had prior ex- 
perience through their food opera- 
tions. These included Sav-On, Osco, 
Pathmark, SupeRx and Medi Mart. 


About this report 


For this, our 1984 Annual 
Report of the Chain Drug 
Store Industry, Drug Store 
News has revised its definition 
of a chain operation. In pre- 
vious annual reports, we de- 
fined a chain as a company op- 
erating just two or more stores. 

In 1984, we decided to adopt 
the National Association of 
Chain Drug Stores’ definition 
of a chain: a company operat- 
ing four or more stores. This is 
also the definition used by the 
A. C. Nielsen Co., whose in- 
dustry overview we wiil pub- 
lish Sept. 3. 

As in earlier years, we have 
again based our Annual Re- 
port primarily on four sources: 
Our own Drug Store News sur- 
vey of stores operated by the 
top 106 chain drug companies; 
Chain Store Guides’ annual 
survey ef chain drug com- 
panies, the U.S. Department of 
Commerce, and company an- 
nual reports. 


We also used research gener- 
ated by A. C. Nielsen and Dun 
and Bradstreet. 


In the Giant store, there were six 
scanners altogether, four at the 
checkout counters up front and one 
each at the pharmacy and cosmetics 
counters. 

At the annual meeting of the Jack 
Eckerd Corp. in November, chair- 
man and president Stewart Turley 
told shareholders that the drug 
chain was about to launch a limited 
scanning test, designed to find out if 
the laser devices could increase. pro- 
ductivity. 

Turley set forth one of the reasons 
that scanning had suddenly become 
attractive: “UPC and bar coding 
now amounts to 60% of the merchan- 
dise and 80% of the transactions in 
drug stores. It’s getting close to the 
point where scanning will be more 
feasible.”

Revco, which introduced scanning 
technology into its deep-discount 
Get It For Less store, was now pre- 
pared to try a limited test in several 
drug stores. 

But Scott Leeseberg, the chain’s 
vp for management information, 
sounded a cautionary note: “This is 
not something we're going to jump 
into full tilt. We’ll begin with a two- 
or three-store test of both hand-held 
and slot scanners, probably in stores 
that are close to headquarters.” The 
proximity to headquarters would al- 
low the chain’s top executives to 
monitor the test closely. 

At the same time, the Twinsburg, 
Ohio-based chain placed a $6 million 
order for up to 2,000 more program- 
mable POS terminals, upgradable to 
scanning. 

At SupeRx, plans were also under 
way for ascanning test. Jerry Thole, 
vp for operations at the Cincinnati- 
based drug chain, told Drug Store 
News that the one- to three-store 
test would begin sometime in 1984. 

“The main thing we’re interested 
in at this point is developing a sys- 
tem that can do our gross profit test- 
ing for us,” he said. The test would 
probably involve both slot and hand- 
held scanning equipment, he added. 

Interest in scanning was not lim- 
ited to the giant chains. Drug Fair of 
New Jersey, the 22-store company 
based in Somerville, N.J., was also 
readying a test.

For Rite Aid, one of the big poten- 
tial pluses of its three-store scan- 
ning test was the chance to try elim- 
inating item price marking—a first 
for drug stores. Savings in labor 
costs was the attraction. According 
to one chain exec, the savings would 
probably allow Rite Aid to recoup its 
equipment investment in a little 
more than a year. 


Pay ’n Save was using the same 
combination approach in its roll-out 
of checkout scanning. Following a 
3'2-month test of both types, the 
Seattle-based chain planned to 
equip a total of 12 stores in its home 
market by year end. According to 
chain execs, it will take three to four 
years to complete installation in the 
remaining stores. 


Expansion surge 
foreseen in 1984 


he past year was not a big one 
Te: acquisitions, despite the 

blockbuster deal involving Im- 
asco and Peoples, but with interest 
rates remaining fairly stable it’s 
likely that 1984 will bring a re- 
surgence of activity. 

Some of the biggest deals during 
the year involved diversification by 
the chains, including. Pay ‘n Save- 
Schuck’s, Rite Aid-ADAP and Per- 
ry-Fleenor’s. 

On the chain drug front, there 
were some smaller acquisitions, 
including Eckerd’s purchase of 11 
Sav-On and Osco stores in Texas, 
Louisiana and Oklahoma; Reveo’s ac- 
quisition of eight Sommers stores in 
Texas; Hook’s purchase of five Hard- 
ing drug stores in Illinois, and Rite 
Aid’s acquisition of six Family Drug 
Stores in Akron, Ohio. 

But in the main, drug chains pur- 
sued the same strategy they used 
the previous year: Filling in existing 
markets with new stores. 

In the coming year, chains seem 


more willing to open their wallets as 
the economy continues to prosper 
and as interest rates remain steady. 
The rate situation has also drawn 
shopping center builders back into 
action, and that development will 
create more sites for the chains. 

Many of the drug retailing com- 
panies that scaled down their expan- 
sion activity in the past two years 
now smell the opportunity for more 
rapid growth. 

Walgreens, for example, has a 
stepped-up expansion plan for fiscal 
1984 that calls for 80 new stores. In 
addition to Chicago, major growth is 
scheduled for the San Francisco Bay 
area (11 new stores), Milwaukee, St. 
Louis, and the states of Texas and 
Florida. A smaller expansion effort 
is aimed at New York, a market 
from which the Deerfield, Ill.-based 
chain had slowly retreated in recent 
vears. There was evidence that New 
York might be only the first step in 
the Northeast. Charles R. Walgreen 
III, chairman and ceo, called that 
region ‘one of the most under- 
chained markets in the country.” 

Fay’s schedules 17 stores 

Fay’s was another chain that 
planned to boost its expansion ef- 
forts. In its most recent fiscal vear, 
the Liverpool, N.Y.-based chain 
opened 10 new stores. In the current 
year, Fay’s has slated as many as 17. 
Unlike Walgreens, whose farflung 
stores make it almost a national 
chain, Fay’s will stick to the markets 
that lie within a 250-mile radius of its 
Liverpool! distribution center. 


Chain stocks: a 


hain drug stocks put on a siz- 
zling show in 1983. 
From year-end 1982 to the 


close of 1983, Drug Store News’s in- 
dex of 18 publicly traded chain drug 
stocks rose from 100 to 146. 

If a savvy investor could have 
spread his money evenly over the 
total number of stocks, the perfor- 
mance would have meant a capital 
gain of $46 for every $100 invested. 

Chain drug stocks even outper- 
formed the high-flying retail indus- 
try as a whole. Kidder Peabody's 
index of 200 retail stocks increased 
from 100 at the beginning of the year 
to 140, six percentage points behind 
the chain drug stocks. 

But if the year-to-year gain was 
outstanding, the performance for 
the first six months of 1983 was even 
better. From the beginning of the 
year to the end of June, Drug Store 
News’s chain drug stock index in- 
creased from 100 to 156. 

The hottest performing stocks for 
the year were Genovese, which rose 
150%, Fay’s (up 110%), Big B (up 
104%) and Dart (up 103%). 

But every chain drug stock turned 
in a strong performance during the 
year. Even the Jack Eckerd Corp., 
which had been suffering from flat 


earnings in the past two fiscal years, 
rode the bull market toa 12.7% yvear- 
to-year stock price gain. 

ine most volatile performer was 
Dart Drug, which reached a high of 
$148 before settling back to $65 at 
year end. Dart’s surge was based on 
its spinoff of Trak Auto and Crown 
Books. In fact, in the month follow- 
ing the Trak Auto spinoff, the price 
of Dart’s stock doubled. 

Filling in markets 

Thrifty, a partner in Crown Books 
and Trak Auto West, also benefited 
from the spinoffs, although to a 
lesser extent because the profits re- 
turned to the Los Angeles-based re- 
tailing company from the two ven- 
tures had less of an impact on total 
corporate earnings than they did on 
Dart’s profit performance. Thrifty’s 
stock price advanced 88% during the 
year. 

In general, chain drug stock priec- 
es have not fared as well in the first 
quarter of 1984 as they did the pre- 
vious year. Almost every stock has 
declined in value from its year-end 
price, following an overall decline in 
stock market prices. 

The big exception was Peoples 
Drug, which rose from $25.50 at 
year-end to $32.75 on April 8. That

C hain drug companies effected 
dramatic changes in 1983 as 
they moved aggressively to 
expand and modernize their ware- 
houses and distribution centers. 
The trend toward centralized, 
streamlined facilities with state-of- 
the-art technology continued at a 
rapid pace as chains focused on cost 
effectiveness and improved delivery

Peoples Drug Stores realized a 
major goal in its eight-year strategic 
planning program with the selection 
of a site in Fredricksburg, Va., for a 
new $20 million, 500,000-sq.-ft. dis- 
tribution center. The facility, which 
will service Peoples 370-plus stores 
in the mid-Atlantic region, is de- 
signed to accommodate as many as 
500 stores by 1990. 

A key factor in the center's suc- 
cess will be the Advanced Inventory 
Management System (AIMS) which 
monitors shipments, providing cor- 
porate level marketing departments 
with more accurate projections of fu- 
ture inventory needs. AIMS is also 
equipped for automatic reorders of 
basic merchandise items and pro- 
vides options for other functions 
such as forecasting and tracking of 
promotional deals and co-op adver- 
tising. 

Eventually, the system wiil play a 
critical role in such areas as quan- 
tifying optimum space allocations in 
store planograms and determining 
optimum gross margin returns on 
investment. 

Expansion effort 

In another expansion effort, 
Reveo Drug Stores boosted its ware- 
house capacity to more than 2 mil- 
lion sq. ft. with the opening of new 
warehouses in Kansas and Alabama 
and the expansion of its facility in 
North Carolina. These three, plus 
the anticipated construction of anew 
400 ,000-sq.-ft. warehouse in Dallas, 
are the operational backbone of 
Revco’s five-year plan aimed at man- 
aging 2,300 stores. 

Once again, technology is the key 
to Revco’s successful operations. An 
upgraded software program for the 
IBM System 38 has enhanced work- 
er productivity by fine-tuning 
batch-picking procedures and 
streamlining receiving functions, di- 
rect put-aways, management of in- 
storage merchandise and store de- 
liveries. Scott Leesburg, vp of sys- 
tems, says that although the system 
was costly initially, it’s a must in to- 
day’s modern warehouse. He pro- 
jects that Revco will realize a 
payback on its investment in ap- 
proximately 2/2 years. 

Walgreens’ third 100% mecha- 
nized distribution center in 
Flagstaff, Ariz., is another success 
story involving sophisticated com- 
puter systems. Computer-guided 
order processing and stock replen- 
ishment, computer-controlled 
mechanized picks of fast-moving 
items and scanner reading of bar 
coded labels on case picks have re- 
duced overall distribution costs by

In many cases, these new units 
have been able to shave as many as 
two days off an order cycle, decreas- 
ing costs and halving delivery time 
to their stores. 

Costs decreased 

Commenting on F lagstaff’s prede-: 
cessor in Orlando, Fla., vp of dis- 
tribution and manufacturing John 
Brown says that distribution costs 
decreased substantially while dollar 


volume processed through the sys- 
tem has increased by 60%. 

Reduced handling costs was also 
cited as a principal reason for com- 
puterized warehouse operations at 
Thrifty Drug. Its Merchandise Con- 
trol System (MCS) totally utilizes 
warehouse space and features auto- 
matic matching of receipts and in- 
voices. It reduces accounts payable 
expenses, shortens the cash receipt 
cycle and, in addition, provides for 
zone retail pricing which fosters im- 
provement of gross margins by di- 
rectly addressing competition in 


ains automate warehouses 


specific geographic areas. 

In other developments, Hook 
Drugs completed a three-year mul- 
timillion-dollar expansion and mod- 
ernization program involving its dis- 
tribution and service center. It now 
relies on a warehouse system which 
has grown to more than 596,000 sq. 
ft. 

One of the major components of 
Hook’s warehouse technology is the 
Barrett Automatic Guided Vehicle 
System which replaced the mechan- 
ical chain-driven carts formerly 
used to handle incoming merchan- 
dise. Productivity has also been en- 
hanced by the installation of three 
flow modules from which merchan- 
dise is selected for store orders and a 
shipping cover conveyor system 
which allows merchandise to be 
transported directly from filling sta- 
tion to trucks. 

Progressive blend 

A progressive blend of people and 
technology characterizes SupeRx’s 
new $10 million, 381,000-sq.-ft. dis- 
tribution center in Bluffton, Ind. It 
relies primarily on a double-deck 
flow rack picking system with 
swing-reach fork lifts guided by in- 
floor electrical wires. 

The Bluffton center is the fourth 
such regional facility to service this 
chain’s growing network of stores. It 
links al! but a handful of Phoenix 
area stores into a centralized dis- 
tribution system stocked by Peyton 
Inc., the Louisville-based nonfoeds 
distribution arm of the Kroger Co., 
SupeRx’s parent. Peyton supplies 
85% of the pharmaceutical, OTC and 
H&BA and general merchandise in- 
ventory of the stores it serves, elim- 
inating reliance on wholesalers as 
well as direct-store and jobber deliv- 
erles. 

In an effort to ease space pressure 
created by the recent addition of 
more centrally warehoused lines 
such as toys, cigarettes and sun- 
glasses, Pay Less NW announced 
construction of a major distribution 
center in northern California. Pro- 
jected size falls within the 600,000- 
to 800,000-sq.-ft range in order to 
accommodate the chain’s 72 super 
drug stores in that area. Pay Less 
also began warehousing prescrip- 
tion drugs for the first time in its 40- 
year history in a further move to 
increase centralized distribution. 

Computers have been instrumen- 
tal not only in their application to 
actual warehousing operations but 
also in the intricate planning stages 
which precede construction and ex- 
pansion. 

Eckerd Drug utilized a computer 
study developed by Bradford Infor- 
mation Systems to select a spot fora 
new warehouse that would maxi- 
mize reduced shipping costs. Taking 
into account such variables as cost 
per driver and speed limitations, the 
study can determine which ware- 
house site can best serve particular 
retail outlets. A similar system can 
pinpoint the least expensive routes 
for drivers delivering merchandise,

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 30. 1984 


Chains to open more combos 


s pig really better? To judge from 

the number of combination stores 

springing up across the country, 
the answer is emphatically “yes!” 

More than one key ingredient is 
needed to make these modern be- 
hemoths successful and although 
there are a number of different 
“combinations” in existence. the 
marriage of food and drugs appears 
to be the most catalytic. 

Why? Chain execs don’t hesitate 
in their response—one-stop shop- 
ping with food generating the traffic 
and drugs boosting the profits. Ex- 
act statistics vary but one industry 
observer, who follows combos in the 
West and Southwest, puts it simply, 
“Supermarkets provide 2% of the vol- 
ume and drug stores % of the prof- 
its.” 

With an average profit margin of 
1% on food and 3% on drug, it’s no 
wonder that many chains have be- 
come converts to the combo phe- 
nomenon. As Larry Nauman, vp of 
advertising and public relations at 
Dominick’s Food Stores, comments: 
“It’s getting harder and harder to 
make a living with just food. The 
combo is an attractive addition be- 
cause it creates a better mix and 
sells more nonfood items at a higher 
margin. The results are on the bot- 
tom line.” 

Dominick’s, which operates 76 
stores In the Chicago area, is one of 
the newcomers to the field. The 
chain’s first combo, Dominick's 
Family Center, opened in November 
1983 and, according to Nauman. it 
quickly became its top-volume 
store. The 63,000-sq.-ft. center is 
open 24 hours, although the phar- 
macy has limited hours, and the 
breakdown is approximately 80% 
food, 20% pharmacy and drug store 
merchandise. | 

“Since site location, such as a 
shopping center, is frequently the 
determining factor for new outlets.” 
says Nauman, “we’ll continue to 
build solo food stores. But we're 
very pleased with the combo and 
hope to open several more in the 
coming year or so.” 

Chains’ commitments to the com- 
bo vary substantially but the heav- 
lest influx of this type of store is still 
to be found in the West and South- 
west, where land is cheaper and 
easier to come by. 

Food and drug partnership 

Sacramento-based Raley’s, one of 
the pioneers in the combo field, is 
100% behind the food and drug part- 
nership in both its combo and super- 
store formats. 

Out of a total of 45 stores, Raley’s 
nas 40 combination-type markets 
and, in 1983 alone, opened four new 
superstores. Another is currently 
under construction in Redding, 
Calif., and others are planned for 
northern California in the future. 

“We have a few freestanding food 
stores, says Frank McMinn, vp of 
advertising and merchandising, 
“but we don’t intend to build any 
more. The combo provides the big- 


gest plus in terms of profitability be- 
cause the higher margin drug items 
benefit from the traffic generated 
by the two-three times a week gYO- 
cery shopper.” 

Another chain experienced in 
combo marketing is Albertson’s 
Inc., headquartered in Boise. 
Idaho. Albertson’s has thrived in 
the combo business since 1970 and. 
at last count, 89 out of its 434 stores 
are combos. Three opened in 1982 
and 11 more are on the boards for 
1984. The average size is 55,000 Sq. 
ft., although newer stores run ap- 
proximately 60,000 sq. ft. with a 
merchandise mix equally divided 
between foods and nonfoods. The 
chain recently announced plans to 
go back into the hot Dallas market. 
Where it will compete with such 
combo giants as Skaggs-Alpha Beta 
and Tom Thumb Page. Albertson’s 
also plans a return to Tacoma, Wash. 

“It’s the popular one-stop shop- 
ping that is the chief advantage,” 
remarks Bob Bolinder, vp of public 
relations. “Combos have bigger vol- 
ume, better margins and. in some 
cases, better average sales per 
square foot.” He notes, however. 
that there is a comparable ROI for 
Albertson’s combos and noncombos, 
most of which are 44,000-sq.-ft. su- 
perstores with pharmacies. 

Enthusiastic support for combos 
is echoed by other large chains such 
as Safeway, which is going full speed 
ahead in 1984. Out of a total 1.999 
stores, 150 are combos, and that 
number will increase dramatically 
this year with the addition of 40-50 
new stores. 


Another leader in the field, Amer- 
ican Stores, increased its number of 
combos by 10% in 1983 (from 70 to 
(7) and plans to open 20 more this 
year. It’s all part of an ambitious 
expansion program that the compa- 
ny says will mean 130 combos by 
year-end 1985. 

But combo activity is by no means 
confined to the area west of the Mis- 
Sissippi. The Eastern Seaboard is 
steadily claiming its share of the 
market. Giant Food Inc. has been 
into combos since 1960 and pres- 
ently numbers 74 combos among 13] 
stores. Two more are planned for 
1984 with computerized, full-service 
pharmacies. Giant’s newer combos 
average about 58,000 sq. ft. with 
pharmacy areas running about 10,- 
O00 sq. ft. 

Integrated format 

One of the principle reasons for 
Giant's success is its innovative use 
of an integrated format in some of 


their newer stores. Boundaries be-. 


tween food and drug areas are more 
subtly defined and encourage shop- 
pers to move freely among areas. 
Increasing sales of higher-profit toi- 
letries and cosmetics. 

“We pioneered this concept and 
certainly expect it to grow,” says 
Barry Scher, director of public af- 
fairs. “Although we have been focus- 
Ing recently on our nonfood areas in 
terms of computerizing pharmacies 
and developing experienced cosmet- 
Ics personnel, it is really accurate to 
say that each department in our 
stores contributes to its overall sue- 
cess. We are committed to that qual- 
ity across the board.”

Other chains have found that a 
mix of stores is better suited to the 
demographics of their area. The 
synergistic effect of food and drugs 
attracted Wellby Super Drugs 
(Portland, Me.) into the combo field 
last year. The chain. a division of 
Hannaford Bros., opened its first 
48,000-sq.-ft. combo in November 
and plens two more 42 ,000-sq.-ft. 
centers this spring. Bill Wood. Vp, 
estimates that the higher gross 
items—health & beauty aids, cos- 
metics and drugs—typically com- 
prise about 15%-18% of a combo’s 
total merchandise. 

While Wellby’s is pleased with the 
combo approach to marketing, it is 
not limited to it. “Several different 
formats work in our area.” Wood 
says. “In addition to the combos. 
well have four new super drug 
stores opening soon, one major ex- 
pansion and we'll also be keeping our 
hand in with 7,500-sq.-ft. mini-com- 
bos and some smaller-scale, solo su- 
permarkets.” 

Supers are initiators 

As Wood and many others at- 
tested to, supermarket chains are 
the traditional initiators in the com- 
bo industry. Supers demand more 
expertise in a number of areas. such 
as handling perishables and are 
often more sophisticated in distribu- 
tion and scanning techniques. But. 
an Increasing number of drug chains 
are exploring the combo field suc- 
cessfully, and some, like Wellby’s 
with Hannaford Bros.. are able to 
rely on the food experience of a par- 
ent company. 

A conservative approach 

Another recent entry into combos 
is Big B, based in Birmingham, Ala. 
Big B’s approach is, perhaps, more 
conservative than some other 
chains, but it too has endorsed the 
one-stop shopping trend. Its first 
combo opened in August 1982, and it 
now has four combos out of a total 
100 stores. Arthur Jones, vp of fi- 
nance, Says that one more is planned 
for this fiscal year, and he predicts 
an average of two per vear in the 
future. 

Big B combos, which measure ap- 
proximately 32,000 sq. ft., are usu- 
ally divided into *4 food and 4 drug 
with the latter featuring the deep 
discounts offered in Big B drug 
stores. “We do substantially more 
volume with the combo than we do 
with a 9,000-sq.-ft. drug store,” re- 
marks Jones. Nevertheless, Big B is 
still committed to the discount-drug 
business and, in addition to the com- 
bos, will open 15 new drug stores 
this year. 

Combos are undoubtedly big busi- 
ness but, like any marriage, they're 
not right for everyone. Industry an- 
alvsts and leaders predict continued 
phenomenal growth in this area, but 
they also foresee a varied marketing 
scenario with mini-combos, super- 
stores, solo supermarkets and dis- 
count drug stores claiming their 
place alongside the progressive com- 
bo. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 30, 1984 


CHAIN DRUG INDUSTRY 


1984 ANNUAL IREPOR! OF TRE 


Pharmacy computer use skyrockets 


be xplosive growth: That’s the only 
way to describe what happened 
to pharmacy computers in 1983. 
This year promises more of the 
same. 

Drug Store News’ annual survey 
Shows that some 3,600 phar- 
macies—22% of the chain drug in- 
dustry—had Rx computer systems 
in operation by year end. 

In 1983 at least 10 companies fol- 
lowed the lead of chains like Pay 
Less, Fay’s and Thrift in outfitting 
all prescription departments with 
computers. They included Wal- 
greens, Standard Drug, Sentry, Ar- 
bor, Cook, Keltsch Bros., Kinney 
Drug, May’s Drug Stores, Muir and 
Medicare-Glaser. 

Among the Canadian companies 
that achieved chainwide installation 
were London Drugs Ltd. of British 
Columbia and Pharm-Escomptes 
Jean Coutu, Quebec. 

Executives at Walgreens, which 
completed installation of its Inter- 
com System, said computerization is 
one reason why script sales rose 25% 
during the vear. 

Intercom allows the Deerfield, 
Ill.-based chain to keep a file of each 
customer's script record. The sys- 
tem also provides for an emergency 
hot-line service that makes drug in- 
formation available to medical spe- 
clalists on a 24-hour basis. Also, the 
system permits transfer of informa- 
tion between hearing-impaired pa- 
tients and selected Walgreens phar- 
macies. 

Two of the biggest benefits of 
pharmacy computerization are eco- 
nomic: improved inventory control 
and greater productivity. 

In an earlier Drug Store News sur- 
vey, chain execs credited Rx com- 
puters as being the prime factor in 
tightening inventory control. De- 
spite the increase in average phar- 
macy inventory cost—from $33,500 
in 1982 to $36,000 in 1983—annual 
stock turns increased to 7.4 times 
from seven times the previous year. 
And cost of inventory as a percent- 
age of sales dropped to &.8% from 
9.2%. 


What’s more, the highly comput- 
erized companies reported dispens- 
ing 11 to 12 scripts per hour of oper- 
ation and 67 to 74 scripts per 
pharmacist day. 

In comparison, companies com- 
puterized on a limited basis or not at 
ali were averaging eight to nine 
scripts per hour and 45 to 49 seripts 
per pharmacist day. 

Gearing for expansion 

Among the other chains gearing 
up for a major expansion of phar- 
macy computers are the following: 
@ Eckerd is in the nrocess of rolling 
out Rx computers all 1,300 of its 
prescription departments. Software 
will be tailored so that pharmacists 
can computerize transactions with 
hospitals, nursing homes and clinics 
as well as with individual patients. 
@ Medi Mart plans to continue in- 
stalling POS terminals that can be 
used in conjunction with its phar- 
macy terminals. Data retrieved 
from both the POS and pharmacy 
terminals will provide management 
with up-to-the-minute inventory re- 
ports for every sku that passes 
through a cash register. 

@ Safeway is expanding tests of its 
IBM Series 1 terminals during 1984, 
and outlets will also evaluate IBM’s 
point-of-sale scanners. At the same 
time, Safeway will also be looking at 


National Semiconductor scanners. 


@ Los Angeles-based Thrifty Drug 
Co. is also going the computer route 
during 1984 in an effort to improve 
its prescription department’s bot- 
tom line. 

@ Perry Drug plans to have 100 
pharmacy computer systems up and 
running in its stores by the end of 
1984. One of the chain’s goals is to 
streamline clerical functions in the 
areas of price updates and third-par- 
ty script processing. 

e Melville, N. Y.-based Genovese 
Drug Stores began installing phar- 
macy computer systems midway 
through 1983. The IBM units will be 
upgraded so that each store man- 
ager can use the system to prepare 
time and attendance records, pur- 
chase orders and cash reports as

well as to monitor inventory and 
buying. 

A number of other chains such as 
Peoples, Gray Drug Fair, Pay ‘n 
Save, Rite Aid, Shoppers Drug 
Mart and Revco are also continuing 
to install computer systems in their 
prescription departments. 

Speeding up work 

Emphasis is on enhancing patient 
services, speeding up third-party 
scripts payment, productivity and 
fast price updates. 


Expanded use of computers con- 
tinues to play a wider role in chain 
drug operations, merchandising and 
distribution as they relate to the

also growing numbers of whole- 
salers making home health care 
products available to their retail cli- 
ents as well as a number of manufac-

Different settings

beds, wheelchairs; stair gliders: 
orthopedic appliances; diagnostic 
aids, incontinence products, ostomy

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 30, 1984

e 1984 ANNUAL PEPORT! OF TAE 


More chains try deep discounting 


he lure of sales volume as high as 

$25 million per store enticed 

eight of the top 25 drug chains to 
venture into the deep-discount drug 
business during 1983. 

This was a departure from the en- 
trepreneurial flair associated with 
this type of low-margin, high-vol- 
ume business pioneered by such fig- 
ures as Bernie Shulman, Fred and 
Margaret Chen and Marc Glassman. 
These operations were usually fam- 
ily affairs, where evervene worked 
long hours to build tremendous vol- 
ume. . 

The original F&M, a tiny 4,: 
sq.-ft. store in Ferndale, Mich.., 
pumped out as much as $10 million 
per vear, or upwards of $2,200 per 
square foot. 

Now with chains entering the 
arena, deep-discounting should 
swell to a cumulative sales volume of 
$14.5 billion by 1985. Already, these 
retailing behemoths produce about 
2% of the total chain drug store bus!- 
ness. 

What has made this business ap- 
peal to drug chains? For one thing, a 
deep-discounter can generate in one 
week the volume that it takes five 
months to reach in a conventional 
store. Moreover, the return on in- 
vestment is greater than that of a 
tvpical drug store, once the unit hits 
the magical break-even point— 
around $3 million to $4 million. Fi- 
nally, chains see deep-discounting as 
an opportunity to diversify or beat 
the competition in hotbed markets. 

Potential pitfalls 

But, Sonny Raichlen of 
Cecille’s, a deep-discounter in Bir- 
mingham, Mich.., and Phil Wilber, 
the originator of the franchised 
Drug Emporium concept, point out, 
there are pitfalls. Raichlen warns of 
the high inventory costs—often $1 
million and more—as well as the 
need to move swiftly and precisely. 
These are both reasons entrepre- 
neurs have fared well in this tricky 
business. 

Phil Wilber adds that the volume 
figures don’t come without hard 
work. “There’s no magic to this busi- 
ness... youcan't doit without hard 
work and sweat.” Wilber attempts 
to keep the entrepreneurial spirit 
present in Drug Emporium by fran- 

chising rather than running a chain- 
like operation. 

Despite the potential snags, 1983 
marked the year that more drug 
chains ventured into this form of re- 


J00- 


as 


tailing. Each chain did it in its own 
way and for its own reasons. 

Perry Drug, for instance, opened 
its first A. L. Price store as a reac- 
tion toan incoming F&M. Its second 
A. L. Price unit, however, was 
planned and opened in a site where 
two other competitors—Arbor and 
Revco—already had conventional 
stores in place. Its third A. L. Price 
store will open in an off-price shop- 
ping center. [ts second store Is al- 
ready exceeding projections and 
should hit $6 million in its first vear 
of operation. 

Other chains plaved it different- 
lvy—leap-frogging into new markets 
rather than cannabilizing its core 
markets. Wal-Mart, for example, 
opened its first deep-discount store, 
called Dot, in Des Moines—miles 
away from its headquarters in Ben- 
tonville, Ark., and miles away from 
any existing Wal-Mart units. A sec- 
ond Dot scheduled for 
Oklahoma City. 

Best chain job 

Reveo is another chain that mi- 
grated to another town to debut its 
Get It For Less units. Chain drug 
sources say that Revco has “done the 
best Job by a chain” with its deep- 
discount entry. Get It For Less 
stores resemble Drug Emporiums, 
but also incorporate merchandise 
from Reveco’s other venture, Odd 
Lot Trading. Says Sidney Dworkin, 
president and ceo, “Odd-Lot mer- 
chandise in Get It For Less is mak- 
ing it possible for us to realize 
break-even point much sooner than 
we anticipated.” 

Revco will open another Get It For 
Less this vear and may open a third 
because “our early results are so 
promising.” 

One president of a deep-discount 
operation believes that testing the 
waters outside of the home markets 
is the smart way to enter the busi- 
ness. “Then, you're not competing 
with your own stores.” 

Others add that it is only natural 
that drug chains want to delve into 
the business, but they predict a 
“shakeout.” Among the chains that 
either opened or announced plans to 
open units in 1983 were: Peoples, 
Perry, Shoppers Drug Mart, Fay’s, 
Genovese, Medicare-Glaser, Path- 
mark and Wal-Mart. Chains already 
operating discount units include: 
Rite Aid, SupeRx, Gray, Heartland, 
Courtesy, Ribordy, May’s and Safe- 


store Is 


Way. 


With so many drug chains entering the deep-discount business last year, cumutative sales 


volume in this market is expected to reach $14.5 billion by 195.

Exec changes in high places 


ajor changes at top executive 

levels had a significant im- 

pact on drug chain manage- 
ment during the past year. In an 
effort to address a variety of busi- 
ness concerns, leading chains 
turned to seasoned execs both with- 
in and outside their companies to 
redefine objectives and to revitalize 
established growth paths. 

Alvin Towle, a well-known figure 
in the industry, took the challenging 
helm of Gray Drug Fair in January 
1982 and had completed a sweeping 
management reorganization when 
he was “relieved of his respon- 
sibilities” in October 1983 by Sher- 
win-Williams, the parent company. 
Although sales were up and Towle’s 
rebuilding efforts were gradually 
progressing, his performance appar- 
ently fell short of goals agreed upon 
when he joined S-W. 


Alvin Towle 


Less than six months later, how- 
ever, Towle, whose track record also 
includes such key positions as vp- 
general merchandise manager at 
Eckerd Drug, senior vp-marketing 
at Peoples and president of Shop- 
pers Drug Mart’s United States op- 
erations, was hired by Dart Drug to 
guide its 73-store, Washington, 
[).C.-based retail drug division. In 
addition to providing a strong link in 
Dart’s “stretched thin” manage- 

-fnent team, Towle will direct his ex- 
pertise to several operational prob- 
lems that have persisted in the drug 
division despite a strong overall per- 
formance. 

In another major move, Eckerd 
Drug Co. appointed Harry W. Lam- 
bert as president in August 1985. 
Like Towle, Lambert is an aggres- 
sive and experienced manager who 
is credited with much of the recent 
turnaround of JByrons Eckerd’s 
department store division, which he 
had headed since November 1978. 
As a 14-year veteran of Eckerd 
Corp., Lambert has held a number 
of other positions including control- 
ler, president of two divisions and vp 
of planning for the drug division, 

The managerial and interpersonal 
skills Lambert utilized so effectively 
at JByrons have already given a 
much-needed boost to Eckerd Drug, 
which just completed the most suc 
cessful first six months in its histo

ry.

At Shoppers Drug Mart, we are 
focusing our attention on three par- 
ticular areas this year. 

Firstly, productivity. We regard 
productivity as a state of mind, a 
way of life and a philosophy of busi- 
ness. It is an absolute strategy for 
survival and growth and we are com- 
mitted to applying it to every aspect 
of our business. 

Our second focus is on our custom- 
ers. We have developed a specific 
program known as “Customers Are 
Really Everything,” or “C.A.R.E.” 
Our commitment at the corporate 
and store level will be to place an 
even greater emphasis on our cus- 
tomers’ needs and requirements, 
and continue to deliver on the value 
and service statement that has been 
the formula of success. 

And finally, our focus is on the 
continued importance of our profes- 
sion. We are drug stores first and 
foremost, and our pharmacists have 
an important role to play in society.

a key role in introducing the “Phar-

palgn.

ith pharmacy leading the 

way, chain drug: stores re- 

corded a strong vear in 1983 
as sales rose 11% to $22.8 billion. 

It was a vear in which more and 
more chains began to use the power 
of computers to aid them in their 
marketing strategies. 

The emphasis was on the core de- 
partments and on building the 
strongest possible health care im- 
age. In that, the chains looked to set 
themselves apart from their food 
and discount store competitors. 

The following is a breakdown of 
the performance of those key drug 
store departments. 

Prescriptions—The rising price 
of the average prescription as Well as 
an increase In the number of scripts 
pushed chain drug pharmacy sales 
up 13.6% to a new high of almost $6 
billion last vear. As the Consumer 
Price Index tor pharmaceuticals 
outpaced the overall CPI by aliiost 5 
to 1, the price of the average script 
rose 95¢@ to $10.60 in chain drug 
stores. 

Drugs/proprietaries—Rx to OTC 
conversions helped propel 1983 
chain drug sales in this department 
upward by 12.6% to $3.2 billion, sec- 
ond only to pharmacy. Leading the 
way In sales growth were analgesics, 
cough cold, eve and lens care and 
family planning products. There 
was also a strong rise In home health 
care sales. 

Toiletries—Driven by strong 
sales of ethnic products, shampoos, 
deodorants and suncare products, 
chain drug toiletry sales rose 11.6% 
in 1983. Many chains recognized the 
potential of the ethnic health and 
beauty aids market last year and ei- 
ther added new ethnic departments 
to their stores or expanded existing 
ones. As a result ethnic sales grew 
14.5% to $152.7 million. Shampoos 
also turned in a strong performance 
last year as sales increased 13.4% to 
$260 million in chain drug stores. 

Cosmetics—Drug chains up- 
graded their cosmetics mix, pro- 
moted more aggressively and were 
in a better in-stock position on hot

Housewares—Chain drug stores 
recorded a steady 7.3% sales in- 
crease in the housewares category 
last vear to $1.6 billion. Consumers 
traded up for better quality plastic 
and rubber housewares, kitchen ac- 
cessories and outdoor furniture. 
Leading the department again were 
plastic and rubber housewares. Re- 
tailers attributed the strong 7.4%

promotional activity and changing 
consumer lifestvles. Sales of plastic 
and rubber housewares totaled 
$368.7 million and accounted for 
23% of total category sales. 

Toys—High tech electronic toy 
sales crashed last year, opening the 
door for a resurgence in sales of such 
traditional toys as dolls and board 
games. Overall category sales 
reached $623.6 million, a 6.4% im- 
provement over the previous vear. 


While drug chains still account for 
of the total toy 


only a small slice 


market, indications are that manu- 
facturers are seeking additional dis- 
tribution channels such as drug 
stores. 

Photo/ineluding processing— 
This category continues to be a suc- 
cessful one for drug store chains 
with sales increasing a healthy 
11.3%. Photo remains strong be- 
cause items, which have gross mar- 
gins of 20% to 25%, turn nine times a 
vear. The ever-popular photo finish- 
ing services along with the new ad- 
ditions of upscale 35mm cameras 
and related products helped this 
$960 million category make up 4.2% 
of total chain drug sales in 1983. 

General merchandise—General 
merchandise sales rose 9% to $1.1 
billion as chains continued to offer 
an appealing mix of products along 
with a range of price points. Small 
personal care appliances, such as 
blow dryers and electric razors, re- 
mained on top with the greatest per- 
centage of sales in the category, 
$203 million or 18%. General mer- 
chandise makes up 4.8% of the total 
drug store sales. 

Do-it-yourself—Faced with in- 
creased competition from high vol- 
ume home centers and discount auto 
parts chains, sales gains in the DIY 
category slowed somewhat last vear. 
Chain drug stores recorded a 6.1% 
increase in DIY sales to $533 mil- 
lion. Once again,’ the automotive 
segment was the DIY department 
leader as chains registered a 7.9% 
increase in 1984 to $156 million. 

Grocery/food/liquor—Led by a 
strong performance by alcoholic 
beverages and snack foods, the food 
and liquor category generated a 
sales gain of 7.7% to $1.1 billion last 
year. Liquor and wine accounted for 
nearly 50% of the department’s total 
volume as sales advanced 8.3% to 
$531 million. Snack foods/cookies 
and nuts combined for nearly 16% of 
the department's sales in 1983. 
Snack foods such as chips and 
crackers and cookies produced sales 
increases of 7.8% with sales reach- 
ing $83.2 million, while nuts sales 
rose 7.9% to $91.8 million.

Generic pharmaceuticals also 
made their presence felt during the 
vear. They now account for 20% of all 
prescription dollar volume. Factors 


contributing to growth in this mar- 
ket segment include programs by 
states like Maryland, which pro- 
vided pharmacists an extra fee for 
dispensing a generic on Medicaid 
scripts. 

Another approach used by Med)i- 
Save Pharmacies also stimulated 
generic sales. At Medi-Save, phar- 
macists are paid 50¢@ per script for 
dispensing a generic. 

Industry analysts said these fac- 
tors represent only a fraction of the 
impact that generics will have on the 
pharmaceutical market once the Ab- 
breviated New Drug Application 
Patent Extension issues are settled. 
A number of well-known products— 
Valium, Serax, Valisone, Di- 
abenese. Motrin and Ativan—will 
be coming off patent over the next 24 
months. As a result, they predict 
that sales dollar growth of generics 
will range from 10% to 15% over the 
next several years.

Many chain buyers pointed to a 
late flu season as the prime reason 
for cough cold preparations grab- 
bing a 14.6% share of total OTC de- 
partment sales. 7 

According to Len Demino, vp of 
professional services, Peoples Drug 
Stores, rapidly changing weather 
conditions were responsible for 
much of the increase in sales. 

“This vear’s changeable weather 
was conducive to the flu,” said 
Demino. “Our prescription and OTC 
sales Were up as a result.” 

Walgreens reported that sales of 
their OTC cough cold preparations 
were up 23.5% in January and in the 
first week of February sales rose 
36.3% over the same period in 1982, 
in large part due to a two-month flu 
that hit the Chicago area. 

But not all the chains felt that a flu 
Was responsible for tneir sales. 

In St. Louis, Medicare-Glaser’s 
director of professional services, 
Ken Anderson, felt that the flu sea- 
son had no effect on upward volume 
movement of OTC cough cold pre- 
parations. 

Consumers who bought cough 
cold. preparations were able to 
choose from wider selection, includ- 
ing those recently converted to OTC 
status after being available only by 
prescription. 

According to an exclusive DrSN 
OTC. study, consumers chose the 
newer OTC conversion products 
over products that virtually had the 
market to themselves for many 
vears. 

For example, within the cough 
cold category, four of the 28 prod- 
ucts in the top 100 (dollar volume) 
and five of the 24 products in the top 
100 (unit volume) were OTC conver- 
slons. 

In particular, Schering’s out- 
standing success with Drixoral and 
Afrin together with Parke Davis’ 
senvlin and Burroughs Wellcome’s 
Actifed, helped retailers stimulate 
cough/cold sales even in those areas 
not hit by a flu. 

Some chain buyers said that not 
only did the flu and bad weather 
favorably affect cough/cold sales but 
an increase in their vitamin sales 
could be seen as well. 

Capturing 10.1% share, vitamins 
were the second highest contributor 
to increased proprietary depart- 
ment sales in 1983. 

Considering the number of retail 
outlets that sell vitamins, drug 
stores did exceedingly well. Drug 
stores accounted for 65% of all vi- 
tamin sales while supermarkets and 
discount stores placed a poor second 
and third with 10% and &% market

Analgesics, which in 1982 was the 
second best-selling category, 
dropped to 3rd place and increased 
only slightly in 1983 to a 9.8% share 
of total department sales. 

The Tylenol tampering incidents 
hit the analgesic market hard. 
Tylenol] had accounted for 43% of all 
analgesic sales when retailers were 
forced to take all Tylenol products 


though McNeil did an excellent job 
of restocking the product, analgesic 
sales plummeted when retailers had 
to look for other nonaspirin products 
to fill the gap. Judging from the 
small increase of analgesic products, 
it appears that many consumers did 
without any analgesic substitutes 
and waited for Tylenol to re-enter 
the marketplace late in 1983.

Toiletry share of chain sales rises 


oiletry sales in chain drug stores 

cracked the $2.4 billion mark 

last year. The category now ac- 
counts for 11.6% of all chain drug 
sales, with the strongest perfor- 
mances coming from the following 
categories: ethnic products, sham- 
poos, deodorants and suntan/sun- 
burn products. 

Ethnic health and beauty aids 
turned in their best year ever in 
1983. Sales jumped 14.5% to $152.7 
million. Much of the gain was gener- 
ated because. many chains either 
added new ethnic departments to 
their stores or enlarged existing de- 
partments. 

Shampoos were the second-fast- 
est growi.y category in the toilet- 
ries department. Sales in 1983 were 
up 13.4% to $260 million. Sales were 
boosted by the influx of new items 
such as salon-style products aimed 
at an upscale market, but budget 
priced shampoos continued to hold 
‘their own as shoppers showed no 
~thusiasm. for ferreting out 
good buys, particularly if they were 
advertised specials. 

Twin packs continued to move, 
helped by the late 1983 introduction 
of a host of new shampoos. 

Suntan/sunburn product sales 
jumped 12.8% in 1983 to $112.5 mil- 
lion. Sales came from both suntan 
items and those with a higher SPF 
(sun protection factors) designed to 
Insure against burns. Additionally, 
volume was up because retailers 
strove to make suncare a year-round 
rather than a seasonal one. Perry 
Drug, for example, merchandised 
suntan items in a cold and blustery 
March. Why? To satisfy shoppers 
headed to warmer climates on vaca- 
tion. 

New suneare products launched 
during 1983 had a cosmeties twist to 
them, which was not surprising be- 
cause the market is predominately
