creams and lotions; sales rose 12.2% 
last vear. 

During -1983, it appeared that 
more women decided to try depilato- 
ries as a sure-fire way to remove hair 
without the trouble of shaving. Al- 
though this category produces only 
0.4% of toiletry sales, volume hit 


$9.1 million last vear, up 11.8% over 
1982. 

Razors, on the other hand, are big 
business in chains, which account 
for better than 20% of all disposable 
razor sales. According to Drug Store 
News’ research, razors/blades sales 
were up 11.6% to $114.9 million. 

And, just as more people are shav- 
ing with disposable, more women 
are coloring their hair. Sales esca- 
lated 11.4% to a total of $230.4 mil- 
lion in 1983. 

Perms and straighteners sales 
flattened out in: 1983, rising 11.3% to 
$20.8 million. Industry sources sug- 
gest that the big perm boom of the 
early 1980's may be over. However, 
the perm business is steady and 
chains dominated the market with 
close to 48% of all perm sales. 

With disposable razors sales ris- 
Ing, men’s shaving creams are inch- 
ing up, too. Sales were 11.2% better 
in 1983 than 1982 for a total of $35.5 
million. 

But sales of products for the rest 
of a man’s needs are still flat as men 
continue to hide in the closet when it 
comes to grooming aids. Sales, be- 
cause of price hikes, rose 10.5% to 
$276.2 million. The industry needs a 
marketing campaign designed to in- 
spire men to purchase their own 
grooming needs. 

Hair notions may not have sales 
figures that shake the earth, but 
they produce a steady volume year 
after year. That was the case in 1983 
when volume rose 9.1% to $93.5 mil- 
lion. Chain drug stores. lead in hair 
notions accessories over discounters 
and supers. 

However, supermarkets are steal- 
Ing share away from chains in hair 
sprays. Sales were up only 8.9% last 
year in chain drug stores to $91.5 
million. This category may also be in 
trouble as the mousse market con- 
tinues to grow.

: million a year in ethnic hair

Hair care, by far, accounts for the 
bulk of ethnic product sales in drug 
stores, but cosmetics sales are slow-

In the past few years, the leading

Walgreens have begun to enlarge 
their existing ethnic product de- 
partments while simultaneously 
putting new departiuents in stores 
with locations with easy acces- 
sibility to black and Hispanic shop- 
pers. 

As part of their growing commit-

well as newsprint ads.

mitment to ethnic 


A recent study executed by the 
American Health and Beauty Aids 
Institute found that while black and 
Hispanic shoppers may only account 
for 5% of an individual store’s traf- 
fic, they are responsible for generat- 
ing 15% of all H&BA sales. 

Just on hair care alone, the study 
found, blacks tend to spend three 
times more than white shoppers. 

The study also found that blacks 
shop drug stores that are close to 
their jobs as well as stores closer to 
home. Partly because of this study, 
many chains. now believe they don’t 
necessarily have to have stores in 
ethnic neighborhoods to justify fea- 
turing an ethnic product section.

stores. Thrift drug has sections in 


nearly 70% of its 363 stores and is 
hoping to roll the department out to 
all stores within two years. 


Flush from success with ethnic hair care 
products, many chains are now turning 
their attention to building ethnic cosmet- 
ics volume.

Upscaling boosts cosmetics sales 


fter the pharmacy, cosmetics 
is the area where drug store 
retailers worked hardest to 
build sales during 1983. 

Their efforts paid off as sales rock- 
eted 12.2% to $1.2 billion. That was 
the highest increase in this category 
for the last five years. 

Chains produced these numbers 
by upgrading their mix, promoting 
harder and working to stay in stock 
on hot merchandise. Indeed, while 
the entire industry growth was 
stagnant, rising only 4%, chains pro- 
duced a volume that grew not only 
from price increases, but unit moye- 
ment as well. At the same time, 
drug chains continued to draw new 
shoppers, especially those who had 
shopped department stores. 

Cosmetics, as a category, pro- 
duces 5.2% of total chain drug vol- 
ume. And, although at 2.2 turns per 
year, cosmetics remain a slow-turn- 
ing department, it produces high 
gross Margins per square foot and a 
healthy gross margin return on In- 
vestment. Cosmetics gross margins 
fall in the 30% to 40% range. 

Perhaps the biggest chain success 
story last year was fragrances. Not 
only did drug stores post whopping 
gains with prestige fragrances, but 
they also enjoyed solid results from 
budget and mass brands. Together, 
toilet water/colognes and perfumes 
generated sales of $355.3 million, up 
12.8% from 1982. Toilet water/co- 
logne sales jumped 12.7% while per- 
fumes picked up steam rising 13.4%. 
Fragrances produce about 30% of all 
cosmetics sales in chains. 

Sweet smell of success 

Prestige, often diverted, fra- 
grances such as Chloé, Opium, Os- 
car, Ciara and White Shoulders 
socked some pizzazz into fragrance 
sales. But, the mass and dual dis- 
tribution items such as Vanderbilt 
and Le Jardin also turned in a strong 
year as did fragrance line extensions 
including Aviance Night Musk. 

In many cases, drug chains them-

The challenge for 1984 will be to 
see if drug chains will continue to 
secure and be able to sell prestige 
brands. There are some indications 
that manufacturers will be clamping 
down on their pricey brands and 
once again limiting their distribu- 
tion to department stores. Drug 
stores, however, have proved they 
can sell these items and buyers hope 
vendors may decide to sell them di- 
rectly. 

Pegged cosmetics are the second 
strongest performers in the cosmet- 
ics category. These items appeal to 
today’s woman whose shopping time 
is limited. Once considered the 
lower-end items, pegged cosmetics 
now also have an upgraded look. 


An increased emphasis on devot- 
ing the proper space per sales to 
pegged lines helped push pegged 
cosmetics sales 13.5% last year to 
$266.9 million or 22.3% of all cosmet- 
ies sales. 

Facial treatments remain an enig- 
ma for the chains. There appears to 
be a need in the mass market, but 
few products have cracked through 


the self-service barrier. Because of 


that. treatment sales have been 
stagnant. Volume rose 10.9% last 
year to $175.3 million. 
Facing the trends 

The biggest trend in this area is 
concentration on the science of skin 
care. It seems that the more clinical 
or natural the skin care item; the 
better the sales. Two good examples 
are the suecess of Revlon’s Euro- 
pean Collagen Complex or Queen 
Helene’s Gift of Life Moisturizing 
items which contain a natural ingre- 
dient called placenta. 


Line extensions of longstanding 


.this burgeoning category. Paced by 


favorites also fared well in facial 
treatments. This includes Oil of 
Olay’s Beauty Bar or Clairol’s Sea 
Breeze moisture lotion. 

The bath is being rediscovered. 
Women are once again using baths to 
pamper themselves. Sales in bath 
preps rose 12% last year to $110.% 
million. What retailers have noticed 
is a trend to the higher-ticket bath 
items such as Vitabath. Also, 19&3 
saw the birth of a new area in bath— 
the shower gels. Bare Elegance and 
Soft All Over were two products pl- 
oneering this trend. 

Lip products enjoyed a healthy 
10.5% sales increase which was In- 
stigated by the debut of lip repair 
products similar to Elizabeth 
Arden’s phenomenal Lip-F ix. There 
are no fewer than six entries into 


these items, lip color and lip product 
sales reached $109 million last vear. 
Nailing down sales 

Even more productive than lip 
was nail during 1983. Retailers are 
amazed at what percentage of total 
sales now come from this category. 
According to Drug Store News, nail 
polish and preps produce 8.6% of the 
cosmetics department volume; the 
fastest-growing products are those 
which help nails grow or those which 
condition the nail. This includes 
hardeners and strengtheners. 

Rounding out the category with a 
6.3% share is eye color, makeup, 
powders, creams and liquids. New 
products as well as a change to mer- 
chandising by line rather than cate- 
gory perked up volume in these 
areas. Kits, coordinated groupings 
of mascaras, shadows and blushers, 
fared well as did the budget lines 
offering trendy colors. 

Increased advertising by manu- 
facturers helped boost this category 
9.3% last year to a total of $74.6 
million. What’s more, retailers peg 
this area as one that will show sub- 
stantial growth in the latter half of 
the 1980's.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 30, 1984 


CHAIN DRUG INDUSTRY 


1984 ANNUAL IREPORT OF THE 


otal chain drug sales in the gen- 

eral merchandise category were 

$1.1 billion in 1983, an increase 
of 9% over 1982. General merchan- 
dise accounted for 4.8% of the total 
1983 drug store sales volume. 

General merchandise products 
typically average five turns per 
vear—with gross margins of be- 
tween 35%-45%. Last year’s gross 
profit dollars averaged between 
$385 billion and $495 billion. 

Personal care accounted for the 
greatest percentage of dollar sales 
in this category, $203 million or 18. 
Sales of personal care items In- 
creased 9.9% in 1983. 

Small personal care appliances 
such as curling irons, blow dryers, 
and electric razors have done espe- 
clally well in drug stores. While 
drug stores are not usually consid- 
ered a popular outlet forsuch items, 
these stores have attracted custom- 
ers by offering the best sku’s along 
with competitive price selection. As 
in the case of hair appliances, it Is 
not usual to find a drug store with a 
lower-price Windmere and a higher- 
end Sassoon. 

These appliances have become 
popular promotional items with 
drug stores, which have been able to 
advertise the lower-end promo pric- 
es along with the more expensive 
brand names. These items also work 
well as seasonal promotions. For ex- 
ample, electric razors are often ad- 
vertised for Christmas and Father's 
Day and hair appliances for Mother's 
Day. 

Advertising effective 

These efforts seem to be working. 
The December results of the Third 
Annual Consumer Study showed 
that almost 20% of those surveyed 
purchased their last small personal 
appliance in a drug store. And while 
many of these items have been pro- 
motional in nature, small appliances 
have still turned out to be profitable. 
Although gross margins sink as low 
as 10% when advertised, the every- 
day margins range as high as 35%.

1984 ANNUAL PEPORT OF TAE 


he DIY boom that sent category 

sales soaring during the late 

1970’s and early 1980's leveled 
off somewhat in drug stores last 
year as sales rose a modest 6.1%. 

However, retailers are quick to 
point out that consumer interest in 
DIY products did not wane last year 
but the growth of home centers, 
hardware “supermarkets” and large 
discount auto parts chains began to 
cut deeper into the drug chains’ 
share of the market. 

As the DIY market became 
crowded in 1983, drug retailers were 
forced in some cases to cut back on 
some home improvement and hard- 
ware items because they simply 
couldn't compete with pricing strat- 
egies set by many high-volume 
home centers. ) 

Overall, DIY department sales to- 
taled $533 million, which repre- 
sented approximately 2.47 of all 
chain drug-sales. 

But while drug chains placed less 
emphasis on their hardware and 
plumbing departments In 1983, the 
automotive products category con- 
tinued to attract a great deal of in- 
terest among drug retailers. De- 
spite the growth of discount 
automotive parts chains, drug store 
automotive department sales in- 
creased by almost 8% to $156 mil- 
lion. The auto segment contributed 
nearly 30% to the total category 
sales. 

It’s no coincidence that the expan- 
sion of drug store automotive de- 
partments has taken place at a time 
when drug chains have been pur- 
chasing auto parts chains. Most re- 
cently, Rite Aid and Pay ’n Save 
joined chains such as Dart Drug, 
Thrifty, Perry and Malone & Hyde 
by diversifying into the automotive 
parts business. 

What has fueled the rapid devel- 
opment of the auto aftermarket in- 
dustry? Observers say that the baby 
boom generation, a group with sig- 
nificant discretionary income, has 
contributed to the industry's growth 
because members of the 18-34 age 
bracket are more likely than their 
parents to attempt their own auto- 
mobile repairs. 

At the same time, hard economic 
times during the past decade have 
prompted automobile owners of all 
ages to perform such minor repairs 
as changing the engine oil and re- 
placing spark plugs and oil and air 
filters. 


Number of autos rises 

In addition, the market continues 
to expand as the number of auto- 
mobiles per household increases 
each year. Since 1970, the number of 
automobiies on American roads has 
increased 38% to more than $123 
million. And while new car sales re- 
bounded dramatically this year, the 
average American automobile on 
the road today is still seven years old 
and a prime candidate for repair 
work. 

Given these factors. it’s not sur-

by,

shoppers.

rate shopping trip to a liquor or

wine, retailers say a consumer will

reasonable.

Beer accounted for an estimated 
6.5% of the food and liquor depart- 
ment sales in drug stores last year. 

Another category in the food and 
liquor department that is rapidly be- 
coming an everyday section in drug 
stores is snack foods. For many 
years snack foods were strictly a 
deal item for most drug chains. 
However, many astute drug retail- 
ers have seen the similarities be- 
tween snack foods and candy, which 
has long been considered a core drug 
store category. 

Snack foods, like candy, generate 
high profits and turns. One mer- 
chandise executive for a Florida- 
based chain. said that snack 
were turning at a rate of nearly 950 
times a year. Items like potato chips, 
corn chips and cookies, retailers say, 
are just as much an impulse item as 
candy. Is. 

In the same vein, drug retailers 
have found that nuts have produced 
outstanding results both as an 
everyday item and as a promotional 
tool. Peanuts, almonds, cashews, 
mixed nuts, besides featuring high 
margins when priced at everyday 
prices and fast turns when sold at 
promotional prices, pose less prob- 
lems in terms of dating than most 
other snack foods. Retailers say that 
the longer shelf life of nuts has 
prompted them to expand the space 
allocated for these products. 

Retailers also have become more 
sophisticated in merchandising 
snack foods. Many chains have de- 
veloped snack food departments 
that rival those in supermarkets. 
Chains are capitalizing on the high- 
impulse appeal of both snack foods 
and soft drink beverages and have 
begun to cross-merchandise them. 

Vendors eye chains 

At the same time drug retailers 
have recognized the potential of 
snack foods, manufacturers of these 
products are viewing the chain dryg 
market with heightened interest. 
Many suppliers have come to view 
accounts as Walgreens, Supekx, 
Peoples and Longs in the same light 


foods 


as they do their supermarket ac- 
counts. In some.cases, drug retail- 
ers say manufacturers have pres- 
ented programs to them that have 
been designed specifically for the 
drug and mass merchandise outlets. 

Measured collectively, snack 
foods/cookies and nuts accounted for 
nearly 16% of all food and liquor 
sales last year in drug stores. Nuts 
alone generated sales of $91.8 mil- 
lion, up 7.9% from 1982, and contrib- 
uted 8.2% to the category’s total vol- 
ume. Snack foods such as chips, 
crackers and cookies produced sales 
of $83.2 million, a 7.8% improvement 
over the previous year. Snack foods 
represented an estimated 7.4 of all 
food and liquor sales. 

Thirst quenchers 
Soft drinks and juices also con- 


ao to grow in importance for 


many drug chains. While chains 


have long been aware of the pulling 


power of a 2-litre soda promotion, 
many retailers have begun to recoup 
some of the lost margins on these 
types of promotions by offering a 
permanent planogrammed soft 
drink department. 

In addition, by installing coolers 
in stores whenever possible, some 
chains have been able to rack up 
margins as high as 35% on single 
cans or bottles of soft drinks. But for 
the most part chains that have intro- 
duced permanent soft drink depart- 
ments are working on margins in the 
20% range, which when combined 
with turns of between 20 and 30 can 
make the soft drink category “ex- 
tremely viable” in the words of one 
buyer. 

During 1983, drug chains rang up 
more than $160.4 million in soft 
drink sales, 6.9% more than. 1982. 
Overall, soft drinks accounted for a 
hefty 14.2'@ of the food and liquor 
department sales.

stant film was 6.9%, far less than 
that of still color.

359mm trend

~ Supekx clustering plan pays off 


CINCINNATI—The SupeRx 
Drug Division of the Kroger Compa- 
ny turned in a strong financial per- 
formance in 1983, fueled by improve- 
ments in marketing and distribution 
strategies. 

For the year ended Jan. 31, oper- 
ating profits were up 80% to $27.2 
million while sales increased 10% to 
$790 million. Parent Kroger Co. did 
not do as well. .Net earnings for the 
year declined 34% to $127 million 
even though sales increased 3% to 
$15.2 billion. 

In addition to the 606 SupeRx 
stores operated at vear end, Kroger 
also operated 1,200 Kroger food 
stores, 226 Dillon stores and 352 Dil- 
lon convenience stores. 

Nineteen eighty-three was the 
second vear in a row SupeRx per- 


Sales at SupeRx 
rise steadily

Source: Company reports 


formed particularly well for Kroger. 
Last year the chain turned ina 133% 
increase in pretax operating profits 
on a sales hike of just 5%. But last 
year’s profits also included a $4.3 
million one-time gain from the sale 
of 21 Houston area stores to Wal- 
greens. are 

SupeRx’s 1983 financial perfor- 
mance seems to indicate that the 
chain’s management has found a 
long-term key to growth. Part of the 
improvement was due to the elim- 
ination of stores in underdeveloped 
markets, while the rest was due to 
better support strategies for exist- 
ing stores. 

Pattern abandoned 

SupeRx has completely aban- 
doned its earlier haphazard pattern 
of growth, which spread the chain 
too thin in too many markets. Today 
the chain is busy “clustering” stores 
in its major markets, seeking the 
economic efficiencies that come once 
a chain has adequate population den- 
sity. 

Just a few months ago, manage- 
ment opened its third regional ware- 
house in Bluffton, Ind., making it 
possible for the chain, for the first 
time, to operate a central distnbu- 
tion system. All SupeRx stores now 
receive service from the warehouse, 
and approximately 70% to 80% of 
the store mix flows through the dis- 
tribution centers. 

In March, Kroger reorganized its 


buying department so that all re- 
plenishment orders are now made 
through the centralized ware- 
houses. 

SupeRx’s management antici- 
pates a $20,000 a year per store sav- 
ings once the system has been in 
effect about a year. That translates 
into a $12 million savings for Supe- 
Rx plus another $24 million for 
Kroger’s food stores. 

Costs lowered 

For the past two years, SupeRx 
has been steadily trying to lower 
overall acquisition costs while simul- 
taneously improving turns, and in 
some highly saturated markets like 
Cincinnati, that goal has been ac- 
complished. 

In those markets, SupeRx has 
launched aggressive Rx and print ad 
campaigns stressing low everyday 
prices and the competence of the 
chain’s pharmacists. 

In 1984, the company will con- 
tinue to open new. stores, but the 
strongest emphasis will be placed on 
remodeling. SupeRx plans to re- 
model at least 50 and possibly 100 
stores in 1984 compared to 20 in 
1983. It hopes to open 20 to 30 new 
stores in 1984, compared to 50 in 
1983. 

The remodels are not just refur- 
bishments, but major upgrades that 
include new graphics and new de- 
partments. 

SupeRx will also continue to ex- 


pand its food and drug combo stores. 
The chain had 19 combos at the end 
of 1983, and management plans five 
mere for 1984. SupeRx liquor stores 
will also be expanded. Five more 
will probably be added in 1984 for an 
estimated year-end total of 23. 

SupeRx also operates five deep 
discounters under the name Drug 
World, but this concept is not yet a 
growth vehicle for the company. 

There will also be a handful of Op- 
tical Centers opened in 1984. there 
are about 45 in the chain now. Supe- 
Rx is also opening drug/food conve- 
nience stores in select markets. 

There are also’a handful of drug 
stores with delis and one with a res- 
taurant, and if these experiments ul- 
timately prove successful, the for- 
mats could be expanded.

~ Walgreens expansion marches on 


DEERFIELD, Ill.—Walgreens 
will hit an important milestone this 
summer as it unwraps its 1,000th 
drug store. The mark will be 
reached with the opening of a new 
unit right where the chain got its 
start—Chicago. 

Reaching 1,000 units this year is 
just one part of the chain’s steady 
and calculated growth pace. During 
fiscal 1983, ended Aug. 31, Wal- 
greens opened 67 new drug stores 
for a total of 941. For 1984, the chain 
has set its sights on 80 new drug 
outlets. It’s all “growth according to 
plan,” says the chain’s president 
Fred F. Canning. 

Established Walgreens markets 
will receive the bulk of new store 
activity. However, Walgreens did 
announce it would seek new markets 
including the surprise announce- 
ment that the chain will increase its 
presence in New York City, a mar- 
ket from which the chain had been 
retreating. Calling the Northeast 
one of the “most underchained mar- 
kets in the country,” chairman 
Charles R. Walgreen III said Wal- 
greens would open in four new loca- 
tions in the “Big Apple.” The first 
should open later this fall in 
Brooklyn. 

Additional expansion is brewing in

Expansion funds 
Walgreens continues to handle ex- 
pansion primarily from internally 
generated funds. Last year $51 mil-

8% of selling space each year. 
Remodeling is also important, and

for remodels in 1984. Last year, 55 
stores were remodeled; 70 will be 
updated this year. Walgreens re- 
ports that the rate of sales “dramat- 
ically improves following a re- 
model.” 

Despite a 59% lower equity in- 
come from Walgreens’ Mexican affil- 
late, Sanborns, overall earnings hit 
a new record of $69.8 million. It was 
the ninth consecutive year of record 
sales and earnings for the chain. 

Sales last year reached $2.4 bil-

greens first cracked the $2 billion 
mark. The drug store division sales 


registered a 16.3% gain, aided by Rx 
sales which jumped 24.7% over last 
year. LIFO-adjusted earnings rose 
24.5% to $69.8 million—double the 
earnings of just three years ago. 
Walgreens has realized a compound 
growth rate of 24% over the past five 
years. 

The chain has made some dramat- 
ic improvements over the years. In 
1979, its net-to-sales ratio was 
2.25%. In 1983 it hit 3%. Each 10th 
of a per cent of this figure, Wal- 
greens says, adds well over $2 mil- 
lion to the bottom line. In addition, 
state-of-the-art warehouses have 
helped lower distribution costs by 
29% over the past five years. The 
company plans to invest $10 million 
more to upgrade existing distribu- 
tion centers in Houston and Mem- 
phis. 

Strong performance 

This strong performance has gen- 
erated healthy dividend growth. 
Factoring in two stock splits in the 
past two years, Walgreens has gone 
from an annual rate of 34 %¢ in 1979 
to 60¢ in 1988, a 75% increase. 

Walgreens’ 941 drug stores each 
pump out about $2.4 million a year in 
sales. The average drug store in 
1983 was about 9,000 sq. ft. with 
sales per square foot of $266.

Peoples acquisition is biggest ever 


ALEXANDRIA, Va.—The mar: 
riage startled the industry. 

Imasco Ltd., the powerful Cana- 
dian retail holding company, took 
the hand of Peoples Drug Stores. the 


11th largest drug chain in the Unit- 


ed States. It was the biggest wed- 
ding in the chain drug history. 

Although startling, the match 
was, on reflection, logical. Imasco. 
whose giant Canadian drug chain, 
Shoppers Drug Mart, faced limited 
growth opportunities in its home 
country, was looking south of its bor- 
der for a quality acquisition. 

And Peoples, with its fast-track 
growth record and strong manage- 
ment team, fit the bill. The purchase 
price, at $34 a share, came to $320 
million. 

Together, Peoples and Shoppers 
Drug Mart operate more than 1.000 
stores, and Peoples president and 


ceo Sheldon Fantle envisions expan- 
sion possibilities that could result in 
the largest drug chain in North 
America. Fantle will sit on Imasco’s 
board along with his Canadian drug 
chain counterpart, David Bloom. 
Kor Peoples, one of the keys to 
accepting the friendly takeover bid 
was Imasco’s “deep pockets.” The 
Alexandria, Va.-based chain for sev- 
eral years has been moving for ward 
with a strategic growth plan whose 
goals is to achieve 1,000 stores. $2 
billion in sales, a 3% net-to-sales 
ratio, four asset turns a year and a 
20% return on shareholder equity— 
all by 1990. Imaseco’s cash is ex- 
pected to accelerate the plan. 
Another key: Peoples will retain 
its autonomy. Imasco has said it has 
no intention of interfering with a 
company that has been moving in 
the fast lane ever since Bud Fantle

TWINSBURG, Ohio—With sales 
increasing sharply in the first three 
quarters, Reveo D. S. Ine. should 
crack the $2 billion barrier by the 
end of fiscal 1984 this May. 

That will be just one more feather 
in the cap for the world’s largest 
drug chain, which was operating 
1,748 stores in 28 states at the close 
of the third quarter on Feb. 4. 

As impressive as its sales growth 
has been, Revco has been racking up 
even stronger growth in profits. 
While sales for the 36 weeks in- 
creased 17% to $1.4 billion, net earn- 
ings advanced 29% to $52.6 million. 

In fact, profit growth has outstrip- 
ped sales growth in every quarter 
for the past two years. The result is 
that the chain’s net-to-sales ratio has 
been moving steadily upward. For 
the year to date, the company’s net 
margin increased by 0.3 of a per 
centage point over the previous peri 
od to 3.7%. 

For the fiscal year ended last May, 
Reveo's profits increased 34% to 
$66.5 million, while sales rose to 
$1.8 billion, a 15.3% gain. Of those 
sales, all buf 5.3% were generated 
by drug stores. 

The strong operating results can 
be attributed to several factors, in- 


cluding one of the tightest cost-con- 
trol programs in the industry, the 
continued impact of lower inflation 
and interest rates, and the dramatic 
turnaround of the former Skillern 
stores in Texas. 

Like-store sale gains 

Sales increases achieved by the 
chain are not solely the result of new 
stores. The sales gain in “like 
stores” (those open a year or more) 
has been outpacing the chain’s own 
inflation index by a wide margin. In 
the most recent quarter, for exam- 
ple, like-store sales shot up by 17%, 
the strongest increase ever. And for 
the first 36 weeks, like-store sales 
rose 13.5%. 

In the former Skillern stores. the 
gains have been especially impres 
sive. In the most recent two quar

Diversification ups Thrifty’s profits 


LOS ANGELES—When Thrifty’s 
sales increased 5.5% in fiscal 1983 
(to $1.188 billion), compared to 6.8% 
in fiscal 1982 ($1.126 billion), Thrifty 
‘watchers expected a profit rerun of 
1982 when net income increased 3% 
(to $18.3 million). 

However, profits galioped to a 
gain of 23% in 1983 (to $22.5 million), 
leaving the pundits talking to them- 
selves. 

However, there is no mvstery to 
the profit breakaway. It can be at- 
tributed to stellar performances by 
Newman Importing, Big 5 Sporting 
Goods, and to cost-reducing elec- 
tronic programs. 

Acquired by Thrifty in November 
1973, Newman Importing recorded 
a compounded growth of 17.8% in 
sales, and 21% in profits in fiscal 
1988. In the past 10 years, sales have

Big 5 was acquired in March 1971, 
when it operated 18 stores. Big 5 
now has 67, and in fiscal 1983, it had 
a compounded growth of 23.6% in 
sales; 26.2% in profits. In the years 
since Thrifty acquired Big 5, sales 
have increased 14.2 times; profits, 
18.3. 

Crown profitable 

Crown Books is another profit 
center. Thrifty and Dart Drug of 
Washington, D.C., each own 34% of 
Crown. As of fiscal 1983, there were 
153 Crown Book stores (78 in Cali- 
fornia; 38 in Washington, D.C.; 26 in 
Chicago, and 11 in Houston. By Au- 
gust 1984, 180-190 Crown Book 
stores should be operating, and 215 
to 225 by August 1985. 

Trak Auto West is another joint 
venture with Dart (Thrifty owns 
50%, Dart 50%). Profit-wise, Crown 
contributed but Trak Auto West 
took away. Trak’s equity losses for 
the first quarter of 1984 (ended Nov. 
30, 1983) exceeded Crown’s income 
by $800,000. 

Start-up costs, plus a new ware- 
house in southern California, 
drained Trak’s profit dollars. As of 
March 1984, Trak operated 38 
stores. By the end of the current 
fiscal year, the total count should 
reach 70 to 80. 

Both Crown and. Trak are deep- 
discount operations. They carry him- 
ited inventory and undercut compe- 
tition severely (35% off best sellers 


oo 


at Crown; 35% to 51% at Trak). How- 
ever, other book chains are matching 
Crown’s discounts on best sellers, so 
a profit squeeze could be in the 
wings. 
Pharmacy slips 

Pharmacy has been a thorn in 
Thrifty’s profit side for many years. 
Fiscal 1979 was the first time in 50 
years that Thrifty’s prescription de- 
partment (accounting for 10% of 
store volume) made money. But 


Thrifty failed to sustain the pace, 


and slipped back into the red. Prices 
have been restructured because 
Thrifty has not been as competitive 
as Sav-On, Longs or Pay Less. 

Thrifty’s top officials attribute 
much of pharmacy’s profit-blight to 
the high wage-benefits of the union 
contract. Claiming that Thrifty pays 
the highest in the nation for both 
pharmacists and clerks, chain execs 
say most of their competition is non- 
union and therefore realizes huge 
cost savings. Thrifty also maintains 
that if the chain were nonunion, it 
could increase its profit margins 2% 
to 3%. 

Thrifty hopes to remove some of 
the cost differential by increasing 
productivity through its comput- 
erized pharmacy terminals. Thrifty 
has ordered 350 IBM Series One 
standalones. Plans call for 50 in- 
stallations in fiscal 1984; 100 in 1985, 
and 150 in 1986, with the rest to be in 
place by 1988.

sent sales and earnings to record

million a vear earlier.

$302.1 million from $286.2 million.

$1.12.

Jewel's Sav-On lags; Osco 


CHICAGO—The Osco drug divi- 
sion of Jewel Companies turned in a 
shining performance during fiscal 
1983, ended Jan. 28, but the Sav-On 
units were termed “disappointing” 
by Jewel’s chairman, W. R. Chris- 
topherson. 

Osco, which operates 322 stores in 
19 states, generated a sales increase 
of 14.3% and pretax earnings that 
rose 19.6%. Sav-On’s sales rosé only 
6.7% while pretax earnings lagged 
93% behind the previous year’s. 
Combined, Osco and Sav-On repre- 
sented 50.3% of Jewel’s United 
States pretax earnings, down from 
00.8% last year. 

According to Christopherson, 
total drug store sales were up 11%, 
but earnings fell as a result of lower 
profits at Sav-On. The two divisions 
combined for total sales of $1.8 bil- 
hon, up from $1.7 billion the year 
before. Pretax earning’ for the drug 
stores were $62 million. 

Jewel’s chairman attributed Sav- 
On’s sagging results to several fac- 
tors, including gross margins that 
fell below traditional levels, costs as- 


sociated with installation of new 
merchandising and distribution SVS- 
tems and start-up expenses for the 
new food-drug combo program in 
the San Joaquin Valley in California. 

During fiscal 1983, the chain pre- 
miered the first of 10 scheduled com- 
bos featuring a mix that is 60% items 
normally stocked in a Sav-Qn store. 

All of these costs, Christopherson 
pointed out, have been largely ab- 
sorbed. Therefore, he expects 1984 
will be an improved year for Sav-On. 
: Earnings decline 

Overall Jewel posted fiscal 1983 
sales of $5.8 billion, a gain of 2.7% 
over sales of $5.6 billion in 1982. 
Earnings, however, slipped from 
$88.1 million, or $6.82 per common 
share, to $83.1 million, or $6.36 per 
common share. That’s a 5.7% decline 
that resulted primarily in reduced 
earnings from its equity investment 
in Aurrera S.A. de C.V. (Mexico). 
Aurrera sales during Jewel's fiscal 
year increased 72.1%, below the 
country’s rate of inflation. With the 
effective rate of translation for the 
peso decreasing from $1.59 in 1982 


to 65¢ in 1983, Jewel’s earnings from 
its equity investment in Aurrera 
were 50.8% below the 1982 level. 

Jewel’s supermarket division is 
hitting snags in the Chicago market, 
Where earnings have been impacted 
by the debut of discount warehouse 
stores into the market. Jewel Foods 
has stepped up its cost control and 
productivity efforts, and most Jewel 
store-level employees were asked to 
accept wage reductions. All savings 
will be translated into lower retail 
prices so Jewel is competitive with 
the warehouse format stores, ac- 
cording to the company. 

Emphasis on combos 

This means the drug division will 
be forced to play an increasingly im- 
portant role for the chain. Jewel will 
continue its emphasis on the combo 
format, which brings in the volume 
and turns associated with a super- 
market, plus the higher margins 
reaped in a drug store. The combo 
format will be important for Sav-On.

Rite Aid drug, specialty units grow 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa.—spe- 


cialty retailing was high on the list of 


priorities last year for Rite Aid as 
the drug retailer expanded its near- 
ly two-year-old toy chain, started a 
chain of variety stores and most re- 
cently, purchased an auto parts 
chain. 

But while the Shiremanstown, 
Pa.-based chain diversified at a 
rapid rate last year, the drug store 
division continued its fast-paced 
growth. Rite Aid opened 73 stores in 
1983. In addition, the chain will roll 
out a new sophisticated comput- 
erized scanning system later this 
vear that will virtually eliminate in- 
dividually priced items in each of its 
stores. 

Collectively, the drug chain and 
other diversified operations com- 
bined to boost fiscal 1984 operating 
income nearly 25% to $62.1 million 
from $49.9 million the previous year. 
Earnings per share from operations 
for the 53-week fiscal vear rose 
16.6% to $1.47 from $1.19 in fiscal 
19835. 

In addition, Rite Aid reported a 
$12 million extraordinary gain from 
the partial sale of Super Rite Foods 
Inc., its grocery wholesaling opera- 
tion through a public offering at the 
close of last year. Taking into ac- 
count the gain from the Super kite 
offering, net earnings for fiscal 1984 


were $74.3 million, up 35% from 
$54.9 million in fiscal 1988, which 


included operating income from 
Super Rite. 


Earnings per share, inclusive of 


the gain from Super Rite and a 2- 
for-1 stock split in January, in- 
creased 34% to $1.76 from $1.31. 

Corporate sales during fiscal 1984 
were up 16.6% to $1.2 billion from 
$1.04 billion in fiscal 1985. 

Given the chain’s ability to gener- 
ate cash, Rite Aid has been able to 
finance expansion and diversifica- 
tion out of its own pockets at a time 
when interest rates still remain un- 
comfortably high for many busi- 
nesses.

Longs upscales cosmetics, profits 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif.—A 
system to track weekly gross prof- 
its, soon to be programmed into 
store computers, helped Longs 
Drug Stores turn sliding profits into 
gains during 1983. 

It was also a year in which sched- 
uling innovations by employees dou- 
bled Christmas cosmetics sales in 
the chain’s Mountain View store and 
a period when cosmetics depart- 
ments got a facelift. 

Longs reported earnings of $36.4 
million in fiscal 1984, which ended on 
Jan. 31, 17% higher than the $30.9 
million garnered in-fiscal 1983. 
Karnings per common share rose to 
$3.43 from $2.92. 

These figures are particularly en- 
couraging after a rather flat fiscal 
1983 when earnings rose only 
slightly, to $30.9 million from $30.3. 

Sales in fiscal 1984 went up by &% 
to $1.2 billion from $1.1 bilhon. The 
percentage: increase was not, how- 
ever, as great as the 12% growth 
achieved in the previous vear. 

The problem of sliding profits 
came to a head in 1982 when Longs 
began experiencing the effect of ex- 
pansion and start-up costs. during 
the recessionary vears. In addition, 
price conscious shoppers did more 
cherrypicking than expected, caus- 
ing the ratio of ad sales to total store 
sales to rise, thereby, lowering: gross 


margins. 

When net income dropped by 6% 
in the third quarter of fiscal 1985, 
the chain took action by creating a 
system that calls on managers to 
project sales volumes and margins 
quarter by quarter. Managers moni- 
tor their progress on a weekly basis 
as a means of reaching or exceeding 
their objectives. 

Plans are to computerize this 
racking system and provide termi- 
nals in store managers’ offices so 
that they can efficiently keep an eye 
on sales and margins. The terminals 
will be installed at locations where 
pharmacy computers already exist. 

While Longs hopes to have com- 
puters in all of its stores, 55 phar-

LIVERPOOL, N.Y.—In the 
wake of the most successful year in a 
25-year history, Fay’s chairman 
Henry A. Panasci Jr. predicted that 
the chain would continue to “outpace 
the economy and the retailing indus- 
try” in 1984. 

On all fronts, the Liverpool, N.Y.- 
based chain is moving ahead ag 
gressively not only to solidify its 
position but. also to break new 
ground. 

Fay’s plans to open as many as 17 
new stores in the current fiscal year 
as well as to maintain the sizzling 
pace that produced such outstand- 
Ing results last year. 

For the year ended Jan. 31, Fay’s 
earnings shot up 48% to $8.1 million 
as sales increased 16% to $312 mil- 
lion. Fourth-quarter gains were just 
as impressive. Earnings soared 51‘ 
to $3.8 million, while sales were up 
17% to $92 million. 

There was strong evidence that 
Panascl’s predictions were right on 
target, as salés in February in- 
creased by more than 30%

formance prim iarily to Increased 
market penetration. But,he

partments have generated addi 
tional sales volume in other depart

Washington, D.C., and mid-Atlantic 
areas.

etched thin, and the drug stores 
suffered in the oe tional area.

and there were severe out-of-stock 
problems.

discount super drug stores and 
drug/home center combos had lost

aygressive expansion track.

lion, up from $42.2 million. segley 
currently operates 45 drug stores.

Care stores, also in Kentucky; one

Cynthiana, Ky.; 110 dry cleaners 
and two Radio Shack franchises.

Even highly advertised prod- 
ucts like deodorants have a 
high-impulse rate even though 
the millions that manufacturers 
spend on advertising specific 
brands within this category 
would make one assume that 
planned purchase decisions 
would be much higher. 

However, according to 
POPAI’s findings, only 49.6% of 
ali deodorant purchases were 
specifically planned before 
shoppers walked into the store. 
Thirty-five per cent were abso- 
lutely unplanned and another 
15% were either substitute 
sales or purchases made by 
shoppers who simply knew they 
wanted to buy some type of de- 
odorant. Decisions as to which 
type, which brand, were made 
while shoppers studied the cat- 
egory selections within the 
stores. 

An old drug store stable, cot- 
ton balls, had an extremely 
high in-store decision rate of 
75%. The findings suggest that 
shoppers tend to be looking for 
bargains and if they see one in 
the store, they will buy a specif- 
ic product even though they 
hadn’t planned to buy that 
product when they first entered 
the store.

an average of 2.27 for the nation.

Generic. branded vendors 
compromise on patents 


NEW YORK—A compromise reached after a marathon 
bargaining session between representatives of the branded 
and generic pharmaceutical industries is expected to pave the 
way for passage of the Drug Price Competition Bill by June. 

Under the terms of the tradeoff, the 
ers will receive limited patent extension for some of their 
drugs and the generic companies will get the right to submit 
Abbreviated New Drug Applications to manufacture generic 
versions of some 125 drugs approved after 1962. 

The measure, if passed, is expected to double the number of 
multisource drugs available to the public. Among them are 
generic versions of such top-selling drugs as Inderal and Val- 


The bill (HR-3605), sponsored by Rep. Henry A. Waxman 
(D-Calif.) is also expected to spur pharmaceutical research as 
4 result of increased effective patent life for drugs.

Spring buying show May 21-23 

NEW YORK—Over 200 chain drug execs will attend the 
combined Associated Affiliated spring buying show at the 
Omni Park Central Hotel here May 21-25. 

The show at the former New York Sheraton will include 
some 120 exhibitors, including the following first-timers: 
Coca-Cola, Mexico Industries, Jordache Electronics, Island 
Magic, Search Marketing, Hyman Products, Higgs Home 
Health Care and H&H International. 

Chain drug members of each buying group will view ex- 
hibits on different floors from 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. on May 21 
and 22, and will be free to visit both floors May 23 from 9 a.m. 
to 1 p.m. 

Prior to the combined show, Affiliated will have showroom 
presentations for its members at its offices May 17-19. 

On May 20 both organizations will have separate meetings. 
Affiliated will host its "What's Good with You” program that 
includes panel discussions on buying plans for the fall and 
producing gift catalogs. 

On the same day, Associated will hold a nonluncheon mem- 
bership meeting, chaired by David Eisenberg. senior vp of 
Peoples Drug Stores, where buyers will exchange ideas. 


Eckerd to open 2nd photo lab 

CLEARWATER, Fla.—Eckerd Drug Co. plans to open its 
second one-hour film processing mini-lab next month in the 
Tampa Bay area. 

A third mini-lab will also be built here but no completion 
date has been given. 

The chain installed its first 600-sq.-ft. mini-lab, called Eck- 
erd Express Photo, last fall in an effort to increase its share of 
the 35mm processing business. Equipment in the center can 
process print film in four formats: 110, 126, 35mm and disc. 


Walgreens changes purchasing personnel 

DEERFIELD, Il]l.—Walgreens has made some changes in 
its purchasing department. Steve Lubin, formerly a house- 
wares appliances division buver, has been named buyer of toys 
and sporting goods. 

Leo R. Titus has been assigned a new divisional purchasing 
position for electrical and personal care appliances. He was 
formerly housewares buyer. William F. Scranton, formerly 
responsible for auto supplies and hardware, has been pro- 
moted to Titus’ former position as housewares buyer. 

Promoted to assistant buyer for housewares appliances, is 
Raymond L. Lalowski. He was previously merchandise coor- 
dinator in the fashion division. Also, Teresa D. Young has 
assumed Lalowski’s previous position. She was formerly coor- 
dinator for fashion accessories. Linda H. Togliatti has been 
promoted from cosmetics supervisor to merchandise coordi- 
nator, replacing Young. 


Paulini named Jax chief 

CLEVELAND—Fisher Foods has hired Bob Paulini to 
head its two-store Jax deep-discount drug store division. 
Paulini, formerly a buyer and merchandiser with Kroger’s 
Cleveland buying office, replaced Fred Barney, who left Jax to 
head up Medicare-Glaser’s deep-discount operations. 

At Kroger, Paulini was in charge of buying and merchandis- 
ing for a wide variety of product areas for both Kroger food 
stores and Kroger’s warehouse supermarket units called 
Barney’s.

CLEARWATER, Fla.—The 
Jack Eckerd Corporation and 
Merck & Company, one of the 
country’s largest manufactur- 
ers of pharmaceutical products, 
are set to go to trial over 
charges that Merck, by adopt- 
ing a one-tiered pricing policy, 
created a monopoly for its prod- 
ucts designed to “squeeze out 
competition at the wholesale 
level.” 

A Federal District court 
judge in Tampa last month de- 
nied Merck’s request for a sum- 
mary judgment which would 
have dismissed the complaint as 
not justified. Judge Terrell 
Hodges said the trial will take 
place in January 1985. 

Eckerd filed the complaint in 
April 1982, ten months after 
Merck switched from a two- 
tiered pricing structure to a 
one-price-for-all program. Be-

Future looks bright for copay relief 


WASHINGTON—The drug 
store industry is now within 
striking distance of securing 
Congressional relief from one of 
its most pressing third-party 
{x reimbursement problems— 
Catch 22 Medicaid rules forcing 
pharmacies to absorb “copay” 
costs for thousands of indigent 
patients. 

At presstime the House had 
already passed legislation pro- 
hibiting states from imposing 
such copayment requirements 
on prescription drugs for Medi- 
caid patients, and according to 
one drug store industry lobby- 
ist, ‘‘we’re at least halfway 
home.” 

Reversing that 1982 Rx 
copay law has been a top pri- 
ority for both chain and inde- 
pendent drug store lobby 
groups concerned that the con- 
troversial requirements would 
create a multimillion dollar 
drain on the profits of par- 
ticipating Medicaid phar- 
macies. 

According to National Asso- 
ciation of Chain Drug Stores 
president Robert Bolger, those 
Federal copay rules have al- 
ready “imposed a loss of more 
than $40 million annually on re- 


tail pharmacies.” 

Congress created the prob- 
lem inadvertently two years 
ago while drafting Medicaid 
“reform” provisions in the Tax 
Equity and Fiscal Responsibili- 
ty Act. 

That law authorized states to 
trim their program costs by re- 
quiring Medicaid patients to 
share part of the cost of health 
benefits. But at the same time, 
that statute prohibited the de- 
nial of health care services to 
patients unable to afford these 
“copays.” 

As a result, drug stores par- 
ticipating in the program are ef- 
fectively forced to absorb these 
costs for all Medicaid patients 
who refuse to pay their share. 

Although the copay amounts 
are nominal (50¢ to $1 per Rx), 
they represent a potentially 
significant profit drain for drug 
stores. 

Despite repeated appeals 
from chain and independent 
drug store groups for Reagan 
Administration relief from the 
copay provisions, it appears un- 
likely that Federal Medicaid of- 
ficials will take any action un- 
less Congress moves to amend 
the law. 


(A Health Care Financing 
Administration response to the 
industry's Medicaid reimburse- 
ment concerns is now under re- 
view by the agency, but report- 
edly that response will not 
provide for any regulatory re- 
lief from the copay trap.) 

Although drug store indus- 
try leaders are encouraged by 
the House action last month, 
they acknowledge that it is still 
far from certain whether the 
Senate will approve similar leg- 
islation. 

The House ban on Rx copays, 
originally drafted by Health 
Subcommittee Chairman Hen- 
ry Waxman (D-Calif.), was 
passed as an amendment to this 
year’s Omnibus Budget Recon- 
ciliation package. 

The Senate has not voted on 
its companion budget bill, and 
at presstime the legislation un- 
der debate in that chamber con- 
tained no provision for Medi- 
caid copay relief. 

Indications are that phar- 
macy groups will wait until the 
two conflicting versions reach a 
joint Congressional conference 
committee before pressuring 
Senate leaders to accept the 
House-passed_ provision.

Inclement weather saps 


Hook 1st gtr. 


INDIANAPOLIS—Incle-

Kor the period ended March 
31, Hook’s sales rose 9.1% to 
$81.7 million from $74.9 million 
in the comparable quarter last 
vear, but earnings dropped 
28.5% to $1.4 million from $1.9 
million. 

Income per share declined 
27% to 32¢ from 44¢ in 1985. 
Reeves said that “weak January 
and February sales” contrib- 
uted to the 12¢ drop in earnings 
per share. 

Reeves added, “More typical 
March levels of sales and earn- 
ings could not overcome the mo- 
mentum lost during the open- 
ing two months of the quarter.

Thrift sales remain steady 


PITTSBU RGH—Sales at 
Thrift Drug Co. for the five 
weeks ended March 31 were $50 
million, the exact amount re- 
ported during a similar period 
in 1983. 

However, Thrift’s parent 
company, J. C. Penney, regis- 
tered a sales increase of 7.7%, 
to $940 million from $873 mil- 


lion in its domestic stores and 
catalogs. 

During the nine-week period 
ended March 31, Thrift’s sales 
increased by 3.7%, to $93 mil- 
lion from $90 million. During 
the same period, sales at Pen- 
ney’s stores and catalog rose 
12.2%, to $1.6 billion from $1.4 
billion. 


Despite the record results, 
Neil kk. Harlan, chairman and 
ceo, sald that “our performance 
did not live up to our expecta- 
tions. 

Harlan cited “margin pres- 
sures in our chemical distribu- 


tion business and the impact of 


the slowdown in the inflation 
rate on our drug distribution 
and wine and spirits busi- 
nesses, 

But he added that he did not 
expect those factors “to have a 
significant impact on fiscal 
1985.” 

For the fourth quarter, reve- 
nues increased 14% to $1.1 bil- 
lion from $962,142, but net in- 
come declined to $13.9 million 
from $15.2 million. However, 
operating profit and pretax in- 
come for the quarter were up. 


Harlan said the reason for 


the decline in the fourth-quar- 
ter net was a higher tax rate 
(46% vs. 38% last year), as well 
asa gain last vear of $2.5 million 
(pretax) from the settlement of 
insurance claims. 

McKesson reported that the 
profits of the drug and health 
care group, the company’s larg- 
est segment, declined 2% to 
$60.1 million for the vear, while 
revenues increased 15.6% to 
$2.5 billion. 

The company said the profit 
decline was the result of a slow- 
down in the inflation rate, a 
change in the business mix to 
lower margin sales and in- 
creased competition in certain 
markets. 

For the fourth quarter the 
drug and health care group's 
operating profits increased 
15.8% to $14.2 million.

of housewares

Housewares manufacturers’ 
total dollar sales jumped 12% 
during 1988 to $22.4 billion. 
That’s the first double-digit 
sales gain since 1980. 

This research comes from the 
17th annual B. Angell & Associ- 
ates study of the housewares In- 
dustry. The study revealed that 
discounters now generate 
about 30% of housewares sales: 
catalog showrooms, 9%: de- 
partment stores, 8%: food 
stores, 6%, and drug stores, 
Others, including variety 
stores and hardware units, ac- 
count for the rest of the pie. 
Although drug chains have 
worked hard to build house- 
| wares sales, their percentage 
| actually dropped from 6% to 5%.

last year.

most popular color in 1984 while 
almond was last year’s winner.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 14, 1984 


37 


John Schlegel: new 
start for pharmacy—p. 40 


@ 


Limited market tests O.K.’d 


ROCKVILLE, Md.—Fresh 
test results from a new Govern- 
ment study of “direct-to-con- 
sumer” prescription drug ad- 
vertising have encouraged the 
Food and Drug Administration 
to authorize manufacturer ex- 
periments of Rx ads directed to 
the general public. 

Among other things, the 
F.D.A. study concluded that 
consumer-oriented prescrip- 
tion drug advertisements can 
successfully communicate “‘a 
large amount of risk informa- 
tion” to patients, and that tele- 
vision commercials are even 
more effective than magazine 
ads for informing the public 
about Rx drug risks and bene- 


F.D.A. gives go-ahead 
for consumer Rx ads 


fits. 

On the basis of those re- 
search findings, F.D.A. offi- 
cials announced that the agency 
will soon propose new regula- 
tions allowing drug manufac- 
turers to conduct “limited mar- 
ket tests” of direct-to-consumer 
Rx ads in order “to obtain morz 
information about the effects of 
such advertising under more 
realistic conditions.” 

Although several major phar- 
maceutial firms are eager to be- 
gin promoting prescription 
products directly to consumers, 
more than a year ago former 
F.D.A. Commissioner Arthur 
Hull Hayes Jr. asked the indus- 
try to comply with a voluntary 


N.Y. Rx group joins 
mail-order script fray 


MAMARONECK, N.Y.— 
The Westchester County Phar- 
maceutical Society is marshal- 
ing opposition to a new pilot 
mail-order drug program by 
General Motors Corporation 
and the United Auto Workers. 

The mail-order program is 
administered by Metropolitan 
Life Insurance Company and 
serviced by Express Phar- 
macies, Pittsburgh, and Na- 
tional Rx Services Inc., Colum- 
bus, Ohio. 

‘“‘General Motors, the 
U.A.W., Blue Cross and Metro- 
politan Life Insurance Compa- 
ny have conspired to put you 
{the pharmacist} out of busi- 
ness,” society president Ber- 
nard Wally warned in a letter to 
members. 

“This is really a concerted ef- 
fort to destroy retail pharmacy. 
We are urging our members 
and other interested parties to 
read thoroughly and under- 
stand the brochure that the 
U.A.W. has distributed to their 
participants.” 

While General Motors is the 
target of the society’s protests, 
all auto manufacturers’ employ- 
ees represented by the 


U.A.W., IUE, URW as well as 


unrepresented hourly and sal- 
aried employees, retirees and 
surviving spouses are eligible 
to participate in the pilot pro- 
gram. 

In its presentation to the 
union membership, G.M. 
claimed that the two-year mail- 
order prescription drug pilot 
program will enable partici- 
pants to meet their nonemer- 
gency prescription drug needs 
with fewer purchases and at a 
lower cost. 

It will be particularly benefi- 
cial, according to G.M., to those 
taking medications for chronic 
conditions. 

“We've been looking at pro- 
posals for this type of program 
since 1981,” said James Ball, 
benefits administrator for the 
auto company. “Mail-order pro- 
grams are really nothing new. 
Many other companies have 
had them for years.” 

Ball explained that saving 
workers’ money and offering 
them extra convenience was 
G.M.’s primary goal for the pro- 
gram. 

Westchester County, N.Y., 
pharmacists are not the only 


ones concerned about the loss of

Consumers may be losers in cost-containment battle 


There’s a quiet struggle going on today in the health 


eabinets. 


Preferred provider organizations (PPO’s) also stip- 


care field, but most consumers are only dimly aware of 


it. It involves their right to select their own pro- 
viders—a right that is slowly being eroded by big 
business, Government and insurance firms in the 
name of cost containment. 

Health care providers and a few knowledgeable 
consumers continue to fight a rear-guard action aimed 
at maintaining some degree of independence from the 
cost accountants and actuaries, but results haven't 
been encouraging. 

The trend really got going when the Reagan admin- 
istration relaxed the freedom of choice provision in 
the original Medicaid legislation, giving states the 
option to experiment with various cost-cutting: ap- 
proaches, including contracting with special pro- 
viders of drugs and services. _ 

Private third-party payers, recognizing a good 
thing when they saw it, began to follow suit. 

Kor example, municipal workers, school teachers 


BENCHMARKS 


By Joseph Caputo, R.Ph. 
Pharmaceutical Editor 


and auto workers have all received letters from the 
administrators of thei: health plans urging them to 
participate in mail-order prescription plans or pre- 
ferred provider organizations. 

Inducements include lower copayments ($2 instead 
of $3) per script and three-month supplies of drugs 
rather than one-month supplies. Never mind that 
there are already too many drugs in most medicine 


ulate what vendors are selected to provide enrollees’ 
prescription services. Besides taking away freedom of 
choice, this type of cost-cutting approach also opens 
the door for all tvpes of under-the-table deals. 

Patient/employees lose a lot when the right to select 
their medical health care providers is taken away by 
Government, employers or insurance companies. Any 
semblance of quality is removed from the system and 
only the lowest cost providers are selected for par- 
ticipation in the plan. 

Such a system may work well in an assem)ly line 
environment which has a built-in system of checks and 
balances between production and quality control. But 
the same system won't work when peoples’ health 1s at 
stake. There is just no way to totally eliminate poor 
quality work by the vendor willing to supply at the 
lowest price. 

When peoples’ lives are at stake, there should be no 
compromise.

To be sure, look for this symbol. 


duced—one with no risk infor 
mation at all, and one contain- 
ing the full text of a “patient 
package insert” (PPI). 

Noting that TV Rx commer- 
clals produced significantly 
higher information recall rates 
among the consumer surveyed, 
K.D.A. project chief Louis Mor- 
ris said that “for the television 
ads, only 3% of the subjects in- 
dicated that they did not re- 
member the main point and 
about 10% indicated they did 
not recall any additional points 
made in the ads.” 

In contrast, one-fourth could 
not recall the main point of the 
magazine ads, “and about half 
said they did not remember any 
additional points,” Morris said. 

Although the consumers 
tended to recall information 
about the drug’s benefits more 
frequently than information 
about risks (even for the ads 
top-heavy with risk informa- 
tion), viewers of the TV com- 
mercials were far more likely to 
remember drug warnings and 
other risk data, the study 
found. 

In addition, “television led to 
significantly higher scores than 
the magazine on virtually all as- 
pects of drug knowledge,” Mor- 
ris noted. “Providing specific 
risk information led to signifi- 
cantly greater recall in total 
and, in some instances, slightly 
greater recall of the promotion- 
al material.” 

Morris, who headed F.D.A.’s 
aborted mandatory PPI project 
during the early 1980’s, also re- 
vealed that displaying a patient 
package insert in a print ad 
proved “inferior” to “most other 
forms of risk disclosure.” 

Although the researchers 
found somewhat better results 
by “scrolling” the text of the 
patient package insert during 
the TV commercial, Morris ac- 
knowledged that “there does 
not appear to be a great benefit 
to including a PPI in” television 
ads, even during a controlled 
experiment. 

Moreover, he said, “whether 
people would read a scroll while 
viewing television in their home 
is doubtful.” 

Although physician groups 
have expressed concern that di- 
rect-to-consumer Rx advertis- 
ing would “undermine the doc- 
tor-patient relationship,”’ 
F.D.A.’s study found that most 
consumers trust their doctor 
more than a drug advertise- 
ment. 

“Three quarters {74% 
agreed that only a physician 
could tell if a drug should or 
should not be used,” Morris 
said. Even more ego-deflating 
for the nation’s pharmacists, 
the study also found that over 
half the subjects agreed that 
“only a physician could tell if an 
advertisement for a prescrip- 
tion drug was truthful or not.” 

Consumers exposed to Rx 
advertising “frequently” drew 
incorrect conclusions about 
“the effects of the products,” 


Morris said, adding that “5% of 


the subjects viewing the high 
blood pressure drug ad said the 
main point of the ad was that 
the drug would make you 
strong.” | 

Although 61% of the consum- 
ers surveyed told F.D.A. “they 
would like to see prescription 
drug advertisements,” only 
half believed such ads would 
benefit the public, and another 
20% said consumer Rx ads 
would drive up drug prices, the 
study found.

Mousse 
takes chains 


by storm 


arely does a new category estab- 
lish itself as quickly as the mousse 
products that have hit the market 
with considerable fanfare during the 
past several months. 


But while the initial success of 
mousse would seem to signal the birth of 


a new hair care category, retailers are 
‘autiously awaiting indications that the 
first-time users of the product will be- 
come repeat buyers. 

In addition, as the mousse segment 
gains momentum, some chain drug 
buyers believe that the fledgling catego- 
ry’s growth may still eventually come at 
the expense of hair care product stand- 
bys such as sprays as well as the newer, 
less established hair gel segment. 

Kor drug retailers, their first intro- 
duction to mousse came during the Af- 
filiated/Associated Buying Show in 
New York a year ago. At that time, 
mousse products marketed by L’Oreal 
and Helene Curtis were already receiv- 
ing considerable attention in hair salons 
throughout the United States. 

With an advertising budget pegged at 


Continued on page 56 


Flood of new shampoos poses risks 


he dilemma shoppers face in select- 
ing which new shampoo or condi- 
tioner to try is nothing compared to 
the difficult choices confronting chain 
drug buyers. | 

They’re in a quandary because they 


must decide which of the multitude of 


new products to find room for in an al- 
ready crowded department. 

Shampoo departments, according to 
Nielsen, now average 69 ft., and drug 
chains report that they can’t enlarge 
them to accommodate new brands. 

“Just because there are new products 
doesn’t mean we expand the depart- 
ment,” said Bill Pories, buyer for Peo- 
ples Drug. 

What makes the category even trick- 
ier is that many of the new selections 
will fail. According to Diana Temple at 
Salomon Brothers, 9 out of 10 new 
shampoos falter. Plus, shampoos and 


conditioners have an average lifespan of 


less than three years. 

What’s more consumption is not ris- 
ing as fast as product proliferation. The 
shampoo category totaled about $1.3 
billion last year—a 8% dollar gain but 
only a 1% unit gain. “How much more 
can people shampoo their hair?” asks 
one buyer. Additionally, it’s a frag- 
mented market with only nine brands 


holding 3% or greater market share. 

Since marketers no longer see oppor- 
tunity for the explosive growth of ves- 
teryear, they've decided to steal market 
share from each other. One way to do 
this is to target specific segments of the 
overall market. For example, Affinity 
by J&J is aimed at women over 40 (that 
market is expected te sw " 15% by 1990 
to a total of 52.4 million). 

Perma Soft is directed toward the es- 
timated 47% of the population with 
permed hair. And, Shulton h: ‘ts 
newly acquired UltraSwim s’~ poo, 
conditioner and soap will appea: co 26 
million plus adults who swim on a regu- 
lar basis. 

But manufacturers aren't letting the 
new brands speak for themselves 
they're dangling the heaviest ad bud- 
gets ever in front of chain drug retailers. 
Revlon, for example, will spend close to 
$60 million in its advertising and cou- 
poning efforts. Lever Brothers is ex- 
pected to shell out $60 million, Clairol 
$14 million (in advertising alone) and 
J&J $10 million with Affinity. If these 
numbers don’t sound impressive, con- 
sider the average brand is backed by 
about $6 million. 

Drug chains are paying attention. 
“You're almost obligated to carry any- 


thing that is backed with substantial 
television advertising,” reports Bob 
Layne, buyer for Wellby Super Drugs. 
“There’s no brand loyalty to speak of 
and that’s why advertising becomes es- 
pecially relevant ina decision to carry a 
product.” 

Adds a Midwest-based buyer, “I make 
sure we have it in our planograms if 
there is a great deal of support behind 
it.” 

Apparently, the ads have been work- 
ing, and chains report requests for the 
new brands. Helen James, Hook's 
buyer, says her stores have already had 
requests for Perma Soft, and Dimension 
and Affinity both appear to be moving.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 14, 1984 


lowly but surely, food stores and 
mass merchandisers are nibbling 
away at the drug store’s market 
share in the four categories that round 
out the $3 billion hair care category. 

The categories—perms, colors, hair 
sprays and accessories—were once to- 
tally dominated by drug chains. How- 
ever, other retailers have taken aggres- 
sive positions in these categories and 
have grabbed away some market points. 
Following are the current trends in each 
of these important category areas: 

Hair color: The aging of America 
portends well for the $500 million hair 
care business. That comes as good news 
to retailers who report sales, have been 
sluggish over the past few years. 
Growth has inched up only 3% in units 
per year and only about 25% to 35% of 
today’s women color their hair. 

But retailers hope that as the total 
number of women over 40 approaches 50 
million by 1990, hair color sales will 
blossom. 

Manufacturers are already anticipat- 
ing the activity. Jhirmack is readying a 
new color product for national rollout 
and Clairol has signed Dynasty’s Linda 
Evans as a spokesman for its brands. 

According to a Clairol representative, 
space and selection are the two keys to 
selling hair color. It has been drug out- 
lets’ willingness to devote almost 70 ft. 
to hair color that has gained them 61% 
of the market. “However,” the source 
added, “drug operators haven’t made 


their departments any larger since 
1978, while supers have increased from 
9 ft. to 13 ft.” 

He also feels giant combos are heating 
up the battle in hair color because “they 
have the traffic and the selection.” This 
source predicts drug outlets’ color gains 
for 1983 will only be 2% vs. a hefty 12% 
for food outlets and 11% for mass mer- 
chants. 

Drug retailers contacted by Drug 
Store News, claimed they’re preserving 
their business by promoting color in 
more ads, including education at point- 
of-purchase and staying in stock on the 
hottest colors. “If a customer can’t find 
her color,” a buyer said, “she'll leave the 
store and take her other health and 
beauty aid business with her.” 

The current best sellers include Nice 
’n Easy, Preference, Miss Clairol and 
Loving Care. Market share by vendors 
breaks down this way: Clairol 62.3%, 
L’Oreal 16.9% and all others 20.8%. 

Hair perms: Four years ago, home 
perming was at its peak, and drug 
stores commanded an impressive 60.5% 
market share. Now the perm business 
has leveled at the same time, drug 
stores lost almost five percentage 
points. 

Last year, Clairol debuted a semi-per- 
manent “perm” that allowed a customer 
to test a perm that could be washed out. 
The goal was to bring in new users and 
Clairol cleverly placed a coupon for its 
Kindness perm in each of the Party

A mall bunny, according to DuCair’s president,

prowls malls (and 
strip centers) search-

is interested in gain-

with DuCair’s new

acquired from Helena 
Rubinstein investors. 

The Candie’s line, 
he says, is perfect for 
this customer and fills a niche in the market. Drug 
stores are a perfect outlet for Candie’s because teen 
girls tend to purchase most of their cosmetics prod- 
ucts in drug stores. 

That’s why one of DuCair’s top priorities in drug 
stores is to regain its former position which had

Rising population, new items fuel ethnic market 


Black-oriented 
mix expands fo 


foiletries, apparel 


ith the ethnic health and beau- 
ty aids market growing at a 
dramatic 15% to 20% annually, 
drug chains and high volume indepen- 
dents are starting to enrich cheir ethnic 
mix. 

Many retailers are expanding their 
existing departments to include a wide 
variety of personal care needs such as 
skin creams, hair colorings, pantyhose 
and soap in addition to the traditional 
high turning hair care needs. 

At least one chain, Walgreens, has 
acknowleged the need to expand into 
broader products by changing the title 
of its ethnic H&BA buyer, Rich Robin- 
son, to buyer of black trade products. 

Other chains are starting to advertise 
ethnic H&BA more frequently and to 
give them more endcap space inside the 
stores. Hook’s Drug in Indianapolis has 
started to bring consultants into its 
stores to answer shoppers’ questions. 

To Lafayette Jones, executive direc- 
tor of the American Health and Beauty 
Aids Institute, this growing aggressive- 
ness on the part of drug store retailers 
“signals expansion and the recognition 
of the needs of black shoppers.” Jones 
says he sees an “improved effort” on the 
part of many drug chains to make their 
shoppers aware of their ethnic sections. 

Retailers, on their part, report that 
the more attention they pay this catego- 
ry, the more it pays off. One West Coast 
chain is currently pumping out over $1 
million a year in some of its ethnic de- 
partments. Revco’s ethnic sales are 
ahead of toothpaste sales—$14 million 
in 1982 compared to $11 million for 
toothpaste. Even smaller chains are 
doing well with this category: Drug 
King, a 20-unit chain based in Califor- 
nia, is currently ordering between 
$6,000 and $9,000 worth of merchandise 
every three weeks to keep up with de- 
mand. 

According to industry statistics, drug 
chains and high volume independents 
are currently capturing about 45% of 
the $1.5 billion ethnic hair care category 
and the numbers are growing. About 
half the category’s current sales are in 
hair care products, traditionally the 
backbone of a typical drug store ethnic 
department. 

What fuels this department is a com- 
bination of a swelling ethnic population, 
increased incomes and the :ntroduction 
of new in-demand ethnic items. Blacks, 
who currently represent 12% of the 
American population, have a distinctive 
need for hair and skin care products for- 
mulated just for them. 

It wasn’t until the 1960’s that the first 
black hair care products appeared on 
the mass market, but the real explosion 
came in the 1970’s with the introduction 
of the California curl. That one look ne- 
cessitated the purchase of a be rage of 
supplemental products. 

In less than five years, the curl style 
created a market of $143 million in ac- 
tivator sales and $79 million in kit sales 
(see related story on p. 64), according to 
Business Trends Analysts. 

Now the cur! product category is sta- 
bilizing, however, leaving future growth 
to come primarily from the following 
areas:

Hispanic market 
continues rapid 
growth pattern — 


ecording to figures compiled for 
the 1980 census, there are cur- 
rently more than 14.6 million His- 
panics living legally in this country, a 
61% increase over the decade of the 70’s. 

In addition, Government sources esti- 
mate that there are another six to eight 
million Hispanics living in this country 
illegally. 

Because of this population’s high 
birth rate and an increasing level of im- 
migration, the Hispanic market is ex- 
pected to grow at a rate some 6.5% fast- 
er than the population at large. 


‘ 2d 


Drug chains are translating their ads into 
Spanish to tap into the $60 billion His- 
panic market. 


Hispanics are particularly expected 
to congregate in markets where they 
already have a presence—such cities as 
New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, 
San Antonio, Denver and Miami. 

Because many Hispanics are “up- 
wardly mobile,” this market holds a par- 
ticular fascination for drug store retail- 
ers, and many top chains are now 
stepping up their efforts to court these 
shoppers. 

Eckerd, for instance, is now advertis- 
ing in Spanish in its Florida markets. 
Walgreens, Revco and Gray are using 
spinner racks to call attention to new 
lines like the popular Que Guapa. 

Suppliers, like Judith Lynn and Ben 
Sheftall, are creating new planograms 
designed to show retailers how best to 
move product and court shoppers in this 
growth category. They are encouraging 
retailers to stock more of the specialized 
products, like toiletries, that Hispanics 
traditionally search for. 

“You need to carry products His- 
panics are familiar with,” says Lou 
Orenstein of Judith Lynn. 

“You have to tailor your mix,” says 
Richard Eichholz of Ben Sheftall. There 
are at least four distinct groups into 
which a Hispanic shopper can be cata- 
loged, and each group has its own 
unique differences, he said. 

“What sells in Miami doesn’t always 
sell in Atlanta,” points out Eichholz. 

Retailers themselves are saying they

; DRUG STORE NEWS, May 14, 1984 


Chains expand ethnic mix in growing market 


Continued from page 61 

Hair Color: Hair colorings are a dy- 
namic category for retailers. The black 
consumer is currently spending an esti- 
mated $50 million a year on ethnic hair 
colors. According to research from Car- 
son Products, as many as 25% of all 
black females color their hair. Their re- 
search also shows that 85% of all shop- 
pers who buy a hair coloring continue to 
repurchase it in frequencies ranging 
from a purchase once every two to six 
months. 

“The influence of Europe has caused 
many women to go lighter with their 
hair,” says Joe Atkinson of Carson Prod- 
ucts. Carson, which just introduced 
three new light shades, hopes to gener- 
ate sales from shoppers who didn’t buy 
before because the colors were too dark. 

Buyers for drug chains are saying 
they expect the new colorings to add at 
least 10% to hair color sales. They also 
report that positioning ethnic hair color- 
ing products in the hair coloring section 
rather than in the ethnic hair care sec- 
tion can increase sales as much as 20%. 

“When you go shopping for hair color, 
you look where there are other hair col- 
orings, not in hair care,” says Atkinson. 
Revco, Walgreens and K mart, among 
others, are now adopting this strategy. 

Skin creams: According to Business 
Trends Analysts, blacks use skin 
creams more frequently than whites be- 
cause they tend to have drier skin. One 
popular seller right now, according to 
several buyers, is Soft Sheen’s Cocoa 
Creme Butter, a deep moisturizing 
cream. 


Cosmetics: Ethnic cosmetics are 
showing signs of life, according to a re- 
cent survey of ethnic suppliers. Yet 
buyers think that the real potential of 
this section won’t emerge until manu- 
facturers come up with more products 
better tailored to the black woman’s 
needs. 

According to Business Trends Ana- 
lysts, less than half of the $348 million 
that blacks are expected to spend on 
cosmetics will go to ethnic products. 
The report concludes that the lower 
sales do not reflect a lack of demand, but 
instead “inadequate availability” of 
good products. 

Fragrances: According to Helen 


James, the buyer for ethnic products at 


Hook Drug, prestige fragrances move 
very well in black markets. However 
manufacturers have not yet started to 
exploit this trend. To date, just Prince 
Matchabelli, MEM and Coty are adver- 
tising their specially formulated scents 
in the black media. Still, according to 
Business Trends Analysts, blacks will 
spend over $247 million on fragrances 
annually and their per capita spending 
is 10% above the national average. 

Other items: “I’d rather put black 
pantyhose into the planogram than cos- 
metics,” said one distributor referring 
to the overwhelming success of black 
oriented hose. Brands such as Afro- 
tique have won over shoppers because of 
their special fit and colors aimed at the 
market. 

Blacks use proportionately less shav- 
ing preparations than other races. But, 
because a 65% share of black men suffer

sales of curl kits flatten, 
but look remains a staple 


here’s no denying that the Califor- 

nia Curl look is flattening out in 

most retail markets. The curl, 
which was the impetus behind hefty 
ethnic hair care sales increases, is giv- 
ing way to the wave ora short and sculp- 
ted look. 

“The curl market just is not what it 
once was,” reported Jerry Davis, presi- 
dent of Paul Sundries Inc., a distributor 
who services Longs, Sav-On, Pay ’n 
save, Pay Less and Drug King. 
‘“Pomades are starting to sell better.” 

tichard M. Eichholz, president of 
Ben Sheftali Distribution, agrees. “We 
have seen the wave become stronger. 
Hair is shorter and the biggest thing 
we've seen are the no-lye relaxers.” 

However, despite a slackening in 
_ Sales, retailérs report that cur! products 
still move, especially in certain geo- 
graphical locations. 

The Sonth, for example, still has a 
higher percentage of sales of curl kits, 
according to sources at Begley, Taylor 
and Eckerd. 

Added, Kirk Bright of Bright Dis- 
tributing, ““These items may have 
reached a plateau, but sales have not 
slackened at all.” 


One Southern-based retailer said he 
doesn't feel the style will ever die out 
because “women would have to keep 
cutting their hair off and that’s expen- 
sive. We just won’t see the same 20% to 
30% sales gains.” Many believe the curl 
will eventually become just another al- 
ternative hair style. 

Presentiy most retailers are leaving 
shelf space for curl kits and mainte- 
nance items intact. However, additional 
space is being cleared for the new gels, 
mousse items, setting lotions and no-lye 
relaxers that are gaining in popularity. 
Carson, for example, just launched a 
new upscale no-lye relaxer called Ex- 
celle, and many chains plan to carry this 
new entry. 

The AHBAI, which has tracked both 
unit and dollar sales to help determine 
how much shelf space each category 
should receive, found that in 1982 condi- 
tioners and hair dressings produced 
47% of unit sales and 29% of dollar sales: 
blow out cremes and relaxers garnered 
11% of units and 21% of dollars; curl 
activators, 17% of units, 20% dollars; 
comb easy lotions, 17% units, 17% dol- 
lars, and hair spray sheens, 3% units, 
2% dollars.
