Eckerd raises eyecare sights 


to include megaoptical unit 


By Gail Appleson 

CLEARWATER, Fla.—The 
Jack Eckerd Corp., an 11-year 
veteran of the eye care busi- 
ness, is taking its expertise one 
step further with a plunge into 
the optical department store 
market. 

According to industry soure- 
es, Eckerd Optical will open a 
10,000-sq.-ft. super store, 
called Vision Works, in Clear- 
water’s Sunshine Mall this sum- 
mer. Eckerd is also considering 
other sites. 

The Eckerd store will be part 
of a new breed of vision centers, 
called megastores or megaopti- 
cals, that range between 6,000 
and 22,000 sq. ft. and offer sev- 
eral cndecd styles of frames 
and as many lenses. Currently 
there are about 20 of these cen- 
“ all less than a few years 
old. 

In fact, one of these stores is 
in the Miami market. Eye- 
world, a 22,000-sq.-ft. center 
owned by the Detroit-based 
D.O.C. Optics Corp., opened in 
Hialeah in January. 

It’s not surprising that Eck- 


erd should once again be on the 
forefront of successful develop- 
ments in the optical business. 
The drug chain made its mark 
in 1973 when it acquired two 
optical centers in the west coast 
of Florida. Today the chain has 
about 150 centers, most of 
which are inside drug stores. 

Opticians in Eckerd Optical 
Centers fill prescriptions for 
eyeglasses and offer full lines of 
standard and fashion frames. 
More comprehensive vision 
care is offered by independent 
professional optometrists at 40 
centers. Eckerd also has three 
labs where eyeglass lenses are 
edged and fitted into frames. 

Industry observers said that 
Eckerd’s decision to open this 
type of optical center is part of 
the national trend toward cor- 
porate ownership of the abun- 
dantly stocked, full service 
megastores where lenses are 
made, as opposed to indi- 
vidually owned stores where 
lens work is often sent 
elsewhere. 

For example, Quaker Oats— 
the diversified holding compa- 


ny primarily known for its cere- 
al products—last year entered 
the eye care business by paying 
some $10 million for an eyewear 
chain called Evyelab, with stores 
in New York and New Jersey. 
Evyelab started the mega trend

Medicare-Glaser: 


Walgreens Rx ads 
confuse shoppers 


By Liz Parks 

ST. LOUIS—Medicare- 
Glaser has begun warning con- 
sumers in its metro St. Louis 
markets that Walgreens televi- 
sion ads stressing the added se- 
curity of their Intercom Phar- 
macy Computer System could 
be dangerously misconstrued. 

The warnings, which come in 
the form of full page open let- 
ters published in three major 
area newspapers under presi- 
dent Harlan Steinbaum’s signa- 
ture, are an attempt to offset 
what Steinbaum and other 
Medicare-Glaser executives de- 
scribe in their letter as “adver- 
tising that is creating a dan- 
gerous misunderstanding.” 

Steinbaum’s letter does not 
name Walgreens directly but it 
specifies that except for Medi- 
eare-Glaser no other retail drug 
chain in St. Louis has the capac- 
ity to monitor drug interac- 
tions. 

Walgreens and Medicare- 
Glaser are the two leaders in 
the St. Louis market but Medi- 
care-Glaser, which has spent 
eight vears developing a phar- 
macy computer system, has 
been advertising the system in 
this market for three years.

CHICAGO—Speculation about a possible 
merger between American Stores and Jewel 
Companies sent Jewel stock spiraling upward 
earlier this month. 

Talk of a possible combination of the two food 
and drug retailing giants surfaced when offi- 
cials at the Phina baned Jewel disclosed that 
a meeting had taken place during the last week 
of April in Denver with executives of American 
Stores. 

‘However, Jewel quickly pointed out that “no 
offer has been made; no offer has been accept- 
ed.” In addition, the company stated that 
American Stores had not accumulated any 


Jewel shares and that it did not anticipate an 
offer for any of its stock. But despite the ob- 
vious attempt to downplay the significance of 
the talk, Jewel’s stock jumped $3.75 to $47.75 
immediately following news of the meeting. 

Heavy trading of Jewel stock continued 
through the first two weeks of May. At press- 
time, , ies stock, which is traded on the New 
‘York Stock Exchange, closed at $54.

flurry of trading activity when it was reported 
that an inside management group offered to 
purchase the company for $65. a share. The

Black ink predicted for Trak Auto 


NEW YORK—Trak Auto West, the auto parts and accesso- 
ries chain jointly owned by Thrifty and Dart Drug, “has not 
turned the profit corner,” but is expected to break even this 
vear, Thrifty chairman Leonard H. Straus told security ana- 
lvsts here this month. 

Straus said that the combined pretax loss of $2.5 million 
from the Trak Auto West operation was due in part to the 
considerable investment involved in opening the auto chain's 
148, 000-sq.-ft., state-of-the-art distribution center as well as 
a less than effective advertising program. 

A new advertising campaign and an auto aftermarket indus- 
trv in southern California that is projected to grow to “double 
the size of the drug store business,” has left Straus “still very 
confident that Trak Auto West will do the volume.’ 

Thrifty and Dart currently operate 40 Trak Auto West 
stores in the Greater Los Angeles Area. Ten new stores will be 
opened by Aug. 31. Thrifty president Richard Ejils said that 
there may be as many as 60 Trak Auto West stores by vear-end 
and 100 units by August 1985. 

Similar expansion plans have been laid out for Crown Books, 
the discount book store chain of which Thrifty and Dart each 
own 34%. There are currently 162 Crown Book Stores in 
operation. By vear-end, the number of book stores may reach 
222, Els said. 

Thrifty’s other major specialty retailing venture will also be 
expanded. Seven new Big 5 sporting goods stores will be 
opened this vear and at aa 10 are planned for 1985. 

In addition to specialty retailing, Thrifty operates 26 foun- 
tain and coffee shops, an import business, a realty division and 
film processing and ice cream manufacturing operations.

Napoli named exec vp at Medi-Save 
BATON ROUGE, La.—Carl J. Napoli Sr., of Medi-Save 
Pharmacies Inc., has been promoted to executive vp, accord- 
ing to Ed Hiller, president of the 10&-store chain. 

Napoli joined Medi-Save in 1962 when the company oper- 
ated four leased pharmacy departments in Louisiana. He was 
named vp of merchandising and marketing in 1974, and re- 
ceived another promotion to senior vp of marketing in 1982, a 
position he held prior to his recent promotion. 

A Baton Rouge native, Napoli graduated from Northeast 
Louisiana State University with a B.S. degree in pharmacy.

“I’m going to be concentrat- 
ing prime irily on the programs 
we are in the process of imple- 
menting,” he says. “rather than 
make drastic changes in other 
directions.”

Perfecto helps boost Thrifty sales 


NEW YORK—After five 
consecutive years of declining 
drug store sales increases on a 


same-store basis, the Los An- 


geles-based Thrifty Corp. has 
apparently reversed the down- 
ward trend. 

Through the first six months 
of fiscal 1984, ended Feb. 29, 
1984, same-store sales in- 
creased 10.6%, a marked im- 
provement over the 6.8% in- 
crease registered during fiscal 
1985 and close to the 11.9% gain 
posted in 1979 and Thrifty’s 
best year-to-year increase in 
the last 10 years. 

Speaking before a group of 
security analysts earlier this 
month, Thrifty chairman and 
ceo Leonard H. Straus said the 
improvements in its drug store 
division have come in part from 


“much larger sales and _ profit 
gains” in Thrifty’s Perfecto pro- 
totype stores, which now con- 
stitute nearly 55% of the chain’s 
539 drug stores. Average store 
sales last year were just over $2 
million. 

“We believe that Thrifty 
stands at the threshold of a 
much more explosive profit and 
sales trend than we have ever 
experienced,” said Straus.

pays off for independents 


NEW YORK—Although in- 
dependent drug stores report- 
ed a higher average cost of 
goods sold last vear, they were 
able to maintain their profit 
margins by trimming expenses. 

This was one of the findings 
of this year’s Lilly Digest pre- 
liminary report on the 1983 op- 
erating results of 860 indepen- 
dent community drug stores 
nationwide. 

According to the report, the 
gross margin of the average in- 
dependent declined 0.4 of a per- 
centage point to 33.2%, the 
lowest since 1953. But the aver- 
age communit, pharmacy was 
able to shave its expenses to a 
new low of 30.3%. 

The two offsetting factors 
left the average net profit mar- 
gin, before taxes, intact at 
2.9%. 

The Lilly Digest also found 
that while average store sales

Pay Less, Bergen Brunswig venture 


Billing process to trim 
Medi-Cal paperwork 


SACRAMENTO, Calif.— 
Pay Less NW and Bergen 
Brunswig have been approved 
by the State of California De- 
partment of Health Services as 
providers for Medi-Cal’s new 
pilot tape-to-tape billing proj- 
ect. 

For Pay Less’ 70 California 
stores, it’s a three-step transi- 
tion: from manual processing to 
tape-and-a-hard-copy to 100% 
tape. 

“Earlier this year,” says Tom 
Eilers, pharmacy systems buy- 
er for Pay Less, “the state al- 
lowed providers to use hard- 
copy backup with tape-to-tape. 
The hard copy enabled us to 
handle edits and rejects expedi- 
tiously.” | 

Eilers notes that “tape-to- 
tape does not change the pro- 
cecures at the Pay Less phar- 
macy except to eliminate hard 


copies—and that reduces pa- 
perwork.” 

With the Pay Less on-line 
computer, the accummulated 
data from the pharmacies is 
transmitted on tape to Comput- 
er Science Corp. (CSC), the 
third-party intermediary un- 
der contract with the state. 
CSC loads the tape into its sys- 
tem, processes the claims, and 
sends the state a payment tape. 
The state then reimburses Pay 
Less. 

As contrasted to the manual 
system, Eilers says there are 
1% to 2% fewer rejections with 
tape-to-tape because “tape has 
been eliminated and therefore 
no human hands are involved.” 

Eilers also notes that reim- 
bursements for Medi-Cal 
claims have been speeded up by 
one week. Pay Less processes

Pending drug price bill benefits public and retailers 


Washington lawmakers occasionally come up with 
legislation that benefits consumers, the pharmaceuti- 
cal industry and retailers alike. One such measure is 
now y ei, 308.2 It has been called “the most signifi- 
cant drug legislation considered by Congress in over 
20 years.” 

he House proposal, sponsored by Rep. Henry A. 
Waxman (D-Calif.), is the Drug Price Competition 
Bill. The Senate companion version is known as the 
Patent Restoration Bill. 

Together, the two bills would effect a tradeoff be- 
tween research-intensive pharmaceutical manufac- 
turers seeking to extend the effective patent life of 
many of their valuable drug properties and generic 
drug makers, who have long been eager to create 
generic versions of pioneer drugs patented after 1962. 

Waxman’s bill would open the door for generic 
manufacturers to market their own versions of some 
125 drugs formerly sold exclusively by their develop- 
ers. It would do so by allowing the generic companies 
to submit Abbreviated New Drug Applications 
(ANDA’s) for post-1962 drugs, where formerly they 
had to spend millions to prove the safety and effective- 
ness of the drugs before marketing them. 

Waxman’s bill would also speed the approval of mul- 
tisource drugs by allowing generic manufacturers to 
import and test new drugs—but not market them— 


BENCHMARKS 


By Joseph Caputo, R.Ph. 
Pharmaceutical Editor 


before the products’ patents expire. The Food and 
Drug Administration would simultaneously be able to 
process ANDA’s, but not approve them until after 
patent expiration. 

The Senate bill would benefit marketers of branded 
pioneer drugs by extending effective patent life and 
thereby providing more time in which to recapture 
investment. Thus, it would offer an incentive to manu- 
facturers to develop innovative new drugs, and the 
cycle toward eventual multisource availability would 
start again. 

The patent extension part of this bill calls for a 
number of modifications in existing patent law. For 
example, pioneer nid such as Peldche. Halcion and 
Cardizem, approved by F.D.A. in the “transition” 


period between Jan. 1, 1982, and the time of enact- 
ment would be afforded 10 years of market exclusiv- 
ity. Drugs with 14 or more years of market exclusivity 
would not qualify for patent extension. 

Patent extension for all other pharmaceuticals 
would depend on whether a drug was currently under 
F.D.A. review. For drugs not yet submitted for ap- 
proval, the period of patent extension would be equal 
to the time required to review the New Drug Applica- 
tion (NDA) plus one-half the time required for the 
Investigational New Drug phase. Total extension 
time, however, would not exceed 5 years. 

For drugs currently under F.D.A. review, a similar 
formula would be used except that only 2 years of 
extension would be granted. In both cases, effective 
patent life would not be extended beyond 14 years. 

As generic firms make these products available to 
the public there wili be more price competition than 
ever before. As a result, the public—especially that 

ortion on fixed or limited incomes—will no longer 
ave to make the desperate choice between eating de- 
cent meals and obtaining needed medications. 

While the public is the ultimate beneficiary, retail- 
ers can also expect to gain from the higher price 
points of new products and the bigger gross margins 
of —— drugs—and, of course, consumer good- 
will.

Pay ’n Save ist qtr. net income drops 64% 


SEATTLE—First quarter net income at Pay ’n Save plum- 
meted 64% to $1.01 million from $2.8 million during the same 
period last year. 

Sales posted by the diversified, Seattle based retailer rose 
18% to $303 million from $256 million the previous year. 

Earnings per share for the first quarter ended April 28 
declined to 7¢ per share from 20¢ per share during the pre- 
vious quarter last year. 

Calvin Hendricks, Pay ’n Save’s vice chairman and ceo, 
attributed the decline in earnings in part to closing of the 
sporting goods departments in the company’s Ernst Home 
Center stores. Hendricks also cited higher than expected 
start-up costs of Pay ’n Save’s Price Saver warehouse division 
and its newly acquired wholesale drug subsidiary, North- 
western Drug. 


Revco completes Odd-Lot acquisition 


TWINSBURG, Ohio—Revco has completed the acquisition 
of Odd-Lot Trading Company, one of the nation’s largest 
wholesalers and retailers of close-out merchandise. Under the 
“pooling of interests” transaction, Revco issued 4.4 million 
new shares cf common stock to purchase the 66-unit chain. 


Peoples’ subsidiary gets new ceo 


ALEXANDRIA, Va.—Peter M. Alexander has been elect- 
ed chairman of the board and ceo of B. H. Krueger, the man- 
ufacturing subsidiary of Peoples Drug Stores, Sheldon W. 
Fantle, Peoples chairman, president and ceo, announced. For 
the past five years Alexander was with ATI Inc., Westport, 
Conn., most recently as corporate vp and general manager of 
the Chem Spray division. Krueger manufactures private 
brand powders, creams, lotions and stick deodorants for a 
number of national chains, including Peoples. It is also in- 
volved in contract packing services for many department store 
lines of fragrances and cosmetics. 


Bob Cole, former Cole chairman, dies 


KNOXVILLE, Tenn.—Robert Cole, former chairman of 
the board of Cole Drug, died last month at the age of 78. Cole, 
an honorary board member of the NACDS, headed the chain, 
which had stores in Alabama and Tennessee, until it was 
merged into Revco in 1971.

Congress O.K.’s crime bill 


WASHINGTON—Final 
Pharmacy crime legislation 
sailed through Congress late 
last month despite bitter op- 
position from independent 
druggists seeking even broader 
Federal jurisdiction over drug 
store robberies and burglaries. 

The compromise measure, 
which was awaiting President 
Reagan’s signature at press- 
time, grants Federal Justice 
Department officials new but 
limited authority to prosecute 
individuals charged with steal- 
ing any controlled substances 
from drug stores, hospital 
pharmacies, drug wholesalers 
or manufacturers. 

Under the new law, Federal! 
authorities will be allowed to in- 
tervene in pharmacy robbery 
cases if the replacement value 
of the controlled substances in- 
volved exceeds $500. 

In addition, the Justice De- 
partment will be authorized to 
prosecute in all cases involving 
“significant bodily injury” or in- 
terstate commerce, regardless 
of the value of drugs involved. 

Although the final compro- 
mise measure drew strong sup- 
port from the National Associa- 


tion of Chain Drug Stores, the 
American Pharmaceutical As- 
sociation and the National 
Wholesale Druggists Associa- 
tion, lobbyists for the National 
Association of Independent 
Druggists openly attempted to 
block passage of the bill, charg- 
ing that the “triggering” condi- 
tions for Federal prosecution 
are too restrictive. 

NARD raised particularly 
vigorous objections to the dol- 
lar threshold, which officials at 
the independent pharmacy 
group charged “might just as 
well be $50,000!” 

Although the author of the 
compromise bill, House Crime 
Subcommittee Chairman Wil- 
liam Hughes (D-N.J.), agreed 
to an NACDS proposal lower- 
ing the original $1,000 dollar 
trigger to $500, NARD officials 
concluded that this “will not 
help us” because “our members 
get shot for one bottle of Di- 
laudid.” 

In House testimony earlier 
this year opposing Hughes’ 
measure, one NARD witness 
told Congress that “three bot- 
tles of Dilaudid 100s might cost 
the pharmacist about $80, but 


bring $15,000 on the street. 
Many criminals will commit 
robbery for much less than the 
$80 replacement value of those 
Dilaudids,” he added, “but the 
robbed pharmacist would need 
to have surrendered /9 bottles 
with a street value of $95,000 to 
qualify for Federal help: 

Other restrictions in the com- 
promise bill—including the pro- 
vision allowing Federal pro- 
secution of dr ‘ug store r obberies 
resulting in “bodily injury” to 
pharmacists and customers— 
also drew fire from NARD as 
too restrictive. 

Although Hughes later com- 
promised on this point to permit 


Justice Department prosecu- 


tion of cases involving * ‘pistol 
whippings,”’ “psychological 
trauma” and other “significant” 
(but not life-threatening) inju- 
ries, NARD stepped up its op- 
position to the bill. 

In the end, however, Senate 
pharmacy crime bill backers 
sympathetic to NARD’s con- 
cerns concluded that further re- 
sistance to the compromise 
would doom all hope-for enact- 
ment of any controlled-sub- 
stance robbery law this year. 


Retailers concerned over vendor 
plans for in-store OTC labeling 


ASHINGTON—Chain and 
inde pe ndent drug stores will be 
expected to post shelf markers 
or display signs listing all inac- 
tive ingredients in a wide range 
of over-the-counter drug prod. 
ucts, under the Proprietary As- 
sociation’s proposed new volun- 
tary disclosure program. 

The thrust of the associa- 
tion’s labeling initative is to 
head off pending Federal legis- 
lation mandating such dis- 
closures by manufacturers of 
thousands of OTC drug prod- 
ucts. (Current law requires 
only that active ingredients be 
listed on labels. ) 

PA member firms participat- 
ing in the program will print 
alphabetical-order lists of the 
inactive ingredients on the la- 
bels of all of their nonprescrip- 
tion drug products, except 
those in packages too small to 
carry such a listing. 

For OTC in “very small pack- 
ages,” retail pharmacies will be 
expected to cooperate by post- 
ing signs or labels listing inac- 
tive ingredients on “counter or 
shelf displays” next to those 
drugs, PA officials told Drug 
Store News 

Although a spokesman for 
the OTC manufacturers’ asso- 
ciation acknowledged that re- 
tail pharmacy groups were not 
consulted prior to the an- 
nouncement of the new label 
disclosure plan late last month, 
she predicted that the program 
would not meet with any se- 


rious drug store industry resis- 
tance. 

sut the proposal has already 
raised eyebrows and concerns 
in key drug store industry cir- 
cies. 

Although PA told DrSWN that 
manufacturers would bear the 
cost of supplying drug stores 
with any necessary signwork, 
officials at NACDS noted that 
retailers would likely be re- 
sponsible for the expense of 


Home health, 


maintaining those small pack- 
age ingredient disclosure no- 
tices. 

In addition, NACDS officials 
voiced concern over the pos- 
sibility that the OTC ingredient 
signs may reduce the number of 
available shelf facings in phar- 
macies and add to “visual clut- 
ter” in drug stores.

ing three deep discounters in

Nyquil, Robitussin and Vicks continue to be the favorite liquid remedies. 


ome of the best-selling products in 

the cough/cold category are ex- 

prescription products recently 
converted to OTC status. 

According to retail drug store buyers 
for the cough/cold category, OTC con- 
verted products have helped boost over- 
all category sales by almost 30% over 
last year. For 1983, according to Drug 
Stores News’ annual survey of chain 
drug stores, cough and cold products 
totaled $463 million. Steven Sorkin, vice 
president of merchandising for Auburn- 
dale, Mass.-based Rix Corp. said the 
OTC preps are doing so well, they're 
“taking over the market.” 

Thanks largely to OTC converted 
products like Actifed, Drixoral, Afrin, 
etc., sales of cough/cold products at Rix 
increased as much as 25% this winter, he 
said. 

Other buyers are reporting the same 
phenomenon. “Actifed and Drixoral 
have been great for us,” said Paige II-

products are perceived by shoppers as 
excellent price values. Many chains and 
independents price Actifed below Con-

At Bartell, the everyday price for Ac- 
tifed 12’s, the chain’s best seller, is nor-

However, while a strong price point 
helps, it does not necessarily assure ag- 
gressive sales. Drixoral still sells well 
even at $5.20 for 20’s and $10 for 40’s. 
“People will spend any amount,” says 
Medicare-Glaser’s Norm Labus, “to get 
relief from colds. Price is not an object.” 

Many buyers reported that during 
the winter when cough/cold preps are 
advertised aggressively, margins on top 
selling products can drop to between 
15% and 20%. However, with every-day 
pricing, margins for the category aver- 
age between 25% and 37%. Margins on 
Actifed are usually higher than on other 
brands. A chain like Bartell commonly 
takes a 37% margin on Actifed com- 
pared to about 20% margin on Contac. 

Turns for the category generally 
average about six times a year with the 
bulk of sales, of course, being seasonal.

By Jim Ricchiuti 

CHICAGO—The battle lines 
have been drawn in what may 
become the most intense corpo- 
rate struggle in chain drug his- 
tory. 

Earlier this month American 
Stores proposed a $1 billion 
takeover bid for Jewel Com- 
panies. The merger, if imple- 
mented, would create a huge 
food and drug retailing con- 
glomerate with total sales in ex- 
cess of $14 billion. Sales from 
the drug division alone would 
top $4 billion. 

The unfriendly proposal 
came only weeks after Jewel 
chairman and ceo Weston 
Christopherson rejected an in- 
formal offer by L. S. Skaggs, 
American Stores chairman and 
ceo. 


In a letter sent to Skaggs 
shortly after a meeting be- 
tween the two ceo’s, but before 
Skaggs made his offer publicly 
Christopherson stated that a 
“combination would not be in 
the best interest of Jewel and 
its people at this time.” 

But despite Jewel’s initial re- 
fusal, American Stores is seek- 
ing to acquire 67% of Jewel’s 
15.4 million shares of common 
and preferred convertible stock 
outstanding. American indi- 


cated that it would offer $70 a 
share for common stock out- 
standing and $49.91 per share 
for preferred stock outstand- 
ing. The remaining 33% of Jew-

$70 a share in securities.

Pay Less looks to future with deep-discount 


WILSONVILLE, Ore.— 
After more than a year of study, 
Pay Less NW, operating 151 
conventional superdrug stores, 
is launching two new formats: a 
deep-discount drug store and a 
10,000-sq. -ft. Revco-type store. 

The first deep-discount 
store, a revamp of a conven- 
tional 30,000-sq.-ft. Pay Less 
store in Mall 205 on Portland’s 
east side, will open around July 
1. The 10,000-sq.-ft. unit. will 
open this fall. Pay Less will not 
reveal the location, but it will 
probably be in Oregon near 
chain headquarters. 

The name selected for the 
deep-discount division is Value 
Giant. Thus, Pay Less returns 
to the name of the northern 


California chain it acquired 10 
years ago and changed to the 
Pay Less logo. Why the return 
to Value Giant? “Because,” says 
a chain exec, “it’s a good name.” 

Pay Less decided to go with 
deep-discount because, an exec 
notes, “the concept Is moving 
West.” 

Pay Less was faced with a 
difficult decision on deep-dis- 
count. Explains an exec: “We 
could have sat tight and con- 
tinued operating only super- 
drug stores. We realize there 
are limited locations for deep- 
discounters, and while they 
may have hurt us in the short 
run, we could win by the num- 
bers—especially if we had a lot 
of stores in one area. However, 


fight the proposed merger 
would be to attempt to make an 
acquisition of its own. There 
also is a possibility that Jewel 
will seek a white knight to initi- 
ate a friendly offer for the Chi- 
cago based food and drug con- 
cern.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 25, 1984 


Compromise generics bill 
gets Congressional priority 


WASHINGTON—The final 
version of Rep. Henry A. Wax- 
man's Drug Pricé Competition 
bill has been put on a fast track 
in Congress. 

The measure, which was be 
in the hopper earlier this 
month, represents a major 
compromise between brand- 
name manufacturers and the 
generic drug industry on one of 
the most heated drug approval 
issues to come along in some 
time. 

Specifically the bill would 
grant generic manufacturers 
fast-track Food and Drug Ad- 
ministration approval of gener- 
ic versions of drugs marketed 
after 1962. 

For brand-name drug pro- 


CesSs., 

At presstime, both the 
House Energy and Commerce 
Committee, chaired by Wax- 
man, and the House Courts 
Subcommittee were planning 
hearings and mark-up sessions 
on the bill before this month’s 
scheduled recess for the Demo- 
eratic National Convention. 

According to aides of the Cal- 
ifornia Democrat, the new bill is 
necessary because “there is a 
pr ocedure at F.D.A. for approv- 
ing generic copies of drugs first 
approved before 1962, but there 
is no such generic approval pra- 
cedure for drugs approved for 
the first time after 1962.” 

The bill generally extends 
the ANDA procedures used to 


that FL. D.A. has determined the 
differences do not require sufe- 
ty and effectiveness testing,” 
Congressional aides explained. 
Generic manufacturers have 
been pushing for this type of 
legislation for several years be- 
cause drug sponsors filing 
ANDAs are not required to re- 
peat safety and effectiveness 


tests conducted by the original 
drug manufacturer. Asa result, 


I.D.A. approval time can be 
substantially reduced. 
According to Congressional 
architects of the legislation, 
the new bill would “make avail- 
able for approval as generics 
over 150 drugs approved since 
1562 that are off patent.’ 
Specific products covered by 


in the legislative arena and would also allow both memberships 
to share a common pool of resources. 

If a merger is effected, DWA, a nine-year-old association

the new planogrammed &-ft. 
and 16-ft. departments (de- 
pending on store size) in April. 
tobert Begley, president and

83 NWDA study 


WHITE SULPHUR 
SPRINGS, Va.—The average 
drug wholesaler increased sales 
aproximately 16% in 1983, ac- 
cording to the preliminary re- 
sults of the National Wholesale 
Drug Association’s 52nd annual 
industry survey. 

However, profits for the aver- 
age wholesaler in 1983 took a 
slight dip for the first time in 
SIX years. 

According to a preliminary 
analysis of NWDA’s 1983 oper- 
ating survey of drug whole- 
salers, sales for the average 
firm increased 16.7% in 19&3 to 
$32.7 million. 

But possibly because whole- 
salers in 1983 were ag- 
gressively pursuing chain and 
liuspital accounts, which typ- 
ically generate lower margin 
percentages and lower profits, 
the industry’s overall prof- 
itability, measured in its after- 
tax net profit to net sales ratio, 
declined from 1.41% in 1982 to 
1.37% last year. 

Gross profits also shrank, 
falling below 10% for the first 
time in the industry’s history. 
According to the survey, gross 
profit to net sales (after cash 
discounts) declined 7% in 1983 
to 9.77%. 

In reviewing the preliminary 
findings before a regional 
gathering of NWDA members 
at the Greenbriar Hotel here, 
association president William 
Ford attributed the decline to 
the industry’s aggressive pur- 
suit of mass merchandise, drug 


chains and hospital accounts, 


forms. 

The new marketing program 
also calls for centralized dis- 
tribution of convalescent aids 
not only to the drug stores but 
also to Begley’s four freestand- 
ing home health care centers. 
Previously, most equipment— 
with the exception of fran- 
chised lines—was housed at the 
main freestanding store in Lex- 
ington. Now such items (except 
those franchised) will be ware- 
housed at the Begley distribu- 
tion center in Richmond. 

This will allow weekly deliv- 
eries to each store, Begtey said. 
Customers should never have to 
wait more than one week for 
any item, and delivery can be 
made immediately in emergen- 
cy situations, he added. 

In addition to the Lexington 
store, Begley operates free- 
standing convalescent aid cen- 
ters in Louisville, Hopkinsville 


and Ashland, Ky. The stores, 
which range in size from 2,000 
to 50,000 sq. ft., are about 2% 
vears old. 

These stores offer 24-hour 
emergency service and free de- 
livery within a 50-mile radius. 
They also have an “in-home” 
respiratory therapist on staff. 
In addition to service within the 
stores, the chain has offered for 
the past 2% years a toll-free 
number that customers can call 
to place orders and ask ques- 
tions. 

It is this toll-free number 
that sparked the idea for the 
new marketing program. Beg- 
ley said he was visiting one of 
the drug stores at the end of 
March when a customer asked 
him if the chain had wheel- 
chairs. Begley told her that it 
did and that she could order 
them through the toll-free num-

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 25, 1984 


FINANCIAL 


Eckerd rebound continues Jewel reports 14.8% 
rise in net earnings 


CLEARWATER, Fla.—Jack 
Eckerd Corp. continued its 
strong rebound from last year’s 
flat earnings growth in its most 
recent quarter. 

Net income for the third 
quarter ended April 28 in- 
creased 8.5% to $18 million, or 
48¢ a share, from $16.5 million, 
or 44¢ a share, in the compara- 
ble period last year. 

Sales rose to $650.1 million, 
10.1% higher than the $590.6 
million posted for the same 
year-earlier quarter. 

Stewart Turley, chairman 
and president, said the compa- 
ny was “gratified” with the re- 
sults even though sales growth 
“slowed somewhat” during the 
quarter. He said the slower 
growth was the result of “lower 
promotional sales in compari- 
son to last year,” primarily in 
the drug company. 

But he sated that Eckerd’s 
“key franchise,” prescription 


sales, “continued to post strong 
increases. We expect a strength- 
ened promotional program in 
the fourth quarter, together 
with continuing consumer confi- 
dence and a strong economy to 
return our sales to their pre- 
vious level.” 

Sales for the first three quar- 
ters increased 12.6% to $1.97 
billion from $1.75 billion in the 
Same year-earlier period. Net 
earnings for the 39 weeks rose 
18.1% to $67.6 million, or $1.80 
from $57.2 million, or $1.53 per 
share. 

For Eckerd Drug, the compa- 
ny’s principal subsidiary, third- 
quarter sales increased 8% to 
$561.4 million from $519.7 
million a year ago. Operating 
profits were up 15.38% to $38.5 
million from $33.4 million. 
Third-quarter comparable 
store sales, for units open a year 
or more, increased a modest 
2.8%. 


Eckerd Drug’s nine-month 
sales increased 11.8% to $1.68 
billion from $1.51 billion, while 
operating profit rose 22.7% to 
$154.8 million from $109.9 mil- 
lion. 

Since the beginning of the fis- 
cal year, Eckerd Drug has add- 
ed 90 stores, bringing the cur- 
rent total to 1,409 in 15 states. 

JByrons, Eckerd’s chain of 55 
junior department stores in 
Flor ida had third-quarter sales 
of $53.4 million vs. $42.5 million 
last year, but its operating prof- 
it dropped to $1 million from 
last year’s $2.2 million. 

American Home Video, the 
subsidiary that operates 188 
VideoConcepts stores in 29 
states, reported third-quarter 
sales of $35.4 million vs. $28.4 
million a year ago. 

Eckerd’s board of directors 
declared a cash dividend of 25¢ 
per common share, payable 
July 2. 


CHICAGO—Jewel Com- 
panies Inc. reported that first- 
quarter net earnings for the 12- 
week period ended April 21 
rose 14.8% to $16.5 million from 
$14.4 million earned during the 
first quarter of 1983. 

Earnings per share on a fully 
diluted basis increased 15% to 
$1.14 from 99¢. 

tesults from Jewel’s United 
States supermarket operations 
were responsible for much of 
the increases. Net earnings 
from the company’s domestic 
operations climbed 19% to $13 
million from $10.9 million the 
previous year. 

First-quarter sales from the 
United States divisions rose 
).6% to $1.34 billion from $1.27 
billion in 19&3. 

The company’s retail drug di- 
visions consisting of 321 Osco 


drug stores and 176 Sav-On 
drug stores generated sales in- 
creases of 13.8% and 11.5%, re- 
spectively. Drug store sales 
were $431.6 million compared 
to $382.7 million last year. 

However, net earnings from 
the drug divisions were signifi- 
cantly below 1983 earnings. 
Earnings plummeted 47% to 
$5.6 million from $10.8 million 
in 1983. | 

Net earnings from Jewel's 
supermarket division, which in- 
cludes 325 stores, soared 160% 
to $19.4 million from $7.4 mil- 
lion the year before. Sales from 
the supermarket division rose 
9.3% to $845 million. 

The company attributed the 
extraordinary earnings gain in 
its supermarket division in part 
from wage reductions, salary 
freezes and bertefits cuts.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 25, 1984

s market. 


Buying flair fuels cosmetics sales 


By Faye Brookman 


ealizing they can no longer be 
everything to everyone, drug 
store retailers are seeking meth- 
ods to provide special perks to entice 
their own segment of the market. For 
1984, buyers report that they’ll be 
forced to work harder and be more crea- 
tive in order to reach out for the cosmet- 
ics customer. 

Some chains and independents are 
trying to set themselves apart from the 
pack by merchandising prestige brands 
while others are going the discount 
route. Still others are emphasizing their 
service through salesclerks and trained 
cosmeticians. 

Coupon books, glossy catalogs and 
sweepstakes are other ploys being used 
to court the all-important female 
shopper. 

“We're all trying to find our own 
niche, to fill the holes in our own par- 
ticular marketplace,” says Pat Duck- 
worth, cosmetics buyer for People’s 
Drugs in Alexandria, Va. 

Another buyer says the situation is 
comparable to Zayre’s current advertis- 
ing compaign which stresses customer 
satisfaction. The ad promises that if a 


customer comes in for an item and it’s 
out of stock, they’ll receive an additional 
10% off the price. 

“That’s the kind of program you need. 
When everyone is after the same pool of 
customers with the same goods and 
prices, it boils down to policies,” the 
buyer says. 

On the whole, drug chains have been 
able to entice cosmetics shoppers by of- 
fering broad selections, good prices and 
service. However, many cosmetic buy- 
ers believe 1984 will end with many 
other competitors throwing their hats 
into the ring. 

“Tt hear Marshall’s [discount apparel] 
now has cosmetics,” reports Giant’s 


Julian Levin. “We’ll have to see what 


they’re up to.” 

Then too, the discount stores are 
moving in. In Michigan, for example, 
Perry’s Eleanor Marshall faces stiff 
competition from Meijer’s Thrifty 
Acres and K mart. 

The most recent Nielsen figures show 
that discount stores (mass merchandis- 
ers) are indeed the outlets gaining sales 
and gaining them at the expense of drug 
stores. Although most drug store retail- 
ers once feared food stores would over- 
come them, Nielsen shows that most of 


the 2.6% share drug outlets lost this 
year went to mass merchandisers. 

Drug stores still hold the lion’s share 
at 61.8%, but mass merchandisers 
climbed from a 19.8% share last year to 
21.6% this year. Food stores stayed 
about even going from 16% to 16.6%. 

The race for the cosmetics dollar be- 
comes even more important when one 
considers that the current growth rate 
of the category is almost stagnant. The 
value of shipments in 1983 climbed only 
1.8% to $10.24 billion last year. Small 
gains of less than 4% throughout the 
industry signaled that most of the 
growth was merely price increases. In 
other words, outlets are all vying for a 
market that is not growing fast enough 
to support all of the outlet sources. 

To overcome the problem, drug store 
retailers are searching for the new cate- 
gories that will entice new users or 
create new markets. Skin care and eth- 
nic are two categories generally con- 
ceded to have growth potential. 

“Treatments certainly afford room to 
grow,” reports Gray Drug Fair’s mer- 
chandise manager John Mirmelstein. 
He believes that the gradual upscaling 
of chain cosmetics departments can en- 
courage treatment and skin care sales. 


Gray Drug Fair, for instance, is semod- 
eling its departments and installing 
chrome and mirrored fixtures. 

As far as ethnic products are con- 
cerned, Duckworth has proven that eth- 
nic cosmetics can indeed move as 
rapidly as black hair care products. She 
embarked on a program last year for 
each store to skim its slowest Caucasian 
items, leaving space for ethnic goods. 
With the lines in clear view sales have

Culver leaves Pay Less 


Ore.—Al Culver, senior vp of merchan- 
dising and distribution for Pay Less NW has resigned. Culver 
says he is leaving to broaden his career opportunities. 
An 18-year Pay Less veteran, Culver was the driving force 
behind the chain’s automated distribution and support sys- 
tems, which have given Pay Less a competitive edge in many of 


A Stanford MBA graduate, Culver joined Pay Less as a 
management trainee and then rose to store manager and vp of 


In 1980, Culver and Ron Schiff, who was then in charge of 
merchandising and distribution, swapped jobs. The purpose 
was to provide both men with a more rounded knowledge of 


At present, it is not certain whether Culver’s position will 
be filled or whether his responsibilities will be divided among 
of the executive staff.

Trinca named to AACP post 

American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy president 
George Zografi has announced that Carl E. Trinea, Ph.D. is 
now acting executive director of AACP. 

Trinea joined the AACP staff in October 1982 as director of 
Pharmacy Affairs, he was previously assistant Dean and Head 
of the Department of Pharmacy Practice at the University of 
Arizona College of Pharmacy. 

Since joining the AACP staff Trinea has been responsible 
for a wide range of activities including the SmithKline Beck- 
man Grant Awards for Pharmacy Schools (GAPS) program.

New chief of F.D.A. faces 
furor over OTC ibuprofen 


WASHINGTON — Incoming 
F.D.A. Commissioner Frank 
Young faces an almost-certain 
“baptism by fire” when he takes 
charge of the agency later this 
month in the midst of the sim- 
mering ibuprofen OTC contro- 
versy. 

At a minimum, the new Food 


and Drug Administration chief 
will be greeted with a growing 


pile of suits second-guessing the 
agency's recent approval of New 
Drug Applications (NDAs) 
from Upjohn and American 


Home Products permitting 


over-the-counter marketing of 
the nation’s top-selling Rx non- 
steroidal anti-inflammatory 
drug (NSAID). 

The latest of those legal chal- 
lenges, filed in Federal District 
Court here last month by ¢

ting a dangerous precedent by 


“hat- 


“granting an effective monopo-

market OTC ibuprofen 

But in addition, Young will 
also face a chorus of profession- 
al critics—including some of 
F.D.A.’s own “expert” advisers 
who originally recommended 
that ibuprofen be switched 
from Rx to OTC. 

Specialists who were ad- 
visers on the F.D.A. panel said 
that ibuprofen labels do not 
specify that the elderly, diabet- 
ics and those with kidney or 
liver problems should not take 
the drug. Those taking diuret- 
ics for congestive heart failure, 
hypertension or for any other 
reason should also avoid the 
drug. 

F.D.A.’s top priority, how- 
ever, will be to sidestep court 
action requiring the agency to 
adjust course, if not reverse di- 


rection on ibuprofen. 

In addition to Chattem’s suit, 
the agency is also fighting a 
separate legal challenge from 
McNeil which claims that 
F.D.A.’s approval of OTC sta- 
tus for ibuprofen was illegally 
conditioned on the agency's ap- 
proval of advertising for the 
product. Under the law, only 
the Federal Trade Commission 
has a say on the content of ad- 
vertising to consumers. 

Chattem’s more recent court 
action questions the appropri- 
ateness and legality of F.D.A.'s 
decision to allow the only manu- 
facturers with approved NDAs 
to market ibuprofen on an OTC 
basis.

Fan giveaways heat up at Carls 


By Faye Brookman 
ROME, N.Y.—At the rate 


customers were lining up at 
Carls Drug Stores recently, vou 


would have thought the chain 
Was giving away merchandise. 

It was. 

It was all part of the chain's 
highly unusual pledge that if an 
advertised item was not in 
stock, the customer would get 
it free at a later date. 

What Carls didn’t count on 
was the record-breaking June 
temperatures that assaulted its 
upstate New York trading area 
same time the chain was 
advertising a $19.99 fan for 
$17.99. 

The fan business was never 
so good. According to chain 
president Neil Roth, about 
10,000 fans were sold through 
Carls’ 3& stores in one weekend. 
When the promotion was over, 
the chain had sold 2!'2 times 


more fans than it had all last 
summer. 

The demand was so intense, 
in fact. that it cleaned out Carls’ 
entire stock, and the chain had 
to give out more than 1,000 cer- 
tificates for free fans. 

Although giveaway had the 

effect of lowering the gross 
mar gins on the fan inventory by 
10 points, Roth says Carls will 
stick with its guarantee. In 
fact. he calls out-of-stoeks one 
of the “sins” of retailing and 
challenges other retailers to 
work to arrest the situation. 

“We'll continue to honor the 
certificates for out-of-stock ad 
items,” Roth says. “It’s a policy 
we eee and we'll stand 
by it. It cost us some money, 
ee we had a heck of aw eek and 
great store volume.” 

Just to make sure Carls holds 
up its end of the deal, the state 
Attorney General’s office is 


handling complaints from cus- 
tomers who don't get certifi- 
cates for out-of-stock ad items. 
According to Michael Hunger- 
ford, assistant attorney gener- 
al, Carls must live up to its 
claim or be in violation of state 
advertising law. 

However, the chain has re- 
aligned its policy to prevent 
future snags by eliminating 
seasonal items from its adver- 
tisements or inserting a dis- 
claimer that seasonal products 
are not part of the campaign. 

The latest item Carls is hav- 
ing trouble supplying is a gas- 
powered weed trimmer at an 
advertised price of $89. 

Despite losing at least $20,- 
000 in sales on the fans alone, 
Roth remains unruffled and op- 
timistic. “In the long run, we're 
O.K.—I think we've gained a lot 
of new Carls customers,” he 
concluded.

Stop & Shop net income up 


BOSTON—The Stop & Shop 
Companies Inc., which oper- 
ates Medi Mart Drug Stores, 
reported that net income for 
the first quarter ended May 19 
rose 44% to $6.4 million from 
$4.4 million during the previous 
quarter last vear. 

Sales for the 16-week period 
increased 18% to $866 million 
from $731 million last vear. 

Earnings per share were up 
28% on a primary basis to 50¢ 


from 43¢. On a fully diluted 
basis, per share earnings rose 
24% to 52e from 42¢ in 1983. 

The company said that its 
Medi Mart division posted a 
record first quarter both in 
sales and earnings. The 55 Medi 
Mart stores registered strong 
sales gains in domestics, toys 
and pharmacy. 

During the first quarter, 
Medi Mart opened one new 
store and remodeled four oth- 


ers. By vear end, the company 
plans nine additional stores as 
part of an extensive expansion 
program. 

In addition to Medi Mart, 
The Stop & Shop Companies 
Inc. also operates 128 Bradlees 
Department Stores, 118 Stop & 
Shop Supermarkets, 952 
Charles B. Perkins tobacco 
stores, 58 Off the Rax women’s 
specialty shops and the Stop & 
Shop Manufacturing Company.

ro go Brunswig posts 
15% net-earnings rise 


LOS ANGELES—Bergen Brunswig Corp. reported that net 
earnings from continuing operations rose 15% during the third 
quarter ended May 31 to $6.4 million, or 51¢ a share, from $5.6 
million, or 44¢ a share, in the year-earlier period. 

Sales and other revenues for the quarter increased to $442 
million, a 21% gain over the $366 million posted a year ago. 

However, the company suffered a $4.8 million loss during the 
quarter on its small appliance and sundry merchandise distribu- 
tion business, which was discontinued. 

The loss resulted in a decline in actual net earnings for the 
company to $1.6 million from $5.3 million a year ago. 

For the first nine months, BBC’s net income on continuing 
operations climbed 18% to $17.8 million, or $1.41 ashare, from $15 
million, or $1.21 a share, for the corresponding period last year. 

Sales and other revenues rose 21% to $1.26 billion from $1.04 
billion. 

Discounting the loss on discontinued operations, the company’s 
actual net earnings for the nine months declined to $12.6 million 
from $13.2 million a vear earlier. 

Commenting on the results, Emil P. Martini Jr., chairman and 
ceo, said: “We believe that after having taken the necessary steps

Personal service is Byerlys byword 


By Harold Cohen, R.Ph. 

ST. LOUIS PARK, Minn.— 
Byerly’s Pharmacy, located 
within tnat chain’s newest su- 
permarket, is working hard at 
projecting a professional image 
that is more in keeping with 
conventional drug store prac- 
tices. 

Because the supermarket 


does little or no advertising of 


its pharmacy, the 400-sq.-ft. 
department must rely on high- 
quality personal service and 
competitive pricing to ensure 
its survival. 

“We try to get to know as 
customers personally by 
said Ann Wye red 
‘Most peo- 


Nalue,

ple do not expect that kind of

macy located in the middle of a

Strachota and her coworkers 


ter area, to answer questions 
from customers about their

vate setting like our consulta- 
tion windows.”

that tracks patients’ records. 
The system is maintained by 
Viking Script Control.

labeling, pricing and receipts, 
the computer contains a com- 
plete interaction data base

Fee limits, waivers for HMOs threaten retail pharmacy 


Government has gone too far. By prohibiting phar- 
macists from collectively bargaining for better dis- 
pensing fee: and by gr anting special waiver pr ivileges 
to PPOs and HMOs, pharmacy as we know it may one 
day be extinct. 


More to the point: When do joint buying efforts of 


health care by groups of eeonomy-minded consumers 
and personnel officers of large industrial corporations 
constitute restraint of trade? 

The question once thought to be a moot issue has 
taken on significant complications for retail pharmacy 
as third party prescription plans increasingly advise 
pi oo? league where to shop for their pharmaceutical 

services. 

An HMO in Philadelphia told its subscribers that 


their prescriptions could only be acquired from one of 


three selected chains in the area, or through a mail- 
order prescription supplier. 
On the surface such an arrangement stinks of cigar- 


filled rooms and deals cut behind closed doors. But if 


each chain and mail-order prescription supplier bar- 
gained without knowledge of the other suppliers’ 
terms then the courts would say trade is not re- 
strained. 

Such arrangements supposedly keep competition 
alive and well, at least in the short term. In the long 
term another picture emerges. As fewer suppliers 
survive, those remaining tend to jack up consumer 


BENCHMARKS 


By Joseph Caputo, R.Ph. 
Pharmaceutical Editor 


| 
| 
| 


prices to prohibitive levels. Then the cycle begins 
again with more small operators entering the market. 
Except here they can’t because the market is effec- 
tively closed. 

These exclusive contracts ultimately cut down on 
the number cf pharmacies servicing an area, and the 
smaller supposely less-efficient ones go out of busi- 
ness. Up until recently most people considered life- 
giving drugs to be a necessity, and these items were 
widely available rather than being confined to a few 
select suppliers. 

A number of chains now se got boas as preferred 
providers, for a wide variety of health plans. But they 
too will soon find themselves in the same dilemma as 
their independent cousins. 

HMOs usually keep chains as suppliers for two-four 


years, then as more people become enrolled and script 
counts soar, a change takes place. HMOs discover the 
savings when the prescription program is moved In- 
house. So, economies dictate that provision of pnar- 
maceutical services be supplied by the health plan or 
one of its satellite pharmacies, thereby preventing 
others from competing when prices escal: i 

Some independents are seexing a solution to their 
dilemma: Realizing that the significance of being 
barred from provider status is a major problem, and 
that the problem can’t be remedied under the anti- 
trust law, a new tack is being employed. 

A group of 200 Florida- based pharmacists is exam- 
ining the feasibility of group-purchasing through se- 
lected wholesalers. Details in the program are yet to 
be worked out, but apparently participants in the 
program will seek chargebacks of the difference be- 
tween bid prices and the prices at which they are 
initially billed. 

A ph 1armacist in this market told Drug Store News 
that this was the only way he could remain competi- 
tive and hold onto his institutional and third-party 
customers. 

If the pharmacy buying group concept fails, per- 
haps the pre fession should apply for endangered spe- 
cies status. Then at least those responsible for killing 
once-thriving businesses could be made responsible 
for preserving and guaranteeing their survival.

COLORADO SPRINGS, Colo.—Longs will launch 
its Colorado division in 1985 with five stores, three of 
them in this fast-growing city. 

In fact, the first two stores will open-in Colorado 
Springs within a few weeks of each other. The third 
store is scheduled for Fort Collins, and No. 4 again for 
Colorado Springs. The fifth store will open in Greeley. 
The site of the sixth store, which will open in 1986, is 
being withheld because it is in the final signing stages. 

The initial six stores will be 27,000 s -28,000 sq. 
ft. overall, as compared with the 25,000-sq.-ft. units 
Longs is opening in other areas. Approximately 70% 
of a Longs store is devoted to selling space 

The merchandise mix in Colorado will follow Longs’ 
well-established pattern in California—except there 
will be no liquor departments. Longs hopes to offset 


this loss (liquor, along with wine and beer, contributes 
8% to store sales) by expanding sporting goods and by 
vigorously promoting t e basics of its mix. This would 
include cosmetics, OTC, H&BA, audiovisual, phar- 
macy and food. 

Longs’ principal supermarket tenants in Colorado 
will be Albertson’s and Safeway. Although both of 
those chains operate some phar macy departments, 
the stores adjoining Longs won't. The main com etl- 
tion for Longs will be Skaggs, Walgreens, a J King 
Soopers, which “own” the Bx and H&BA business in 
Colorado. 

Longs’ strategy in Colorado closely resembles its 
incursion into Arizona. That is, initially, Longs’ stores 
ring the outlying cities and move into the metro- 
politan areas only after a strong cluster has been 


DRUG STORE NEWS, July 23, 1984 


Longs to launch Colorado drive with 5 stores 


forged. However, at this point Longs is not sure 
whether it will go into Denver. 

Longs is sure of two things: one, that the Colorado 
stores will open faster than in Arizona, where it took 
five years to open 11 stores. And two, the chain wants 
to avoid the fate of both Hart Drug (Pay Less NW) and 
Eckerd, which opened drug stores in the Denver area 
and then pulled out. Lacking top locations as well as 
name identification, both chains were crushed pri- 
marily by King Soopers and Skaggs. 

Observers note that if Pay Less had continued to 
spend heavily on advertising and promotion for an- 
other year, the chain could have turned the six Hart 
stores around. However, Pay Less execs felt that the 
funds could be better spent in their Pacific Northwest 
stronghold. Subsequent events proved them right. 


==News in brief 


Malone & Hyde Stock purchased 


MEMPHIS—Malone & Hyde Inc. has reported that 60% of 


its common stock outstanding has been acquired by Pitco 
Acquisition Corp., a company formed by several top execu- 
tives from Malone & Hyde and Kohlberg, Kravis, Roberts and 
Co., an investment banking firm. 

According to Malone & Hyde, Pitco has acquired 9.1 million 
shares of the food/drug wholesaler and retailer outstanding 
common stock. In addition, Malone & Hyde said that it re 
purchased 1.02 million shares of its common stock. 

Last month, a group of senior Malone & Hyde executives led 
by Joseph Hyde III, chairman and president, offered $35 a 
share in a $585 million leveraged buyout. 


Pathmark buys Purity Supreme 


WOODBRIDGE, N.J.—Supermarkets General Corp., op- 
erators of Pathmark supermarkets and drug stores, has 
reached a definitive agreement to purchase Purity Supreme 
Inc. for $79.3 million in cash. The purchase had been expected. 

The acquisition will afford Supermarkets General access 
into New England’s retail food and drug market. Purity Su- 
preme operates 43 supermarkets and Heartland food ware- 
houses in Connecticut, Massachusetts, Maine and New Hamp- 
shire. The company’s retail drug store holdings include 24 
Pharmacity drug stores and Heartland deep discount drug 
stores.

Cash offer for Jewel McKesson sets yearly goal 
of 15% per-share growth 


draws 75% of stock 


SALT LAKE CITY—American Stores has reported that its 
cash tender offer for the Chicago-based Jewel Companies has been 
oversubscribed. 

American’s tender offer for the food and drug retailing concern 
indicated that the company was seeking to acquire 67% of total! 
common stock and preferred stock outstanding. By the time the 
offer had expired on July 5, American said a preliminary report 
showed that approximately 11.8 million common shares and 2. 
million preferred shares of the Jewel stock outstanding were tend- 
ered, which represents approximately 75% of the total shares. 

A meeting of shareholders of both American Stores and the 
Jewel Companies is scheduled to take place in August.

SAN FRANCISCO—Mc- 
Kesson Corp. has set a corpo- 
rate goal of 15% annual com- 
pound growth in per-share 
earnings over the next three 
years, according to Neil E. 
Harlan, chairman and presi- 
dent. 

“This three-year goal will be 
updated annually to take into 
account changes in the inflation 
rate, real growth of the Gross 
National Product and other ex- 
ternal factors,” Harlan said ina 
letter to stockholders contained 
in the 1984 annual report. 

Other company objectives: a 
15% return on average equity 
by 1987 (17% by 1989) and a 


debt-to-capital ratio that will 
provide the company with con- 
tinuing access to capital mar- 
kets on favorable terms. 

At the end of the 1984 fiscal 
vear, McKesson’s return on 
average equity was 11.8% and 
the debt-to-capital ratio was 
20%. 

Harlan’s letter also said the 
company Is nearing the end of a 
transition period. ““We are 
shedding those businesses with 


either unsatisfactory returns or 


limited growth prospects. In 
their place we have expanded, 
through acquisition and inter- 
nal development, into new 
areas of distribution and ser- 


vices,” he said.

company has almost abandoned 
is the food business.

dropped by McKesson were

1982 and the C. F. Mueller pas-

through acquisition and inter- 
nal development, into vet- 
erininary supplies, personal

equipment, fragrances and of- 
fice supplies.

Script survey 


Generics play smaller role 
inamoxicillin/ampicillin field 


NEW YORK—The amoxicil- 
lin‘ampicillin drug store market 
experienced significant chang- 
es during the 15-month period 
from January 1983 through 
March 1984. Among them: 

e Beecham tightened its grip 
on the market, as the firm’s 
drug store script volume ad- 
vanced nine share points. The 
firm now commands 43% of ail 


amoxicillin/ampicillin scripts. 


@ Generics are playing a less 
significant role among the lead- 
ing 24 ampicillin/amoxicillin 
products dispensed through 
drug stores. This year, for the 
first time, only generic ampicil- 
lin 250mg capsules made the list 
of leading products. In 19&2, 
however, 
ampicillin 2 50mg and 500mg as 
well as amoxic illin 250mg held 


perc versions of 


positions among the top 24 


products dispensed. 

® rare the price of an 
average ampicillin/amoxicillin 
script remained unchanged at 
$7.72, the average price of the 
market leaders’ scripts gained 
40¢ and now stands at $8.15. 
Prices among the all other 
group averaged $6.02 per 
script, a decline of almost $1.60. 

Tnese were some of the main 
findings of a survey conducted 
by Texas-based PharmAssist 
from script data collected dur- 
ing March 1984. 

Other findings indicated that 
retailer margins for ampicillin 
amoxicillin products averaged 
14%, a2— point gain over pre- 
vious levels. The margin gain 
was even stronger among the 
top 24 products, which chalked 


up a record average of 46%. 
Although retailer margins 
advanced for almost all leading 
dopa the average prescrip- 
tion price paid by consumers for 
seven of the top 10 amoxicillin 
ampicillin products declined. 
i i his means manufacturers such 
s,eecham, Wyeth and Parke- 
Davis cut prices to retailers and 
a portion of the price decline 
passed through to consumers. 
Retailer margins for the “All 
Other” category fell 2 points to 
36% during the audit period. 
Products appearing for the 
first time among the top 24 in- 
clude Amoxil Chewables 250mg 
(Beecham), Amoxicillin 250mg 
Caps and Suspension 250mg 
4m] (Parke-Davis) and Wymox 
200mg C my, and 125mg/5m! 
Suspension (Wyeth).

hat is a Triple A product? 

Basically, it is a product 
that shoppers know by 
name, by reputation and by pack- 
age and purchase by price. 

Thus began the editors’ introduc- 
tion to the first Triple A Product 
Study published 15 years ago in 
Chain Store Age Drug Edition, 
Drug Store News’ predecessor. 

In the end, the editorial went on to 
say, the primary function of Triple A 
merchandise is to draw traffic. 

There have been a lot of changes in 


drug store merchandising in the 
past decade and a half, but the basic 
premise set down in that first Triple 
A study remains as true—and as 
fresh—today as it ever was. 

The Triple A products are the 
ones that provide drug store retail- 
ers with promotional heat. They are 
featured in ads and they are given 
preferential in-store treatment. 
They pull the traffic and they gener- 
ate hefty gross profit dollars. 

Typically, the same products and 
manufacturers turn up on the Top 


100 list year after year. What would 
a Triple A Study be, for example, 
without a Procter & Gamble or Col- 
gate-Palmolive, without a Kodak or 
Polaroid, without a Gillette or John- 
son & Johnson? 

These are the super marketers. 
Tney create consumer demand with 
useful products, and they spend the 
money to keep those products alive 
in customers’ minds. 

But while the basic core of prod- 
ucts remains the same year after 
year, the Top 100 list continues to 


undergo change as new consumer 
needs create fresh product introduc- 
tions. The recent growth of products 
geared for contact lens users is a 
good example. 

Although retailers in the past 15 
years have grown a great deal more 
sophisticated in tracking item move- 
ment, the concept of a national list of 
best-selling products remains as 
useful today as it ever was. It can 
still serve as a promotional barome- 
ter and as a checklist against which

Film dominates lists 

In this year’s Triple A Product 
Study, the top 10 places on the dol- 
lar, unit and profit charts are again 
dominated by film products, with 
Polaroid’s SX 70 instant film emerg- 
ing as the No. 1 dollar producer and 
Kodak’s C110 film heading the unit 
list. 

In fact, Kodak managed to grab 
five places on the Top 10 unit list and 
three on the Top 10 dollar list, while 
Polaroid’s SX 70 film took two of the 
places on the Top 10 dollar list—first 
place for its single pack and sixth for 
the twinpack. 

As for gross profit dollars, film 
was even more dominant, with six of 
the Top 10 places going to Kodak 
products. 

This year batteries were tracked 
for the first time in the Triple A 
Study. Highly consumable and 
placed at heavy traffic locations, 
batteries scored in the survey, gain- 
ing 12% of the places on the unit list, 
9% of the dollar places and 13% of 
the profit dollar spots. 

On the Top 10 lists, batteries were 
particularly strong in generating 
gross profit dollars, gaining 3 of the 
10 places. 

In terms of profit dollars, the only 
other category besides film and bat- 
teries to gain a place on the Top 10 


list was eye/lens care—Bausch & 
Lomb’s Softlens 24s. 

Other categories that took places 
on the Top 10 lists in dollars and 
units included cough/cold, laxatives, 
baby needs, dental/oral care and re- 
ducing aids. 

Computerized data 

To compile the 1984 Triple A Prod- 
uct Study, Drug Store News com- 
puterized and ranked warehouse 
withdrawal data from a wide variety 
of retail drug store chains and major 
wholesalers. The data was for a full 
year, which eliminated seasonal 
skews. 

We originally started out compar- 
ing item movement, dollar sales and 
gross profit dollars within 21 spe- 
clally selected general merchandise 
and health and beauty aid catego- 
ries. 

By the time we had finished rank- 
ing and computerizing the data, 
however, only 13 categories 
emerged as major players in the Top 
100 rankings. 

In the Top 100 unit sales list, there 
were a total of 17 categories, but 
only 13 of these had more than three 
products represented. 

Fifteen categories emerged in the 
dollar sales ranking, but only 11 had 
more than three products repre- 
sented. 

On the gross profit dollar list, 
there were also 15 categories, but 
only 11 of these had more than three

Five top categories 

Stories on the major categories 
appear throughout this section, but 
to summarize the results, there 
were five categories that repeatedly 
made it into the top rankings in all 
three dimensions. 

Kilm, again, was the top-produc- 
ing category. In addition to its domi- 
nation of the top 10 lists, it also 
scored heavily on the Top 100. Film 
gained 14% of the places in unit 
sales, 17% in dollar sales and 15% in 
gross profit dollars. 

Only in dollar sales was there a 
product category that gained more 


places than film on the Top 100 list, 
and that was baby needs. 

saby needs, with 12 products 
ranked in the Top 100 unit sales list, 
tied with batteries (12 products 
ranked in the Top 100) for the second 
most productive category. 

The baby needs category, with its 
thin margins, was not as productive 
interms of gross profit dollars, but it 
did manage to come in fourth with 
seven places on the Top 100 list. 

Dental needs, which placed 14 
products on the Top 100 list, tied 
with film in that area, but the cate- 
gory took third place in gross profit 
dollars with eight products.

Large size baby care products draw traffic 


Predictions that the baby boomlet 
would increase sales throughout the 
1980's are coming true, with various 
types of diapers, formulas and baby 
washcloths peppering the list of Top 100

products. 

Not only have these products grown 
in sales, but new, larger sizes have par- 
ticularly caught on, causing some drug 
chains to expand the sizes of their baby 
departments and weed out slower-mov- 
ing products. For example, 32-0z. sizes

in unit sales. 

These sales parallel findings by A. C. 
Nielsen that show disposable diapers, a 
$2 billion market, grew 13% between 
1982-83. Sales in drug stores make up 
10.5% of this total. Other findings show 
that disposable washcloths, a $135 mil- 
lion market, grew by 22%, and that 
baby lotions and powders, a $110 million 
market, increased by 19%. Drug stores 
sell 29% of baby lotions and powders, 
and 16% of washcloths. 

Popular large-quantity boxes of dis- 
posable diapers have caused a dilemma 
for drug stores. While these space-tak- 
ing packages draw traffic, they also 
must be footballed to compete with su- 
permarkets and mass merchandisers. 
Not only are the Huggies’ 33’s good sell- 
ers, but other industry leaders include 
the 48-diaper boxes of Luvs, Pampers 
and Huggies and the 60-count Pampers. 

To overcome the squeeze on margins 
from diapers, and formulas, drug chains 
mix profitable items in the baby care 
department, such as private label 
cloths, shampoos, powders and oil, 
which can bring in margins as high as 
50%. Even brand name cloths can yield 
margins of anvwhere from 25% to 40%.

Razors, blades retain 


their sharp profit edge 


Despite heavy competition from su- 
permarkets, drug chains continue to 
record strong sales results from the 
razors and blades category. 

According to Drug Store News’ an- 
nual report on the chain drug industry, 
razor and blade sales last year climbed 
11.6% to $114.8 million. Overall, razor 
and blades account for 4.8% of the toilet- 
ry department sales. 

Not surprisingly, the moderately 
priced razors and blades placed higher 
in the Top 100 listing by unit sales than 
by dollar sales. However, razors and 
blades, with their strong profit mar- 
gins, figured strongly in the list of Top 
1°9 by gross profit margin. 

The leading razor and blade products 
by unit movement were Good News dis- 
posable razors 3’s, Bic men’s shavers 5’s 
and the Atra cartridges 5’s. 

In dollar sales, the leading sellers 
were Atra cartridge 10’s, Gillette Trac 
II, Atra cartridges 15’s and Atra car- 
tridges 5’s. According to the Triple A 


Product Study, the biggest money- 
makers in the shaving products catego- 
ry were Atra cartridge 10’s, Good News 
disposable razors, Bic men’s shavers 5’s 
and Atra cartridges 5’s. 

Disposable razors are the best per- 
former in the category for most drug 
chains. Drug retailers have been able to 
offset the competition from supermar- 
kets and discount stores with disposable 
razors by taking advantage of off-shelf 
display fixtures from manufacturers 
such as dump bins. 

In addition, many drug store oper- 
tors merchandise disposable razors and 
replacement blades in key traffic loca- 
tions, such as the front-end checkouts. 

While drug chains appear to be hold- 
ing their own in the battle to retain the 
razor and razor blade business, only one 
shaving cream product managed to 
make the Top 100. Barbasol regular 11 
oz. made the Top 100 of leading sellers 
by units, based on its low average price 
point.

Batteries score high on every AAA product list 


With the exception of film, no catego- 
ry had as many products featured in the 
Triple A Product Study as did batteries. 

Batteries finished among the leading 
products in dollar sales, unit sales and 
overall profit dollars. In addition, the 
Triple A report reveals considerable 
selling strength in the three major 
sizes—D, C and AA—as well as in the 
alkaline and heavy-duty varieties. 

Six batteries were listed among the 
Top 20 selling products by unit sales. 
Duracell and Eveready each nad three 
products in the Top 20. Duracell’s al- 
kaline D battery 2-pack placed high- 
est—seventh overall in the Top 100 in 
unit sales. Its AA alkaline 4-pack and 
alkaline C battery 2-pack also finished 
strongly. 

Eveready also had its D, C and AA 
batteries in the Top 20 in unit sales. 
Eveready’s heavy duty D, C and AA 
batteries dominated the remainder of 
the Top 100 unit movement chart. 

The higher-priced alkaline batteries 
were the only battery products listed in 
the Top 100 by dollar sales. However, 
Eveready still had five and Duracell had 
four different batteries listed in the top 
100 by dollar volume. 

Batteries are among the most profit- 
able products carried in drug stores. 
This point was driven home by the Tri- 
ple A survey. Of the Top 25 products in 
terms of gross profit dollars, eight were 
battery products. Duracell’s alkaline 
AA 4-pack batteries was the highest 
gross-profit-dollar producer.

Cough/cold products accounted for 
approximately 9% of all unit sale prod- 
ucts in Drug Store News 1984 Triple A 
Product Study. 

The fastest-moving product was 
Chap Stick, which ranked first in its 
category and fourth in the total unit 
rankings. Its closest competitor, 
Robitussin DM 4 oz., a cough medica- 
tion, ranked second in the category but 
29th in overall rankings. Chap Stick’s 
advertising, low price, ease of use as 
well as its relative high consumability 
accounted for its strong showing in the 
unit category. 

In total profit dollars, Chap Stick also 
did well, showing up second in its cate- 
gory and 20th in the overall Top 100 
rankings. Actifed tablets 24’s was the 
most profitable item in the category in 
gross profit dollars, a reflection in part 
of its relatively high ticket, which also 
helped place it No. 1 in dollar sales. 

Actifed was also the only OTC conver- 
sion product to make the list in unit 
movement. In the Top 100 unit sales, it 
ranked 43rd. 

Only two products that made it into 
the Top 100 dollar sales rankings failed 
to also make it into the Top 100 gross 
profit dollar rankings: Contac Caps 10's 
and Drixoral tabs 10’s. It is possible that 
intensive promotions within these cate- 
gories shortened overall margins just 
enough to keep them out of the Top 100 
gp dollars. Contac 10’s was eighth in its 
category on unit movement and 80th 
overall.

By Jim Ricchiuti 

NEW YORK — Genovese 
Drug Stores has opened its first 
full-line automotive depart- 
ment in the basement of a new 
12,000-sq.-ft. store in Jackson 
Heights in the New York City 
borough of Queens. 

The 3,000-sq.-ft. automotive 
department, which the Mel- 
ville, N.Y.-based drug retailer 
has dubbed the Genovese Auto 
Warehouse, is considered by 
some analysts as a test project 
in what may become another 
area of specialty retailing for

the company opened its first 
home health-care store not far 
from the location of the first 
Genovese drug store.

tite Aid’s newest unit,

than the depot unit. The new 
Dayton store averages 15,000 
sq. ft.: 10,000 is allocated for 
backroom; 1,000 is for office 
support space, and 4,000 is de- 
voted to the selling area.

Patterson Avenue doesn’t look 


like a retail store. There are no 
gondola runs, merchandise is 
displayed on pedestals rising 
from the floor and on shelving 
against perimeter walls. “We 
tried to provide a professional 
appearance, like a physician's

Drug Castle Franchises to open 
four new deep-discount stores 


SPRINGFIELD, Ohio — 
Drug Castle Franchises Inc., a 
deep-discount franchisor head- 
quartered here, plans to open 
its first four franchised stores in 
Houston, Orlando, Fla., and 
Fort Wayne, Ind. 

The stores will be fashioned 
after the two-year-old Drug 
Castle deep-discounter in 
Springfield, which is owned by 
Brown Drug Co. Drug Castle 
Franchises is a separate opera- 
tion, but its president, Richard 
Brown, is also president of 
Brown Drug Co., a 15-year-old 
chain of six traditional drug 
stores in south central Ohio. 

If the Drug Castle franchise 
operation is successful, it will 
become the second major fran- 
chisor of deep-discounters. 
Drug Emporium, headquar- 
tered in Columbus, Ohio, has 22 
franchised stores out of a total 
of 32 units. 


Like Drug Emporium, initial 
capitalization for Drug Castle 
stores is $600,000. The one- 
time initiation fee for Drug Cas- 
tle franchisees is $20,000, com- 
pared to the $25,000 required to 
become a Drug Emporium, ac- 
cording to industry sources. 

Drug Castle franchisees 
must also pay royalty fees, but 
the corporation would not say 
how much. 

According to Dale Obracay, 
vp of Drug Castle Franchises, 
options to franchise have al- 
ready been signed for two 
stores in Houston and one in Or- 
lando, with one in Fort Wayne 
soon to be signed. He said the 
franchisor would like to open at 
least one other location this 
year and possibly 10 more in 
1985. Markets that are being 
considered are Philadelphia, 
New Orleans and areas in New 
Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio 


and Michigan. 

Obracay said there are also 
plans to convert the existing 
Drug Castle to a franchisee. 

Drug Castle prefers to open 
stores in locations where there 
are no other deep-discount 
stores, Obracay said. 

While there may not be any 
other deep-discount stores in 
the first locations, the franchi- 
sees Will be facing stiff competi- 
tion from mass merchandisers, 
supermarkets and drug store 
chains. In Houston, for exam- 
ple, not only are there a large 
number of Walgreens and Eck- 
erd drug stores, but kK mart and 
Target discount stores. 

In Orlando, there are also a 
number of Eckerd and Wal- 
greens stores as Wellas K mart, 
Zayre and Albertson's. Fort 
Wayne has Hook's, Revco, 
Walgreens, Kroger, K mart

inserted into newspapers varies by location, according to Budd

more chainwide runs were tried around Christmas and a fourth in 
February 1984. Revco’s fiscal vear ended in Mav.

Nielsen vp says chains 
losing race for H&BA sales 


Continued trom page o 


Dic k Schaefer, vice president of 


H&BA for Majors Corp., and 
Richard Aubry, the company's 
marketing manager, presented 
data that suggested that such a 
reversal might indeed be under 
way. The firm specializes in ad 
and promotion analysis. 

In the first quarter of 1984, 
after two vears of reducing ad 
space for H& BA, drug stores 
increased ad space in that cate- 
gory by 27%, Majers discov- 
ered. 

At the same time, they said, 
food and mass-merchandise 
stores were devoting less space 
to H& BA. 


Aubry and Schaefer said they 


saw this return to increased 
drug chain emphasis on core 
H&BA items as a “positive shift 
that should be continued.” 
They said the way to regain 
and continue to experience mo- 
mentum with I He BA products 


is by aggressively using lead 
features and hot prices. 
“Aggressive tle-Ins In Sun- 


day ads backed up with store 
displays will dramatially in- 
crease volume,” they advised. 
In other presentations at the 
show, Allen Karcher, director 
of Trade Relations for Eastman 
Kodak, and Vincent S. Zuccaro, 
vice president of professional 
services for Barnes-Hine Hy- 
drocurve, discussed new trends 


In the photo and eve care cate- 
gory, respectively. Dave Rob- 
Inson, National marketing man- 
ager tor Hallmark, and Bill 
Marter, national sales director 
for Ambassador, discussed 
trends in the greeting card cate- 
gory. 

Howard Stumpf, president of 
the Point of Purchase Advertis- 
ing Institute and John Kawula, 
vp, discussed the preliminary 
findings of their 1983 drug store 
consumer buying habit study. 
A full in-depth analysis of that 
study will be presented in Drug 
Stores News Dee. 10 issue. For 
the results of the initial find- 
ings, please see our April 16, 
1984 issue.

group seeks stronger voice 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — The 
National Wholesale Druggists’ 
Association (NWDA) is expect- 
ed to give the go-ahead to a 
merger with the Drug Whole- 
salers Association during an 
NWDA membership meeting 
here Aug. 27. 

The merger was previously 


approved by DWA’s member- 
ship and NWDA’s board of di- 
rectors. Final authorization 
rests with NWDA‘’s members. 

Both groups have been push- 
ing for the action, believing that 
if unified, they would have a 
stronger voice with Govern- 
ment representatives.

NEW YORK — Strategic 
growth plans at Genovese Drug 
Stores call for a vearly 10 in- 
crease In neW stores, and chain 
chairman and president Leon- 
ard Genovese expects most of 
that growth to come from exist- 
ing markets. In fact, Genovese 
believes the chain can event ual- 
lv double the number of stores 
Within its trade area. 

The 79-store Melville, N.Y.- 
based chain operates in some of 
the most heavily populated and 
lucrative markets in the coun- 
trv. “Our markets [metropoli- 
tan New York, New Jersey, 
Connecticut and Massachu- 
setts] have 10% of the nation’s 
population and 20 of the dis- 
posable income,” Genovese 
pointed out. 

Although the chain has avoid- 
ed Manhattan—the heart of 
New York City’s business and 
cultural activities—Genovese 
hinted to a recent gathering of 
retail analysts that the chain 
might take astab at the Big Ap- 
ple. 

“We will perhaps go vinto 
Manhattan shortly,” he told the 
zroup, but would not elaborate.

should have no problem meet- 
Ing its growth goals. For exam

accommodate up to 12 more

Jersey.”

ovese, Pathmark is the biggest 
competitor. However, he feels 
Pathmark’s combo shoppers 
differ from those who use Geno- 
vese for drug store needs. 

“They have their peas and

the right locations and fair
