DRUG STORE NEWS, August 20, 1984 


FINANCIAL 


Second-quarter results at Hook 
end period of downward earnings 


INDIANAPOLIS — Sec- 
ond-quarter 1984 results ended 
a downward earning trend that 
had spanned two quarters at 
Hook Drugs Inc. Hook’s chair- 
man and president, J. Douglas 
Reeves, reported that this 
should mark the end of de- 
pressed earnings for the chain. 

“With two difficult earning 
periods now behind us, we an- 
ticipate steady improvement in 
our overall performance the re- 
mainder of the year,” Reeves 
said. He added that the im- 
proved second-quarter figures 
represent efforts by the chain to 
control expenses. 

Sales for the quarter, ended 


June 30, rose 10.1% to $86.6 
million from $78.6 million in the 
same period last year. Net 
earnings advanced 3.5% to 
$1.94 million. 

For the first six months of the 
fiscal year, sales reached $168.3 
million, up 9.6% over last vear. 
Net earnings, however, 
dropped 12.7% to $3.3 million 
from $3.8 million. Much of the 
earnings decline dates back to 
the first quarter, when Hook 
Drug wrestled with some of the 
worst weather on record in its 
trade area. 

Reeves said the most recent 
results “indicate areas in which 
further sales and expense con- 


trol efforts are required to pro- 
duce respectable increases in 
both sales and earnings by 
year’s end.” 

He added, “While much work 
lies before us, it is the type of 
work with which every employ- 
ee is familiar—and I have every 
confidence that 1984 will end as 
another fine year for the share- 
holder.” 

During the second quarter, 
Hook’s added five new stores, 


bringing to 310 the number of 


retail units. Four of them were 
Hook’s drug stores, the fifth a 
Hook’s Convalescent and Home 
Health Care Center, the chain’s 
14th such unit. 


Investment income cited 


Bindley Western 
posts earnings rise 


INDIANAPOLIS — Bindley Western Industries, a major drug 
wholesaler specializing in the distribution of ethical pharmaceuti- 
cals to drug chains, reported that earnings for the second quarter 
ended June 30 increased 59% to $1.3 million from $791,000 in the 
corresponding year-earlier period. 

Sales for the quarter advanced 15% to $133.5 million from $115.7 
million. Earnings per share rose to 40¢ from 36¢. 

For the first six months, earnings increased 68% to $2.3 million 
from $1.4 million a year earlier. 

Sales rose to $264.9 million from $232.7 million, and earnings per 
share increased to 72¢ from 62¢. 

William E. Bindley, chairman, attributed the strong gains to 
continued improvement in gross margins, effective inventory and 
cost-control programs and a “significant increase in investment in- 
come generated from the working capital management system.”

Based on the latest FLE.C.

Overall, drug store industry 
PACs have made 1983 contribu-

and Senate candidates since the 

1982 elections.

channeled nearly $40,000 into 
state and local campaigns, as 
Well as $19,850 into allied indus-

run by NACDS and NARD.

sis found that industry political 
fund-raisers gave nearly 70% of 
their contributions to Republi- 
can Congressmen during the 
1982 races.

figures—which reflect PAC 
payments made since the 1982 
elections—show that political 
contributions for the 1984 race 
are almost evenly divided.

pumped 54% of their Federal 
contributions into Democratic 
campaigns. 

The amount of these contri- 
butions varied greatly, ranging 
from as little as $100 to several 
thousand dollars. 

Most of the contributions 
weighed in between $200 and 
$750, however, with Democrats 
and Republicans receiving an 
average Of 3939 each.

coffers bulging 


WASHINGTON — Trade 
association PAC’s representing 
the nation’s prescription and 
over-the-counter drug manu- 
facturers have been significant- 
lv less active than drug store in- 
dustry political fund-raisers, 
the latest FLE.C. filings re- 
vealed. 

Specifically, the Pharmaceu- 
tical Manufacturers Associa- 
tion PAC raised only $2,745 
since the 1982 election while po- 
litical fund-raisers at the Pro- 
prietary Association collected 
Just mb. 

In contrast, the National As- 
sociation of Chain Drug Stores 
has nearly $40,000 in its 1984 
campaign coffers and the Na- 
tional Association of Retail 
Druggist’s PAC receipts for the 
upcoming November elections 
Lops $27,000.

fund-raisers had contributed 
$1,275 to three Congressional

fedolphus Towns (New York).

Was Senate Labor and Human

ardiovascular drugs are the 

most productive pharmaceuti- 

cals, according to the first Drug 
Store News Top 100 Prescription Prod- 
uct Movement Survey. 

The survey is based on rankings pro 
vided by Decision Data, a North Arling- 
ton, Tex.-based supplier of pharmaceu 
tical marketing research. 

The Drug Store News survey shows 
that cardiovascular drugs account for 26 
of the 100 products ranked by number of 
scripts dispensed, 32 of all products 
ranked by dollar sales and a whopping 
27 of all Top 100 products ranked by 
gross profit dollars. 

Cardiovasculars had twice as many 
products in dollar sales than the nearest 


competitor, antiarthritic drugs, which 
placed 15 in the Top 100. The category 
almost. doubled its nearest. rivals” in 
scripts dispensed and profitability. 

Antibiotics, our analysis found, was 
the second most productive pharmaceu- 
tical category in terms of number of 
scripts written (16) and highest volume 
gross profit dollars (16). 

Antiarthritics, with 15 produets in 
the Top 100 dollar sales ranking, was 
second to cardiovascular drugs in that 
category and third in number of prod 
ucts in the gross profit dollar rankings. 

Survey results were based on product 
movement data gathered in more than 
2,000 retail outlets. An expanded Top 
200 movement rankings is available in 


the April 1984 edition of Drug Store 
Veuw's Pharmacy Reterence. 

[In most cases, the products that made 
It into our Top 100 on all three rankings 
were “old standbys” such as Dyazide, 
Tylenol w codeine, Tagamet, Valium, 
Cte. 

Newer “specialized” medications 
such as calcium channel blockers have 
not had enough exposure vet to propel 
them into the highest movement rank- 
ings. But industry sources agree that 
the potential for these and other new 
specialized products is great. 

At the bottom of the most productive 
drug category list were decongestants, 
Victims possibly of the recent trend to- 
ward conversion of prescription prod-

Tranquilizers 


America is a stress-producing  soci- 
ety, and one of the consequences of that 
fact of life is the prominence of Valium in 
all three of our Top 100 rankings. 

Valium was the fourth most produc- 
tive product on both our Top 100 fastest 
moving scripts and highest volume dol- 
lar rankings, and it was the fifth most 
productive product on our Top 100 list- 
ing of gross profit dollar producing prod- 
ucts. 

In fact, Roche's Valium accounted for 
half of the tranquilizers that made it into 
our Top 100 listing of fastest moving 
scripts. 

All three strengths of Valium were 
represented: Valium 5mg was the No. 1 
tranquilizer dispensed; Valium 10mg 
was No. 3 and Valium 2mg was No. 5.

Antiarthritics 


Since its launch Feldene has 
enjoyed tremendous levels of 
acceptance by the medical com- 
munity, and this success is re- 
flected in terms of script counts, 
dollar sales and gross profit dol- 
lars. 

The drug captured the No. 3 
position in dollar sales among 
the Top 100 drugs sold in drug 
stores, thereby making Fel- 
aene 20mg the No. 1 brand 
among all antiarthritics. Fel- 
dene 20mg also captured the 
ninth position among the lead- 
ing Rx products generating the 
greatest gross profit dollars for 
retailers. 

Motrin tablets 600mg regis- 
tered 15th place on our Top 100 
chart, thereby capturing the 
leading spot among antiarthrit- 
i¢ scripts dispensed. In addition 
to being the fastest moving 
antiarthritic drug, Motrin 600 
placed second among. antiar- 
thritic dollar sales and gross 
profit dollars. 

Antiarthritic products from 
MSD surprisingly made up half 
the entries in the antiarthritic 
groupings. These include Indo- 
cin capsules 25mg, which 
ranked 37th among the Top 100 
scripts dispensed, Flexeril Tab- 
lets 10mg, which ranked 52nd in 
the Top 100 and Clinoril Tablets 
200mg, which ranked 57th in 
the Top 100. 

The antiarthritic category 
was fourth in terms of the num- 
ber of products contributed to 
the three Top 100 rankings. The 
category had four products in 
the Top 100 scripts dispensed, 
three in the Top 100 highest 
gross profit dollars and two in 
the highest dollar sales.

Analgesics 


Analgesics had a total of 11 
products in our Top 100 highest 
gross profit dollar rankings, 
making it, in conjunction with 
antiarthritics, the third most 
profitable category in DrSN’s 
survey. 


Two of the category’s most 
profitable products, Tylenol 
tabs with codeine 30 mg and 
Davrocet-N tabs 100mg made it 
into the Top 10 most profitable 
products in the Nos. 2 and 4 po- 
sitions, respectively. 

Tylenol was also No. 2 in 


our Top 100 listing, while Dar- 
vocet-N was fifth in both dollar 
sales ana number of scripts. 
Prices of analgesics are often 
less competitive than mainte- 
nance medications, which are 
prescribed for long periods of 
time. Analgesics are prescribed 
in smaller quantities for rela- 


number of scripts dispensed in 


tively shorter periods of time, 
which adds to the profitability 
of that category. 

In terms of scripts, the anal- 
gesic category captured eight 
positions among the Top LOO 
pharmaceuticals dispensed in 
drug stores.

EDITORIAL 


Buying allegations may spur Revco power play 


By Elizabeth Parks 

There are a E : 
lot of words you | 
can use to de- | 
scribe the cur- 
rent unsettled 
condition at 
Revco: confus- 
ing, ambiguous, 
provocative, cu- 
rious, dramatic. 
Riveting, given : a’ 
the current #?y @ Baya... 
state of rumors and eounter. rumors, is 
probably the most apt description. 

' At this point in the story, it is very 
hard to say exactly what is going on in 
the company or exactly what the out- 
come might be. But the situation looks 
like it’s shaping up as a battle for control 
of a $2 billion organization. The possibil- 
ity exists that the man who built Revco 
from a small, 30-unit local chain to a na- 
tional institution may be iced out of the 
picture by partners that friends say now 
they warned him to be leary of. 


At the heart of the controversy are al- 
legations about “purchasing impropri- 
eties” made by two dissident stockhold- 
ers, Isaac Perlmutter and Bernard 
“Bernie” Marden, president and chair- 
man, respectively, of Odd-Lot Trading, 
a recently acquired Revco subsidiary. 

Until recently Perlmutter and Mar- 
den were close friends of Sid Dworkin, 
Revco’s president and ceo, and his two 
sons, Marc, executive vp of marketing 
and operations, and Elliot, senior vp of 
marketing. 

Suddenly in mid-August, however, 
Perlmutter and~Marden went public 
with allegations that Revco’s purchas- 
ing department, under the supervision 
of Elliot Dworkin, was overbuying. 

A special committee made up of out- 
side directors at Revco was appointed to 
investigate the allegations and to exam- 
ine transactions allegedly involving a 
number of brokers and manufacturers. 
However, only one manufacturer was 
specifically mentioned as being under 
investigation, Joseph DeKama, a Pa- 


ramus, N.J.-based broker who is a 
friend of the Dworkins and whois said to 


have done between $40 million and $60: 


million in business with Reveo during 
the past year. 

Nospecific charge has been leveled 
against DeKama. 

The committee will soon determine 
whether the allegations about “impro- 
prieties” are founded on any real basis 
or whether there is, as many suspect, 
another reason for the charge: a power 
play meant to embarrass the Dworkins; 
discredit theix management; provoke a 
proxy fight, and permit control of the 
company to pass from the Dworkins to 
Perlmutter and Marden. 

There are a number of people in the 
industry who agree with that analysis. 
“T’ve known Budd (Elliot’s nickname) all 
my professional life, 20 years,” says one 
broker, “and I’ve never known him to do 
a dishonest thing.” 

“Perlmutter and Marden are tough, 
tough businessmen,” says another 
source. “They have 12% of the stock and

Pharmacy crime law squabbles continuing 


By Ken a 

The chief Con- si 
gressional archi- 
tect of the new 
Federal pharma- 
ey-crime bill 
signed by Presi- 
dent Reagan 
earlier this sum- 
mer—House 
Crime Subcom- 
mittee Chairman 
William Hughes 
(D-N.J.)—will address the NACDS 
Pharmaceutical Conference this month in 
an effort to clear the smoke still surround- 
ing the lobbying activities of various 
pharmacy groups that led to passage of 
the compromise measure. 

Hvghes will have his work cut out for 
him, thanks to the continuing accusa- 
tions from officials at the National Asso- 
ciation of Retail Druggists that indepen- 
dent druggists were double-crossed by 
most other national drug store and phar- 
macy groups during the fashioning of 
that compromise legislation. 

NARD, which opposed the Hughes 
pharmacy-robbery bill at every corner 
and then took full credit for its enact- 
ment in a letter to President Reagan, is 
now claiming that the legislation “bears 
NARD’s* imprint throughout because 
the association’s lobbyists worked 


steadfastly at every step of the legisla- 
tive process to improve it.” 

(The key “improvement” obtained by 
NARD lobbyists allows Federal au- 
thorities to prosecute drug store rob- 
beries resulting in significant—rather 
than serious—bodily. injury. Other, ar- 
guably more important changes in the 
Hughes bill, including a reduction in the 
dollar threshhold for ‘Federal involve- 
ment from $1,000 to $500 worth of 
drugs, were actually made at the re- 
quest of NACDS.) 

But the legislative infighting between 
NARD and other pharmacy groups dur- 
ing the debate over the Hughes bill was 
miid in comparison to the post-enact- 
ment recriminations surfacing now as 
both sides attempt to claim credit for the 
new law. 

NARD?’s latest enemies list, pub- 
lished in the association’s July Journal, 
includes virtually all of the major indus- 
try supporters of the final new pharma- 
cy-crime law, including APhA, NACDS 
and NWDA (which according to NARD 
“sold out the profession” by endorsing 
the Hughes bill). 

Significantly, however, NARD’s pub- 
lished list of “SOBs” who “caved in” by 
backing the pharmacy-crime legislation 
now also includes the Pharmaceutical 
Manufacturers Association, the Propri- 
etary Association, the Drug Wholesal- 


ers Association and the National. Drug 
Trade Conference which may have “out- 
lived its usefulness” after refusing to op- 
pose the Hughes bill, NARD officials 
said. | 

Even Drug Store News niade the lat- 
est NARD enemies list for portraying 
the independent druggist group as “the 
stumbling block” in the way of final 
pharmacy-crime legislation this year. 

And Hughes himself came under 


heavy fire from NARD officials who de- . 


scribed the committee chairman as 
“mean spirited” after he publichy fin- 
gered lobbyists for the independent 
druggists group for repeatedly causing 
“dissension” among pharmacy organiza- 
tions working for a new robbery bill. 

Unquestionably, however, NARD’s 
sharpest barbs are being directed at 
representatives of the nation’s drug 
wholesalers—particularly NWDA ex- 
ecutive vp William Ford. 

In a letter to NWDA‘s board of direc- 
tors, NARD Executive Committee 
chairman H. Joseph Schutte accused 
Ford and other staffers at the wholesale 
druggists association of “blind obstina- 
cy” for failing to “defer to NARD’s wish- 
es” during the debate over the bill. 

NWDA‘s 


Schutte charged. 


they know their own power. I think they 
see an opportunity and they’re going for 
the jugular.” 

The feeling on the street is that Perl- 
mutter and Marden want to take over 
the company either by spending another 
$200 million to $300 million to acquire a 
controlling interest, probably with addi- 
tional partners, or by pushing for a 
proxy fight and settling for a compro- 
mise position that gives them control of 
either the presidency or some other key 
management position. 

Perlmutter and Marden, in fact, have 
informed the Securities and Exchange 
Commission that they might pursue 
such a course, depending partly on the 
findings of the investigation committee. 
They could also, of course, choose to sell 
their holdings to another company, to 
the Dworkins, or the Dworkins might 
sell their holdings to them. 

At presstime, none of these outcomes 
was certain. But the general conviction _ 
on the part of everyone we interviewed 
was that a war was imminent and with 
each passing day, a compromise was be- 
coming less and less likely. 


“betrayal of NARD is far 
worse or different than that of NACDS 
which has never posed as a friend,”

lobbying against direct-to-consumer ad-

with its suit te relax the three- year-old 
consent decree: 

At issue in the controversy: a 1981 


. Federal order resolving Justice Depart- 


ment charges that APhA’s past policy of 
discouraging Rx price advertising rep- 
resented an illegal and anticompetitive 
trade restraint. 

That consent order—which is sched- 
uled to remain in force until 1991— 
sharply restricts APhA from taking for- 
mal association action to prevent or dis- 
courage the advertisir g of prescription 


drugs, including direct-to-consumer ads 
by pharmaceutical manufacturers 

Key APhA leaders as well as many 
rank-and-file pharmacists are deeply 
concerned over the prospect that Food 
and Drug Administration officials may 
relax the agency’s longstanding ban on 
‘Rx drug ads directed to consumers, but 
‘without a modification of the existing 
antitrust order tie association will be 
severely restricted in participating in 
that debate. 


The present battleground is a Federal 
court in Michigan, where APhA has 


filed suit for relief from those restraints. 


Justice Department attorneys, how- 
ever, urged the court to keep that order 


intact.

Adams Drug Co. reports 


rise in 2nd quarter earning 


PAWTUCKET, R.I. — Aa- 
ams Drug Co. reported that 
second-quarter earnings. rose 
42.7% to $1.28 million 
$898,000 during the same peri- 
od a year ago. 

Sales for the second quarter 
ended June 30 increased 12.4% 
to $81.8 million from $72.7 mil- 
lion in 1983. The company at- 
tributed the sales increase to 


the Easter selling season ae 
curred in the second quarte¥ 
this year as compared with last 
year, when the Easter season 
fell in the chain’s first quarter. 
Adams also cited an overall in- 


the fact that a major eacon 


from . 


crease in volume for the strong 
sales results. 

On per-share basis, net earn- 
ings rose 41% to 31% per share 
from 22% during the same peri- 
od last year. 

Net income through the first 
six months of the year were up 
26% to $1.85 million from $1.46 


during the first six months of 


1983. Net earnings per share 
for the first half of the fiscal 
year rose 254 40 45¢ from 36¢ 
the previous year. 


During the first six months of 


the year Adams said sales were 
up 9.1% to $156.5 million from 
$143.4 million in 1983. 


As of June 30, Adams was op- 
erating eight fewer stores than 
a year before. The company 
said the store closings were the 
result of a chainwide effort to 
“phase out smaller, less-profit- 
able stores. and focus on opening 
larger stores with pharmacy 
departments.” 

The Pawtucket, R.I.-based 
chain also reported: that its 
board of directors declared a 1¢ 
per share dividend. 


Adams operates 420 stores in ~ 


10 states in the Northeast un- 
der the names Adams, Brooks, 
Eckerd of western Pennsylva- 
nia, Nescott and Whelan.

with our 1984 Drug Review and at the same time send a

W: would like to salute the drug industry once again this year 


in 1983, consumer dollar sales through retail drug stores in- 
creased at a 10% rate vs. 1982 while overall inflation was 3.2% 
over the same interval. Sales through chain drug stores continued 
to expand during 1983 at a faster rate than total drug store dollar 
volume, as chains carved out a new high of 57.4% of the retail drug 
business.

the drug industry.

Chapter 1 


During 1983, total U.S. Retail Sales 
reached $1.2 trillion dollars, a9% in 

crease over 1982. Strong gains as 
our economy gets back on its feet. It 
is important to note that much of the 
gain in retail sales can be considered 
“real” gains since prices rose very 
little in 1983. 


Drug and proprietary stores sales 
accounted for 3.3% of total U.S. re- 
tail sales holding on to a position 
they achieved in 1982. The areas of 
greatest retail growth during 1983 
included retail automotive sales 
(+21%) and the hardware & lumber 
sector (+ 18%). 


Allindications point to 1984 as being 
another year of strong growth as 
well. Increasing employment and 
low rate of price inflation continue 
to help fuel consumer retail sales de-

PRICE INFLATION IN GENER- 
ALISSLOWING BUT THE COST 
OF MEDICAL CARE I5 STILL 
MOVING UPWARD QUICKLY 


Price inflation has definitely 
slowed. The Consumer Price Index 
for all items rose only 3% during 
1983. However, there were steep 
gains within the medical care seg- 
ment. Hospital room costs, already 
6 times greater than 1967 (double 
the all item inflation rate), in- 
creased by another 11% from 1982 
to 1983. 

Prescription drug .prices also rose 
by 11%, while over-the-counter 
drug prices grew by 7% from 1982.

Chapter 2 


RETAIL DRUG STORE SALES 


During 1983, retail drug store sales 
reached $39.7 billion, 10% greater 
than 1982. Part of this increase can 
be attributed to the rising cost of 
prescriptions and part from “real” 
growth. 


Chain drug store sales increased by 
11% during 1983 and now account 
for 57.4% of total drug store sales. A 
chain is defined as four or more 
stores under common ownership. 
Continued expansion and acquisi- 
tion, competitive merchandising, 
and aggressive inventory manage- 
ment are all factors contributing to 
the strong chain drug store growth 
trend we have seen over the past 
several years. 


Independent drug store sales grew 
by 8% in 1983. The $16.9 billion of 
sales generated in independents 


now represents 42.6% of total drug 
store sales. 


The strongest growth from within 
the chain drug store universe has 
come from those stores with a sell- 
ing area of between 10,000-15,000 
sq. ft. These types of stores now ac- 
count for 26.8% of total chain drug 
store volume, up 12.8 points from 
1978. | 


Chain drug stores under 5,000 sq. 
ft. and those between 5,000 to 
10,000 sq. ft. are no longer account- 
ing for the same level of sales en- 
joyed in 1978. The 5,000 to 10,000 
sq. ft. stores still account for the 
largest portion of chain drug sales, 
38.7%, but their share has declined 
six points since 1978. The very large 
chain stores, with over 15,000 of 
of selling area, have also declined 
slightly in importance since 1978, 


dropping 1.1 points toa 10% share in 
1983. 


DRUG STORE SALES IN- 
CREASE UNIFORM ACROSS 
a... 


During 1983, drug store sales 
growth by geographic area did not 
vary much from the U.S. average 
increase of 10%; with the exception 
of Metro New York where sales in- 
creased only 6% over 1982. 


Drug chains, whose overall sales in- 
creased 11% over a year ago, either 
ther held or increased their impor- 
tance in all Nielsen Territories. This 
is true even in Metro Los Angeles 
and the Remaining Pacific areas of 
the country, where they already 
dominate the market, and account 
for almost three out of every four 
dollars spent in drug outlets.

HEALTH & BEAUTY AID 
SALES ACHIEVE 6% REAL 
GROWTH IN 1983... 


During 1983 sales of the total Niel- 
sen 49 Health and Beauty Aid cate- 
gories in drug, food and mass mer- 
chandisers combined grew by 6% on 
a weighted unit or “real” basis. 
Drug outlet real sales held better 
than steady actually increasing 1% 


over 1982. However food stores. 


(and most combos are included 
here) increased unit sales 7%; while 
mass merchandisers realized a 12% 
increase in sales. 


Total dollar sales in drug, food and 
mass merchandisers combined in- 
creased by 10%. However drug 
stores increased sales just 6% while 
food and mass merchandiser stores 
increased their H&BA sales by dou- 
ble that amount. Apparent price in- 
creases were lowest in mass mer- 
chandisers (+3%) while drug 
(+6%) and food (+5%) prices for 
the 49 categories increased at about 
the same rate.

INTERNAL MEDICINES ARE 
STRONGEST DRUG OUTLET 
CATEGORIES... 


Within drug stores, the strongest 
categor y growthcame from internal 
medicines, up 3% on a unit basis and 
12% on a dollar basis. Men’s prod- 
ucts, up 7% in dollar sales and 2% in 
unit sales, and oral hygiene, up 4% 
in dollar sales and 2% in unit sales, 

also enjoyed strong growth in 1983. 


Within the internal medicine group- 
ing the headache remedies, and 
cold/sinus products categories were 
quite active during 1983. And with- 
in the oral hygiene grouping, 
mouthwash and dentifrice items are 
enjoying strong sales. 


INVENTORY MANAGEMENT 
BECOMING MORE EFFICIENT 


“Real” or weighted average inven- 
tory levels in food, drug and mass 
merchandise stores combined for 
Nielsen’s selected 49 Health & 
Beauty Aids increased 3% during 
1983. However, drug outlet inven- 
tory levels did not rise. They fell 1% 
from 1983, marking the third year in 


a row that drug inventories have | 


been reduced. 


Some of the inventory declines in 
drug cutlets is due to a slowing of 
sales as food outlets continue to ac- 
count for a greater portion of 
HB&A purchases. On the other 
hand, drug retailers are also making 
more efficient use of their inven- 
tories by gradually increasing their 
rate of inventory stockturns. 


DRUG OUTLET INVENTORIES 
REDUCED 1% AS EFFICIENCY 
INCREASES... 


During 1983, drug stores reduced 
their “real” or weighted average in- 
ventory levels by 1% for Nielsen’s 
select 49 Health & Beauty Aid cate- 
gories. There were commeasurate 
increases in stockturns (inventory 
efficiency) as sales grew by 1%. 


Since 1978, stockturns for the 49 
H&BA’s have increased 21% to a 
1983 average of 4.6 turns per year in 
drug outlets. 


Measuring from a year ago, stock- 
turn rates increased in all groupings 
except hair care and paper goods. 
Inventory build ups within these 
two groupings were slightly greater 
than sales increases.

HEALTH AND BEAUTY AIDS 


IN DRUG CHAINS HEADACHE 
REMEDIES GENERATE ONE 
OF THE HIGHEST PER FOOT 
PER MONTH SALES VOLUME. 


The categor y of headache remedies 
generated the highest sales per lin- 
ear foot in chain drug stores in 1983, 
averaging $43.96 per foot per 
month. Face creams & lotions were 
a close second with $42.75 in sales 
per foot per month, followed by dis- 
posable diapers and sanitary pro- 
tection at $36.98 and $34.75 respec- 
tively. 


Within drug independents, as in 
chains, the highest selling categor y 
was headache remedies averaging 
$33.63 per linear foot per month fol- 
lowed by face creams & lotions at 
$24.18. Laxatives were third with 
sales per linear foot per month of 
$21.68 and alkalizers were fourth 
with sales of $22.73 per linear foot 
per month. 


The amount of linear feet of shelf 
space allocated in 1983 to most of the 
selected 49 H&BA categories being 
tracked by Nielsen remained rela- 
tively stable for drug stores as a 
whole. 


However there were some signifi- 
cant shifts in allocations within 
chain drug outlets. Cold remedies 
and sinus product space allocations 
increased 4 linear feet im 1983 over 
1982 while headache remedies and 
OTC vitamin products both grew by 
2 linear feet. In large independents, 
there were similar increases in 
these categories. All of these cate- 
gories have been very active during 
1983.

Chapter 5 


SCANNING 


SCANNING STORE UNIVERSE 


During 1983, the number of grocery 
stores with scanning installatiens 
grew by 26% to 8,150. These stores 
currently account for 35% of total 
food store dollar sales volume. We 
project that within three years, the 
number of scanner equipped food 
stores will increase by an additional 
55% and that these stores will ac- 
count for 50% of total food store 
sales. 


By December 1983, scanner 
equipped supermarkets accounted 
for 69% of total food store sales in 
Denver, the major market with 
highest scanner development. 
Closely following are Los Angeles 
(60%), Miami-Fort Lauderdale 
(59%), Chicago (55%), St. Louis 
(55%) and Seattle-Tacoma (54%). 


Rapid increases in the number of 
UPC coded products and sharp de- 
clines in the cost of scanning sys- 
tems have not only helped to main- 
tain the trend of new scanning 
installations in retail food stores,

but also have encouraged the devel- 
opment of scanning point-of-sale 
systems in other types of retail out- 
lets. Drug retailers such as Revco, 
Pay-N-Save, Eckerd, SuperX, 
Medi Mart (Boston), Drug Fair 
(New Jersey), Save-On and Peoples 
are well into experimenting with 
the systems and the McKesson Cor- 
poration, a drug wholesaler, has 
just announced an integrated cash

scanning system. 


Of course the list of hard cost sav- 
ings that are used to initially justify 
the system installation keeps grow- 
ing. Improved price control, shrink 
reduction, and improved employee 

roductivity are immediate gains 

or any type of retailer. Direct store 
delivery control, price remeva!, and 
automated reordering are addition- 
al significant hard cost benefits that 
are being realized by those retail or- 
ganizations using or experimenting 
with scanning technologies. 


Ir addition to the hard cost savings 
available to retailers installing scan- 
ning systems, there are soft savings 
that can be realized. Of particular 
interest is the ability to link the ef- 
fects of retail level promotions on 
consumer sales. 


The promotional evaluation chart, 
drawn from the Nielsen experi- 
ence with scanning generated infor- 
mation in grocery stores, is an ex- 
ample. Here, a mouthwash 
manufacturer offered a large trade 
allowance to encourage retailer pro- 
motional support on his item. For 
the item alone, average weekly 
sales jumped 652% (752 index 
points) above sales during non-pro- 
motione! neriods in stores that sup- 
ported the item with both a display 
and a major ad; and, average week- 
ly sales for the entire category in- 
creased by 62% (162 index points) at 
the same time.

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 3, 1984 


OTC Buyer Survey 


Detailers visit Top 100 chains most freq 


NEW YORK — Can a retail- 
er who is an independent drug 
store operator or an over-the- 
counter product buyer for a 
chain ranked somewhere be- 
tween 101 and 200 in dollar vol- 
ume expect the same service 
from over-the-counter product 
manufacturers as Top 100 
chains? 

According to a recent 
Lebhar-Friedman study com-

On average, detail sales per- 
sonnel from over-the-counter 
product manufacturers service 
the drug store retailer quite dil- 
igently. However, there are 
significant differences in the 
frequencies of service provided 
to Top 100 chains as compared 
with second-tier chains and in- 
dependent drug store retailers. 

According to the Lebhar- 
Friedman survey of chain and 
independent OTC buyers, 97% 
of all Top 100 chain buyers re- 
port that they see an OTC detail 
person at least once every three 
months. However, only 80% of 
buyers for second-tier chains 
and just 77% of buyers for inde- 
pendent retailers report that 
they see an OTC person that 
frequently. 

Furthermore, the survey 
found that specific manufactur- 
ers have a habit of visiting Top 
100 chain buyers much more 
frequently than they visit ei- 
ther independents or buyers for 
second-tier chains. 

When we tried to assess how 
effective vendor salesman real- 
ly are as sources for communi- 
cating important product infor- 
mation to OTC buyers, we 
found that twice as many Top 
100 chain buyers found sales- 
men to be “very effective in 
communicating information” 
than did their second-tier and 
independent counterparts. 

We also found that most OTC 
buyers rely heavily on trade 
news stories and trade news ad- 
vertising for learning about 
particular OTC products. Buy- 
ers for second-tier chains and 
for independents are especially 
dependent on this information. 


Visits from manufacturers

uently then they did buyers 
or second-tier and independent 
operations.

how often they saw detail peo-

70% of our respondents at least 
once every three months.

were visiting 9 out of every 10

least once every six months. 
These companies included 
Parke-Davis, Upjohn, Lederle,

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 3, 1984 


Top chains introduce the most new products 


NEW YORK — In the OTC, 
Proprietary category, the Top 
100 chains introduce the most 
new products during the course 
of a year and their buyers again 
report feeling the most satisfied 
with the support and service 
levels they received from man- 
ufacturers. 

Buyers for the Top 100 chains 
reported introducing an aver- 


age of 86 new products in the 
course of a year while buyers 
for second-tier chains intro- 
duced an average of 72, and in- 
dependents an average of 40. 
When a Top 100 chain intro- 
duces a new product, manage- 
ment usually takes space from 
existing products rather than 
expand the department. Seven 
out of 10 Top 100 merchandisers 


weed out slower movers or poor 
profit-producers to make way 
for promising new products. In 
contrast, second-tier chain 
merchandisers are just as in- 
clined to expand the depart- 
ment as they are to pare it (50- 
50). Six out of every 10 
independents will expand a de- 
partment rather than pare it. 
Chains are also much quicker

Total sales in the over-the- 
counter category in drug stores 
increased more than 12% iast 
year, sparked by a late break- 
ing flu season and the public’s 
acceptance of former prescrip- 
tion-only products converted to 


OTC status. 


The addition of just one OTC 
converted product, Drixoral, 
hypec sales 54% in the cough/ 
cold category for Page Drug in 
Dallas while a see, convert- 
ed decongestant, Actifeds took 
seventh place in unit volume 
sales in Drug Store News’ Top 
100 volume OTC products 
study. 

Obviously aware of the posi- 
tive impact of conversions on 
OTC sales, most of the retailers 
contacted in Drug Store News’ 
recent OTC industry study, re- 


port that they are currently in- 
creasing shelf space for the cat- 
egory, and doing so primarily 
because of conversions. 

They also report that they 
are getting more requests from 
customers for help in shopping 
the category and that there is 
growing customer confusion 
about the OTC products in the 
category. 

Nearly 8 out of 10 indepen- 
dents in our study reported that 
they have increased space for 
OTC preducts. Three out of 10 
say they see “growing customer 
confusion.”

say they are taking advantage 
of this increased exposure and 
contact with consumers to im-

How the study 
was conducted 


Findings in this survey are 
based on a total of 90 15-minute 
telephone interviews with buy- 
ers of over-the-counter drug 
products for chains and inde- 
pendently owned retaii drug 


| stores. 


Thirty completed interviews 
were conducted among inde- 
pendents, and 60 interviews 
were completed among chains. 
The number of respondents 
among chains was evenly divid- 
ed among the 100 largest drug 
retailers and smaller chains. 
These second-tier units ranked 
between 101 and 200 in dollar 
sales volume for 1983. 

Some 22% of the chain re- 
spondents in the survey worked 
for companies with five or fewer 
stores; 20% worked for compa- 
nies with six to 19 units; 20% 
worked for firms with 11 to 20 
units; 15% worked for compa- 
nies with 21 to 99 units, and the 
remaining 20% worked for com- 
panies operating 100 or more 
units. 

Qualified chains were select- 
ed at random from the 1983 
Lebhar-Friedman Directory of 
Drug Stores and H&BA 
Chains. Independent stores 
were randomly selected from a 
combination of Drug Store 
News circulation lists and the 
Dun and Bradstreet listing of 
independents. 

A qualified respondent was 
the individual responsible for 
purchasing OTC health aids and 
raedications.

INTRODUCTION OF NIELSEN 
SCANTRACK MAJOR MARKETS 


In November of 1984, the A. C. 
Nielsen Company will incorporate a 
new scanning based food store anal- 
ysis and reporting service into its 
regular consumer sales measure- 
ment services. The enhancement, 
called Nielsen ScanTrack Major 
Markets, wiil initially be availavle 
in ten major market areas where 
scanning based food retailers ac- 
count for between 70% to 80% of to- 
tal large supermarket dollar volume 
(supermarkets are defiaed as those 
stores with annual volumes of $4 
million and over). These markets 
are Boston, Chicago, Houston, In- 
dianapolis, Kansas City, Los Ange- 
les, Jacksonville/Orlando, Subur- 
ban New York, San Francisco and 
Seattle. 


Nielsen ScanTrack Major Market 
Service will be available to both 
manufacturers and cooperating re- 
tailers. It represents a major in- 
vestment on Nielsen’s part to begin 
transforming the mass of data avail- 
able from scanning into manageable 
reportsthat can enhance the making 
of major marketing sales and mer- 
chandising decision. 


The advent of scanning based re- 
porting technology will add several 


new analytical dimensions to help 
increase marketing and merchan- 
dising productivity. This includes 
the ability of scanners to record all 
important consumer sales transac- 
tion elements on a store-by-store, 
i a and UPC-by-UPC 
asis. 


A second new analytical dimension 
opened up by scanning technology 
will be the direct linking of mer- 
chandising tactics with sales. The 
information can be tabulated in time 
intervals that fit the analysis allow- 
ing greatly improved promotion and 
retail price analysis as well as new 
item evaluation. 


A third dimension, really a by-prod- 
uct of scanning technology, will be 
the development of a product identi- 
fication language common to manu- 
facturers, distributors and retail- 
ers. The key to this common 
language is the universal product 
coding system, a numeric code that 
will remain the same throughout 
the distribution channel. This will 
permit the development of reports 
that can be understood by all partic- 
_— involved in manufacturing, 

istributing and retailing consumer 
goods.

By Jim Ricchiuti 

TWINSBURG, Ohio — The 
volatile struggle for control of 
Revco D.S. showed no signs of 
dissipating late last month as 
dissident shareholders Bernard 
Marden and Isaac Perlmutter 
requested that Revco manage- 
ment provide them with a 
shareholders’ list. 

The latest salvo fired by the 
two Odd Lot principals, who 
own nearly 12% of Revco, fur- 
ther fueled speculation that 
they were considering a move 
to take control of the $2 billion 
drug chain. 

In a filing with the Securities 
and Exchange Commission, 
Marden and Perlmutter also 
stated that they had retained 
Drexel Burnham Lambert Inc. 
to provide them with financial 
advice 

But while the threat of a 
proxy fight remained a possibil- 
ity, industry analysts believe 
that even with a shareholder 
list the two dissident sharehold- 

rs lack the necessary time and 
support to oust Revco chair- 
man, president and ceo Sidney 
Dworkin. 

Earlier last month, Revco 
mounted a counteroffensive 
against Marden and Perlmutter 
by rejecting as “self-serving” 
their demands that they receive 
six seats on Revco’s 13-member 
board. 

In proxy material mailed last 
month, Revco also asked share- 
holders to allow the chain’s 
board to “exercise the right of 
first refusal” to buy back the 4.4 
million shares Marden and Perl- 
mutter received when they sold 
Odd Lot to Reveo in May. 

However, in an apparent con- 
cession to Marden and Perlmut- 
ter Revco said that it would not 
ask shareholders to approve 
any antitakeover measures in 
its annual meeting next week. 
The chain also agreed to pro- 
vide the two Odd Lot execu- 
tives with two seats on the 
board, which Marden and Perl- 
mutter in turn rejected.

Herrlich purchase bolsters Rite 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. — Rite Aid’s acquisition 
late last month of the six-store Herrlich’s Drug Stores 
in Flint, Mich., is the chain’s second move into Michi- 
gan within the last three months. 

With the Herrlich’s purchase so close on the heels of 
the 24-store Muir deal, industry sources say that Rite 
Aid has pegged Michigan as a prime growth area. 

Although the state is dominated by Pontiac, Mich.- 
based Perry Drug, it is also home to a great number of 
smaller chains and independents. ; 

“It only makes sense that Rite Aid is preparing an 
assault on Michigan,” said one observer. “It's the last 
remaining market where there are stores left to buy.’ 

Local small-chain operators confirmed that the 
1,206-store chain is pursuing growth in Michigan. Said 
one chain president, “Feelers are out for acquisitions. 


They want to fill in markets where they aren’t and 
push closer to 2,000 stores.” 

Pat Early, Rite Aid’s spokesman, said the chain’s 
emphasis on Michigan is “only natural because of our 
presence in northern Ohio.” 

However, despite signs that Rite Aid is set to in- 
vade Michigan, Sentry’s vp Chuck Fugate points out 
that the chain is steering clear of Detroit and relying 
on fringe markets. 

“It’s not Rite Aid’s style to butt heads with the large 
chains,” he said. “They want to find their own niche.” 

But Rite Aid will go head-to-head in Flint (popula- 
tion 523,600) with Perry, which, according to Metro 
Market Studies, controls better than 15% of the area 
volume. Additionally, the former Herrlich’s stores, 
which average 7,000 sq. ft., will compete with strong

thought they were going out of business,” a competi- 
tor said. “They have two good stores, the other four 
are in bad areas.” 

Added another Flint operator, “Herrlich’s had poor 
locations and untidy housekeeping.”

Morris Axelrod of Thrifty dies 


LOS ANGELES — Morris Axelrod, who died last month at 
76, left his imprint on Thrifty Drug’s buying department for al- 
most a half-century. 

Axelrod—known by his contemporaries as “Ax”—started 
with Thrifty in 1936, seven years after Thrifty opened its first 
store, as an advertising copy writer. In the ensuing years, he 

vitated to buying. For many years prior to his death, he 
eld the title of executive vp, buying, and supervised a staff of 
25 to 30 buyers. 

He became a director of Thrifty in 1969 and was also a mem- 
ber of the chain’s finance committee. 

Despite a gruff exterior, Axelrod was “morally good and 
kind,” says a Thrifty exec who worked with him for 40 years. 
His son Ellis is assistant vp in operations. 

Suppliers describe Axelrod as “hard-nosed but fair.” He had 
the reputation of being a shrewd bargainer, and with the im- 
mense power of Thrifty’s 500-plus stores, he not only cut some 
sharp deals but made sure his buyers used the leverage fully. 

As a result, suppliers rate Thrifty buyers as among the 
toughest in the business when it comes to rock-bottom prices. 
By the same token, a sale to Thrifty meant a large order. Thus, 
negotiations were not always conducted in subdued tones. 


Perry to. buy Pappy’s 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores has reached an 
agreement in principle to acquire the three-store Pappy’s Dis- 
count Auto Stores Inc. heeed in St. Louis. The stores range in 
size from 4,500 sq. ft. to 7,000 sq. ft. 

This marks Perry’s second acquisition in the St. Louis mar- 
ket. The chain recently proposed a takeover of the 24-store 
Jack Lambert-Singer Auto Parts chain, St. Louis’ largest 
auto-parts retailer. 

Perry currently operates 52 FAS auto stores and 26 Auto 
Works outlets. 


Bartell scales down nutrition dept. 


SEATTLE — After two years of testing nutrition depart- 
ments in four stores, Bartell Drug spent months fine-tuning 
the mix and scaling down the size. 

Now the chain has installed streamlined departments in 13 
of it 21 stores. The other eight stores will be phased in within 
the year. 

Originally, Bartell devoted 20 to 36 ft. to nutrition, depend- 
ing on store size. Now the department is 12 to 20 ft. The origi- 
nal mix was 50% food and 50% natural vitamins. Because vita- 
mins weie accounting for 75% of sales, Bartell changed the 
allocation to 70% vitamins, 20% food and 10% H&BA. 

In the final shakeout, food was eliminated and H&BA re- 
turned to its regular home. The mix now consists of natural vi- 
tamins and books.

tions, including the chain’s deep-discount Drug Palace stores.

Victory for chains is seen 
in court ruling on imports 


WASHINGTON — The Fed- 
eral Court of International 
Trade has slammed the door on 
efforts by multinational manu- 
facturers to choke off supplies 
of “gray-market” imports to 
drug chains and other Ameri- 
can retailers. 

In a precedent-setting deci- 
sion upholding the Customs 
Service’s current policy that 
prevents foreign manufactur- 
ers and their United States sub- 
sidiaries from blocking “unau- 
thorized” imports of their own 
products, the court concluded 
that Congress never intended 
to give foreign suppliers such 
power over the domestic mar- 
ketplace. 

The ruling represents a clear- 
cut victory for a number of ma- 
jor drug and discount store 
chains that have been quietly 
lobbying Congress and the Rea- 
gan Administration to resist 
pressure from foreign manufac- 
turers for sweeping new re- 


strictions on “gray” or “paral- 
lel” imports. 

At issue in the dispute: a 
nearly 50-year-old Customs 
Service interpretation of Fed- 
eral law under which American 
subsidiaries or other corporate 
relatives of foreign manufactur- 
ers: are not entitled to prevent 
the unauthorized importation of 
their own legitimately trade- 
marked products. 

Since many multinational 
manufacturers price their prod- 
ucts sabetmatialls higher in the 
United States than in other 
countries, drug chains and oth- 
er domestic retailers are often 
able to secure significant sav- 
ings on brand name watches, 
cameras, fragrances and other 
products by bargain-shopping 
overseas markets. 

Even relatively inexpensive 
items such as Duracell flash- 
light batteries can be purchased 
from European distributors at 
as much as 40% below the prices 


charged by the manufacturer in 
the United States market. 

In seeking authority to block 
unauthorized chain imports of 
these products, foreign firms 
maintain that retailers who 
purchase their goods abroad 
and ship them to the United 
States without authorization 
are “free riding” on their trade- 
marks. 

But the Court of Internation- 
al Trade rejected these argu- 
ments as immaterial by ruling 
that the only real question is 
whether Congress intended to 
give this degree of marketplace 
power to foreign manufactur- 
ers. 

That ease, which involved at- 
tempts by a Japanese camera 
manufacturer (Vivitar) to re- 
verse the Customs Service’s 
pclicy, hinged on the court’s 
finding that Congress intended 
the law to protect American 
firms from unfair practices by

Key Drug is new name 
for Pay Less’ small stores 


WILSONVILLE, Ore. — 
Pay Less NW has selected Key 
Drug as the name for its new 
small-store format. 

The first Key Drug will open 
around the first of November in 
Sequim, Wash., approximately 
65 miles northwest of Seattle. 
The freestanding store, with 
17,000 sq. ft. overall and 11,500 
*) ft. of selling area, is the site 
of a former grocery store. 

Upcoming Key stores will ei- 
ther be takeovers of vacated 
premises or built from the 
ground up. 

During 1985, Pay Less plans 
to open five to 10 Key Drugs in 
the states where it now oper- 
ates—Washington, Oregon, 
Idaho and California. 

Pharmacists will manage the 
stores, which are expected to 
generate between $1.5 million 
and $2 million in sales. Size of 
the units will vary from 10,000 
to 17,000 sq. ft. overall and 
8,000 to 12,000 sq. ft. of selling. 

Sequim (pronounced squim) 
has a trading area of 12,000 sq. 
ft. and is called the “Sunbelt of 
Washington” because it has less 
rainfall than the rest of western 
Washington. Sequim’s claim to 
fame is its wild animal farm, 
which trains animals for the 
movies. 

Key Drug stores, called “mini 
Pay Lesses” by chain execs, will 
contain most of the depart- 
ments of a conventional 30,000- 
sq.-ft. Pay Less but will be 
scaled to size. Altogether there 
will be about 15,000 sku’s in the 
store, compared with 25,000 in 
conventional Pay. Less units. 

The mix will also be tailored 
to the community. For exam- 
ple, if there is a sporting goods 


store nearby, then Key will not 
have one. 

The stores are pegged for 
small towns with populations of 
5,000 to 10,000 which cannot 
support a conventional Pay 
Less drug store. Two major de- 
partments—Rx and OTC—are 
expected to account for 35% of 
the store’s volume. 

Key Drug completes a triad 


of store formats which 
strengthens Pay Less’ market- 
ing flexibility. The other two 
types are the conventional 30,- 
000-sq.-ft. superstore and the 
Value Giant deep-discount. 

The first Value Giant opened 
in Portland in July. Two more, 
both in Hayward, Calif., are 
— to open in Septem- 

er. 


NWDA merger signed: 
Treffrey named exec vp 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. —Just 
one day after members of the 
National Wholesale Druggists’ 
Association approved a merger 
with the Drug Wholesaler As- 
sociation, executives from both 
associations formally signed the 
merger agreement. 

The NWDA now represents 
more than 95% of the wholesale 
drug industry, making it the 
single organization responsible 
for all drug wholesalers. 

“For the first time in the his- 
oF of our industry,” said 
NWDA chairman Elmer Fiery, 
“all wholesalers can now speak 
with one voice.” 

Fiery said the unity will per- 
mit NWDA to play an even 
greater leadership role in rep- 
resenting the interests of 
NWDA’s member companies. 

Prior to the merger, 
NWDA‘s membership. repre- 
sented approximately 90% of all 
shistaaiioes: About 66% of all 
DWA members were members 
of NWDA. 

The merger agreement was 
signed by Fiery and DWA pres- 


ident Robert W. Meyer Aug. 
28. Meyer is a one-year elected 
official, as is Fiery. 

Charles Treffrey, DWA’s ex- 
ecutive vp, now becomes execu- 
tive vp and coo of NWDA—sec- 
ond in command to president 
Bill Ford—while his assistant 
Janet Cordiano becomes assis- 
tant director of member ser- 
vices, reporting to Bob Mc- 
Hugh, NWDA’s vp of member 
services. 

Cordiano, who officially 
joined the NWDA staff Sept. 4, 
will be responsible for coordi- 
nating all program services and 
meeting activities for NWDA’s 
independent members (those 
who operate single distribution 
centers as opposed to multiple 
distribution centers). 

According to NWDA sourc- 
es, the proxy vote by the 
NWDA membership to deter- 
mine the merger was “well in 
excess of the two-thirds major- 
ity required.” 

DWA’'s membership had al- 
ready approved the merger at 
an earlier meeting.

Pay ’n Save earnings drop for second quarter 


SEATTLE — Pay ’n Save’s 
earnings dropped substantially 
for the second quarter in a row, 
the company reported. 

According to the diversified 
Seattle-based retailer, net in- 
come for the quarter ended July 
28 fell 64% to $3.1 million, or 20¢ 
a share, from $8.4 million, or 
58¢ a share, in the correspond- 
ing year-earlier period. 

Sales for the quarter ad- 
vanced 14% to $342.2 million 


from $301.5 million. 

Cal Hendricks, vice chairman 
of the board and chief financial 
officer, said the lower earnings 
were the result of several fac- 
tors, including “disappointing” 
same-store sales gains and 
“comparative weakness” in 
gross margins, particularly in 
the Ernst Home Center divi- 
sion. 

In addition, Pay ’n Save took 
one-time losses from the sale of 


six unprofitable California 
stores and the closing of two 
others, one in California and the 
other in Hawaii. Start-up costs 
associated with Price Savers 
Membership Warehouse and 
Northwestern Drug Co., the 
wholesaler acquired earlier in 
the year, also hurt earnings. 
“We are confident that our 
long-term strategies to im- 
prove operating efficiencies and 
merchandising methods will 


pay off in greater future profit- 
ability despite the disappoint- 
ing results of the present,” 
Hendricks said. 

He added that the opening of 
a second Price Savers eacher- 
ship Warehouse in Fife, Wash., 
had been “very well received by 
customers” and two more are 
scheduled to open, in Seattle 
and Anchorage, later this year. 

“Another bright spot,” he 
said, “is the warehousing po- 


tential of the highly mechanized 
Northwestern Drug Co. North- 
western has recently expanded 
warehousing of merchandise 
for our Pay ’n Save and Bi-Mart 
drug divisions. We expect to be- 
gin warehousing additional 
items for the Ernst Home Cen- 
ter Division later this year.” 
For the first two quarters, 
earnings declined 64% to $4.1 


million, or 26¢ a share, from - 


$11.3 million, or 79¢ a share.

Convenience, quality remain photo dept. assets | 


Continued from page 13 


Quality problems still plague 
some one-hour operators. Many 
have gone belly up from the 
large investment outlays for 
equipment and high rental 
rates. And still another prob- 
lem facing many mini-labs is the 
consumer resistance toward 
paying the higher processing 
costs in one-hour service. 

‘The difficulties experienced 
by many one-hour operators is 
now causing. many industry ex- 
perts to re-evaluate market 
share projections for mini-labs 
over the next few years. Indus- 
try estimates now are that mini- 
labs may penetrate only 15% of 
the market in the near future. 

In some eases, the predicted 
shakeout in the one-hour indus- 
try has left some drug store 
photo-processing executives 
wondering if they reacted too 


quickly to the mini-lab threat. 
When Crest Photo, the pho- 
to-processing division of the 
Chicago-based Osco Drug, 
launched its seven-day-a-week, 
next-day service it mounted a 
major advertising program to 
promote the faster turnaround 
service. But while the chain’s 
photo processing volume in- 
creased, it was only a tempo- 
rary increase. Once the adver- 
tising campaign was over, 
Osco’s volume slipped back to 
its pre-express service level. 
A spokesman at White Drug 
Stores, a 43-unit chain in North 
Dakota, said the chain has de- 
cided not to compete directly 
with the one-hour labs by 
stressing turnaround time. 
“Customers come into our 
stores and drop off their film be- 
cause it’s convenient,” he said. 
“I don’t think the average per-

son knows how fast they can get 
their film developed.” 

According to the PMA con- 
sumer survey, 35.7% of the re- 
spondents said that one week 
was a reasonable amount of 
time to wait to have their film 
aeveloped. Twenty-nine per 
cent said three days, while 
18.8% felt two days an accept- 
able amount of time. Less than 
10% of the respondents felt they 
should receive next-day ser- 
vice. 

In fact, among consumers 
who rely on drug stores for their 
photo-processing needs, speed 
in returning pictures was re- 
garded as the most important 
factor in-choosing a particular 
photo-processing outlet by only 
10.4% of the respondents in the 
PMA consumer survey. 

The survey clearly indicated 
that the two most important 
reasons why consumers drop 
their film off in a drug store are 
still convenience (35.7%) and 
quality reputation (28.6%). 

Some retailers have likened 
the mini-lab phenomenon to the 
explosive growth of photo ki- 
osks in the 1970’s. Kiosks had 
been considered the mrt seri- 
ous threat to the drug store pho- 
to-processing business in recent 
years. However, as many opera- 
tors reached the maturation 
point and as many areas of the 
country became saturated with 
these outlets, kiosks began de- 
clining in overall numbers and 
market share. 

For the most part, chains 
have put most of their efforts 
behind promoting quality. 
Chains such as Eckerd and Gen- 
ovese Drug in Melville, N.Y., 
which operate their own photo- 
processing plants, offer con- 
sumers larger prints. 

Genovese two years ago also 
began providing its photo-pro- 
cessing customers with Photo- 
gard, a protective coating devel- 
oped by 3M that prevents 
photographs from fading, 
smudging, scratching or wet- 
ting. 

Sal Giaramitta, general man- 
ager at Genovese’s Living Color 
photo-processing division, said 
that the chain is attempting to 
communicate to customers that 
it provides the same careful ser- 
vice with photo processing as it 
does with pharmacy. 

Many drug retailers view su- 
permarkets and discount stores 
as their most serious competi- 
tive threat. Supermarkets with 
their large network of store lo- 
cations and sharp pricing tactics 
may pose the biggest challenge. 

Drug chains have tried to off- 
set the competition by offering 
additional services. White 
Drug was able to boost its pho- 
to-processing volume by ap- 
proximately 50% last year by 
kicking off a twin print pro- 
gram. White now provides all of 
its customers with two prints 
‘or one low price. 

While offering two prints for 
one price is not a new strategy 
in the industry, White Drug 
spotted the demand for such a 
program in its operating mar- 
kets, and thus far the program 
has paid dividends.

1984: Boom year for computer hookups 


ndustry sources are fore- 

casting a boom year for new 

pharmacy-computer instal- 
lations as computer technology 
improves and prices fall. 

It is now estimated that by 
the end of this year, about 15,- 


000 drug stores, approximately 
30% of the industry, will have 
pharmacy computers. 

“With this evolution in tech- 
nology and decline in the cost 
over a period of time, we have 
Seen a general proliferation of 


computers by both the indepen- 
dent and the chains,” says Wil- 
liam A. Lockwood, president 
and publisher of Computer- 
Talk, a publication specializing 
in pharmacy and medical com- 
puter systems.

Many of the chains and inde- 
pendents that have pharmacy 
computers are also finding so- 
phisticated new applications for 
them, such as running software 
that links electronic in-store 
communicating cash registers 
to in-store mini and micro com- 
puters. 

To date, independents have 
been more aggressive in phar- 
macy-computer installations, 
but. Lockwood sees the chains 
quickly closing the gap. 

“Right now 25% of the inde- 
pendent pharmacies are using 
pharmacy-computer systems, 
compared with 20% for the 
chains,” says Lockwood. He es- 
timates that by the end of 1984 
the number of independents 
and chains using computers will 
be equal. “We project that 
about 30% of all independents 
and chains will be operating a 
puarmacy-computer system by 
year end,” he added. 

With entry-level-prices aver- 
aging around $15,000, Lock- 
wood says the current payback 
on a system is excellent. 


“When paid out over a five- 
year period, it costs the phar- 
macy only $8.22 a day before 
taxes to own his own computer 
system,” says Lockwood. “Now 
that’s a real bargain.” 

One chain in the computer 
fast lane is Genovese Drug 
Stores. According to Wayne 
Carona, assistant vp, pharmacy 
services, of the 72-store Mel- 
ville, N.Y.-based chain, new 
computer systems are being in- 
stalled at the rate of one or twoa 
week. “We’ve taken the IBM 
pharmacy-computer package 
and rewritten the software to 


-tailor-make it to our needs,” 


said Carona. Genovese plans to 
have the entire chain computer- 
ized by the end of 1984. 

In the past, stores that did 
the highest volume of prescrip- 
tion business were the first to 
get pharmacy computers. But 
with third-party workloads in- 
creasing, chain executives are 
rethinking their criteria for 
computer-system installations. 

Ina study conducted by Drug

In some cases, the master

such as Pay ’n Save and Pay

either is or will be facilitating

Says ComputerTalk’s Lock- 
wood, “The initial thrust of the 
pharmacy computer was pro- 
duction-oriented, but today the 
computer is being used more as 
a decision support system.” 

The point-of-sale system 
works via an interface—an elec- 
tronic connecting device— 
through which information im- 
pulses, such as cash register 
sales, can be received and 
stored in the same computer the 
pharmacist is using to fill pre- 
scriptions. The information is 
held in the computer’s memory 
until access is made in the form 
of preprogrammed manage- 
ment reports, the software that 
tells the computer what to do 
with the data. 

Mark Braunstein, president 
of National Data Corporation, a 
pioneer in POS, says the new 
technology will enable the phar- 
macist to use his computer to 
the fullest extent. 

“What has previously been 
available to department stores 
and supermarkets is now avail- 
able to the drug store at a frac- 
tion of the cost,” he points out. 

Several chains have installed 
pharmacy systems, with the ad- 


dition of POS in the near future 
a major priority. 

Once installation is complete, 
Big B plans to hook up its Na- 
tional Data Corporation com- 
puter systems with special 
TEC America electronic cash 
registers that will enable com- 
munication of information be- 
tween the two. 

Boots Drug Stores Ltd. has 
installed its first of 30 stand- 
alone pharmacy systems pur- 
chased from JTS Computer 
Systems Ltd. of Canada. 

According to Jan Weisiolek of 
Boots’ management informa- 
tion services, a major consider- 
ation in choosing the JTS unit 
was for future POS conversion. 

The role of the wholesaler in 
the pharmacy computer busi- 
ness has become clear in recent 
months. At least three of the 
top 10 wholesalers have pur- 
chased computer companies, 
with sights set on the pharmacy 
systems developed by the com- 
panies. 

According to Lockwood, the 
drug wholesalers, which al- 
ready have a solid customer 
base to work with, are the most 
likely candidates to do well sell- 
ing the new high-tech computer 
systems. 

“According to our statistics,” 
says Lockwood, “67% of the 
_ wholesalers we polled are sell- 
ing a pharmacy-computer sys- 
tem. And of those wholesalers 
not offering a system, 60% said 
_ they planned to offer one for 

_ gale in the future.” Com -

and POS systems 


offering a system were using a 
national brand as opposed to an 
internally developed system. 

In California, McKesson 
Corp. has unveiled a moderate- 
ly priced computerized scan- 
ning system with full POS func- 
tions. The 3PM system (3PM is 
a McKesson subsidiary) is cur- 
rently being tested in a 4,000- 
sq.-ft. Wrigley Drug store in 
Pontiac, Mich. If testing is suc- 
cessful, Allen Stotsky, presi- 
dent of the chain, plans to install 
the equipment in all of his nine 
stores. 

A spokesman at Spectro In- 
dustries Inc., Jenkinton, Pa., a 
drug wholesaler that recently 
acquired S. B. Systems, says 
his company will begin to phase 
in the new computer system as 
soon as an existing sales con- 
tract with 3PM expires. Mar- 
keting of the new S. B. Systems 


computers is expected toward 
the end of this year. 
FoxMeyer Corp., Dallas, 
which acquired TBL Inc., a firm 
that already provides pharma- 
cy-computer hardware and soft- 
ware to more than 700 indepen- 
dent and chain drug stores, 
plans to provide retailers with 
software packages that include 
electronic-order entry, POS, 
nightly maintenance, third-par- 
ty billing, and inventory control 


systems. 
A wholesaler that took the 


plunge into the computer busi- 
ness by developing its own sys- 
tem rather than buying a com- 
pany is Bergen Brunswig, 
“We have the technology now 
to-upgrade our original Compu- 
phase computer to a state-of- 
the-art system,” says Craig To- 
yama, director of Bergen’s 
computer division.

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 17, 1984 


43 


Chains use TV, mail 
1O promo service 


n an effort to boost store 
traffic, many chains with 
pharmacy computer sys- 
tems are now heavily promoting 


‘them through TV, newspapers, 
‘direct mail and in-store displays 
‘and events. 


Standard Drug, forexample, 
acting on the assumption that 
its pharmacists are in the best 
position to promote the compa- 
ny’s computer system, hired an 
ad agency to produce a commer- 
cial featuring an actor in the role 
of a pharmacist. To add realism 
to the production, Standard 
chose one of its pharmacy de- 
partments as the filming site. 

As-a result, Dick Barnes, vp 
of professional relations for the 
Richmond, Va:-based chain, be- 
lieves that the consumer will as- 
sociate the actor in the film with 
Standard’s own pharmacists. 
“Even our pharmacists who 
have seen the commercial have 
been asking me which store we 
took him from to do the com- 
mercial,” says Barnes. 

“Our pharmacists feel they 
played a major role in the com- 
puter advertising campaign,” 
he added. “They are eager to 
discuss the system with our cus- 
tomers.” 

In addition to the commer- 
cial, bag-stuffers and direct- 
mail advertising are used for 
the computer promotion. 

Standard’s direct-mail adver- 
tisements are targeted to the 
physician as well as to custom- 
ers. “The doctors love our com- 
puter,” said Barnes. “Once they 
are made aware of the advan- 
tages, the doctors actually be- 
come a source of promotion by 
passing the information along to 
their patients.” 

The physicians especially like 
the computer’s avility to cross- 
reference drug interactions 
with the patients’ medical pro- 
file to catch any potential prob- 
lems before they occur. 

In Oregon, Wilsonville-based 
Pay Less NW stresses the con- 
fidentiality of information re- 
ceived from the patient in its ad- 
vertising. 

“By telling the public through 
our advertisements that all per- 
sonal information they furnish 
is kept strictly confidential,” 


explains Tom Wilers, pharmacy 
systems coordinator for the 
chain, “it lessens the ‘Big 
Brother’ image of which so 
many shoppers are afraid.”’ 
This point is stressed through 
local television and newspaper 
ads, as well as through in-store 


‘banners and posters. 


At Gray Drug Fair in Cleve- 
land, Irwin Livon, vp of profes- 
sional services, uses his advertis- 
ing to increase the consumer’s 
awareness of the types of work 
the computers can do. 

Livon is convinced that cus- 


tomers’ familiarity with the 


computers, through constant 
exposure, increases a sense of 
security with stores that have 
computers. Therefore,. if they 


‘switch to a pharmacy that does 
‘not have a computer, they would 


not be satisfied. 

“It’s a lot like an automatic 
garage-door opener,” says Li- 
von. “Nobody really thinks they 
need one until they buy it. Then 
try to take it away and see the 
reaction.” 

Currently operating 119 com- 
puters in its chain, Hook Drug, 
Indianapolis, advertised its 
pharmacy computer system on 
the customer’s receipt. 

Realizing that there was 
empty space on the store’s label 
sets, Keith Johns, assistant vp 
and director of professional ser- 
vices, saw to it that the blank 
space was filled with a message 
that promotes the chain’s phar- 
macy computer. 

“We weren’t using the space 
anyway,” says Johns, “and what 
better time to alert the public to 
the advantages of the system 
than when they receive their re- 
ceipt. This way it is always in 
front of them.” 

Features common to all com- 
puter advertising being done by 
the chains include: 

@ Shorter waiting time for fill- 
ing prescriptions, especially 
those on third-party plans. 

@ The ability to give the cus- 
tomer a record of drug pur- 
chases for tax-reporting. 

e Accurate record keeping on 
new as well as refill prescrip- 
tions for quicker retrieval. 

@ Programmed drug interac. 
tions to alert the pharmacist.

Model computer guidelines 
released by Rx association 


s pharmacy-computer in- 

stallations continue at a 

breakneck pace, The Na- 
tional Association of Boards of 
Pharmacy (NABP) has re- 
leased model computer regula- 
tions for review by its state 
board of pharmacy member- 
ship. 

The model computer regula- 
tions have been written into the 
newly revised Model State 
Pharmacy Aci and Model Regu- 
lations of the NABP. This docu- 
ment updates institutional reg- 
ulations, nuclear pharmacy 
regulations, and includes a 
model institutional pharmacy 
inspection form. 

According to NABP execu- 
tive director, Fred T. Mahaffey, 
the model computer regulations 
are geared to “serve as a guide- 
line for all NABP member 
states wishing to utilize such a 
composite in developing their 
own regulations.” 

The computer regulations 
were developed by the NABP 
Committee of Law Enforce- 
ment/Legislation after careful 
review of existing state regula- 
tions, model regulations devel- 
oped by individual state boards 
of pharmacy, model language 
developed by the chain drug in- 
dustry, input from computer in- 
dustry executives and help 
from pharmacy associations. 

Serving on the committee 
were: chairman and member of 
the Arizona Board of Pharmacy, 
Joseph J. Rowan; Elaine Dunn, 
president, New Jersey State 
Board of Pharmacy; Len De- 
Mino, vp, professional services, 
Peoples Drug Stores, and 
George McFarland, senior vp, 
Reed Drug Company, a division 
of Peoples. 

According to committee 
members, the intent of the mod- 
el computer regulations is “to 
deal with and to define proce- 
dures that will not only comply 
with state and Federal regula- 
tions, but will assist to facilitate 
the inspection of those pharma- 
cies employing the use of a com- 
puter.” 

“These regulations are not 
mandatory,”’ said chairman 
Rowan. 

The model regulation is divid- 
ed into seven sections. The first 
two sections deal with a review 
of pharmacy regulations that 
most states are already enforc- 
ing. The remaining five sections 
deal directly with computer 
systems being used in the phar- 
macy department: 
® Section three is devoted en- 
tirely to how sections one and 
two should be carried out if the 
pharmacy is using a computer 
system. Highlights of this sec- 
tion are: 

The system shall have the ca- 
pability of producing sight- 
readable documents of all origi- 
nal and refilled prescripticn 


information. These records may 
be read from the computer’s 
CRT, microfiche, microfilm or a 
computer printout. To provide 
completeness and accuracy of 
computer entries, the pharma- 
cist filling prescriptions en- 
tered into the computer must 
provide documentation in the 
form of a printout of each day’s 
prescription activity or in the 
form of a bound log book. 

The printout must be dated 
and signed by the pharmacist 
verifying the correctness of in- 
formation. The documents must 
be maintained for five years 
from date of last dispensing and 
must be in the pharmacy within 
72 hours of date of dispensing. 

Should the computer be inop- 
erative, an auxiliary record- 
keeping system should be es- 


tablished for documentation of 
refills. Once the system is work- 
ing again, this information must 
be transferred to the computer 
to be made part of the patient’s 
permanent profile. 

@ Section four states that there 
must be adequate safeguards or 
security of the aforementioned 
records. 

@ Sections five and six deal 
with the ability to satisfy all in- 
formation requirements in pre- 
scription transfers to another 
store. This includes transfer of 
schedule III, IV, and V con- 
trolled and dangerous sub- 
stances for refill purposes.

Such connectors are now 


available from IBM, Sweda, 
National Data Corp., Fox- 
Meyer’s TBL division and 
McKesson’s 3PM company to 
name but a few. 

Pay Less NW seems to have 
won the distinction of being the 
first drug chain to “fully auto- 
mate” (i.e., to communicate 
with any electronic subsystem 
within the store thereby fully 
integrating all in-store data into 
one common base), but other 
chains are either testing or pre- 
paring to test some version of 
an integrated system including 
Eckerd, Revco, Rite Aid, 
Thrifty, Medi Mart and Big B. 

At year end, Eckerd should 
have about 100 of its approxi- 
mately 1,500 stores tied to a 
communicating front-end sys- 
tem. The front end, in the Eck- 
erd system, has its own price 
look-up file stored on a hard 
disk in the master cash register. 
That master can literally “com- 
municate” or interact with a 
personal computer located in 
the manager’s office handling 
scheduling and other activities 
plus it (the front-end) and the 
manager’s computer can “com- 
municate” with the per al 
computer in the pharmacy de- 
partment. A company spokes- 


report: 
_ pharmacy 


computers 


and POS 
systems 


man said Eckerd plans to auto- 
mate another 100 stores by next 
July. 

Unlike the Pay Less integra- 
tion system, the Eckerd test as 
well as most of the other cur- 
rent tests are not considered 
“fully integrated’’ because 
there is no one master computer 
storing all available data in its 
memory and acting as a “facili- 
tator” by which one in-store ma- 
chine talks to another or the 
host computer at headquarters 
talks to the front end. 

Eckerd, sources say, is also 
using a mini-computer, the 
IBM Series I, in its integrated 
high-volume stores where the 
number of pharmacy scripts 
processed in a single day ex- 
ceeds 150. 


e 


Thrifty is also using a mini, 
again the Series I, to talk to its 
electronic point of sale as well as 
to perform a variety of other 
management programs. Thrif- 
ty, sources say, began impie- 
menting the link-up in five 
stores about six months ago. 
The chain hopes to have all 540 
stores interactive in about 
three years. 

Rite Aid is also testing an in- 
tegrated front-end/computer- 
management system in six 
stores, but sources say the 
chain is taking its time about 
implementation, waiting to be 
sure management knows exact- 
ly what hardware it wants and 
exactly what software package 
to be developed to manage the 
system.

DRUG STORE NEWS, September.17, 1984 


Reveo, which began testing 
an integrated system about a 
year ago, is also taking its time, 
testing various combinations of 
front-end/computer-manage- 
ment packages in about 20 
stores. 

Medi Mart is currently in- 
stalling upgraded point-of-sale 
registers and pharmacy sys- 
tems in all 54 stores, and they 
are expected to have the system 
chainwide within the next 12 
months or less. 

Big B, the 100-unit, conven- 
tional-sized chain headquar- 
tered in Birmingham, Ala., is 
planning to test one or two inte- 
grated stores sometime next 
year. (See Drug Store News, 
Aug. 20.) 

Bridging the gap 

Generally most chains and in- 
dependents are bridging the 
gap from a purely pharmacy 
computer system to a fully inte- 
grated in-store management 
system by putting a stand-alone 
pharmacy system in first and 
then building or adding on to 
that system later by adding “in- 
store communicating” electron- 
ic cash registers. Some chains, 
like Medi Mart, however, are 
putting the POS in first. 

Once the operators feel they 
have the “right software to link 
the two systems and get them 
to do exactly what that specific 
operator wants them to do,” 
they begin “tieing” or connect- 
ing the two together, allowing 
the master computer to control 


»the flow of data into and out of 


the front end. Generally that 
computer then transmits the 


data back te the host computer 
at either.a chain or wholesaler’s 


headquarters. 

At this early stage in the 
game, hard statistics are hard 
to come by, but most point-of- 
sale manufacturers estimate 
that currently less than 10% of 
all the cash registers in the drug 
store universe are truly up- 
gradable to integration. 

However, that is not seen as a 


-major drawback to full-scale 


implementation because chain 
management has apparently 
been anticipating this develop- 
ment since scanning first elec- 
trified the supermarket indus- 
try. 

“Will depreciate quickly” 

“If you look at the types of 
registers most chains have been 
buying to date,’’ says one 
source, “you'll see they are basi- 
cally intermediate investments 
of between $800 and $1,000 
each. They’!! depreciate quickly 
and the chains will be ready to 
write them off when they make 


their final decision about which 


kind of in-store communicating 
system they should select.” 

The source also pointed out 
that most independents are 
even in a better position to con- 
vert to “in-store communicat- 
ing EPOS.” 

“They haven’t been buying 
new equipment as fast as chains 
and most are now in a position 
where they’re ready to replace 
their mechanicals or their first 
generation electronic regis- 
ters,” he said. 

“Independents are also buy- 
ing pharmacy computer sys- 


tems at a very rapid rate so 
what would be more natural 
then to buy asystem that would 
let you integrate your entire 
store. They know it’s coming. 
They know the chains are going 
to do it. They know supermar- 
kets are doing it. How else are 
they going to compete?” 

As far as pharmacy compo- 
nents go, the penetration is 
even deeper. By the most re- 
cent count, approximately 25% 
of all independent stores and 
20% of all chain stores now have 
mini- or micropharmacy com- 
puters and that estimate is ex- 
pected to exceed 30% for both 
segments by the end of 1984. 
(See DrSN’s special feature on 
pharmacy computers in this is- 
sue.) That will mean that by the 
end of 1984, there will be about 
15,000 stores out there with 
pharmacy computers, about 
4,000 of them chain stores. 

This count doesn’t even in- 
clude the approximately 1,000 
combination food/drug stores, 
some of which are already add- 
ing pharmacy department ap- 
plications to the software pro- 
grams for their own in-store 
minis. 

With the costs of the hard- 
ware down to approximately 
$30,000 to $40,000 for a four- 
register drug store, the soft- 
ware is really the only stum- 
bling block to a wide scale roll 
out of integration technology. 

Getting the bugs out 

Most retail sources say that 
the rest of 1984 and early 1985 
will be spent “tinkering” with 
existing packages and with new 
programs until all the potential 
buyers are satisfied they have a 
system that can do everything 
they want it to do. 

“That’s how Reveo and Rite 
Aid are proceeding,” says a 
source. Toward the end or mid- 
de of 1985, however, sources 
say they expect to see enor- 
mous flurries of activities in this 
area as chains like Revco, Rite 
Aid, Eckerd, Big B, etc., make 
a decision on the route to follow. 
Once that happens, they say 
they expect to see the smaller 
regional chains quickly follow- 
ing up on the trend, and some 
sources are estimating that the 
industry might be “more than 
50% integrated” by the end of 
1990. 

The approximately 38,000 
stores that belong to indepen- 
dents and two or three store op- 
erators might even achieve 
penetration faster because, as 
sources pointed out, they do not 
have to wait for s<”eral dozen 
committees to make a decision. 
Most independents are pharma- 
cists and when they see the sys- 
tem that they like, they can just 
say: “I’ll take it.” 

The independents, too, of 
course, will be aided in their roll 
out by wholesalers. McKesson, 
whose 3PM computer division 
created the integrated package 
just announced at McKesson’s 
trade show last July, sold more 
than 125 systems, mostly to in-
