WASHINGTON — Top Congressional leaders and 
Reagan Administration officials joined representa- 
tives of the nation’s generic drug manufacturers in 
predicting a sharp increase in pharmaceutical indus- 
try price competition following final passage of com- 

romise ANDA/Patent Term Restoration legislation 
ate last month. 

Health and Human Services Secretary Margaret 
Heckler, for one, predicted that the new law will “save 
$1 billion in consumer costs over the next 12 years” by 
allowing generic pharmaceutical houses to obtain fast- 
track marketing approval for scores of me-too ver- 
sions of “new” (post-1962) drugs. 

Generic Pharmaceutical Industry Association pres- 
ident William Haddad forecast a 100% increase in “the 
number of low-cost generic drugs in the marketplace,” 
and predicted that the legislation will “cut the price of 
many popular drugs in half.” 

Under the final bill, upward of 150 off-patent single- 
source drugs with total sales of some $4.5 billion annu- 


More competition seen in wake of 


ally are now likely to face competition from lower- 
priced generic versions that will become “approvable” 
under the streamlined “Abbreviated New Drug Ap- 
plication” (ANDA) process. 

Among the prime targets for generic competition: 
@ SKF’s Dyazide, which went off patent in 1980 and 
generated sales of nearly $177 million in 1982; 
@ Wyeth’s Ativan ($55 million in ’82) which lost its

@ Upjohn’s Tolinase, which produced sales of more 
than $49 million in ’82 after its patent expired in 1979;

lion in annual sales); 
@ Lilly’s Keflin ($43 million) which went off patent in 
1982, and

Jewel-Pay Less trial set 


SAN FRANCISCO — In the latest fallout from the bitter 
1979 battle for control of Pay Less California, Jewel Cos. has 
won the right to a full trial in its claim for damages against Pay 
Less NW, the company that acquired the California chain. 

Jewel originally sued Pay Less NW in late 1979, but in June 
1982 the Wilsonville, Ore.-based drug chain won a summary 
judgment from the U.S. District Court of Northern California. 

Jewel then appealed to the U.S. 9th Court of Appeals in San 
Francisco, and that court has now reversed the decision and 
ordered a full trial. 

Jewel, recently acquired by American Stores, claims it is en- 
titled to damages because the Chicago-based food/drug chain 
had signed an agreement with the board of directors of Pay 
Less California before Pay Less NW made its offer. Pay Less 
NW subsequently completed the acquisition of the 61 Califor- 
nia stores. 

Jewel’s suit for damages did not specify any dollar amount. 

Regardless of the outcome of the case, the acquired Califor- 
nia Pay Less stores will remain part of the Pay Less N W chain. 


Rite Aid buys Jays 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. — Rite Aid has acquired the 
five-store Jay’s Drug Stores Inc. , based in Lockport, N.Y. The 
stores are located upstate, near Buffalo, where the chain al- 
ready has a strong presence. Rite Aid is currently on a strong 
acquisition streak, bringing more than four new chains under 
its belt in the last three months. 


Second discount Pathmark opens 


GLEN BURNIE, Md. — Supermarkets General Corp. has 
opened its second deep-discount Pathmark Super Drug Store 
here. Modeled after its successful 22,000-sq,-f unit in Dun- 
dalk, Md., the new store offers discounts up to 50%. 

Pathmark’s entry with a deep-discount unit into this market 
has caused a price war, with Giant and Safeway both slashing 
prices to meet Pathmark head on. 


Bortnick retires from Giant 


LANDOVER, Md. — Morris Bortnick has retired from his 
post as sr. vp professional services at Giant Food. Bortnick 
was with the food/drug combination chain for 23 years. 

Replacing Bortnick is Emanuel Richman, also a 23-year em- 
ployee of Giant. Richman’s title is director of professional ser- 
vices. 


Four new Fay’s stores 


LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — Fay’s Drug has unveiled four new 
stores, bringing to 111 the total number of stores operated by 
the chain. The new stores are in Norwich, Cheektowaga and 
Saugerties, N.Y., and Eynon, Pa.

stg Markets for about $55 mil- 

ion.

steps to raise cash needed to re- 
tire the debt accrued when 
American purchased Jewel at a 
sweetened price of $75 per 
share.

In chain drug stores, buyers said all- 
year merchandising of the category 
should lead to a 15% sales increase over 
the $157.6 million produced by sun- 
glasses last year. 

“We've found the business is strong 
all year because people want fashion 
glasses, even for skiing,” said Anna Ia- 
cono, buyer for Douglas Drug Inc., 
Providence, R.I. 

Recent figures from A. C. Nielsen 
Co. support the strong upward sales 
trend in the category. For the first four 
months of 1984 vs. 1983, overall sun- 
glass sales jumped 27% in dollars and 
41% in units; that’s compared with only 
a 7% dollar increase and a 1% unit gain

Now that the business has become so 
trendy, retailers are critiquing manu- 
facturers by their fashion offerings. 
One company receiving high grades for 
its fashion entries is Opti-Ray with its 
Flash Fashion line. According to Bud- 
dy Sklar, sr. vp, the line was so success- 
ful last year that it has been extended 
from five sku’s to 11. “There will be 
new cords and coordinated colors, new 
styles and gradients—it’ll be wild,” 
Sklar told Drug Store News. 

A survey of drug chains and suppli- 
ers revealed that the following styles 
should command sales for 1985: 

@ Glasses with leashes or cords. This 
style, reminiscent of the glasses librar- 
ians wore, was inspired by TV star 
Tom Selleck and later picked up by 
fashion magazines and department 
stores. Drug stores were quick to add 
them to the mix and sold both glasses 
with cords and the cords separately. 
For 1985, the look will still be strong, 
however, new colors will dominate 
sales. 

@ Tinted lenses and those with differ- 
ent colors. 

e Beveled, rimless glasses. This style 
will continue to be a popular hit. Also, 
buyers pick any frame with an Italian 
influence as a winner for 1985.

tone Sun Protectors by Opti-Ray, will 
be ultraviolet, impact resistant and 
available in fashion tints. 

In addition to fashion, buyers look 
for a price/quality ratio in the sunglas¢ 
category. “Today’s customer wants 
quality and wants to feel the price he or 
she paid is worthy of the product,” ex- 
plained a buyer from a Southern chain.

Drug chains find niche 
with small food depts. 


t Walgreens president Fred F. 
Canning doesn’t fear the on- 
slaught of the giant food/drug 
combos. He is convinced that there’s 
still plenty of room for the relatively 
small, conveniently located drug store 
with a limited food mix that appeals to 
busy shoppers. Walgreens has more 
than 100 of these mini-combo stores. 
Cincinnati-based SupeRx also sub- 
scribes to the theory that hurried shop- 
pers prefer the in-and-out convenience 


ft. convenience food department. 
Wellby plans to open four more such 
stores this year. Previously, Wellby de- 
voted only 1,000 sq. ft. of space to foods. 

These are three examples of drug 
chains that are reacting to today’s life- 
styles by adding more food to the drug 


store mix. Buyers report that sales per 


square foot in food can exceed $125 and 
volume can account for as much as 20% 
of store sales. 

Why are drug stores enjoying bus- 


ing food selections. To date, chains in- 
cluding Begley, Longs, Peoples, Perry, 
Carls and Douglas have introduced con- 
venience foods into the mix. In total, 
drug chains produced better than $1 bil- 
lion in food and beverage sales in 1983. 
By most indications, sales should rise 
12% in 1984, buyers said: 

Bob Upthegrove at Perry said his food 
sales have been strong, especially in 
markets where there are no large food 
stores. “We’re in a unique situation in 
Michigan. There’s so much grocery com- 
petition here that a lot of food stores 
have closed down. We’ve added grocer- 
ies in those markets and it has been suc- 
cessful.” Perry’s department, he added, 
averages 32 ft. to 4& ft. 

For Perry, it makes sense to open a 


of a drug store. The chain now operates 
28 stores with 25% of the selling space 
devoted to convenience foods. SupeRx 
will even add a snack bar complete with 
a microwave and fountain in select loca- 
tions. 

And Wellby Super Drug Stores in 
Portland, Me., just upped its commit- 
ment to food with the opening of a new 
7,500-sq.-ft. store housing a 2,500-sq.- 


tling food sales? There are several rea- 
sons, but an underlying message is that 
the increasing demand for one-stop 
shopping is fueling growth of conve- 
nience food sales. 

“T think more and more chains are get- 
ting involved in convenience foods,” rea- 
soned K&B’s Mark Blandford. “It en- 
hances the one-stop shopping image.” 

Indeed, more drug chains are enlarg- 


convenience food department in loca- 
tions where supermarkets have folded. 
What guidelines can other drug chains 
rely on to target the best food locations? 
A representative of SupeRx devised the 
following points for a location with food: 
@ Ample parking or a downtown loca- 
tion with a dense population.

Service important 

A third factor a retailer con- 
siders when selecting a sun- 
glass company is service. The 
‘acks must be kept clean and 
stocked. Also retailers do not 
want to be saddled with items 
that won’t move. 

A survey of drug chains found 
that most carry at least two, 


and sometimes three brands of 


sunglasses. In some chains, the 
buyer splits his or her stores be- 
tween companies. 

“Then we compare them to 
see who gives us the best ser- 
vice and where we get better 
turns and gross margins,” said 


one buyer who is currently re- 
viewing several lines before 
making a final decision. 

Indeed, the search to boost 
margins and improve the turns, 
which average two the three 
times per year, is paramount in 
the category. Drug stores ac- 
count for about 25% of the total 
sunglass business but must sac- 
rifice the hefty 45% margins 
during price promotions in or- 
der to compete with other re- 
tailers. To date, most retailers 
have relied on half-price promo- 
tions which boost sales, but sap 
margins. 

Better promotions sought 

“T wish someone would devise 
a better promotion than half- 
price,” lamented one buyer. 
“No one is making anything on 
that promotion.” 

He suggested more coupon- 
ing and import programs to 
boost margins. And, several 


manufacturers offered item ad- 
vertising as an alternative. 
“Promote the fasnion looks on 
the ads,” one supplier said. 

Buyers did cite several ven- 
dors as improving the support 
for the category. For example, 
Corning was applauded for its 
$3.6 million promotion of its 
Chameleon line. Others select- 
ed Visual Scene’s co-op adver- 
tising program as a power hit- 
ter. CVS, for example, teamed 
up last May with Visual Scene 
for a television and print ad blitz 
that “was very successful,” ac- 
cording to a CVS manager. 

Although coupon programs 
and co-op ad dollars are adding 
to the profitability of the cate- 
gory. Several chains prefer im- 
port programs. 

Perry Drug. for example, 
opted for its import program 
four years ago and now stocks 
only its own line on racks of 340 


frames in all stores. The chain 
prefers this method because it 
yields greater control. 

“Everyone in our markets 
discounts sunglasses at least 
40%,” said Peterson. “The im- 
port program helped us im- 
prove our profits.”

Look for a new engine lubri- 
cant designed to restore lost 
compression to aging automo- 
bile engines. Dubbed Restore 
(appropriately enough), the 
new product was test marketed 
in a number of southern Florida 
retail outlets, including several 


Walgreen and Eckerd drug 
stores. Pic N Save, headquar- 
tered in Jacksonville, Fla., also 
had the product on the shelves 
in a number of its stores. 

Test results appear to have 
been favorable because Restore 
is currently being rolled out na- 
tionally. The key ingredients to 
the oil-based product are min- 
ute particles of combined cop- 
per, silver and lead that fill 
scratches and grooves in engine 
cylinders. Restore comes in 
three sku’s—for cars with four, 
six and eight cylinders. 

A national advertising cam- 
paign is scheduled to break this 
fall. The print portion of the 
campaign will include such 
books as Car and Driver, Road 
and Track and Popular Me- 
chanics. A spot television cam- 
paign also is in the works. 

Among the drug chains that 
may take the product on a 
chainwide basis in January are 
Eckerd, Revco and Walgreens. 
Skaggs Drug Centers and 
Skaggs Alpha Beta combos 
have already committed to car- 
ry Restore.

highly effective against most vi-

Fay’s, Carls, Rite Aid and 
CVS.

be $1.39 in Buffalo and Roches-

sell for $1.09.

media advertising campaign

Eckerd earnings rebound 


as sales top $2.6 billion 


By Bruce Buckley 

CLEARWATER, Fla. — 
With its drug store company 
leading the way, Jack Eckerd 
Corp. returned to strong earn- 
ings growth in fiscal ’84 after 
two years of depressed results. 

The corporation reported 
that net profits for the year end- 
ed July 28 increased 19% to 
$85.4 million as sales rose 12% 
to $2.62 billion. As a result, the 
company’s net-to-sales ratio 
moved up to 3.3% after bottom- 
ing out in 1983 at 3.1%. 

“This has been a year of sig- 
nificant improvement for Jack 
Eckerd Corp.,” said Stewart 
Turley, chairman and presi- 
dent. “In the new 1985 fiscal 
year we anticipate additional 
progress in our operating com- 
panies’ performance as we con- 
tinue to sharpen the merchan- 
dising and operating programs 
in our markets.”

Pa. installations complete 


Rite Aid readies POS scanners 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. 
— Rite Aid launched its plan to 
install point-of-sale scanning 
systems chainwide. 

The chain has installed a few 
dozen of the 400 LS-7000 hand- 
held laser scanners, purchased 
from Symbol Technologies, in 
stores in the Philadelphia and 
Harrisburg, Pa., areas. Be- 
cause installation of scanning is 
tied to training (it takes at least 
a week to train store person- 
nel), roll out will depend upon 
training capacities. Rite Aid 
hopes to have the system chain- 
wide by 1988. 

According to Martin Binder, 
Rite Aid’s vp Management In- 
formations Services, the cost of 
equipping stores for scanning is 


“spiraling” downward and is 
now under $20,000 per store. 
He said Rite Aid selected hand- 
held devices because of the effi- 
ciencies this system offers drug 
stores. 

“We are totally committed to 
hand-held scanning as the pri- 
mary scanning vehicle for POS 
applications,” Binder said. “We 
p an to install some 7,000 hand- 

eld laser scanners in 1,500 to 
2,000 stores by 1988.” 

He added Rite Aid research 
showed that Symbol’s gun has 
the highest successful read rate 
of universal product codes. 

Hand-held laser scanners 
have some advantages over slot 
scanners in smaller drug stores 
because such stores generally 


process fewer items per trans- 
action, according to Jerry Gul- 
ley, vp sales and marketing for 
Symbol. Therefore, the prima- 
ry goal of scanning becomes to 
gain movement information 
rather than increase checkout 
productivity. 

Also, hand-held laser scan- 
ners are more cost-efficient for 
drug stores because they do not 
require expensive conveyor 
belts to move items past the slot 
scanning devices. And finally, 
the new hand-held devices are 
more accurate than previous 
readers. 

As Rite Aid installs scanners, 
the chain will start eliminating 
individual pricing on items.

Abe Plough dead at 92 


MEMPHIS — Abe Plough, 
Inc. and a generous philanthropist, died in mid-September at 
~— Hospital Medical Center here. 


In the early years of this century, Plough began his career as 
a soda clerk in a drug store. Over the years he was instrumen- 
tal in establishing the Plough Pharmaceutical Co., which was 
merged with Schering Corp. to form Schering-Plough Co., one 
of the world’s largest pharmaceutical firms. 

Schering-Plough employs 25,000 people worldwide and did 
$1.3 billion in sales in over 100 countries last year. 

Plough retired from business in 1976 as chairman of the 
board of Plough Inc. and Schering-Plough. He continued to 
work six days a week as a philanthropist after retirement. 

He claimed his philosophy was to help the greatest number 
of people, because that is when the most good is done.

sion to operate one of its Jupiter

store will have little impact on 
neighboring drug stores, ac-

Troy, Mich.-based retailer re-

promoting department dis- 
counts. 

The spokesman said that 
K mart is advertising the store 
as Super Jupe in local newspa- 
per ads.

flect a discount image. A Wal-

Rite Aid posts record first-half sales, earnings 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. 


— Rite Aid Corp.’s 


; aggressive 


fe program helped pro- 
pel sales and earnings for the 
first half of fiscal 1985 to record 


levels. 


The company reported that 
net income for the second quar- 


ter ended 


Sept. 1 


increased 


16.8% to $14.7 million from 
$12.6 million for the corre 
sponding period a year ago. 


Earnings per share increased to 
36¢ from 30¢. 

Sales for the quarter rose 
21% to $344.6 million from 
$284.8 million. 

For the six months, net earn- 
ings climbed 17.6% to $28.2 mil- 
lion from $24 million a year ear- 
lier. Sales were up 18.8% to 
$669 million from $563.1 mil- 
lion. Earnings per share were 
68¢ vs. 56¢ a year ago. 


Earnings per share figures 
were changed to reflect a 2-for- 
1 stock split on Jan. 30, 1980. 

Alex Grass, chairman and 
president, noted that the com- 
pany had aggressively expand- 
ed during the second quarter in 
both its drug store business and 
specialty retailing operations. 

During the quarter, Rite Aid 
diversified into discount book 
retailing with tlix acquisition of 


Encore Books, a 19-store chain 
based in Philadelphia. In the fis- 
cal year ended Jan. 31, Encore 
had revenues of $10.2 million. 

Rite Aid also began a vigor- 
ous penetration of the Michigan 
market in the second quarter by 
acquiring 24-store Muir Drug in 
Grand Rapids. Other acquisi- 
tions followed swiftly, including 
Herrlich’s, Lippert Drug and 
Remes. 


Ina flurry of new-store activ- 
ity, the company launched 28 
new units in the second quarter. 
The acquisitions and new store 
openings brought the total 
number of Rite Aid outlets to 
1,235 in 20 states, making the 
chain the third largest next to 
Revco and Eckerd. 

Other specialty divisions in- 
clude 180 Circus World toy 
store in 23 states.

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 15, 1984 


~ MERCHANDISER 


Auto part ads renewed as user profile changes 


uto aftermarket manufacturers 
A:: stepping up their consumer 
marketing efforts through in- 
creased mass advertising and new 


packaging innovations in an attempt to. 


reach what the industry considers a 
large untapped market. 

In past years, auto products con- 
sumers conjured up images of blue-col- 
lar men with grease under their finger- 
nails. The most popular outlet for 
purchasing automotive products was 
the professional auto parts dealer and 
general merchandise retailers such as 
Sears. 

However, that stereotype no longer 
appropriately describes the typical 
auto parts consumer. The declining 
number of full-service gasoline sta- 
tions, rising labor hour costs for me- 
chanics and the fact that people are 
holding on to their automobiles longer 
(the average is seven years) has 
prompted more car owners than ever 
before to undertake simple repair jobs 
themselves. 

Recognizing this very fundamental 
change in demographics, manufactur- 
ers in recent years have reached out to 
embrace the new auto aftermarket 
consumers, a growing number of 
whom are women. Advertisements for 
easy-to-install-and-apply automobile 
products frequently feature women us- 
ing the product. 

One of the best examples of the new 
consumer-marketing strategy by auto 
parts suppliers is the move by oil man- 
ufacturers, which in the past year have 
rushed to introduce resealable funnel- 
top quart oil containers. 

Similarly, manufacturers of air and 
oil filters and windshield wiper blades 
have improved their point-of-sale ma- 
terial, enabling consumers to find re-

placement parts for their cars. 


This shift “from a professionally ori- 


ented market to a more consumer-ori- 
ented market,” as described by the in- 
vestment research firm of Charles H. 
Kline & Co. has not been lost on drug 
retailers. 

While drug chains rang up only a 
small portion of the estimated $30 bil- 
lion auto aftermarket sales last year, 
the chain drug automotive department 
was the biggest gainer in the do-it- 


yourself category in drug stores in 
1983. According to the Drug Store 
News annual survey, automotive de- 
partment sales registered close to an 
8% increase in sales to $156 million. 
Drug chains have long been success- 
ful moving auto supplies on an in-out 
basis. And an increasing number of 
chains are expanding their everyday 
automotive mix and realizing full 


markup on motor oils and chemicals, 
which can often generate impulse 
sales. 

Some chains have even begun test- 
ing 8-ft. oil and air filter sections. 
These sections, which generally fea- 
ture 12 top-selling sku’s of air filters 
and seven best-selling sku’s of oil fil- 
ters, contain enough merchandise to 
fit 85% of the automobiles on the road 
in the United States. 

One source for a large Midwest drug 
chain said the chain has been success- 
ful with this type of merchandise. “We 
stay away from the industrial auto 
parts,” he said. “We carry things that 
are readily recognizable to the layman.’ 

Says Fran Massey, customer service 
manager at the Fort Lauderdale-based 
STP Corp., one of the companies that 
manufactures oil and air filters: “Drug 
chains are not sleeping giants. The 
drug trade has offered additional 
growth opportunities for us. 

The problem with limited selection 
auto departments is space. Many re- 
tailers, particularly those with stores 
10,000 sq. ft. or less, are quick to point 
out that they simply don’t have the 
floor space to carry products such as 
headlamps, belts, hoses and filters. 

While small store operators may not 
be able to allocate 1,000 sq. ft. to 2,000 
sq. ft. to automotive, there are oppor- 
tunities to exploit in the auto accesso- 
ries market. Retailers favor accessory 
items such as compasses, steering 
wheel covers, car mats, battery cables, 
fuses, tire gauges, oil spouts, funnels 
and filter wrenches because they don’t 
require a great deal of floor space to 
merchandise. Moreover, accessory 
items such as these boast margins of 
45% to 50%. 

Motor oil remains one of the biggest 


draws in drug store auto departments. 
Continued on page 10 


Rebates on personal care 
set what’s hot, what’s not 


manufacturers of personal care ap- 

pliances may determine which lines 
win and which lose a place on drug store 
shelves. | 

Buyers say that the amount of the re- 
bates in relation to the consumer’s cost 
can be a deciding factor on whether they 
carry the line. And today with most 
manufacturers offering rebates from $2 
to $7 on products like blow dryers and 
curling irons that sell for under $20, the 
fight to capture a buyer’s attention is fu- 
rious. 

So along with rebates there has beena 
flourishing of new product designs like 
Black & Decker’s “Black Tie” grooming 
tools for men, Sunbeam’s compact prod- 
ucts for working women called Perfect 
and Clairol’s “Time Wave,” a curling iron 
with a timer. 

However, buyers say that it is the re- 
bates that have been the major factor in 
increasing personal care appliance 
sales. The rebates have allowed drug 
stores to offer prices competitive with 
mass merchandisers and therefore to re- 
main a popular outlet for such appli- 
ances. In fact, sales of these items 


T he rebate war being waged among 


reached over $203 million in chain drug 
stores last year, a 9.9% increase over 
1982. 

While chains report increases in sales 
volume, buyers say space devoted to the 
category has remained the same over 
the years—usually about 6 to 8 ft. Mar- 
gins average 30% when personal care 
products are sold at an everyday price. 
On promotion, however, they can sink to 
10% and lower. When advertised, per- 
sonal care products are often footballed. 
Buyers report that such items are usual- 
ly advertised at least once a month and, 
during holiday periods, weekly. 

While the personal care appliance cat- 
egory includes products like electric 
shavers and massagers, buyers say the 
bulk of sales are in hair care appliances, 
primarily blow dryers. Other popular 
items are curling irons, styling brushes 
and electric rollers. 

The two manufacturers most fre- 
quently named in this category are 
Clairol and Conair. However, other 
strong leaders are Sassoon, Norelco, 
Sunbeam, Black & Decker (formerly 
G. E.) and Windmere.

ALEXANDRIA, Va. — For 
the first time in its history, the 
National Association of Chain 
Drug Stores has opened its 
membership to hospital groups 
with retail pharmacies. 

The two hospital groups that 
have joined—Shawnee Medical 
Center in Shawnee, Okla., and 
Carle Foundation Hospital in 
Urbana, II].—both fit NACDS’ 
requirements of operating four 


or more retail outlets. Carle has 
a total of seven retail stores av- 
eraging 1,000 sq. ft., while 
Shawnee owns five pharmacies, 
including two full-line stores. 
The admission of hospitals 
into the association has caused a 
stir among many chain pharma- 
cy executives. However, most 
said that since the groups run 
four or more retail stores, they 
can’t be denied entry. Also, the 


chains said they would rather 
deal directly with the new com- 
petition, than try to second- 
guess them.

rather sit down at the table with

they’re talking about than wor-

Two groups join forces 
fo publicize Rx crime law 


PHILADELPHIA — The 
National Association of Chain 
Drug Stores (NACDS) and the 
American Pharmaceutical As- 
sociation (APhA) have 
launched a national public infor- 
mation campaign designed to 
increase awareness of the new 
pharmacy crime law. 

The campaign, announced at 
last month's NACDS Pharma- 
ceutical Conference here, is de- 
signed to use editorials written 
by NACDS president Bob Bol- 

er and APhA president John 

chlegel, as well as public ser- 
vice announcements, local news 
releases and other media, to 
warn potential law-breakers 
that stealing narcotics or stimu- 
lants from an American phar- 
macy is now a Federal crime. 


The objective of the cam- 
paign, says Bolger, is “to let the 
ublic know that a major step 
as been taken, both to make it 
safer to patronize community 
pharmacies and to reduce ille- 
gal drug trafficking.” 

Schlegel, who was represent- 
ed at the NACDS press confer- 
ence by Dr. Richard Penna, 
APhA board member, said in a 
prepared statement that the 
campaign is intended to convey 
two fundamental messages. 

“First, we want the public to 
know something is being done 
to protect them against crime,” 
he said, “and we want the crimi- 
nal and potential criminal to 
know that the stakes have just 
gone up drastically.”

PHILADELPHIA — Four 
out of 10 people who take pre-

recent American Association of 
Retired Persons study.

study commissioned by D 
Store News suggest that the in- 
cidence of side effects may be so 
high because pharmacists are 
not as informed about the po- 
tential negative consequences 
of prescription drugs as they’d 
like to be.

New products fail 
tO spur rep visits 


@® ince the average pharma- 
ey stocks approximately 
33 new products a year, it 
would be logical! to assume that 
the average pharmacist re- 
ceives frequent and very careful 
attention from the average de- 
tailist, who must explain the po- 
tential benefits and limitations 
of new products. 

However, according to the re- 
cent Drug Store News Pharma- 
ceutical Store Detailing Survey, 
it would be wrong to make that 
assumption: the average phar- 
macist is not visited that often 
by representatives of compa- 
nies with new products on the 
market, nor are they given all 
the information they want when 
they are visited by detailists. 
According to the Drug Store 


News study, only 40% of the 575 
respondents in the survey were 
visited within six months of a 
product launch by representa- 
tives from 12 selected compa- 
nies. 

The number of pharmacists 


Store detailing study 


who had seen a rep within a six- 
month launch of a new product 
from these 12 select companies 
ranged from a high of 70% toa 
low of 10%. On a median basis, 
40% of our respondents had 
seen a rep from one of these 
companies at least once within 
the six-month launch. 

Pharmacists who work for in- 
dependent stores saw reps 
more often than pharmacists 
who work for chain stores. In 
the case of a few manufacturers, 
their reps got to independent 
pharmacists twice as often as 
they got to chain store pharma- 
cists. However, ifarep from one 
of these companies had 
reached, say, 85% of the inde- 
pendent pharmacists, he, she or 
a counterpart would have 
reached about 66% of the chain 
pharmacists. If 5 out of 10 inde- 
pendents had seen a rep from 
one of these companies, then 
generally 3 out of 10 chain phar- 
macists would have also seen a 
rep from that company. 

In all cases, the pattern was 
consistent. There was no com- 
pany that had reps reaching 
more chain pharmacists than in- 
dependent pharmacists. 

As one would expect, the 
companies who had reached the 
least number of pharmacists 
within a six-month launch of a 
new product received the lowest 
overall satisfaction ratings. 

The three companies on our 
list who had only reached be- 
tween 10% and 20% of our over- 
all respondents in the six-month 
launch period barely received a 
‘somewhat satisfied” rating 
while the three companies who 
had reached at least 5 out of 10 
of our respondents received a 
close to “very satisfied” rating: 
2.6 out of a possible 3.0 score. 

Pharmacists in the survey 
aiso complained that when de- 
tailists visited, buyers were not 
giving them all the information 
they needed to adequately eval- 
uate the product. 

Pharmacists said they were 
not getting enough information 
about possible side effects, pos- 
sible interactions and adverse 
reactions, and that some of the 
information they were getting 
was either “too vague” or “too 
technical.”

oo are entering the mar-

“In today’s world, there are

and these new drugs place cer-

Caputo pointed out that the 
recent AARP survey of over 
1,000 people 45 years old and up 
found that 30% of all people who 
experience side effects describe 
them as “very serious.” 

Some 3% of those in the 
AARP study who experienced 
side effects were hospitalized 
because of side effects and that 
figure was as high as 6% for re- 
spondents over 65. 

According to the study, some 
60% of all consumers stop tak- 
ing medicine when they experi- 
ence a side effect. Cohen said 
one of the reasons they give up 
so quickly is because their phar- 
macists and their doctors “nev- 
er” warned them about the pos- 
sibility of side effects in the first 
place. 

“Some 55% of the respon- 
dents in the survey,” Cohen 
said, “reported they had never 
received any information about 
‘normal’ side effects or possible 
reactions.” 

“More than 6 out of 10 respon- 
dents,” he said, “were never 
told what to do if a serious side 
effect or bad reaction material- 
ized.” 

Rxers overworked 

Part of the problem, both 
men agreed, was that pharma- 
cists are often overworked and, 
according to studies done by 
pharmaceutical associations, 
spend only about 20% of their 
work time counseling or educat- 
ing patients. 

owever, the computer is 
liberating today’s pharmacist 
from much of the old paperwork 
and there is an opportunity to 


get more involved in counseling 
if the pharmacist is well in- 
formed.

have a very effective product,”

properly could really help the 
patient. But many patients may 
never get to use the drug prop- 
erly because pharmacists have

Only good news 

Caputo also pointed out that 
manufacturers generally tell 
pharmacists the “good news” 
about their preduct, but often 
hold back the bad. “They irony 
is,” he said, “that most pharma- 
cists are not as anxious for the 
commercial as they are for real- 


istic presentations that outline

about a product.” 

Most manufacturers achieve

chain by selling their products

chain headquarters. Cohen

seem to be assuming that most 
product information will filter 
down from the corporate buyer

case,” he said. “Just 37% of all

fied with the information they 
were receiving from chain 
headquarter bulletins.”

through physician and consum-

by less than 4 out of 10 respon- 
dents. 

It’s very likely that chain 
pharmacists see detailmen less 
frequently than independents 
because chains discourage in- 
store visits, instead chains rely 
on their corporate pharmaceu- 
tical buyers to distribute prod- 
uct information to the pharma- 
cists in the stores. But it is clear 
from our study, that this infor- 
mation source is not working 
very effectively, and chain phar- 
macists as a result are less in- 


formed or at least they feel less 
informed about all the various 
aspects of pharmaceutical prod- 
ucts than their independent 
counterparts. 

At a presentation on the 
Drug Store News findings given 
earlier this month at the 
NACDS Pharmaceutical Show 
in Philadelphia, pharmaceutical 
editor Joe Caputo warned that 
lower detail frequencies and 
lack of adequate patient product 
information pose a_ potential 
threat to patient well being 
while they may also contribute 
to an increase in adverse side ef- 
fects, potentially dangerous in- 
teractions and noncompliance. 

Caputo said manufacturers 
should take a “serious look” at 
their detailing frequencies, par- 
ticularly in reference to the indi- 
vidual chain stores, and that 
they should make every effort 
to give the chain store pharma- 
cist the service levels and prod- 
uct information they require to 
remain “America’s No. 1 trust- 
ed professional.” 

“We have a situation where 
the manufacturer and the phar- 
macist could be doing more to 
help each other,” he said, “and 
they are not taking advantage 
of it.”

Walgreens tops $2.7 billion in fiscal ’83 sales 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Despite a slackening of its 
pace during the fourth quarter, the Walgreen Co. re- 
ported record fiscal sales and earnings for the 10th 
consecutive year. 

For fiscal 1984 ended Aug. 31, Walgreens recorded 
corporate sales of $2.74 billioin up 16.3% over iast 
year’s $2.36 billion. In reaching that mark, Walgreens 
remained the top drug store chain by sales. 

Net earnings for the year rose 22.4% to $85.4 mil- 
lion, putting Walgreens neck-and-neck with Eckerd, 
which two weeks earlier also reported fiscal year 
earnings of $85.4 million. 

Walgreens’ earnings, however, included a gain of 
$3.6 million on the fourth-quarter sale of its equity in- 
vestment in its Sanborns Mexican operation. 

The drug store division, which accounts for 90% of 
the chain’s corporate sales, registered a 16.8% gain in 
sales for the year, while comparable store sales rose a 
solid 11.2%. 

Pacing the drug division results were prescription 
sales, which jumped 22.8%. Chain president Fred F. 
Canning attributed sharp gains to Walgreens’ Inter- 
com pharmacy computer system, now on-line chain- 
wide.

Genovese opens Long Island unit 


LINDENHURST, N.Y. — Genovese Drug Stores has 
opened a new 20,000-sq.-ft. drug store in Lindenhurst, Long 
Island, that features a 4,000-sq.-ft. home health care depart- 
ment and a full-line automotive department. It is the first Gen- 
ovese store to group both the auto and home and health care 
retailing concepts under one roof. Earlier this year, Genovese 
opened its first freestanding home health care unit in Queens, 

.Y., and more recently, unveiled a full-line automotive de- 
partment in a new store in Jackson Heights, N.Y. 


Sherwin-Williams earnings up 


CLEVELAND — Sherwin-Williams reported third-quar- 
ter earnings of $25.3 million on sales of $552.5 million. This rep- 
resents a 9.6% increase in earnings and a 4.2% gain in sales. 

According to company chairman, president and ceo John G. 
Breen, the paint store segment reported healthy sales and 
earnings. The Gray Drug Fair division, however, “lost the 
sales momentum of the first two quarters of the year, and our 
new management team is working to regain it.” 


SupeRx’s Thole new Fla. vp 


CINCINNATI — SupeRx has named Jerry Thole to the 
new position of vp of Florida operations. Thole will be respon- 
sible for the food/drug combination store operations in that di- 
vision. Thole was formerly vp operations. 

According to SupeRx spokesman Bob Griffith, the move 
was made to “strengthen our commitment to the growing F lor- 
ida division.” 


McKesson antitrust order ends 


WASHINGTON — The Federal Trade Commission official- 
ly eliminated the final remaining provision of a 17-year-old 
antitrust order against McKesson. 

That order, triggered by Foremost Dairies acquisition of 
McKesson & Robbins almost two decades ago, stemmed from 
FTC charges that the takeover “lessened competition in dru 
wholesaling and in the manufacture and sale of pharmaceutica 
preparations.” 

Over the years most of the restrictions imposed on McKes- 
son by the 1967 order were lifted in response to shifts in the 
marketplace. 

FTC set aside the sole remaining provision—a requirement 
that the firm sell crude lactose at “reasonable, nondiscrimina- 
tory prices” to other United States producers of pharmaceuti- 
cal grade lactose—because McKesson sold its lactose produc- 
tion facilities earlier this year.

Stiffer penalties approved 


for Rxers who divert drugs 


WASHINGTON — Pharma- 
cists convicted of diverting con- 
trolled substances will soon face 
up to 15 years in prison for a 
first offense. 

That is one of the provisions if 
a new Federal anticrime law 
passed by Congress last month. 

The new law, which won final 
approval only hours before 
Congress adjourned for the 
election campaign recess earli- 
er this month, triples the maxi- 
mum Federal prison sentences 
to 15 years for first offenders, 
and allows the courts to incar- 
cerate drug-diverting pharma- 
cists convicted of repeat of- 


fenses for as many as 30 years. 

These stiff new penalties— 
which apply also to nonpharma- 
cists who illegally distribute or 
manufacture amphetamines, 
barbiturates or other Schedule 
IT nonnarcotic substances—are 
on top of increased fines of $20,- 
000 to $50,000 per violation. 

Although Congress acknowl- 
edged in an accompanying re- 
port that only a “small number” 
of the nation’s pharmacists en- 
gage in diversion, that report 
makes it clear that retail phar- 
macies are considered the main 
trouble area. 

“The retail level is believed to 


be the principal source from 
which drugs are ‘diverted’ from 
legitimate medical use to drug 
abusers,” the committee report 
noted. 

The law permits the Justice 
Department to use more flexi- 
ble standards in suspending or 
revoking pharmacy registra- 
tions. 

Under the previous law, 
D.E.A. could lift a pharmacy’s 
registration in following the 
pharmacist’s conviction of a 
controlled substance-related 
felony, a decision by state offi- 
cials to deny, revoke or suspend

he wholesale drug industry in 1984 is continuing to expand dra- 
T matically-—both in product lines carried and in types of custom- 
ers serviced. 

The major companies are either expanding their product lines to 
achieve greater sales penetrations from their current customer base 
or are studying the possibilities of such an expansion. 

There is an intense effort to attract new customers, specifically hos- 
pitals, nursing home suppliers, HMO’s and other similar accounts. 
There is some trend toward consolidation of facilities so that compa- 
nes can achieve the operational efficiencies that come from pumping a 
higher sales volume through single centers. And there is a major 
thrust in automating programs so that productivity savings can be re- 
alized. 

There is a growing emphasis on developing voluntary or coopera- 
tive advertising customers so that independent retailers can be armed 
to compete on a more aggressive level with the chains, and there is a 
great amount of energy being devoted to the development of new mer- 
chandising programs that will support the retailer as he or she ex- 


pands in-store mix of products, particularly in such hot growth cate- 
gories as home health care convalescent aids. 

There is also a new onslaught of “acquisition fever” sweeping the in- 
dustry as price-earnings multiples return to more acceptable pur- 
chasing levels and as growth-minded tigers such as FoxMeyer knuckle 
down to the business of spending the capital they raised from going 
public. 

Almost all of the companies interviewed by Drug Store News for 
this report were broadening their product line base in 1984. McKes- 
son has developed a full-line stationery and home and school supplies 
program as well as a full line of medical-surgical supplies. It was add- 
ing such new lines as pet care, reading glasses, hosiery, hair lotions 
and fragrances to its mix. 

Bergen Brunswig was rolling out a stationery program and filling in 
products for such categories as watches, pantyhose, batteries, baby 
care, lawn chairs and other seasonals, etc. McPike was expanding its 
selection of home health care and durable medical equipment, as well

as continuing its emphasis on fra-

Amfac was studing the possibility of 
product-line expansions. Durr-Fillauer 
was diversifying into stationery and 
school supplies. Drug Service, a division 
of Synergex, which only a few years ago 
expanded heavily into H&BA products, 
was investigating a wide variety of other 
product expansions, including electron- 
ics, candy, tobacco and food. Ketchum 
Distributors had completed the rollout 
of 16 new merchandising departments 
and was preparing to launch a second 
phase of rollouts. 

Just about everyone was developing 
or introducing home health care pro- 
grams. 

“You know that because of automated 
order/entry systems, most retail cus- 
tomers are using one wholesaler as their 
primary or main vendor,” said Mel Whit- 
mire, president of Drug Service, “and 
that means that since they’re buying pri- 
marily from one source, they’re continu- 
ing to demand additional products. 

“From a wholesaler’s point of view, of 
course, the more we can sell them, as 
long as we can turn it fast enough and 
handle it efficiently enough, the more 
we can grow,” Whitmire added. 

“When we had shorter product lines, 
we got less of the retailer’s business,” 
said Doug Thompson, sr. vp of distribu- 
tion planning for McKesson Corp. “We 
prosper by expanding our product lines. 
We get deeper penetration into the drug 
Stores we service.” 

Fuller-line companies such as McKes- 
son and Bergen were estimating that 
they were now supplying 63% to 65% of 
an average retail customer’s wholesaler 
needs, as opposed to less than 50% four 
or five years ago. 

Home health looks promising 

Home health care, because of the gen- 
eral aging of the population and because 
more hospitals are discharging patients 
earlier today to improve their own cost 
efficiencies, was regarded by nearly ev- 
ery wholesaler as a particularly promis- 
ing potential new market. 


Drug Store News’ first Wholesal- 
er Trends Survey was done in the late 
summer and fall of this year with the 
assistance of the National Wholesale 
Druggists’ Association (NWDA). 

The survey was sent to the corpo- 
rate headquarters of 107 companies 
operating a total of 321 distribution 
facilities. — 

The companies we surveyed gener- 
ated more than $10.3 billion in sales in 
1983, approximately 90% of total sales 
for the wholesale drug industry. 

Response rate for the survey ex- 
ceeded 19% and included companies 
operating as few as one, to as many as 
50 distribution centers. 


Joe Polastri, general manager of 
McKesson’s Drug Services, was devel- 
oping a new program for McKesson cus- 
tomers in the belief that home health 
care sales are going to continue to go 
“straight up.” McKesson, like Drug Ser- 
vice, was using the resources of one of its 
divisions, the Sun Mark Home Health 
Care Company, to support and enrich its 
developing home health care program. 

Drug Service was planning to use the 
sources and contacts developed by its 
sister division, Hospital Services and 
Supplies, to strengthen its particular 
home health care program. 

“This is a very large potential mar- 
ket,” said Whitmire, “and it’s going to 
grow rapidly.” 

Tom Coulbourn, executive vp of Ow- 
ens & Minor, called home health care 
“one of the most significant areas of op-

portunity for the retail druggist to come 
along in years.” John Wilcox, director of 
sales and marketing for McPike, said 
the growth prospects were “phenome- 
nal.” 

“In the past year, we have more than 
tripled our sales in this category,” he 
said. 

Entwined with the enthusiasm for 
home health care lines was a comparable 
enthusiasm for hospital accounts, seen 
by most wholesalers as an area for 
strong and dramatic sales gains. 

Some wholesalers such as Owens & 
Minor and Drug Service were already 
generating a substantial percentage of 
total sales (45% and 50%, respectively) 
through hospitals, while others such as 
McKesson were experiencing growth 
rates in excess of 30%. For fiscal 1985, 
approximately 12% of McKesson’s total 
sales for its wholesale division is expect- 
ed to come from hospitals. 

In contrast, most wholesalers report- 
ed that their growth rate among inde- 
pendent retailers, traditionally the 
wholesaler’s strongest customer base, 
were flat or up only slightly. 

Chains, surprisingly enough, were 
also considered a growth area for many 
wholesalers, and not just for those locat- 
ed on the West Coast. Because the 
wholesale industry in the past 10 years 
has consistently been able to lower oper- 
ating expenses, pricing has become 
more and more competitive. 

“Chains are finding that in many cases 
they can acquire products more effi- 
ciently from us than they can buying it 
direct,” said a source from Bergen. 

Hospital share targeted 

Hospitals were also learning that 
same lesson. Emil Martini Jr., chairman 
and ceo of Bergen, estimated that within 
five years the wholesale industry will 
have a higher share of the hospital mar- 
kets sales than they have today from re- 
tail drug stores. 

“The hospitals are learning,” said 
Martini, “that most wholesalers can 
supply them cheaper than if they buy di- 
rect. Plus, wholesalers can help keep 
their costs down by keeping their inven- 
tories down. And if they buy from a pri- 
mary wholesaler, they deal with one in- 
voice and one delivery. If they buy 
direct, they’re dealing with dozens of in- 
voices and deliveries. The cost savings 
are substantial.” 

Much of the dollar growth that the 
wholesale drug industry has been able 


to generate in the past few years has re- 
sulted from operating efficiencies that 
have reduced margins and made the 
wholesalers riore price-competitive. 

To some wholesalers and to some ana- 
lysts on Wall Street, the decline in profit 
margins (down to 9.77 on average in 
1983 compared with 10.48 last year and 
11.63 in 1978) is serious, portending a 
worrisome return to the dog-eat-dog 
days that threatened to destroy the in- 
dustry in the early to mid-70’s. 

But to the bigger and more progres- 
sive companies that have been able to re- 
duce margins and lower prices through 
operating improvements, the trend was 
not frightening, but promising. 

They agreed with National Wholesale 
Druggists’ Association president Bill 
Ford, who pointed out that the decline in 
margins is offset “by an almost parallel 
reduction in operating expenses.” 

Operating expenses to net sales, Ford 
said, were down 7% to 7.21% in 1983 
while operating expenses to gross prof- 
its were down nearly 8% to 73.82%. 

“Very strong year” 

Ford called 1983, a year in which the 
wholesale industry generated a 17% in- 
crease in sales to nearly $12 billion, “a 
very strong year for drug wholesalers.” 
He said NWDA’s findings indicate that 
the industry is continuing “to move 
ahead aggressively in such areas as sales 
growth, expense reduction, averase line 
extensions, inventory and tota! « set 
turns and receivables.” 

“What you’re seeing today is what I 
call ‘value-pricing,’ ” said Whitmire of 
Drug Service. “Wholesalers may be cut- 
ting their prices but when they do they 
compensate by reducing collection peri- 
ods.” 

In fact, NWDA’s latest operations 
surveys show that the average collection 
period for a wholesaler today is 26.44 
days, compared with 28.42-days in 1982 
and 37.03 days in 1975. 

The NWDA survey also shows that 
wholesalers are doing an excellent job 
on other significant profit indicators in- 
cluding: return on total assets, average 
line extensions, inventory turns, reduc- 
tion of operating expenses as a percent- 
age of both gross profits and net sales, 
net profit percentages and return on net 
worth. 

“Our volume is going up and our costs 
of handling are going down,” said Bill 
Williamson, chairman and ceo of Durr- 
Fillauer, “and that makes us the most 


cost-effective distribution industry in 
America.” 
Automation continues 

To continue to fuel that trend, most 
wholesalers in 1984 were continuing to 
automate, upgrade or expand existing 
distribution facilities. 

McKesson, Southwestern Drug and 
others were continuing to consolidate by 
closing older and smaller facilities while 
replacing them with larger ones capable 
of handling higher volumes and operat- 
ing more efficiently. In eight years, 
McKesson has gone from more than 90 
facilities to 50, while Southwestern has 
gone from 11 to four d.c.’s. 

The higher-volume facilities are also 
being automated; automation sortation 
systems are being added, more pro- 
grams are being computerized, scan- 
ners are being installed into higher vol- 
ume d.c.’s to route orders, and at least 
one wholesaler, Bergen Brunswig, is 
testing automatic single-item picking 
machines in one of its highest-volume 
d.c.’s—while Southwestern is prepar- 
ing to go on line with a “state of the art” 
perpetual inventory automatic replen- 
ishment system.

says Steve Westall, senior vice presi- 
dent of LAD Drug, “we are shrinking 
the size of the areas we work in, picking 
more efficiently, computerizing stock 
repienishments, computerizing sorta- 
tion systems, conveyor systems, etc. 

“Even though all of our d.c.’s except 
one are unionized, we’ve still managed 
to reduce operating expenses as a per- 
centage of sales from a high of 8% a few 
years ago to 5% today.” 

A few wholesalers think the industry 
today may have gone about as far as it’s 
able to go in reducing operating ex- 
penses, but Westall disagrees. 

“T think the wholesale industry is go- 
ing to continue to grow like this. The 
companies in this industry have always 
been innovative. Look at order/entry. In 
a Short while, you’re going to see a great 
surge in automatic order replenish- 
ments and that will lead to additional 
cost savings.” 

“Value added services” 

And, in what promises to be an in- 
creasing boon to retailers, as wholesal- 
ers Save money, they are plowing more of 
it into marketing programs in the form 
of what is now popularly known as “val- 
ue added services.” 

This means the typical drug store re- 
tailer, whether chain or independent, 


can increasingly turn to his or her 
wholesaler for help with inventory man- 
agement, planograms, pricing, financial 
services, promotional assistance, ac- 
counting, etc. 

Drug Service, for instance, has a new 
automatic in-store accounts-receivable 
program that permits a retailer to auto- 
matically transmit accounts receivables 
to wholesaler headquarters. Drug Ser- 
vice, in turn, prepares the statements 
for its customers. 

McKesson has a number of customer- 
service programs including a rapidly 
growing service merchandise program 
called Cos Mck; Bergen has a space man- 
agement program, plus a number of pro- 
motional programs in additional to the 
traditional merchandising and pricing 
programs that most of the major whole- 
salers offer; FoxMeyer has a broad 
range of promotional programs, etc. 

“Service orientation is a trend now,” 
said Chester Milligan, president of Am- 
fac Distribution and Health Care. 
“McKesson and Bergen have done an ex- 
cellent job of molding the industry to- 
ward a marketing concept that stresses 
service. It really started with the shift 
to automated order/entry systems. Out 
of that came velocity reports, inventory 
management reports, planogramming, 
the whole marketing/merchandising 


value added services concept.” 

“For the past 10 years, the industry 
has been moving toward a service dis- 
tinction, not just a price distinction,” 
said Doug Thompson, McKesson’s se- 
nior vp of Distribution Planning. “A ser- 
vice distinction makes it possible for a 
wholesalee to stand out from his compe- 
tition. Plus it makes it easier for the 
more cost-efficient companies to com- 
pete. They’re able to attract customers 
from those companies that are not as ef- 
ficient.” 

Co-op advertising expanding 

The thrust of competition is also cre- 
ating another trend that is benefiting in- 
dependent retailers: the creation and 
expansion of voluntary or cooperative 
advertising programs. 

McKesson has the largest and per- 
haps oldest voluntary group, the 1,600- 
member Valu-Rite based in Los Ange- 
les, but Bergen Brunswig has a growing 
voluntary association called Good 
Neighbor. FoxMeyer has its thriving 
Health Mart, Durr-Fillauer has Price 
Guard, Drug Service has Prime Value, 
Owens & Minor has Cardinal Drug, Dik 
Drug has Centsible, ete. 

Many of these groups are less than a 
few years old, but all seem to be grow- 
ing. 

“There will have to be more action 


with voluntaries,” said Rex Molson, 
president of McKesson’s Drug and 
Health Care Division. “Independents 
need to belong to something so that over 
the long run, they can get the advan- 
tages and economies of scale. That’s the 
only way they’re going to be able to com- 
pete with chains.” 

Bergen, whose Staff for its Good 
Neighbor program were recruited di- 
rectly from the retail side of the busi- 
ness, is investing about $500,000 a year 
in advertising revenues for the program 
and hopes to use Good Neighbor to cre- 
ate a strong identity for its approximate- 
ly 500 members. 

In certain pockets such as Fresno, 
Calif., where the program has been in 
place for over a year, vp of merchandis- 
ing Tom Allison reports “a growing 
awareness on the part of the consumer 
to the Good Neighbor names and ser- 
vices.” 

“All voluntaries,” said Ron Bone, 
president of McKesson’s Valu-Rite, “try 
to provide independents with the pro- 
motional tools that will make them more 
successful. The idea is to provide them 
with a way to keep their autonomy, but 
at the same time take advantage of the 
kinds of purchasing and distributional 
and promotional economies a chain can 
enjoy.” 


he wholesale drug industry in- 
creased sales 17% in 1983 to $11.9 
billion. 


According to the most recent Nation- 
al Wholesale Druggists’ Association’s 
Operating Survey, about 10 points of 
that total growth is “real,” or minus in- 
flation. The NWDA inflation index, 
which measures increases in product 
prices, rose only 7% in 1983. 

If the industry simply maintains that 
same rate of growth for 1984, as it seems 
to be doing, total wholesale drug sales 
will come close to and possibly exceed 
$14 billion. 

To date most of the major companies, 
such as McKesson, Bergen, ALCO and 
FoxMeyer, are already ahead of that 
growth, with sales increases generally 
averaging more than 20%. 

Many of the midsize to smaller compa- 
nies, however, are generating sales in- 
creases in the 12% to 20% range. 

The industry suffered some criticism 
in 1983 for alleged “profitability slip- 
page,” but that slippage was mostly tied 
to a decline in the average profit margin 
for the industry. Those who criticized 
the trend failed to take into account off- 
setting factors such as substantial de- 
clines in average operating expenses 
with simultaneous increases in average 
volume sales. 

“NWDA’s numbers show that there’s 


a decline in net profit from 1.41% in 1982 
to 1.37% in 1983,” said Joel Liffman, an 
analyst for Drexel Burham, “but I don’t 
consider that a meaningful number. 

“If you round off the number, there is 
really a zero change. Much more mean- 
ingful is the fact that as a general trend, 
gross profitability in the industry is in- 
creasing. 

“Operating expenses are not growing 
as fast as sales. Revenues in this indus- 
try are growing quicker than expenses, 
which means that this industry is fairly 
well leveraged.” 

Bill Ford, president of NWDA, points 
out that the ratio of net sales to total as- 
sets in 1983 hit “an all-time high” while 
average annual inventory rates in- 
creased substantially and the average 
collection period in days went down dra- 
matically. 

The result was that net profits after 
taxes declined slightly in 1983, down 
from an all-time high of 15.55% in 1982 
to 15.23% in 1983. Ford said the 15.23% 
return was a “very strong showing.” 

“Some people say the wholesale in- 
dustry has already done so much to im- 
prove profitability by reducing expenses 
and improving productivity that there’s 
very little room for any further growth, 
but I don’t agree with that,” said Gene 
Vykukal, president of Southwestern 
Drug.

Most wholesalers are aggressively 
pursuing volume growth from a variety 
of strategies. They range from acquisi- 
tions through the consolidation of distri- 
bution facilities through the search for 
new customer markets: hospitals, 
HMO’s, nursing homes, veterinarian 
services, department stores, food

with greater varieties of products: home

stationery, pet care, fragrances, cos-

Wholesalers are also continuing to 
capture an ever-increasing share of the 
United States pharmaceutical business. 
According to the most recent study done 
by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers 
Association, wholesalers have increased 
their share of total pharmaceutical sales 
to 60% in 1980 from just 48.5% in 1976.

have been the strongest growth ar- 

eas for wholesalers, with most in- 
dustry members projecting that the 
trend will continue strongly for the next 
two years. 

According to Drug Store News’ first 
Wholesaler Trends Study, nearly 9 out 
of every 10 wholesaling companies have 
experienced sales increases in hospital 
business for the past two years while 
80% of all wholesalers believe this 
growth will continue at least for the next 
two years. 

According to the survey, many whole- 
salers have increased their hospital 
sales between 30% and 50% in the past 
year alone. 

More than 60% of the companies who 
responded to our survey were doing 
more than 20% of their total business 
with hospitals, while several of our re- 
spondents had total sales in excess of 
40% and 50%. 

Only 1 out of every 10 respondents be- 
lieved their sales to hospitals might de- 
crease in the coming two years, while 8 
out of 10 believed their sales would go up 
dramatically. 

Many respondents (70%) also report- 
ed dramatic increases in sales direct to 
chain drug stores, while a smaller num- 
ber, 20%, also reported that at the same 
time sales to chain warehouses had also 
gone up considerably over the past two 
years. 

More than 80% of our respondents felt 
that sales direct to chain stores will con- 
tinue to increase in the future, while 4 
out of 10 felt this pattern would continue 
with respect to chain warehouses. 

The current percentage of sales direct 
to a chain store ranged from a low of 2% 
to a high of 30% for respondents selling 
to this marketplace. Most respondents 
were doing only between 1% and 10% of 
their business with chain warehouses, 
but there were exceptions: one respon- 
dent was currently doing more than 80% 
of its business with chain warehouses. 

The prime customer for most of our 
wholesaler respondents was still the in- 
dependent community retailer. More 
than 80% of our respondents reported 


that business with independents had in- 
creased in the past two years, while 80% 
also felt it would continue to increase. 

In addition to hospitals, the most 
promising areas for future new sales 
growth were the following: indepen- 
dents, chain stores direct, chain ware- 
houses, nursing home suppliers, nurs- 
ing homes direct, food stores, mass mer- 
chandise stores, convalescent aids 
stores, HMO’s and clinics. 

Some respondents were currently 
generating as much as 28% of their total 
sales through mass merchandisers, but 
the average ranged from 2% to 4%. For 
most respondents, sales to HMO’s and 
clinics ranged from a low of 1% to a high 
of'5%, while sales to nursing home sup- 
pliers, for those in this business, ranged 
from 3% to 5%. Sales to nursing homes 
direct hovered between 1% and 3%, but 
some respondents reported they would 
not pursue this line of business because 
it would put them in competition with 
retail customers. 

For those respondents doing business 
with food stores, the per cent of total 
sales ranged from 1% to 3%. 

Over the course of the next two years, 
however, nearly 45% of our respondents 
felt that sales to nursing home suppliers 
would increase while 15% believed this 
would also happen with food stores. 

Five out of 10 of our respondents also 
felt sales to clinics and HMO’s would go 
up in the next two years, while 20% be- 
lieved the same would happen with mass 
merchandise stores. 

Despite the fact that only one whole- 
saler was currently selling direct to phy- 
sicians, 15% of our respondents felt this 
market would grow. 

More than half the respondents in our 
survey supported a voluntary or a more 
limited form of promotional advertising 
program. The percentage of total whole- 
saler sales generated by these various 
memberships varied widely, ranging 
from a low of 0.03% of sales to a high of 
15% of sales. The average, however, was 
around 12%. 

In marketing services, just about 
every respondent featured a broad as- 
sortment of merchandising support pro-

programs (profit and loss reports, labor 
scheduling reports, etc.) to their stable 
of marketing services, while another 
15% were planning to add private-label. 

Ten per cent were also planning to add 
site selection assistance and in-store

Most of our wholesaler respondents 
were also giving their retailers help in 
developing a zone-pricing program. 
Nearly 9 out of every 10 wholesalers had 
such a service available for H&BA and 
OTC products, while 50% also offered it 
for pharmaceutical products. 

In the area of product mix, all of our 
respondents were generating the bulk of

maceuticals as a percentage of sales 
ranged from a low of 60% for the most di-

90% for those houses that were primari-

Service translates into growth at McKesson 


SAN FRANCISCO — McKesson 
Drug & Health Care, the largest divi- 
sion of the McKesson Corporation and 
the nation’s No. 1 drug wholesaler, is 
continuing to court growth by putting 
its marketing emphasis on service. 

The group, which was the first to coin 
the term “value-added services” now 
used by the entire drug-wholesaling in- 
dustry, has just developed a new finan- 
cial and business study package for its 
retail customers. 


M-Kesson 


The study package, which McKesson 
plans to make available to any interest- 
ed retailer, consists of a series of seven 
modules built around video cassettes 
addressing specific problems. 

“It’s like a Harvard case history,” 
says Joe Polastri, a group executive vp 
and general manager of the drug compa- 
ny. “We taped a retailer trying to cope 
with a specific problem. It might be cash 
management or inventory control or 
gross-margin analysis. We’re showing 
those tapes at seminars that we’ve set 
up in various sections of the country. 
Our merchandising reps lead the semi- 
nars and they try to help retailers figure 
out the best strategies to adopt given 
the nature of that particular problem.” 

Both Polastri and Rex Malson, presi- 
dent of the Drug & Health Care Group 
and a corporation vp, feel that the era of 
chains madly gobbling up market share 
at the expense of independents is end- 
ing, but that independents still need to 
improve their business and financial 
- skills if they are going to prosper. 

“The weak,” says Polastri, “have al- 
ready been weeded out by the chains. 
But there are still lots of retailers out 
there having a tough time, and this kind 
of program is designed to help them.” 

McKesson is also continuing to ex- 
pand its Cos Mck service merchandising 
program. For an agreed upon fee, a 
McKesson rep will set, stock, replenish, 


price label and maintain just about any 
department in a retail drug store. The 
most commonly repped departments, 
however, are cosmetics, costume jewel- 
ry, hosiery, pet care, stationery and fra- 
grances. 

“The service levels we provide are a 
way to distinguish ourselves from our 
competition,” says Doug Thompson, 
McKesson’s senior vp of distribution 
planning. 

“For the past 10 years, this industry 
has been moving toward service distinc- 
tions rather than just price distinctions. 
Price competition is still a logical and 
plausible business strategy, but it 
doesn’t take a genius to figure out how 
to give away profit. As an industry, 
we’ve been in that loop for a long, long 
time.” 

Like its closest competitor, Bergen 
Brunswig, McKesson has been aggres- 
sively moving to automate its opera- 
tions and expand into new customer ar- 
eas. 

The chain’s newest warehouse in Sac- 
ramento has an automated sortation 
system as well as a picking system se- 
quenced by “families” of traditional 
drug store departments. All dental care 
products, for instance, are in the dental 
care “department” of the warehouse 
and each incoming order from a retailer 
is presorted by computer so that pickers 
can fill all dental product orders at one 
time. 

To get even more productivity out of 
its distribution centers, McKesson is 
also putting in mezzanines that allow 
pickers to work from storage space that 
was previously just “empty air.” The 
cube in a McKesson warehouse is now 
averaging 30 ft. instead of 24 ft. “It’s 

just more efficient to stack higher,” says 
Polastri.

Because of its operational efficien- 
cies, Sacramento is now McKesson’s 
most active facility. In mid 1984, it was 
running at 1987 sales projections and 
with a capacity of a million lines a 
month, handling close to 750,000. 

Consolidated centers 

For the past eight years, McKesson 
has been consolidating its warehouses, 
closing smaller facilities and replacing 
them with much larger more centralized 
facilities like the one in Sacramento. 

The move from smaller to larger, ac- 
cording to Polastri and Thompson, per- 
mits each facility to stock from between 
1,000 to 1,500 more items, enabling 
McKesson, in Thompson’s words, “to 
improve customer service.” 

“Even though our consolidated cen- 
ters may be further from the customer 
service point,” says Thompson, “they 
usually have larger inventories and that 
means that our retail customers now 
have many more unique items available 
to them.” 

The move, of course, also enables 


yo _ Wholesaler Profiles — 


McKesson to improve its operational ef- 
ficiencies because each consolidated 
center handles larger volumes of busi- 
ness. 

Thompson points out that McKesson 
is more than 50% ahead of the industry’s 
median average on office productivity 
(number of order lines processed per 
man-hour) and 80% ahead on warehouse 
productivity (number of lines picked per 
man-hour). 

More products 

The centers are also continuing to car- 
ry more and more diversified products. 
In addition to pharmaceuticals, H&BA 
and OTC products, McKesson now 
stocks a full line of stationery and school 
and office supplies, pet supplies, read- 
ing glasses, hair notions and fragrances 
(also available through McKesson’s Fra- 
grance Division, one of nine subdivi- 
sions now grouped into the Drug & 
Health Care Division). 

“We are carrying more products that 
go into the center of the store,” says Po- 
lastri. “And we’re also filling in more 
products for the perimeters of the store. 
We feel the more orders we can fill, the 
more we can grow.” 

McKesson’s management feels inde- 
pendents, chains and hospitals will be 
the strongest avenues for future 
growth, but the company is also continu- 
ing to supply product to food stores and 
mass merchandisers and there is a 
chance McKesson may form a service 
merchandise division to help food stores 
market H&BA and OTC products. 

“The hospital business is growing by 
leaps and bounds,” says Polastri. “We 
were up 35% in sales last year and so far, 
this year, we’re up 32%.” 

Like most wholesalers, McKesson is 
trying to position itself as a “prime ven- 
dor” for both its retail and hospital cus- 
tomers. So far, the concept is working. 
McKesson’s management estimates 
that the company is a prime vendor (the 
No. 1 source of supply for an individual 
account) to at least 80% of its drug store 
retail customers. 


LOS ANGELES — Bergen Bruns- 
wig, the wholesaler with the second- 
highest volume in the country, is pro- 
jecting a growth rate of between 20% to 
25% annually for the next five years. 

Bergen’s chairman and ceo Emil Mar- 
tini estimates that the company’s most 
dramatic growth will come from its con- 
sumer electronic division. Sales for the 
division for the past 10 years have al- 
ready increased 10-fold. 

However, in the drug distribution

arena, growth is expected to come from 
two key areas: an expanded customer 
base and an extended product mix. 

Bergen’s vice president of merchan- 
dising Tom Allison estimates that the 
company’s nearly two-year-old volun- 
tary, the Good Neighbor program, will 
have about 500 members by the end of 
1984. “We’re growing at a rate of about 
20% a year,” Allison said. 

Like many wholesalers, Bergen is 
also aggressively going after more hos- 
pital business as well as “aggressively 
pursuing,” in Martini’s words, more 
sales to HMO’s.

than retail business,” said Martini. 
“Hospitals are where retail drug stores

starting to discover the economic bene-

customers. Today, they account for 
26%. Chains are also a source of growth 
for the company. In 1977, chains only ac- 
counted for about 24% of Bergen’s over- 
all business. Today, they account for 
about 33%. 

But with more than 4,200 indepen- 
dent retail accounts currently being ser- 
viced, independents are still the heart of 
Bergen’s business. Last year, they ac-

total sales. 

Bergen has been trying to nurture

wide variety of retailing and merchan-

which about 60% of its retail accounts 
belong, and a Super Saver program that 
Allison believes helps independents add 
a “bargain atmosphere” to their stores. 

Bergen’s space management program 
is a planograming support and merchan- 
dising system, while Space Saver is 
more promotional. 


About 80% of Bergen’s retail custom-

bership fee, participants get complete 
in-store monthly promotional packages, 
which usually feature eight to 10 spot- 
lighted, high-velocity products that 
change every other week. 

With the package comes color coordi- 
nated signs that, when hung within a 
store, create a “carnival atmosphere.” 
Also shelf talkers, window signs, hand 
bills, and a black and white velox for ads 
are offered. Bergen supports the pro- 
gram with spot TV as well as radio and 
print ads. 

In the area of line extensions, Bergen 
is currently working on the develop- 
ment of anew home health care program 
while simultaneously rolling cut 2 new 
line of about 1,000 stationery sku’s. 

“Sundries and stationery are getting 
a lot of attention from us,” Allison said. 
“We'll be expanding even more next 
year.” Through its new line of consumer 
products, Bergen is already distribut- 
ing pantyhose, watches, batteries and 
baby care. It is considering adding more 
seasonal items such as lawn chairs and 
barbecue grills. 

Earlier this year, Bergen began test- 
ing an automatic picking machine in its 
San Jose, Calif., warehouse. Martini 
said the $750,000 system will probably

years.

distribution centers “wherever the vol-

Of Bergen’s 50 distribution facilities, 
29 are currently used for drug wholesal- 
ing. The Drug Wholesale Group ac-

total sales last year.

Acquisitions push Alco Health into third place 


VALLEY FORGE, Pa. — With its 
voracious appetite for acquisitions and 
its keen ability to tune into thriving 
trends, Alco Health Services has be- 
come the third-largest full-service phar- 
maceutical distributor in the country 
within a span of only six years. 

Aleo Health Services is the drug 
wholesaling arm of Alco Standard, a 
huge conglomerate that posted 1983 
earnings of $57.2 million on sales of $2.8 
billion. During 1983, Alco Standard 
shed several of its manufacturing opera- 
tions in order to concentrate on its thriv- 
ing distribution properties, including 
Health Services. In fact, Aleo Health 
Services, which posted a 19% increase in 
1983 sales for a total of $691.3 million is 
the company’s fastest-growing segment 
and second largest behind its paper divi- 
sion. 

Alco Standard’s president and ceo, 
Ray B. Mundt, sees big things ahead for 


full-service pharmaceutical distribut- 
ing. In fact, he said that as new drugs hit 
the market and manufacturers continue 
to sell more pharmaceuticals through 
wholesale channels, the market could 
swell to more than $14 billion by 1985. 
That’s more than double its size four 
years ago. For Alco, the Health Ser- 
vices division is attractive because of a 
25% return on capital. 

Acquisitions have played a key role in 
Alco Health Services growth. When the 
company “acquires” another, it actually 
merges all operations (including person- 
nel) into its corporate umbrella. Accord- 
ing to the company, this encourages an 
entrepreneurial spirit within the com- 
pany. 


’ . ” “Wholesaler Profiles 


One of the most recent acquisitions 
was that of Brown Drug, which serves 
stores in Sioux Fall, S.D., Council 
Bluffs, lowa and Maxato, Minn. With 
the addition of Brown, Alco thrust itself 
into new markets. Its existing base in- 
cludes: The Drug House Inc., Brother- 
ston Health Care Services, Brotherston 
Hospital Supply, Duff Brothers Inc., 
The Geer Drug Company, The Kauff- 
man-Lattimer Company, Rita-Ann Dis- 
tributors, Smith-Higgins Inc., William 
T. Stover Company Inc., Strother Drug 
Company and Spetrum Corporation. 
The Alco Health Services serves 23 
states from New York and Pennsylva- 
nia south to Georgia and west to Texas. 
It is obvious that Alco Health Ser- 


vices’ growth has not only been geo- 
graphic, but into new categories, as 
well. Last year, for example, Alco ven- 
tured into the prestige fragrance, cos- 
metics and gift business with the pur- 
chase of Rita-Ann Distributors. 

Additionally, Alco is entering the 
home health care business with its Total 
Home Health Care programs. Under 
this plan, retailers can gain access to Al- 
co’s home health care products and tap 
into the company’s merchandising sav- 
VY. 

Another important program is Alco’s 
Family Independent Pharmacy volun- 
tary program. The voluntary program 
is set up to attract small pharmacies into 
Aleo’s distribution network. It offers 
them advertising support, access to Al- 
co’s computers to manage inventories, 
planograms, traffic analysis, value-add- 
ed product lines, store graphics and oth- 
er managerial tools. 


Purchases put FoxMeyer in new markets 


DENVER — FoxMeyer began fiscal 
1985 the way it closed the books on fiscal 
1984—-with a series of acquisitions. 

In April, FoxMeyer completed the 
the acquisition of I. L. Lyons, the New 
Orleans wholesaler, which last year 
posted operating earnings of $1.9 mil- 
lion on sales of $98.3 million. 

Four months later, FoxMeyer signed 
a letter of intent to purchase Yahr- 
Lange for $15.25 million in cash. The 
purchase of Yahr-Lange, which last 
year earned $2.5 million on sales of 
$118.6 million, opens up two more im- 
portant markets to FoxMeyer. To the 
north, Yahr-Lange is the No. 1 whole- 
saler in Milwaukee and the surrounding 
markets. Headquartered in Elm Grove, 
Wis., the company also operates distri- 
bution centers in Rockford, Ill., and La 
Crosse, Wis. In Florida, Yahr-Lange 
commas the No. 2 position in many 
markets, with distribution centers in 
Miami and Lakeland, Fla. Prior to the 
acquisition, FoxMeyer had no facilities 
in Wisconsin and only a marginal pres- 
ence in the Florida panhandle. 

Last month, FoxMeyer struck again. 
This time it was the Arlington, Tex., 
computer services firm, PharmAssist. 
When the purchase is completed Fox- 


Meyer will have doubled its base of 
pharmacy computer system users to 
nearly 2,600. PharmAssist provides 
computer services and products to an 
estimated 1,300 pharmacies in 29 states. 

FoxMeyer’s seemingly insatiable ap- 
petite for other wholesale operations 
and pharmacy computer firms has been 
well received on Wall Street. The 
wholesaler last month raised nearly $44 
million in a stock offering of nearly two 
million shares. Proceeds from the offer- 
ing were to be used to retire bank debt 
from previous acquisitions, the compa- 
ny said. 

Part of the reason that FoxMeyer has 
had little difficulty raising capital for ex- 
pansion is that the wholesaler has been 
ahle to quickly assimilate each of the ac- 
quisitions into its own operations. In ad- 
dition, many analysts have been im- 
pressed with the company’s outstanding 
financial performance. 

For the fiscal year ended March 3, 
FoxMeyer’s net income soared 126% to 
$5.2 million from $2.3 million earned in 
the previous year. Sales advanced 32% 
to $464 million from $351 million in fiscal 
1983. 

In addition, first-quarter results 
seem to indicate a continuation of the 


upward trend. Net income for the first 
quarter, ended June 30, jumped 102% to 
$1.4 million from $704,000 from the first 
quarter of the previous year. Sales rose 
56% during the first quarter to $159.4 
million from $102.3 million last year. 
The pending purchase of PharmAs- 
sist ranks as one of FoxMeyer’s most 
significant acquisitions since the compa- 
ny went public in 1983. It complements 
the wholesaler’s acquisitions of TBL, 
the pharmacy computer product and 
services firm in Texas that FoxMeyer 
merged into its Pharm-Data computer 
service division almost one year ago. 
FoxMeyer has exploited the pharma- 
cy computer as a means of attracting 
new accounts, particularly nontradi- 
tional pharmacy retailers, better than 
most other wholesalers. This year for in- 
stance, FoxMeyer contracted to install 
more than 1,000 Pharm-Data microcom- 
puters in K mart pharmacy stores 
throughout the country over the next 
three years. Sales to K mart, alone, rep- 
resent approximately 6% of FoxMeyer’s 
total volume. Overall, the wholesaler’s 
business with discounters and super- 
market chains such as Wal-Mart, 
Safeway, King Sooper and Albertson’s 
accounts for approximately 25% of its
