Investments aid Bindley income spiral 


INDIANAPOLIS — While other 
drug wholesalers made a concerted ef- 
fort last year to accelerate expansion 
through the acquisition of smaller 
wholesalers, Bindley Western parked 
much of its internal reserves in cash and 
marketable securities. 

The strategy has paid off handsomely 
for Bindley thus far. Together, earnings 
from the distribution of ethical pharma- 
ceuticals and income derived from in- 
vestments sent total corporate income 
for the first half of fiscal year 1985 sky- 
rocketing 68% to $2.3 million from $1.4 
million during the same period last year. 
On a per-share basis, earnings rose 16% 
to 72¢ from 62¢ during the first two 
quarters of 1983. Bindley’s sales for the 
first half of the year were up nearly 14% 
to $264.9 million from $232.7 million. 

Last year, Bindley raised nearly $20 
million from its first stock offering. At 
the time, William E. Bindley, chairman 


and ceo of the company, indicated that 
the wholesaler would be looking to ex- 
pand in existing markets by acquiring 
smaller companies. However, while ac- 
quisition opportunities presented them- 
selves, Bindley has been very selective 
and instead has directed its efforts to- 
ward growing internally. 

“We've looked at a number of possible 
acquisition targets,’ said Jack 
Laughner, president of Bindley West- 
ern Drug Co. “But we’re not going to 
buy something just for the exercise of 
buying another company.” 

Part of the reason that Bindley has 
been so selective in making any acquisi- 
tions is that the wholesaler is one of a 
dwindling number of houses whose prin- 
cipal business is the distribution of ethi- 
eal pharmaceuticals. Approximately 
95% of Bindley’s total sales are generat- 
ed through the sale of pharmaceuticals. 

Bindley has not ruled out purchasing 


a full-line wholesaler. According to 
Laughner, while Bindley would make 
some “modifications” to anything it 
bought, “we’d probably leave a full-line 
house intact.” 

But until Bindley makes such an ac- 
quisition, Laughner says, the compa- 
ny’s cash position and absence of any 
long-term debt is a “win-win situation.” 
At the close of fiscal 1984, Bindley had 
amassed nearly $25 million in cash and 
marketable securities. Of the $9.44 per- 
share in shareholders’ equity, $7.53 per 
share represented cash and other liquid 
instruments. In addition, Bindley has a 
line of credit totaling approximately $21 
million. However, Laughner said that 
any future acquisitions will likely be fi- 
nanced internally. 

Bindley also has used some of its capi- 
tal reserves to open a new distribution 
center in Dallas and relocate te a larger 
facility in its Phoenix operating region. 


Though supermarkets and discount- 
ers represent a growing segment of 
Bindley’s business, its principal custom- 
ers remain chain drug stores. Laughner 
said that five chains aceount for about 
80% of the total business Bindley does 
with the chain drug industry. The com- 
pany’s biggest customers are Eckerd 
Drug, Reveo, Rite Aid and Hook 

Bindley is able to supply West Coast 
chains such as Thrifty without having a 
distribution center closer than Phoenix 
because it ships full case lots directly to 
chain drug warehouses. 

In addition to its retail customers, 
Bindley like other wholesalers, has seen 
its hospital supply business increase 
sharply. “Ne question about it,” says 
Laughner, “this will be a big part of the 
wholesale business.” Bindley’s sales to 
hospitals, while accounting for only 5% 
to 6% of total volume, have doubled in 
the past year. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1984 


1984 Annual Report 
of the Wholesale Drug Industry 


Amfac focus the same despite name change 


BURLINGAME, Calif. — The name 
has been changed from Amfac Drug 
Supply to Amfac Health Care, but the 
primary focus remains the same: doing 
better at what it does best. That is, sup- 
plying pharmaceuticals and OTC to 
drug stores and hospitals as a second- 
ary-source wholesaler. 

Even so, the Health Care Division is 
keeping its options open. The tip-off is 
the name-change. Says Chester Milli- 
gan, president of the Health Care Divi- 
sion: “The name Drug Supply, which im- 
plies drugs for humans only, no longer 
reflects our current or future plans be- 
cause of our acquisition of two veteri- 
nary supply companies last June. Also, 
we intend to get into other health-care 
related areas—probably by acquisition 
ona selective basis.:’ Milligan declines to 
be more specific at this time. 

The Health Care Division prides itself 
on being a lean-and-mean operation. 
The pay-off? “Our return on investment 
is among the best in the industry,” says 
Milligan. 

Currently, the Health Care Division 
is trying to maximize its strengths in re- 
tail/hospital services in order to fill what 
Amfac perceives as a widening vacuum. 

The vacuum is due to full-line whole- 
salers reducing frequency of deliveries, 
and to a large extent, dictating delivery 
days. In addition, full-line wholesalers 
are setting minimum orders that im- 
pede the flexibility of retailers, 

milligan says his division is keying its 
growth expectations on two product ar- 
eas—pharmaceuticals/OTC and veteri- 
nary supplies—and two market areas— 
chains and hospitals. 

Pharmaceuticals and OTC. He pro- 
jects a 20% increase in product lines for 
both. He also says the company is plan- 
ning to open new branches in the North- 
east and Southeast, both by acquisition 
and start-ups. 

Veterinary. This represents a quan- 
tum leap for Amfac. Why veterinary? 
“It is a totally different business than 
our traditional pharmaceutical whole- 
saling role. It is a sales representative- 


intensive business rather than product- 
oriented. So expenses are high—but so 
are sales and gross margins.” 

The acquisition of Holmes Serum Co., 
and Connrex-Mosher Veterinary Ser- 
vices Co., provided a distribution base 
in 15 states. 

Veterinary pharmaceuticals repre- 
sent a $2.4 billion market in the United 
States, and the wholesaler’s share is $1 
billion. The market is expected to grow 


12% to 15% a year over the next five 
years. 

Chains According to Milligan, “inde- 
pendents own 60% of the retail drug 
business. The growth is in the chains. In 
the last few years our sales to chains has 
been increasing 16% annually, and I 
think this trend will continue.” At pres- 
ent, Amfac services 12,000 indepen- 
dents and 3.000 chain stores. 

Hospitals. Growth has been about

JENKINTOWN, Pa. — Spectro In- 
dustries is celebrating its 16th year of 
steadily rising sales, crediting much of 
its success to its constantly expanding 
home health care and pharmaceutical 
lines for the growing number of elderly. 

It’s no wonder that Spectro, based in 
Jenkintown, Pa., has adopted an un- 
equivocal corporate objective to concen- 
trate on the burgeoning health care in- 
dustry and is currently developing and

However, Spectro, which calls itself 
The Healthcare Company, is not limit- 
ing its growth to this market. In the past 
year, it purchased Harry Toub & Sons 
Inc., a New Jersey-based distributor of 
stationery, school supplies and notions. 
The new division, Toub Distributors 
Inc., provides planogramming, promo- 
tional and regular merchandise to all of 
Spectro’s distribution areas. 

During fiscal 1984, which ended in 
March, Spectro recorded sales of $395.4 
million, a 16% increase from the previ- 
ous year’s $33.9 million. Sales in 1985 
are expected to increase 15%, to about 
$450 million. 

Net income reached a record level of 
more than $7.2 million, a 34% increase 
from the $5.4 million earned the previ- 
ous year. This is Spectro’s third year of 
annual income increases of more than 
27%. 

Spectro is divided into a manufactur- 
ing and a distribution division, the latter 
accounting for 95% of the company’s 
sales. The company distributes to more 
than 3,000 independent pharmacies, re- 
tail drug chains and hospitals, primarily 
located in the Northeast and Middle At- 
lantic States. Among products supplied 
are more than 27,000 individual phar- 


maceuticals, proprietary medicines, 
stationery, cosmetics home health care 
and medical equipment. 

The Pharmaceutical Products Distri- 
bution Group reported a 15.8% increase 
in sales between fiscal 1983 and 1984, 
rising to almost $52 million, of which 
$2.3 million was attributed to the Toub 
Distributors acquisition. 

The company predicts that sales will 
continue to rise with the increase of new 
pharmaceuticals such as antiulcer drugs 
and beta blockers, and general mer- 
chandise like toys and stationery of- 
fered through Toub. 

While the Healthcare Products Man- 
ufacturing Group makes a smaller con- 
tribution to overall corporate sales, rev- 
enues from this division have been rap- 
idly rising. Between fiscal 1983 and 
1984, sales rose by 41.5% to $4.5 million. 

This group, which manufactures du- 
rable medical equipment under the 
name of Sci-O-Tech, added several new 
items during fiscal 1984 and is currently 
developing a number of others. 

It was also during fiscal 1984, that 
Spectro saw the solidification of Spectro 
Medical, an offshoot of the distribution 
operation that supplies durable medical 
supplies, exercise equipment and relat- 
ed items to dealers and pharmacists on a 


sales climb 16% at Spectro Industries 


same-day basis. Spectro Medical is 
staffed by professionals who provide 
training and advice to retailers. 

Now, during fiscal 1985, Spectro is in- 
volved in the development of a propri- 
etary in-store computer software pro- 
gram for pharmacies, hospitals and 
durable medical equipment dealers. The 
company hopes to develop a program to 
provide a complete inventory and cash 
control system for pharmacies. 

Spectro, itself, is heavily computer- 
ized. For example, the majority of the 
company’s customers use Spectro’s or- 
der-entry system, which is capable of 
transmitting a 300-item order in sec- 
onds. Computers are used in the compa- 
ny’s five distribution centers to assem- 
ble orders and prepare them for 
same-day or next-day delivery, while at 
the same time printing invoices and 
maintaining perpetual inventories on 
some 27,000 items. 

In the Philadelphia center Spectro 
uses computerized order-picking ma- 
chines capable of selecting over 6,000 
items an hour. 

Computers also allow Spectro to keep 
track of inventory levels; make use of di- 
rect electronic links with suppliers, and 
provide those suppliers with marketing 
information about product sales.

NEW YORK — The sales of 
generic drugs are surging so 
strongly that some security an-

will erect, 30% of the pa

Analysts attribute much of 
the anticipated growth to the 
generic drug ro recently 
passed by Congress and signed 
into law by President Reagan. 

The new generic drug law 
grants a number of relatively 
new drugs extra years of mar- 
keting exclusivity. The law’s 
10-year exclusivity provision 
applies to any “new” drug which 


was approved from Jan. 1, 1982 
to Sept. 24, 1984, the date the 
bill became a law. For example, 
Feldene’s patent was slot to 
expire in 1988, but now the 
product will enjoy some degree 
of marketing exclusivity until 
1992. 

“The generic drug law is the 
best thing that could happen to 
the generic drug industry,”’ 
Says Robert Uhl, a research an- 
alyst at L. F. Rothschild. 

Wall Street analysts are Say- 
ing that because of the law, the 
industry can expect to see as 
many as 125 new generic drugs 
hit the market in the next two to 
three years. 

Some analysts are estimating 
that the new generics will gen- 
erate approximately $1 billion 
in sales by 1990, coking gener- 
ics a $4 billion industry by the 
end of this decade.

about the potential for growth,

AN ABC PUBLICATION, October 29, 1984 


#

HARRISBURG, Pa. — The 
Pennsylvania Department of 
Aging (DOA) is cracking down 
on pharmacists who try to build 
traffic by offering senior citi- 
zens discounts, coupons or re- 
bates on copays for prescription 
products that are already 
heavily subsidized by the 
state’s new Pharmaceutical 
Contract to the Elderly 
(PACE) program. 

Fearful that further dis- 
counting by retail pharmacists 
may result in either abuse or 
overuse of prescription prod- 
ucts by the elderly—as well as 
drive up program costs and pos- 
sibly the copay—the DOA is 
threatening to audit and possi- 
bly suspend from the PACE 
program pharmacists who dis- 
count the $4 copay to PACE 
members. 

“The offering of discounts, 
coupons or gifts by pharmacies 
to entice PACE customers to 
shop in their stores is strictly 
prohibited by the PACE agree- 
ment,” said Carmen A. DiCello, 
executive director of the Penn- 
sylvania Pharmaceutical Asso- 
ciation. 

Currently, PACE customers 
are required to pay a $4 copay 
for each prescription purchased 
and it is mandatory for the 
pharmacist to collect it. DiCello 
is concerned that any discounts 
offered to offset the copay 
would lead to abuse and over- 
utilization of the program. 


Correction 


In Drug Store News’ special 
report on pharmacy computers 
and POS systems that appeared 
in the Sept. 17 issue, ComCo- 
Tec was misspelled in the 
“Guide to Hardware Suppliers” 
and inadvertently left out of the 
“Guide to Software Versatili- 
ty. ” 

ComCoTec, headquartered 
in Westmont, Ill., offers a com- 
plete pharmacy software pack- 
age that runs on Digital Equip- 
ment Corp. (DEC) hardware. 
Included in the basic entry-lev- 
el price of $19,500 is a hard- 
ware/software package that 
will provide the user with the 
following functions: label/re- 
ceipt, patient profile, drug in- 
teractions, including drug-to- 
allergy and drug-to-illness, 
third-party processing, ac- 
counts receivable, perpetual in- 
ventory and DEA reports. 

The following software en- 
hancements are available at an 
extra cost: nursing home forms, 
$1,500; payroll, $1,000; price 
updates, $30/mo.; durable med- 
ical equipment, $1,500; general 
ledger, $1,500, and accounts 
payable, $1,500. The total 
maintenance charge on the soft- 
ware is $50/mo. and includes 
any enhancements to the sys- 
tem that may be added in the fu- 
ture. 

ComCoTec calls its pharmacy 
computer system RxExpress 
and it features communication 
by modem as well as multitask- 
gy om 

he RxExpress system will 
also interface with DTS and 
Sweda cash registers, making it 
a complete POS interactive sys- 
tem. 

The company plans to offer, 
in the very near future, an auto- 
matic-ordering feature through 
its POS function. 

For more information, write 
to ComCoTec Inc., 825 N. Cass 
Ave., Westmont, Ill. 60559. 


“If the copay were discount- 
ed by the participating pharma- 
cy, I fear many PACE custom- 
ers would refill prescriptions 
even if they weren’t needed,” 
explains DiCello. “That would 
drive the cost of the program up 
and would probably lead to a 
higher copay.” 

DiCello says that the PACE 
program, initiated in July, has 
been well received by consumer 
and pharmacist alike. He says it 
took months of negotiations be- 
fore PPA and its members were 
satisfied with the program. 


“We've only had reports of 


about 12 or 13 pharmacies that 
have offered discounts on the 
copay,” says DiCello. ‘The 
DOA and the PPA are not going 
to let a few rotten apples spoil 
the program’s effectiveness.” 
The DOA hopes early interven- 
tion will discourage other phar- 
macists from violating the pro- 
gram’s regulations.

Chains staking claim in home-health market 


he list of independent and 

chain retailers investing in 

home health care continues 
to expand dramatically. 

To date, at least 18 major 
chains accounting for approxi- 
mately 26% of the nation’s top 
00 chains have begun to chip 
away at the $3 billion home 
health care market. 

Those include Hook Drug, 
the nation’s 17th largest drug 
chain, which has 14 freestand- 
ing home health care stores; 
Harco Drug, the 47-unit North- 
port, Ala.-based chain with 
nine freestanding stores, and 
Peoples Drug Stores, the na- 
tion’s 11th-highest-volume 
drug chain, which has three 


freestanding locations. 

Other chains with freestand- 
ing home health care stores in- 
clude: Medicare-Glaser, one 
store; Genovese, one store; Wal- 
greens, three stores; Thrift, 


one store, and Big B, two. 


In addition to those chains 
with freestanding units, some 
have in-store departments de- 
voted to home health care—in- 
cluding Revco and Kinney 
Drug. 

Predicasts, a Cleveland- 
based business information and 
market research firm, forecasts 
that the home health care mar- 
ket will reach $5.2 billion in 
sales by 1988 and top $10 billion 
by 1995.

some money in home health 
care,” said Russell Paylor, di- 
rector of pharmaceutical and 
home health care products for 
Peoples Drug. “But we are also 
aware that it costs more to oper- 
ate a home health care store.” 

Most chains are accustomed 
to operating a payroll between 
2% to 10%. But Paylor says Peo- 
ples, in its home health care 
stores, is looking at a payroll 
that can run as high as 25%- 
30%. 

“This is a service-oriented 
business,” said Paylor. “Some- 
body has to be on the road all the 
time to detail the health profes- 
sionals. That all costs money.”

Compared to the incidence in fetuses from the control group
